No roofs, no toilets, no teachers: TOI check finds minuses in Rajasthan govt schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
03:05:27 UTC
12:05:27 KST

TOI Special Report From Rajasthan: Where 'school' means a tree, tin shed, or locked gate
TOI reporters visited govt schools across six Rajasthan districts after the row over CJP volunteers inspecting campuses. What they found, from Kota’s coaching hub to desert villages and tragedy-hit Piplodi, was a system in which children study under tin sheds, squeeze into unsafe rooms, and sometimes find their school locked.In Kota, a primary school with 78 students operates from municipal parking kiosks and tin sheds. Three teachers run the school on deputation, with no permanent teaching posts sanctioned. A PWD survey found 61 school buildings in the district ruined and hundreds of classrooms unsafe.
Across Barmer, Jaisalmer and Balotra, some schools lack buildings, while transfers have left senior-secondary streams without teachers. In Piplodi, Jhalawar, where a roof collapse killed seven children in July 2025, classes still run from a farmer’s two-room home as construction of a new school drags on.In the CM’s Sanganer constituency, 404 students at one school have been pushed into four rooms after a second building was declared unsafe.Assembly data shows 611 govt schools have no building of their own; 2,047 lack toilets; and 1,049 lack drinking water.
Another 3,768 buildings and 83,783 classrooms are classified as completely dilapidated. Rajasthan also has 7,200 single-teacher schools and 1.5 lakh vacant teacher posts.
List of Rajasthan districts TOI visited.
It has 78 enrolled students from classes I-V who study in six classrooms but there can be no building inspection at Govt Primary School on MBS Road in Kota. The school, established in 2023, doesn’t have one.Children who come to study here gather under small tin sheds created next to municipal parking ticket kiosks. Pathways to success that all of India chases are all around them. But it’ll take a miracle for anyone in this batch to one day make that short walk to one of the city’s many fabled coaching centres, where many of India’s brightest prospects in medical and engineering come to hone their skills in a widely publicised ‘topper-producing’ machinery.Kota’s higher education success, riding entirely on private enterprise, hasn’t pulled up with it the city’s own govt education system. It’s a constituency that Rajasthan’s education minister Madan Dilawar represents, but that too has made little difference to many children who have been going to ‘school’ on footpaths, cramming into single rented rooms or under tin sheds in a state that sees extreme temperatures.Last week, a Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) delegation led by Ashutosh Ranka was chased away by a mob after it went on an inspection of a govt school in Jaipur. In Kota, though, there’s little that’s hidden behind walls about the state of primary schools. Within a day after this non-inspection, however, Rajasthan’s BJP govt led by CM Bhajan Lal Sharma pledged to spend Rs 12,000 crore on schools over three years.Shobana Gupta, the in-charge of the primary school on MBS Road in Ward 33, says, “We operate out of six municipal kiosks and from under a tin shade. We have adequate arrangements for drinking water, electricity, and basic toilet facilities available onsite. There are no sanctioned permanent teaching posts here yet. Three teachers are currently deployed on deputation to manage the classes.”At Govt Senior Secondary School in Vigyan Nagar — a designated centre for JEE and NEET — the school sits inside a Rajasthan Housing Board building that is falling apart. Nine classrooms need major repair. Two are unusable but funds haven’t been allocated yet for demolition or repairs. Mold has eaten into walls of functional classrooms and the school’s ‘smart classroom’. A part of the perimeter wall has given way. Thieves have stolen the school’s water taps and CCTV cameras worth Rs 70,000. Principal Anita Sharma is still waiting for funds.At Shiv Nagar, Govt Primary Sanskrit School has been running for eight years now out of a single rented room, reached by a muddy track that’s impassable in the rains. Enrolment has fallen to 8-10 students under one teacher in a locality of around 60,000 people.“This locality has children who want to study Sanskrit. I have repeatedly submitted memorandums, but no permanent building has been sanctioned yet,” said former ward councillor Dhanraj Gurjar Chechi.Dilawar, incidentally, publicly champions Sanskrit learning as part of Indian cultural values.
What TOI investigation found
At Govt Upper Primary School in Devripunia, Dharmpura — in Ladpura constituency of BJP MLA Kalpna Devi, roughly 10 km from Dilawar’s residence — 130-plus enrolled students share three classrooms built decades ago under Rajiv Gandhi Swarn Jyanti Pathshala scheme. The school was upgraded to upper-primary status in 2021, but the promised classroom expansion never came.On full-attendance days, children sit under trees, on the veranda, or on open ground. Drinking water comes via a temporary line from an adjoining field. Principal Chandra Prakash Meena has written to both the MLA and the minister. Days before this report, 27 students fell ill after eating their mid-day meal.A Public Works Department survey of Kota district’s 1,088 govt schools found 61 buildings entirely ruined and marked for demolition, plus two classrooms flagged as unsafe in each of 318 school buildings, and one classroom each in a further 98. Only 41 full buildings and 29 partial structures have been demolished so far.District collector Peeyush Samaria’s office has no record of any personal inspection visit to a govt school. Samaria remained unavailable for comment. Sanganer, Jaipur: The CM’s constituency
Bhajan Lal Sharma won the Sanganer assembly constituency in 2023
At Bojyawas Govt Primary School, there are toilets, but they have no water. The water tank has cracked and dense cobwebs, indicating it hasn’t been in use for some time. The school shares space with a sub-health centre, where fungus covers medicine boxes and water stains mark chairs and registers.A staff member said open defecation has become routine for her. She does her best by consciously holding off the urge to use a toilet. The school itself has 10 students in classes 1 to 5 under a single teacher.
Govt Secondary School, Kalyanpura, looks well-kept from the gate, till you learn that one of its two buildings has been shut as unsafe, leaving 404 students across classes 1–12 to squeeze into four rooms.The school runs two shifts, 7am–12 noon and 12:30–6pm, and some second-shift students sit under a tin shed outside because the classes can’t accommodate them. Washrooms don’t have regular water supply and are cleaned only twice a month, said a Class 12 student.With no security guard and a broken, low boundary wall, the campus has seen repeated thefts. As a result, each classroom door has three latches and three separate locks.At Govt Upper Primary Sanskrit School in Hasampur Basdi, 85 students from classes 1 to VIII are taught in four classrooms — one of which is assigned to a booth level officer for special intensive revision (SIR) work.
Teacher Rajendra Verma produced letters he has submitted seeking a playground, boundary fencing and a tubewell. The school has been running on tanker water for close to a year, he said.At Govt Primary School in Hasampura, there was no need to interview anyone about the school’s condition. The gate was locked at 9.30am on a weekday. Former ward councillor Ram Singh Choudhary said he has been writing to govt for three years about the school’s lack of facilities. Jaisalmer & Barmer: Studying under treesIn Rajasthan’s desert border districts, several schools have no building.In Ramsar panchayat, Barmer, Govt Upper Primary School Azad Nagar was sanctioned in the 2022–23 budget and began classes in March 2023. But its 37 students study in a hut built by villagers or under trees.“Whether it rains, there is a storm or it is extremely hot, we have to study under trees,” said a Class V student.Land for the school was allotted only in 2024, and construction funds await sanction.At the Govt Higher Secondary School in Majal village, Samdari block (Balotra district), students and parents locked the school gate after nine teachers were transferred out at once, leaving senior secondary arts, science and agriculture streams without lecturers.“When there are no lecturers in the school, how will we study? How can Grade-II teachers perform the duties of lecturers?” a student asked.The protest ended after education officials agreed to post three teachers on deputation.Assembly data, drawn from UDISE 2025-26 figures, shows both districts have building-less schools: 36 in Barmer and 25 in Jaisalmer. Jaisalmer also features among districts hit hardest by a separate supply failure — a shortfall in the milk powder needed for the state’s Pannadhay Bal Gopal Yojana. Jhalawar: After 7 deaths, wait on for a new buildingOn the morning of July 25, 2025, the roof of Govt Upper Primary School in Piplodi, a tribal village in Jhalawar, collapsed during class hours. Seven children died; 21 were injured.A year on, Piplodi has visibly changed — better roads, more power connections, regular health camps, rising enrolment — but the one thing it still lacks is a functioning school building.Classes at the school have run since last August out of the two-room house of Mor Singh, a 60-year-old farmer and shepherd who vacated his own home so children would not lose another year of school.A new school building — eight classrooms, an anganwadi centre and a kitchen — is under construction, originally due by July 24, 2026. It has since been delayed after villagers raised concerns about construction quality when work began last November. Officials demolished the substandard work and restarted.“Construction of the school is taking longer than expected as villagers raised concerns about the quality of construction,” said Jhalawar collector Ajay Singh, adding that surprise inspections are now held every few weeks and the building should be ready by October.
Among Rajasthan’s blocks, Jhalawar has the highest concentration of building-less govt schools. District-wide, 81 schools lack toilets.Assembly data show 611 govt schools statewide with no building of their own, including 10 girls’ schools, 2,047 schools with buildings that lack toilets, and 1,049 that lack drinking water. It’s not that govt doesn’t spend on educationRajasthan’s 2026–27 budget allocates Rs 64,205 crore to school and college education. Of this allocation, around 75% goes into staff salaries and only 10–15% goes infrastructure.The state employs the second-highest number of teachers in the country, at 7.93 lakh, second only to UP. Yet, it has 7,200 single-teacher govt schools serving over 1.5 lakh students. Around 1.5 lakh sanctioned teacher posts remain vacant.The state’s own infrastructure data lays out the scale of the problem: 3,768 school buildings, 83,783 classrooms and 16,765 toilets are classified as entirely dilapidated while another 2,19,902 classrooms and 29,753 toilets need repair.Over the past two years, govt says it has spent Rs 2,723 crore building 179 new school buildings and 7,945 new classrooms to replace dilapidated ones.With govt funds in scarce supply, state-run schools increasingly lean on voluntary and community money. Statewide, philanthropic donations for school development totalled Rs 138 crore in 2024 and Rs 140 crore in 2025.In Pali district, a donor-led ‘Aao Gaon Chalen’ campaign — connecting migrants and philanthropists to their native villages — has targeted raising Rs 300 crore for infrastructure work.“There are around 23,000 such teachers in the state who are posted in a school where they are not needed, and their posting should be in another school, but they have not accepted their new posting. For instance, in an English-medium school, a Hindi-medium teacher who was earlier posted does not accept their new posting after a transfer, and the Hindi medium school, where the teacher is needed, students are suffering in that school,” said Mahendra Pandey, chief general secretary of Rajasthan Primary and Secondary Teachers Association.
TOI Special Report from Rajasthan
Gen Z, Gen alpha protestsThe consequences have spilled onto the streets.In Sikar, Class 12 students protested dilapidated buildings that force school closures every time it rains, alongside a shortage of subject teachers.In Gangapur City (Sawai Madhopur), girls locked the gates of the Mahatma Gandhi English Medium School in Meena Badoda, Wazirpur, after the principal was pulled onto local-body election duty, compounding an existing teacher shortage.At Govt Senior Secondary School in Majal village in Balotra district, students locked the gates after nine teachers were transferred simultaneously.A Class XII student at Govt Higher Secondary School at Majal in Balotra said: “If we had to study without teachers, then we could have studied at home. What is the need to come to school? If a school is operational, teachers must be posted.”
TOI Ground Report
The infrastructure debate has become an open political fight.A civic campaign, ‘School Thik Karo’, backed by CJP, has sent volunteer teams to inspect schools across nine districts — Jaipur, Ajmer, Jodhpur, Udaipur, Dholpur, Bharatpur, Kota, Barmer and Hanumangarh — after receiving what it says are public requests.“It has been over a year since the school collapse tragedy in Jhalawar, and the education minister has still not shared a concrete plan on how over 80,000 classrooms in dilapidated conditions will be fixed. Students are being forced to study in unsafe buildings, risking their lives,” said CJP national spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka.One inspection, in Jaipur’s Bagru constituency, found a school that had been operating out of a buffalo shed for two and a half years after its own building was declared unsafe; it was shifted to a house only after drawing media attention.
The state education department has now issued an order requiring prior permission for any outsider to enter school premises, and barring photography, videography, interviews or livestreaming involving students without the principal’s consent.Opposition leader Tikaram Jully called it an attempt to hide failures: “Instead of fixing schools, if you introduce ‘no entry’ measures just to hide your own failures, how can such accidents be prevented? A useless ‘double-engine’ govt,” Jully said.Additional reporting by Vimal Matta, Suparna Roy, Somdutt Trtpathi, Suntl Parmuwal & Shoeb Khan

U.S. Strikes Iran in First Military Action in a Month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
03:05:16 UTC
12:05:16 KST

U.S. forces attacked two Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, according to the U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), marking the first publicly confirmed strike on Iran in weeks.
In a statement to TIME, CENTCOM spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins confirmed the strikes on the launchers on Larak Island, adding that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) forces “were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines” into the strait.
Last week, U.S. forces finished clearing sea mines from the strait’s international shipping routes.
“U.S. forces are monitoring the area closely and remain prepared to protect the free flow of commerce through this essential waterway,” Hawkins added.
Axios later reported, citing a U.S. official, that Iran launched ballistic missiles at a U.S. base in Jordan in retaliation for the strikes. Jordan’s armed forces said it intercepted eight missiles that entered the country’s airspace early Monday morning.
Iranian state news agency IRNA carried a statement from the Revolutionary Guards issued soon after the U.S. strikes saying that Iran will respond to the attacks on Larak Island “with punishment for the aggressor”.
In a statement, CENTCOM rebuffed the Revolutionary Guards’ claims, describing the Sunday attack as “limited, precise action against IRGC minelaying forces posing an imminent threat” to the strait.
Before the Sunday strikes, the last time the U.S. military confirmed targeting Iran was on July 29, announcing a “heavy wave of strikes” on dozens of IRGC targets in Iran, including command centers, missile and drone facilities, and coastal surveillance and defense sites.
On Aug. 1, President Donald Trump said that he agreed to “hold off” strikes in Iran at the request of the U.S.’s regional allies in the Middle East.
The strikes mark the latest escalation of the war in Iran that began on Feb. 28, and from which Trump has struggled to find an off-ramp.
The war has led to a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, which before the hostilities was one of the world’s most important energy transit routes, through which about a fifth of the world’s oil supply previously passed.
A U.S. naval blockade on Iranian ports was lifted in June, but it proved temporary, with the President reimposing the blockade after a deal to cease hostilities fell apart.

Without additional $6.75 billion, Ukraine unable to pay its military
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
03:02:57 UTC
12:02:57 KST

MOSCOW, August 31. /TASS/. Ukraine will run out of funds to pay its servicemen in mid-October if it fails to adopt budgetary amendments to secure at least $6.75 billion in additional financing for its armed forces, according to TASS calculations based on data from the country’s Finance Ministry.
In the first months of 2026, the Defense Ministry of Ukraine was forced to tap into funds allocated for the end of the year, including money earmarked for military salaries. The ministry needs at least $6.75 billion to compensate for these expenses. However, maintaining combat operations at the current level will require roughly three times that amount, or around $20 billion.
Kiev needs approximately $2.7 billion every month to pay military salaries, or approximately $8.1 billion between October and December 2026. Consequently, without supplemental funding, money for these disbursements will be depleted by mid-October.
As a result, Ukraine will need to urgently amend its budget in September. At the same time, external borrowing is being considered as its only source of financing.

China Focus: Centuries-old artifacts bear witness to vibrant Sino-Italian cultural exchanges
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
11:01:34 CST
12:01:34 KST

A visitor takes photos during an exhibition titled "Crown of Glory: 18th-Century Italian Court Treasures from the House of Savoy" at the Tianjin Museum in north China's Tianjin Municipality on July 2, 2026. (Xinhua)
TIANJIN, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Chinese silk and decorative motifs found their way into the art of 18th-century European courts, while European tastes and designs came into contact with Chinese porcelain.
At an exhibition at the Tianjin Museum in the northern Chinese metropolis, more than 150 Italian artifacts offer a vivid glimpse into the rich cultural exchanges between China and Italy centuries ago.
Jointly presented by the Tianjin Museum, the Tianjin Digital Art Museum and the Turin City Museum of Ancient Art in Palazzo Madama, the exhibition, titled "Crown of Glory: 18th-Century Italian Court Treasures from the House of Savoy," ran from Feb. 10 to Aug. 31. The exhibition showcases centuries-old treasures from the House of Savoy, one of the most influential royal houses in Italy in the 17th and 18th centuries.
Rather than simply showcasing the splendor of the Italian royal court, the exhibition traces how Chinese art and craftsmanship influenced European tastes and how Chinese artisans, in turn, responded to European demand, providing a window into the cultural interaction between East and West.
A French court gown from the collection of Palazzo Madama is among the highlights at the exhibition.
According to Li Jun, deputy director of the artifacts research department at the Tianjin Museum and curator of the exhibition, the gown incorporates Chinese silk and embroidery techniques, offering evidence of the popularity of "chinoiserie" at the time. By the mid-18th century, the style had become a hallmark of European aristocrats and the wealthy bourgeoisie.
Another exhibit, a men's robe with decorative patterns, provides further evidence of the influence of Chinese craftsmanship.
According to scholars, the ivory-colored robe with floral patterns was made from precious Chinese fabric. The silk was produced using a combination of weaving, block printing and hand painting techniques.
Such oriental-style fabrics became highly fashionable in European society in the second half of the 18th century. They were used not only for luxury garments but also extensively in interior decoration, becoming an important carrier of the "chinoiserie" aesthetic.
In the 17th and 18th centuries, Chinese porcelain, silk, lacquerware and other goods featuring distinctive oriental aesthetics became increasingly popular in Europe. Travel accounts, images of exotic people and landscapes, and Chinese-inspired decorative motifs further shaped European perceptions of the Orient.
The 18th century also witnessed the Enlightenment in Europe, with thinkers challenging feudal autocracy and religious constraints.
The thoughts of Chinese philosophers emphasizing openness and rationality resonated with some Enlightenment ideas, said Yan Guodong, dean of the School of Foreign Languages at Nankai University and an expert in the history of cultural exchanges between China and foreign countries.
Against this backdrop, an unprecedented craze for Chinese-style art and design, known as "chinoiserie," swept across European society and courts, leaving a lasting imprint on Western art and aesthetics.
The influence of cultural exchanges is even more vivid in the exhibition's "East Meets West" section, where Chinese-style porcelain, round fans and bird-and-flower paintings evoke interactions between Chinese and European artistic traditions.
A Qianlong-period Guangcai porcelain plate with a Swedish coat of arms from the Tianjin Museum's collection is one example.
Li said the piece was commissioned by Count Carl Gustaf Tessin, a prominent European art collector of the 18th century.
"Its value goes far beyond an ordinary commercial transaction. It represents a profound cultural dialogue between East and West based on mutual aesthetic appreciation and romantic imagination," Li said.
Such exchanges were by no means one-way, as Chinese kilns also accepted bespoke orders from European aristocrats, producing armorial porcelain tailored to Rococo tastes, Li added.
Yan said European consumers regarded the patterns on Chinese porcelain, silk and lacquerware as representations of life in China, while Chinese artisans sought to cater to European tastes in the selection and design of porcelain motifs.
"These exchanges were not simply the movement of commodities, but also the interaction of aesthetics, craftsmanship and cultural imagination," Yan said.
The exhibition has so far attracted more than 24,000 visitors.
"I was amazed by the material culture and artistic achievements of the House of Savoy, and even more struck by how some of the pieces ingeniously incorporated traditional Chinese craftsmanship, vividly recreating the 'chinoiserie' craze in 18th-century Europe," said a visitor surnamed Wang in Tianjin.
The artifacts, he added, bear witness to cultural exchanges between China and Italy along the Maritime Silk Road.
For Giovanni Carlo Federico Villa, director of the Turin City Museum of Ancient Art in Palazzo Madama, the journey of these artifacts across mountains and seas to China tells a story that extends far beyond artistic beauty.
"These artifacts not only allow us to look back on exchanges between ancient civilizations, but also provide a historical reference for contemporary cultural cooperation between China and Italy, further strengthening the bonds between our peoples," Villa said.
Massimo Ambrosetti, Italian ambassador to China, said the exhibition reveals the profound influence of Chinese art on European "chinoiserie" aesthetics and the porcelain industry in the 18th century, demonstrating the mutual enrichment of Chinese and Italian cultures and arts.
He expressed hope that cultural exchanges between China and Italy will continue to deepen and deliver lasting benefits. ■
People visit an exhibition titled "Crown of Glory: 18th-Century Italian Court Treasures from the House of Savoy" at the Tianjin Museum in north China's Tianjin Municipality on July 2, 2026. (Xinhua)

Chinese yuan weakens to 6.7828 against USD Monday
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
11:01:27 CST
12:01:27 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- The central parity rate of the Chinese currency renminbi, or the yuan, weakened 17 pips to 6.7828 against the U.S. dollar Monday, according to the China Foreign Exchange Trade System.
In China's spot foreign exchange market, the yuan is allowed to rise or fall by 2 percent from the central parity rate each trading day.
The central parity rate of the yuan against the U.S. dollar is based on a weighted average of prices offered by market makers before the opening of the interbank market each business day. ■

Japan's July industrial output up 0.1 pct on month

TOKYO, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Japan's industrial output in July edged up 0.1 percent from the previous month, as stronger semiconductor-related production was offset by weakness in transport equipment, government data showed Monday.
The uptick came on the heels of an upwardly revised 1.9 percent gain in June, according to a preliminary report released by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry.
The seasonally adjusted index of production at factories and mines stood at 104.7 against the 2020 base of 100.
Ten of 15 industrial sectors covered in the report saw output increases in July, including production machinery, which was boosted by stronger exports of semiconductor manufacturing devices.
Transport equipment excluding motor vehicles was among the four sectors that declined, while electric machinery and information and communication electronics equipment held steady.
Based on a survey of manufacturers, the ministry expects output to climb 6.4 percent in August and contract 4.2 percent in September. ■

Factbox: Latest relief and rescue progress at mudslide-hit border port in China's Xizang

BEIJING, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- A fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal, struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Aug. 26, causing heavy casualties and leaving many missing.
Chinese rescuers immediately launched an all-out effort to reach the mudslide-hit port area and search for the missing. Here is what we know about the deadly mudslide and the latest rescue and relief progress in China:
-- Sixteen people have been confirmed dead and 546 others remain missing as of 6 p.m. Saturday, according to the regional government.
-- A total of 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries have been identified as unaccounted for. The figure was announced on Sunday morning at a press conference held by the information office of the regional government, following a joint search and cross-checking of information by foreign affairs, public security, culture and tourism, and emergency management authorities.
-- At the press conference, the regional government noted that the mudslide was triggered by an ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-mountain glacier in Nepal.
A glacier on Mount Langtang Lirung in Nepal fractured at an altitude of about 5,200 meters, triggering the ice-rock avalanche. The avalanche plunged rapidly to an altitude of around 4,000 meters, scouring the mountainside and developing into a massive debris flow, which surged about 22 kilometers before reaching Gyirong Port at an altitude of around 1,800 meters.
-- A total of 2,141 personnel have joined search and rescue operations, including personnel from the People's Liberation Army, the People's Armed Police Force, and China Anneng, a state-owned engineering and rescue enterprise. And 269 rescue vehicles and 3,922 sets of rescue equipment have also been dispatched to the front line.
-- The barrier lake above Gyirong Port has basically drained, forming a flowing state of the river channel, China's Ministry of Water Resources said Sunday, citing drone footage and panoramic images captured in the morning and reports from emergency response teams.
-- Communications have been restored at the core rescue site, as successful phone calls have been made with rescuers at the port via a newly-built base station on Sunday, according to the regional communications administration.
The first emergency base station adjacent to the border gate of Gyirong Port was put into operation at 1:30 p.m. on Sunday. Up to now, telecom operators in Xizang have restored one damaged base station and built eight new ones near the port.
-- On Sunday morning, the People's Liberation Army Xizang Military Command mobilized an epidemic prevention team to the disaster-hit area to carry out environmental disinfection, food and water quality testing, emergency vaccinations, and routine medical rounds for injuries and illnesses. This relief mission also included psychological support personnel, who will regularly provide psychological counseling for rescuers and the disaster-affected local residents.
-- China has provided emergency humanitarian assistance to Nepal, the China International Development Cooperation Agency said on Sunday.
At present, Chinese aid supplies have been delivered to Kathmandu, tunnel rescue experts have arrived at the disaster-stricken area in Nepal, and the Chinese side is simultaneously sharing important information such as images, satellite and hydrological data of the disaster area.
-- Gyirong County is expected to see more rainfall in the coming days, with significant nighttime precipitation, the National Meteorological Center said on Sunday. ■

Will fixing Hong Kong’s childcare bottleneck help lift the city’s birth rate?
Parents and social welfare groups say demand for childcare services remains high even as births fall below 30,000 for 12-month period
Shortly after Erica Lam found out she was pregnant with her second child, submitting a day care application for her unborn daughter became a top priority, as places at Hong Kong childcare centres were insufficient to meet demand.
Even though Lam, a nurse in her early forties, tried to secure a place early, her daughter Ho-yan only managed to enrol in day care services operated by the Sheng Kung Hui church’s St Christopher’s Home, a social welfare group, when she turned eight months old.
Meanwhile, her elder son, born in late 2020, had not been able to secure a place. The boy’s grandparents helped care for him during that period.
To raise two children and give them a good quality of life, Lam and her husband could not give up their jobs. Sending Ho-yan to day care helped take pressure off their shoulders.
“Childcare service is essential for working parents like us. The government encourages childbirth, and we have two children,” Lam said.

====================================================================================================

Les think tanks musclent leur jeu en vue de 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

À l’approche de l’élection présidentielle, les think tanks passent comme tous les 5 ans à la vitesse supérieure. Et s’interrogent plus que jamais sur le ton à adopter, dans un paysage politique fragmenté et polarisé.
Les laboratoires d'idées se livrent une rude concurrence pour faire avancer leurs propositions auprès des candidats à l'Elysée. | Amaury Cornu/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
Si la campagne présidentielle démarre à peine pour les candidats comme pour la plupart des Français, les think tanks, eux, entrent dans le money-time de leur saison, prêts à faire assaut de propositions choc pour se servir de la campagne comme vitrine.
L’Institut Montaigne, laboratoire d’idées libéral qui dispose du plus gros budget, publiera ainsi vingt-cinq notes thématiques le 6 octobre et recevra plusieurs directeurs de campagne au fil de l’automne. Cochez également le 10 septembre, pour les préconisations de l’Institut de l’entreprise sur l’éducation (la santé et l’innovation suivront) —toutes chapeautées par des patrons qui en sont membres — et le 12 du même mois pour la journée des idées du plus jeune Institut Rousseau, présidé par l’économiste Nicolas Dufrêne. Mais encore : le 14 octobre ce sera la présentation du plan “robuste” du Shift Project de Jean-Marc Jancovici pour l’économie française. Spécialisé sur les questions économiques et écologiques, l’Institut Avant-garde annoncera quant à lui ses solutions sur le financement des transitions cette semaine dans le Nouvel Obs, qui en a obtenu l’exclusivité.
L’exercice est un passage obligé pour ces clubs de réflexion à cheval entre le monde académique, économique et de la haute fonction publique, qui tous cherchent à montrer sa capacité d’influence. Par le passé, certains think tanks avaient réussi à marquer les campagnes présidentielles de leur empreinte : ainsi du “produire en France” défendu par la fondation Concorde, thème de François Bayrou, en 2011 ; l’organisation d’une primaire au PS revendiquée par Terra Nova ; la “règle d’or” de la Fondapol qui suggérait il y a quinze ans d’inscrire une norme de déficit dans la Constitution ou encore le dédoublement des classes dans les quartiers populaires, soufflée par l’Institut Montaigne au candidat Macron dès 2016.
Advertisement
Qu’en sera-t-il pour le cru 2027, dans le contexte d’un débat champ médiatique et politique très polarisé ?
Bataille culturelle
Une chose est sûre : les laboratoires d’idées conservateurs ou d’extrême droite occupent une place grandissante. Le cercle Orion voit d’ailleurs dans la campagne l’occasion de “rouvrir la guerre des idées” dans son premier document, tout comme l’Institut de l’espérance “d’inspiration chrétienne”, fondé il y a un an par Vincent Bolloré, qui achève avec un peu de retard son manifeste pour le début de l’automne.
L’Observatoire de l’immigration et de la démographie, qui accumule les reprises dans les médias plutôt classés à droite, a préparé un projet de révision constitutionnelle. L’Institut Thomas-More, un franco-belge, a déjà dressé son inventaire des “50 décisions qui ont coulé la France” ces cinq dernières décennies. C’est aussi l’angle retenu par les nouveaux venus Hexagone ou Hémisphère droite, tous les deux de tendance conservatrice. Ces structures sont financées par Périclès, l’organe d’influence du milliardaire Pierre-Edouard Stérin, décrit comme une “pépinière d’initiatives métapolitiques” par son directeur général Arnaud Rérolle.
Face à la prégnance des thèmes imposés par le Rassemblement national et La France insoumise, la fabrique des idées se double donc d’une bataille culturelle. Mais les modérés ne sont pas en reste : ce printemps déjà, plusieurs think tanks se sont attelés à une rare tribune collective pour se dresser comme un “outil primordial de stabilité et de modération”, alors que le “débat public s’électrise de plus en plus”, nourri aussi par “les nouveaux diktats de la communication politique”. L’Institut Montaigne, l’Institut Terram, la Fabrique de l’Industrie ou encore la fondation Robert-Schuman étaient signataires.
Thierry Pech, qui dirige le progressiste Terra Nova, explique par exemple que des textes “de riposte” seront préparés sur les “propositions les plus contestables” du Rassemblement national, comme prochainement l’analyse des votes de leurs eurodéputés. Il aborde toutefois cette campagne inquiet : “La campagne va se dérouler dans un climat dégradé avec un contexte géopolitique assez stressant.” “Les producteurs d’idées sont soit tétanisés, soit à court d’idées ou totalement idéologisés dans une forme de radicalité”, déplore encore le libéral Dominique Reynié, qui entame sa quatrième campagne présidentielle à la tête de la Fondation pour l’innovation politique. Celle-ci creusera tout de même plusieurs sillons sur la fiscalité, l’énergie, la productivité ou l’éducation.
La floraison d’écrits qui s’annonce est aussi à l’image d’un paysage contrasté, à l’influence diffuse aussi, loin de l’assise des think tanks en Allemagne, au Royaume-Uni ou aux Etats-Unis où ces organisations sont plus installées et financées. Le risque : une multiplication de structures, toutes couleurs politiques confondues, à l’image de la fragmentation de l’offre politique. “Si vous avez des propositions et des chiffres dans tous les sens, vous ne retenez plus rien”, estime le cadre d’un labo d’idées qui a requis l’anonymat.
Advertisement
Questions d’écurie
Le timing comptera lui aussi : “Si on veut vraiment avoir une influence, il faut le faire de manière précoce. Notre rôle est d’aiguiser la capacité des candidats à bien appréhender les problèmes”, soutient Thierry Pech.
L’Ifrap, l’Institut Montaigne et l’Institut de l’entreprise ont tous trois discuté avec l’équipe d’Edouard Philippe de sa proposition d’un “deal fiscal XXL” de 50 milliards d’euros de baisse des impôts de production contre une réduction équivalente des aides publiques aux entreprises. Présidé par Pierre-André de Chalendar, l’Institut de l’entreprise a par ailleurs reçu ces derniers mois Bruno Retailleau, Gabriel Attal et Raphaël Glucksmann autour d’un petit-déjeuner devant pas plus d’une trentaine de dirigeants. Le 29 septembre, ce sera au tour d’Edouard Philippe.
Lors des échanges avec les politiques, les questions ont tourné autour des normes, des impôts de production, mais aussi de la stratégie politique. Avec une interrogation incontournable : “Comment allez-vous faire pour repousser les extrêmes ?” Ni Marine le Pen ni Jean-Luc Mélenchon n’ont été conviés par l’institut.
Le leader Insoumis phosphore, lui, dans d’autres cercles. Son concept de “nouvelle France”, qui a déjà marqué la campagne, a été travaillé dans les rangs de l’Institut de la Boétie, les mois précédant la campagne des municipales. C’est à ce jour le seul think tank qui participe aussi directement à la réflexion et à la formation des Insoumis, qui dévoileront en novembre l’actualisation de leur programme. Dans les prochains jours, Eric Berr, le coresponsable du département d’économie, fera la promotion de son livre intitulé Mélenchonomics (éd. Les liens qui libèrent). “Nous, on a fait l’inverse des partis qui piochent ailleurs. On crée un think tank et on construit avec, on continue le travail intellectuel à côté du mandat parlementaire”, revendique le député Hadrien Clouet, coordinateur du programme avec Clémence Guetté.
De son côté, l’Institut Rousseau, qui œuvre aux “conditions d’une République sociale, écologique et démocratique”, s’est félicité du débat rouvert sur l’annulation des dettes publiques détenues par la BCE, une proposition défendue dès sa création en 2020 auprès des Insoumis et des Ecologistes.
Savoir se raconter
Quelle que soit leur coloration politique, une conviction semble avoir gagné les cercles de pensée : l’expertise sans récit articulé est prédestinée à l’échec.“On a beaucoup réfléchi au récit qu’on voulait raconter autour de l’urgence d’une politique économique des grandes transformations”, explique Clara Léonard, cofondatrice de l’Institut Avant-garde, conseillé par l’agence GreenLEX. “Les mots que vous installez dans le débat public sont fondamentaux”, insiste Jean-Michel Blanquer, à la tête du Laboratoire de la République. L’ancien ministre de l’Education a accueilli ce week-end Edouard Philippe, François Hollande, Sébastien Lecornu, Xavier Bertrand ou encore Bernard Cazeneuve lors de ses universités d’été à Sens (Yonne). “Faire sens ensemble” est son slogan, aidé pro bono par le communicant Nicolas Bordas, pour défendre un “projet de société avant même des mesures techniques”, explique-t-il.
Advertisement
La mise en récit est la capacité à “vendre politiquement” les mesures auprès des électeurs, résume Julien Chartier, le directeur des études des Républicains. D’où le soin apporté à la communication par les think tanks. Chez Montaigne, où d’anciens et actuels adhérents déplorent la perte de vitesse et le manque d’incarnation des rapports par des grands patrons, Publicis — adhérent du think tank — aidera à multiplier les retombées en ligne de leurs publications, tout comme l’institut Verian mesurera l’acceptabilité citoyenne de certaines propositions.
Vouées d’abord à éclairer le débat public, les notes de l’Institut Montaigne — sur l’Europe, la sécurité nationale, le logement, les ordonnances de début de mandat etc. — seront toutes construites autour d’un état des lieux, des options politiques sur la table et des conséquences notamment budgétaires de chaque arbitrage. “On assume des redondances entre les notes, on veut rendre les interdépendances visibles entre chaque sujet”, explicite sa directrice générale, Marie-Pierre de Bailliencourt dont le recrutement à la tête de l’institut fondé par Claude Bébéar en 2000 est passée par un changement de méthode.
Parmi les nouveaux arrivés, l’institut Terram, fondé par Victor Delage, aborde sa première présidentielle en variant les formats autour de l’étude des territoires : une itinérance de cafés-débats en France pour aboutir à une dizaine de recommandations qui devraient nourrir un futur débat entre des candidats ou encore un baromètre à l’échelle locale des plus importants sujets de discussion en ligne avec une startup d’IA Magic LEMP. “L’entrée par les territoires nous permet déjà de sortir de cette extrême polarisation des débats”, avance cet ancien de la Fondapol.
Une concurrence grandissante
Si les think thanks redoublent d’efforts pour percer le mur du son, c’est que leur champ d’action est aujourd’hui grignoté par les ONG, les fédérations d’entreprises et les associations qui, comme acteurs d’influence, investissent plus que jamais le terrain des prescriptions clé en main à l’oreille des politiques et sont parfois plus efficaces dans le service après-vente, jauge un fin observateur.
Preuve en est l’un des rendez-vous animés au siège du parti Horizons d’Edouard Philippe sur le climat, mi-février, autour d’une dizaine de représentants comme WWF ou encore le Réseau Action Climat. D’autres échanges ont été organisés sur la simplification, la démocratie ou la décentralisation.
“Je ne crois pas au désintérêt pour les think tanks, mais les responsables politiques les regardent comme un thermomètre ou un indicateur de tendances”, tempère Jérémie Peltier, codirecteur de la fondation Jean-Jaurès, qui prévoit des publications resserrées sur les politiques publiques pour des catégories de populations, comme les jeunes ou les familles monoparentales.
Advertisement
Des figures individuelles, associées ou non à des structures, s’arrogent également l’accès aux candidats lors de rendez-vous ou de repas confidentiels. “Je fais voir à Edouard Philippe des gens qui écrivent, plutôt que des institutions”, relève le coordinateur de son projet présidentiel, Clément Tonon.
Cités à droite et au centre, les noms d’Antoine Foucher sur le travail et les salaires, qui publie Pour que nos enfants vivent mieux que nous (éd. de l’Aube) en cette rentrée, de l’économiste Maxime Sbaihi sur la baisse de la natalité, qui écrit un livre sur la “gérontocratie” pour le début d’année prochaine, du directeur général de Bpifrance Nicolas Dufourcq, de l’historien de l’immigration Patrick Weil ou encore celui du professeur de droit public Benjamin Morel reviennent régulièrement. “C’est la logique des influenceurs appliquée à 2027”, commente l’un de ces experts courtisés. “Bien sûr, ces deux sphères ne sont pas des vases clos et les couloirs de nage des think tanks et des têtes pensantes se croisent fréquemment. J’observe plutôt des interactions personnelles que des discussions organiques entre les think tanks et les entourages des candidats”, relève un expert qui collabore à plusieurs d’entre eux.
De nombreuses structures mettent un point d’honneur à écarter l’idée que certains candidats jouent à domicile ou bénéficient d’un passe-droit supplémentaire pour disposer d’une note en avance. Classée à gauche, la fondation Jean-Jaurès, qui fêtera ses 35 ans en 2027, publie des contributions de parlementaires socialistes, comme récemment celle de Boris Vallaud sur l’exercice de l’opposition, mais se garde de prendre parti en tant que fondation reconnue d’utilité publique.
A l’Institut Montaigne, le double pied en 2017 de son président Henri de Castries et de l’ex-directeur Laurent Bigorgne dans les campagnes respectives de François Fillon et d’Emmanuel Macron a laissé des traces en interne, quitte à adouber une “position d’une prudence exacerbée”, juge un ancien. L’entrepreneur Arnaud Vaissié (International SOS), membre du comité directeur, fait partie des chefs d’entreprise qui conseillent Bruno Retailleau.
Face à la concurrence des nouveaux laboratoires d’idées qui revendiquent un discours de radicalité, dans un paysage politique morcelé, les structures plus installées cherchent à consolider leur espace. L’année 2027 sera celle d’un défi : comment trouver sa place, sans perdre son identité.

On edge of the abyss? Treasury warns IDF spending could swallow a third of Israel’s budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
02:57:35 UTC
11:57:35 KST

The Finance Ministry pushed back Sunday against warnings from senior defense officials that the military is nearing a financial breaking point, accusing the defense establishment of mismanaging its budget and making misleading claims about billions of shekels in additional funding.
A senior Finance Ministry official said the military was far from the “edge of the abyss” described by defense officials and warned that meeting the defense establishment’s demands could eventually push military spending to nearly one-third of Israel’s entire state budget.
“That would be a situation unprecedented anywhere in the world,” the official said.
The unusually sharp exchange comes as Israel continues to face security threats on multiple fronts and as the government wrestles with the mounting cost of years of military operations.
Earlier Sunday, defense officials warned that the military faced serious shortages because the Finance Ministry’s Budget Department was blocking the transfer of 15 billion shekels, or about $5.1 billion, in funding that had already been agreed upon.
The warning followed comments last week by IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, who said the Israel Defense Forces was operating with “empty coffers.”
Senior defense officials said the military was now facing acute shortages of Humvees and munitions. They also said major purchases from the United States, including a deal for Apache attack helicopters, had not gone ahead.
Finance Ministry officials rejected the accusation that they were holding up the 15 billion shekels, saying the funding request had been submitted to the Knesset Finance Committee in early August and had been awaiting parliamentary approval since then.
“We transferred the budget to the Knesset on Aug. 2, and despite that, the defense establishment prefers to attack us even though it knows it is no longer with us,” Finance Ministry officials said. “We are acting exactly according to the agreements reached by the National Security Council. It is outrageous to say that it is stuck at the Finance Ministry.”
Finance Ministry officials said their department had been fully committed to supporting IDF operations and had financed the military’s activities on all fronts with hundreds of billions of shekels while also working to raise government debt and maintain the functioning of the wider economy.
The ministry’s Budget Department said defense spending had nearly tripled over the past two years. It said all funding approved in the state budget, as well as additional budget agreements, had been transferred in full.
“There is no agreement that the Finance Ministry has failed to honor,” officials said, adding that funding had gone “far beyond the original budget approved by the Knesset.”
A senior Finance Ministry official called on defense leaders to treat the billions of shekels allocated to them each year with greater care to ensure the money was used efficiently and responsibly for national security.
The criticism was also aimed at what Finance Ministry officials described as wasteful spending and benefits distributed without sufficient transparency.
Other senior ministry officials suggested that the defense establishment’s accusation that the money was being held up by the Finance Ministry reflected a lack of understanding of the process for transferring funds and the requirement for parliamentary approval.
“That reflects precisely the defense establishment’s negligent management when it comes to the budget,” the officials said. “They are acting with ingratitude. For three years, we have met every budgetary demand from the military. We have stood at attention and financed this entire costly war, including funding beyond the amount approved by the Knesset in the state budget.”
The officials said the government had been raising large amounts of debt on international markets under challenging conditions to finance military spending.
“All of this is being done to channel that money directly to the defense establishment,” they said. “Instead of recognizing that, they treat us as ‘another front’ simply because we point out failures and wastefulness and shine a spotlight on the fact that they are managing an independent budget contrary to the law.”
Another senior Finance Ministry official said defense leaders should recognize the trade-offs involved in allocating additional billions to the military.
“They should understand that this budget comes from funding for patients in hospitals, the national basket of subsidized medicines, money for struggling populations, road construction and infrastructure,” the official said.
The official accused defense leaders of responding to the government’s willingness to fund the military at the expense of public services, tax cuts and economic growth by promoting claims designed to frighten the public into supporting ever-higher defense spending.
The official warned that the current trajectory could eventually undermine Israel’s ability to finance a future war.
“If the defense establishment’s budgetary conduct does not change and they demand billions more and more, the economy will no longer be able to sustain it,” the official said. “Perhaps in several years we will face a large-scale confrontation, and this time there really will be nowhere to get the money for it.”

Google Maps updates Lake Ontario to 'Lake America' in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
02:57:08 UTC
11:57:08 KST

Google has modified its Maps service to reflect a US government directive renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America", highlighting escalating diplomatic and trade tensions between Washington and Ottawa.
"Since we update Google Maps to reflect name changes in official government sources ... people using Maps in the US will see 'Lake America'," Google said Saturday.
US President Donald Trump, who ordered the change, noted the adjustment on Truth Social, posting: "Google Maps changes Lake Ontario to 'Lake America' on US phones."
The company clarified that users in Canada will continue to see Lake Ontario, whilst those outside both countries will see both designations displayed as "Lake Ontario (Lake America)".
The update follows formal changes implemented by the US Geographic Names Information System, the federal agency tasked with standardising geographic names.
The adjustment stems from an executive order signed by Trump directing American government agencies to adopt the name across all official databases, with Trump stating the move takes immediate effect in response to recent bilateral friction.
Collapse of bilateral trade
In January 2025, shortly after returning to office, Trump similarly ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed the "Gulf of America", prompting comparable regional display adjustments on Google Maps.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford rejected the measure, unveiling a new "Lake Ontario" sign on Saturday to reaffirm the waterway’s historical identity.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney also condemned the executive order, citing the Wendat, an Indigenous people of North America, as the origin of the historic name.
The dispute unfolds alongside an intensifying trade conflict.
Canada is scheduled to impose counter-tariffs ranging between 15 percent and 50 percent on $20 billion worth of US imports starting on September 8.
The retaliatory measures follow the collapse of bilateral trade talks and the subsequent US imposition of 50 percent tariffs on CAN$27.6 billion worth of Canadian products on August 22.

Nepal floods: could foreign rescue teams have been brought in earlier?
In the immediate aftermath of the floods, the government refused overseas help, only to reverse its decision days later
Kathmandu’s apparent reversal reflects caution born from its chaotic experience with foreign teams after the 2015 earthquake, according to observers. Other factors include the government’s need to tightly control relief operations and failure to anticipate how quickly domestic capabilities can be overwhelmed in the aftermath.
Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said the country had requested “specific specialised assistance” – including technology to locate people in affected areas and provide quick forensics and DNA analysis, as well as mortuaries to preserve dead bodies. He dismissed media reports rejecting international help and support as “false”.
“The scale of devastation is extremely huge and support and assistance are required, not just in the phase of rescue and relief but more so in the phase of reconstruction and rehabilitation,” Khanal told a press conference on Saturday. “Given these very complex challenges of geography, we had to be very sensitive.”
The ice-rock avalanche and ensuing floods on Wednesday along the Nepal-China border, which is flanked by towering mountains and deep gorges, have obliterated settlements in both countries, with the churning water swallowing villages hundreds of kilometres downstream.
In Nepal, the death toll has climbed to nearly 800 with over 2,500 people still missing, including 592 foreigners, as of Sunday, though the numbers are expected to rise. Across the border, China has reported at least 16 deaths and 546 people as missing.

Philosopher’s Annual for 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
02:41:07 UTC
11:41:07 KST

Philosopher’s Annual for 2025
The articles that made it into the latest edition of Philosophers Annual have been announced.
The list aims to “select the ten best articles published in philosophy each year—an attempt as simple to state as it is admittedly impossible to fulfill.”
This volume—the 45th—covers the literature from 2024.
The selections are:
Evan Behrle (Harvard), “Desert and Economic Interdependence” from the Journal of Philosophy.
Outside of philosophy, the idea that workers deserve to be paid according to their productive contributions is very popular. But political philosophers have given it relatively little attention. In this paper, I argue against the attempt to use this idea about desert and contribution to vindicate significant income inequality. I claim that reward according to contribution fails on its own terms when the following condition holds: the size of each worker’s contribution depends on what other workers only together do. When workers only together make another more productive, that is not reflected in the sum of their own contributions. Thus reward according to contribution recognizes individual accomplishments without recognizing their dependence on collectives, dependence that is, in complex economies, ubiquitous.
Sam Berstler (MIT), “The Structure of Open Secrets” from the Philosophical Review.
In conversation, we often do not acknowledge what we jointly know to be true. This article identifies a distinctive kind of non-acknowledgment norm, open secrecy norms, and analyzes how such norms constrain our speech. First, the author argues that open secrecy norms are structurally different from other everyday non-acknowledgment norms. Open secrecy norms iterate: when is an open secret, then there’s a norm not to acknowledge that , and this norm is itself an open secret. Then, the author argues that the non-acknowledgment at issue in open secrecy norms motivates a more complex understanding of discourse structure. When interlocutors are conforming to open secrecy norms, they rely on at least two disjoint common grounds, one of which has a privileged status. To understand why and how it is privileged, the author develops Erving Goffman’s notion of defining a social interaction. Finally, the author shows how strategic speakers can exploit the structure of open secrecy norms in order to both communicate about the open secret and shield themselves from retaliation for what they communicate.
Kyle Blumberg (Melbourne) and Ben Holguín (Johns Hopkins), “Fictional Reality” from the Philosophical Review.
This article defends a theory of fictional truth. According to this theory, there is a fact of the matter concerning the number of hairs on Sherlock Holmes’s head, and likewise for any other meaningful question one could ask about what’s true in a work of fiction. This article argues that a theory of this form is needed to account for the patterns in our judgments about attitude reports that embed fictional claims. It contrasts this view with one of the dominant approaches to fictional truth, which originates with David Lewis. Along the way it explores the relationship between fiction, counterfactuals, and vagueness.
Liam Kofi Bright (LSE), Nathan Gabriel (UC Merced), Cailin O’Connor (UC Irvine), and Olúfẹ́mi O. Táíwò (Georgetown), “On the Stability of Racial Capitalism” from Ergo.
What is the connection between capitalism and racial hierarchy? In line with the tradition known as ‘the theory of racial capitalism’ we show that the latter can functionally support the former. As a social construction, race has just those features which allow it to facilitate the sort of stable, inequitable distributions of resources that tend to emerge in capitalist systems. We support this claim using techniques from evolutionary game theory and cultural evolutionary theory, and end by discussing the normative political consequences of this relationship.
Colin Chamberlain (UCL), “How To Eat a Peach: Malebranche on the Function of the Passions” from Mind.
Nicolas Malebranche (1638-1715) holds that the senses, imagination, and passions serve the body’s needs. In this paper, I explain how the passions keep us alive by situating them in Malebranche’s account of ordinary bodily action. Malebranche holds a consent-based view of action. An agent translates her inclinations or motives into action only when she consents to them. The passions contribute to the preservation of life by helping the agent close the gap between inclination and action. The passions, according to Malebranche, are complex psychophysiological phenomena whose various elements—perceptions, shifts of attention, evaluations, bodily preparation, feelings, and so on—work together to elicit the agent’s consent.
Dai Heide (Simon Fraser), “The Transcendental Aesthetic and the Leibnizian Theory of Space” from the Journal of the History of Philosophy.
In considering Kant’s response to the Leibnizian theory of space in the Transcendental Aesthetic, scholars have overwhelmingly emphasized Kant’s response to Leibniz’s relationalism. They have largely missed the metaphysically realistic aspects of Leibniz’s theory with which Kant is primarily concerned. As such, scholars have failed to appreciate the threat Leibniz’s theory poses to Kant’s idealism, a point made publicly as early as 1786 by H. A. Pistorius. I argue that the Aesthetic does indeed contain a compelling argument against the Leibnizian theory of space. This argument crucially depends upon Kant’s claim that space is monistic: that the whole of space is prior to the parts of space and, as such, spatial representations are not decomposable.
Elselijn Kingma (KCL) and Fiona Woollard (Southampton), “Can You Do Harm to Your Fetus? Pregnancy, Barriers, and the Doing/Allowing Distinction” from Ethics.
When pregnant persons do not behave in the way deemed optimal for their fetus, they are often framed as doing harm. This framing acts as a justificatory bypass for defenses of widespread expectations of pregnant persons, allowing such defenses to avoid substantial questions about special obligations in pregnancy. Our main claim is that this justificatory bypass is unwarranted: in many cases either the pregnant person does not count as doing harm or substantive questions about special obligations cannot be avoided. Our secondary claim is that direct engagement with these substantive questions is unlikely to justify widespread expectations on pregnant people.
Alexander Meehan (Wisconsin) and Snow Zhang (UC Berkeley), “Bayes Is Back” from the Philosophical Review.
A core tenet of Bayesian epistemology is that Bayesian conditionalization is the rule of rational credal revision. But it has been pointed out in the recent literature that if learning can be nontransparent, then Bayesian conditionalization does not universally maximize expected accuracy. This result raises an explanatory challenge for any externalist Bayesian who does not want to give up on a connection between accuracy and epistemic rationality: Why is Bayesian conditionalization the rule of rational credal revision, despite the fact that it does not universally maximize expected accuracy? This article proposes an answer to this challenge. The article argues that an updating rule can be evaluated, not only on the basis of its expected accuracy in particular learning situations, but also on the basis of its total expected accuracy across different learning situations. The article proposes a notion of global evidential constancy, and shows that, out of all globally evidentially constant rules, Bayesian conditionalization has the highest total expected accuracy across all learning situations, including nontransparent ones. Bayes is back!
Paulina Sliwa (Vienna), “Changing Minds and Hearts” from Russ Shafer-Landau, ed., Oxford Studies in Metaethics, vol. 20.
Suppose you are uncertain about some moral question. Are you falling morally short, if you rely on moral advice? A popular line of thought is that the problem with relying on moral testimony is that it can change beliefs but not feelings. An agent who forms a moral judgment based on testimony will be emotionally alienated from the moral judgment they accept. They may come to believe—even know—that a given course of action is right or wrong. But they won’t feel it. The aim of this chapter is to challenge this diagnosis: that moral deference will leave the agent emotionally disconnected from the features that matter. It does so by examining the phenomenon of hermeneutical advice: this is moral testimony that aims at helping an agent to make sense of her moral situation. Hermeneutical advice, it is argued, has the power to change minds and hearts.
Quinn White (Harvard), “Love First” from Philosophy and Phenomenological Research.
How should we respond to the humanity of others? Should we care for others’ well-being? Respect them as autonomous agents? Largely neglected is an answer we can find in the religious traditions of Judaism, Christianity and Buddhism: we should love all. This paper argues that an ideal of love for all can be understood apart from its more typical religious contexts and moreover provides a unified and illuminating account of the the nature and grounds of morality. I defend a novel account of love for all that avoids serious worries about the incoherence or impossibility of loving everyone. Doing so requires countenancing a neglected form of love. Love admits as its object not just individual entities like people and groups; we can also bear a love for the Fs in general—for all the Joneses, all the philosophers, or even all the human beings. I go on to argue that while it is possible for ordinary agents like us to love all, we shouldn’t. Instead, we should approximate love for all. The minimal approximation of love for all is, surprisingly, respect; I derive the basic, structural features of deontological ethics (including anti-paternalism and anti-aggregation) from the ideal of loving all.
The editors of Philosopher’s Annual are Daniel J. Singer (University of Pennsylvania), Lila Graham, Lorenzo Manuali, Brett Thompson (University of Michigan). The executive editor is Patrick Grim (Center for the Study of Complex Systems, University of Michigan; Logic & Formal Semantics, Philosophy, Stony Brook).
The nominating editors this year were: Jc Beall, John T. Bengson, Brian Berkey, Ned Block, Ben Bradley, Liam Kofi Bright, Tyler Burge, Victor Caston, Andrew Chignell, Kathleen Creel, Roger Crisp, Cian Dorr, Elizabeth Edenberg, Adam Elga, Iskra Fileva, Branden Fitelson, Will Fleisher, Graeme Forbes, Aaron Garrett, Michael Glanzberg, Alexander Guerrero, Alan Hájek, Ned Hall, Gary Hatfield, Christopher Hitchcock, Des Hogan, Lily Hu, Simon Huttegger, Gabbrielle Johnson, Simon Keller, Zoë Johnson King, Niko Kolodny, Marc Lange, Harvey Lederman, Brian Leiter, Ernie Lepore, Neil Levy, Martin Lin, Ting-an Lin, Colin McLarty, Jeff McMahan, Lauritz Munch, Derk Pereboom, Duncan Pritchard, Theron Pummer, Greg Restall, Geoffrey Sayre-McCord, Anat Schechtman, Barry Schein, Ted Sider, Scott Soames, Roy Sorensen, Quayshawn Spencer, Katie Steele, Una Stojnić, Eric Swanson, Johan van Benthem, Mark van Roojen, Sergio Tenenbaum, Peter B. M. Vranas, Eric Watkins, Daniel Wodak, Gideon Yaffe, José Zalabardo, and Kevin Zollman.

NATO's Arctic activity poses 'direct threat' to Russia, Lavrov warns

NATO's Arctic activity poses 'direct threat' to Russia, Lavrov warns
Russia views NATO’s growing activity in the Arctic as a direct security threat, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said on Monday. NATO launched its Arctic Sentry mission in February to strengthen its presence in the region amid tensions with Moscow and US President Donald Trump’s push to acquire Greenland.
Russia sees NATO activity in the Arctic as a direct security threat, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said in an article published on Monday, as the alliance members boost their presence in the region in the wake of Russia's war on Ukraine.
In February, NATO launched a mission called Arctic Sentry to bolster its presence in the far north, underscoring the alliance's increased focus on the Arctic amid tensions with Russia and US President Donald Trump's push for the acquisition of Greenland.
Russia, which has a naval fleet including nuclear-armed submarines in the Arctic, sees the region as its sphere of interest where it also develops a shipping route to connect with the Asian nations.
Read moreIcelanders vote in tight referendum on restarting EU membership talks
Moscow earlier protested the Arctic Sentry mission and in the article, Lavrov, President Vladimir Putin's long standing foreign minister, said Russia sees NATO military exercises in the region as "aggressive".
"Such military activity in the Far North poses direct threats to Russia's security. The risks of incidents that could trigger an armed confrontation, with potentially catastrophic consequences, are increasing," he said in the article published by the Russian foreign ministry.
Russia has the largest military presence and the most extensive military infrastructure in the Arctic, and in recent years China has started to increase its activity in the mineral-rich area, mostly in partnership with Moscow.
Norway, Russia's neighbour, this month expanded a recently created military brigade headquartered in the Arctic, in what constitutes the latest move by a NATO nation to boost its defence footprint in the wake of the Ukraine war, which Russia started in 2022.
Moscow has previously dismissed allegations that it poses a threat to NATO.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

One dead, many feared missing after Grand Canyon flash flood (VIDEOS)
One person has been confirmed dead and around 14 others are feared missing after a powerful flash flood tore through Arizona’s Grand Canyon, forcing dozens of hikers to be airlifted from the remote inner canyon.
The flooding struck Bright Angel Canyon and the Phantom Ranch area at around 2:30 PM on Saturday, sending muddy torrents, boulders and debris surging through Bright Angel Creek and into the Colorado River.
The US National Park Service (NPS) said Sunday evening that the body of a 46-year-old man had been recovered near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River, around ten river miles downstream from where the flooding occurred. The body was transported to the Coconino County Medical Examiner’s Office, but the victim was not immediately identified.
Some 14 people may still be missing or unaccounted for, down from more than 20 earlier in the day. At least 62 people were evacuated by helicopter from Phantom Ranch and the lower North Kaibab Trail.

Footage from the area showed swollen brown water roaring through the canyon and carrying debris, while campers described scrambling to higher ground as the water rapidly rose.

Nearly all footbridges across Bright Angel Creek were destroyed, while Phantom Ranch, Bright Angel Campground and sections of the North Kaibab Trail were closed indefinitely. The flood also damaged the park’s water pipeline, prompting conservation measures.
The Grand Canyon flash flood comes days after a far deadlier flood and mudslide disaster struck Nepal and neighboring Tibet. At least 788 people have been confirmed dead in Nepal, while around 2,500 remain missing. Over the weekend, dramatic footage emerged showing rescuers pulling a six-year-old girl alive from beneath mud and debris, as search teams raced against time to find possible survivors five days after the calamity.

Ben-Gvir tells party to play down crocodile prison plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
02:32:43 UTC
11:32:43 KST

National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has instructed his far-right Otzma Yehudit party to stop highlighting his controversial plan to use crocodiles to help secure Israeli prisons, amid concerns that voters see the proposal as a gimmick that is hurting the party’s election campaign, ynet and its parent newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth have learned.
During internal party discussions, Ben-Gvir directed campaign officials to play down the crocodile initiative in media appearances, social media posts and campaign messaging. He argued that continued attention to the plan was damaging the party because the public viewed it as unserious, according to information obtained by ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth.
The shift comes after Ben-Gvir repeatedly promoted the proposal in recent months, including in media interviews and official statements to journalists.
The initiative, developed with the Israel Prison Service, calls for crocodile-filled moats to be used as an additional security measure around prisons. When excavation work began as part of a pilot program at Ketziot Prison in southern Israel, Ben-Gvir dismissed criticism of the idea.
“Anyone who thought it was a gimmick was wrong,” he said at the time.
As recently as Aug. 4, Ben-Gvir, who heads Otzma Yehudit, visited Ketziot Prison with Environmental Protection Minister Idit Silman. The two toured the site and filmed a video beside moats dug around a wing holding members of Hamas’ elite Nukhba force, which played a leading role in the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel.
The video was filmed after a district court halted the use of crocodiles for prison security in response to a petition by animal welfare organization Let the Animals Live. The court, however, allowed excavation and other infrastructure work for the Ketziot pilot project to continue.
While Ben-Gvir has sought to lower the profile of the crocodile proposal, his election campaign has increasingly focused on attracting voters from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and the ultra-Orthodox Shas party.
Ben-Gvir has repeatedly warned right-wing voters that Netanyahu could choose to form a government with former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the centrist Yashar! party, rather than form another exclusively right-wing coalition. The message is aimed in part at persuading Likud voters to support Otzma Yehudit instead.
During a Facebook livestream earlier this month, Ben-Gvir repeated that warning.
“If Bibi decides to go with Eisenkot, it will be a mistake that will live in infamy,” Ben-Gvir said, using Netanyahu’s nickname. “If he prefers the center-left over us, then a government like the one we just had — everything will go backward.”
Ben-Gvir also criticized Likud over the government’s stalled effort to overhaul the judiciary.
“Unfortunately, those who dealt with it did not succeed,” he said. “If they had done what I did with the police — the changes in the prisons — then we would have seen things differently.”
Ben-Gvir’s office said in response that the minister remained focused on changes to the prison system.
“Minister Ben-Gvir continues to lead an unprecedented, historic reform of the Israel Prison Service — from toughening conditions for terrorists to upgrading security and protection systems,” his office said. “We will continue to focus on genuine security measures for the safety of Israel’s citizens, not media spin.”

The Jordan strikes targeted US bases used to launch and support the attack on Larak, the foreign ministry said in a statement.
Iran’s army said its drone attack on the United Arab Emirates’ air base targeted sites where US forces and helicopters were stationed, in response to the Larak casualties.
The Revolutionary Guards used air defence missiles to shoot down a US drone that crashed in Gulf waters, the Mehr news agency said on Aug 31, citing a statement from the elite force.
A supertanker caught fire and was brought to a complete halt after being struck by two naval mines in the southern Strait of Hormuz, Iran state TV said, citing a Guards’ statement.
The return to hostilities followed weeks in which the Trump administration has stepped up efforts to punish Tehran and its business partners with costly economic sanctions, shifting away from military options.
More sanctions on Iran
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Reuters on Aug 30 new secondary sanctions were likely to be unveiled weekly in the effort to pressure Iran, with an initial focus on banks.
“We’re starting with the banks, and we’re telling the banks it’s not okay to have Iranian money and to aid the regime,” Bessent said in an interview.
After imposing penalties on the United Arab Emirates branches of Egypt’s Banque Misr on Aug 28 over alleged financial links to Iran, Bessent said the next step may be cutting off an institution entirely from the dollar-based financial system.
“You’re going to see a lot more of these every week,” Bessent told Reuters, ahead of a meeting of Group of 20 finance leaders.
In describing the first known US military strikes since late July, a US official said forces attacked two Iranian launchers on Larak, a small island in the Strait of Hormuz near the strategic port of Bandar Abbas overlooks shipping lanes at the mouth of the Gulf.
“Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz,” the source added.
In a statement, the US Central Command said it took “limited, precise” action against mine laying forces of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards that posed an “imminent threat” in the Strait of Hormuz. It gave no details.
Jordan’s armed forces intercepted eight missiles that entered its airspace, state television said, while a Fox News reporter said on X nearly all incoming missiles had been intercepted.
Amid threats to shipping, the number of visible commodity vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz dropped to five a day over the weekend, shipping data showed.
The actual number could be higher as some vessels have switched off automatic identification systems to evade attacks.
The Guards said the supertanker on fire after being hit by mines had been attempting to pass through the waterway illegally, but gave no details of the vessel or crew, according to a statement cited by state television.
It warned of the same fate for other ships infringing its mandatory regulations to transit the strait.
Last week, US President Donald Trump said all mines had been detonated or removed from the international waters of the strait and Iran had been warned that any vessel placing new mines would be destroyed.
While Trump has repeatedly said the Strait of Hormuz is open, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards’ navy had called those statements “an obvious lie”, reiterating that it remained closed to ships without Iranian permission.
The waterway carried nearly a fifth of global crude oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before it was blockaded in the six-month-old Iran war.
Iran is the third largest producer in the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries. REUTERS
