Aon is nearing a roughly $17 billion deal, including debt, to acquire insurance brokerage USI from private-equity firm KKR, The Wall Street Journal reported Sunday.
A deal could be announced as soon as Monday, the Journal said, citing people familiar with the matter.
USI is an insurance brokerage and consulting firm based in Valhalla, N.Y., that specializes in risk management, employee benefits and retirement consulting. The company has about $3 billion in annual revenue, according to its website.
KKR bought USI from private-equity firm Onex in 2017 and has since increased its ownership stake, becoming the company's largest shareholder in 2023.
A possible deal for USI would follow a string of prominent exits for KKR, including sales of data-center cooling firm CoolIT and Circor's commercial and defense aerospace business earlier this year. KKR reported a record $1.29 billion in asset sales for the quarter that ended in June.
A USI deal would help Aon — a large insurance broker and consultancy with a market capitalization of $75 billion — extend its reach into midsize businesses and boost earnings per share as soon as 2028, the Journal reported, citing a person familiar with the matter.
Aon reported second-quarter adjusted earnings of $3.81 per share on July 29, topping Wall Street analysts' estimates. The stock has since fallen by 5.6%, closing at $355.40 on Friday.

Details
According to the U.S. National Hurricane Center, Karina's maximum sustained winds are reaching 130 km/h, which corresponds to a Category 1 hurricane.
Forecasters expect the cyclone to continue rapidly intensifying over the open waters of the Pacific Ocean. Within 1–2 days, it could become a powerful Category 3 hurricane or stronger.
Dangerous waves threaten Mexico's coast
Karina is located approximately 1,400 km west-southwest of the southern tip of Mexico's Baja California Peninsula and is moving farther into the Pacific Ocean.
Although the hurricane is not expected to make landfall, the waves it generates could lead to dangerous surf and strong rip currents along the southwestern coast of Mexico and Baja California.
In another part of the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm "Lowe" is also intensifying; it is located east-southeast of Hawaii. According to forecasters, it could also become a hurricane in the coming days.

CJP netas not saints... nothing wrong in having political ambitions: Wangchuk
TNN / Aug 31, 2026, 03:29 IST
Comments

Small

Large
Sonam Wangchuk says CJP organisers may have political ambitions, but that's acceptable if platform remains non-party.
NEW DELHI: Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk has said Abhijit Dipke and his fellow organisers of the Cockroach Janta Party movement appear to have political ambitions, but there is nothing objectionable in this as long as the student platform retains its non-party character.Wangchuk, in a Prakhar Gupta Xperience podcast, said Dipke and the others had not disclosed any plans to him and his view was based on his own assessment. “Political ambition is very normal,” he said. “Past political connections I don’t care about, present and future political aspirations are not a problem.”“They are not such saints that they want absolutely nothing and are doing all this entirely selflessly,” he said, referring to the possibility that the organisers had personal or political aspirations.Assessing their suitability for leadership, Wangchuk described the organisers as “well meaning”, “quite skilled” and “above average”.“Well meaning but unskilled” could create difficulties, while “very skilled but ill meaning” would pose a much greater danger, he said.
Asked whether they could become corrupt, Wangchuk said he had seen no such indications. “People go through changes, and I hope they won’t,” he said.
Wangchuk said the organisers could join an existing party or launch a new one later, but must not turn the CJP platform into their political vehicle. He said he had advised them to preserve it as a “neutral, apolitical pressure group”, arguing that this would help retain the trust of supporters who saw it as a students’ movement rather than an organisation aligned with BJP, Congress or AAP.Wangchuk acknowledged that his own standards sometimes led him to expect public figures to have no political ambition. That, he said, could be unrealistic because the organisers were ordinary people entitled to pursue political careers. Beginning such a career by championing an education-related cause could, in fact, be positive.He also expressed hope that participation in the movement would help them emerge as more mature and grounded politicians. “I am actually happy about that,” Wangchuk said of their taking up public issues.

Russia is preparing to return a missile cruiser to service after nearly 30 years of repairs
Kyiv • UNN
The nuclear-powered cruiser “Admiral Nakhimov” is completing trials after modernization. The ship will receive 80 missile launchers and cost more than 200 billion rubles.
Russia expects to return the nuclear-powered missile cruiser "Admiral Nakhimov," which has been undergoing repairs and modernization for nearly 30 years, to the fleet's active service. The ship is currently completing its shipyard and sea trials, Defense Express reports, according to UNN.
Details
By the end of the year, the Russians plan to conduct state trials of the ship, after which it could theoretically return to the Russian Navy.
In fact, the "Admiral Nakhimov" arrived for repairs as early as July 1997, although it was officially placed under repair in August 1999. The cruiser entered service in 1988.
The cruiser can carry up to 80 missiles
After modernization, the ship is to receive 80 launchers for Kalibr, Oniks, and Tsirkon missiles, which would make it one of the most heavily armed ships in the Russian fleet.
According to Russian estimates, the repairs and modernization have already cost more than 200 billion rubles, or approximately $2.3 billion. At the same time, the project's cost was previously estimated at roughly $5 billion.
Defense Express notes that the advisability of such expenditure on a single large ship raises questions, particularly due to the development of naval drones and other means of destruction that increase the vulnerability of large surface platforms.

ASEAN and Japan’s Updated Free and Open Indo-Pacific Initiative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:55:00 UTC
06:55:00 KST

A decade has passed since Japan proposed the Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP) initiative. The “Updated FOIP,” announced in May 2026, carries on the original philosophy while adding a new focus on AI and data infrastructure, supply chains for energy and critical goods, public-private sector market co-creation, and security cooperation. It marks a shift from philosophy to building regional resilience in practice.
Asian growth has benefited from interdependence, but that same interdependence has created vulnerabilities. Disruptions to navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea ripple outward to affect Japan and ASEAN through energy prices, ocean freight, insurance premiums, and component supplies. Economic security is not merely about preparing for great-power competition; it is about protecting the shared foundation of sea lanes, energy, resources, and digital infrastructure from threats including armed conflict, disasters, cyberattacks, and economic coercion.
Japan is a U.S. ally, yet it is not pressing ASEAN to choose between Washington and Beijing. Japan’s role is to strengthen each country’s capacity to make its own decisions and expand the alternatives available to it in times of crisis. Japanese companies have invested in ASEAN for decades, building factories and logistics networks and developing technology and human resources. Japan and ASEAN share the same supply networks and maritime routes, making ASEAN’s resilience inseparable from Japan’s own.
If the FOIP and the ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific (AOIP) are pursued independently, AOIP priorities risk going underimplemented, while the FOIP risks being seen as little more than a vehicle for Japanese interests. The AOIP defines ASEAN priorities; the FOIP links funding, technology, and enterprise to drive implementation. This allows ASEAN to choose the cooperation projects itself and ensure that they are implemented in line with regional needs.
Concrete cooperation could take three forms. The first is joint preservation of maritime routes. The Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and the Malacca and Singapore Straits constitute a single maritime logistics network. Japan, ASEAN, China, and South Korea, despite their different political positions, share a common interest in safe and stable navigation. What this requires, however, is not “joint defense” by extra-regional powers, but navigation safety, anti-piracy, search and rescue, and accident and disaster response that respect the sovereignty and initiative of coastal states.
The model here is the Malacca Strait patrols conducted by the coastal states of Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. Japan has bolstered navigational safety through hydrographic surveying, navigation aids, maritime security information-sharing, and training. Such coastal-state-led, user-state-supported mechanisms can be extended to port and submarine cable protection, information-sharing on alternative routes, and rescue cooperation, with user countries including China participating as well.
The second is critical minerals supply chains. In 2026, Japan successfully conducted a test extraction of rare earth mud from 6,000 meters depth in its Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) around Minamitorishima Island. Though still at the demonstration stage, it marks a step toward supply diversification. Japan should advance collaboration with ASEAN on separation and purification, environmental monitoring, processing, magnet and motor production, and waste-product recovery. Linking future Minamitorishima output with ASEAN mineral and processing capabilities would reduce excessive dependence on single sources.
Third is energy mutual aid. In 2025, ASEAN renewed the ASEAN Petroleum Security Agreement (APSA), which governs cooperation on emergency oil supply. Similar arrangements will also be needed for natural gas disruptions. Japan and ASEAN should consider joint stockpiling of crude oil and petroleum products, shared use of regional storage, emergency mutual accommodation, and LNG-vessel scheduling adjustments. Crisis response can be accelerated by integrating Japan’s stockpiling system with ASEAN’s emergency mechanisms.
The moment is right to expand cooperation with countries such as Australia, South Korea, India, and the EU, building outward from the Japan-ASEAN relationship. But this does not require creating an entirely new bloc. Maritime routes should involve user countries like China, critical minerals should draw in reliable supply-chain partners, and energy should engage both consumer countries and oil- and gas-producing states. A functional approach to open collaboration is realistic: membership varies by issue, with no single grouping required for all.
There is no need to build from scratch. In addition to the ASEAN-Japan Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and ASEAN Plus 3, the supply-chain agreement of the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework for Prosperity (IPEF), in which seven ASEAN countries participate, can serve the FOIP as well. The agreement enables signatories to share risks of critical-mineral supply disruptions, develop alternative sourcing, and coordinate emergency response procedures, with lessons that can inform broader ASEAN-wide cooperation under the AOIP.
What the Indo-Pacific needs is not exclusive blocs but a system of collective stability across sea lanes, resources, and energy. The updated FOIP can take root only by working in tandem with the AOIP and broadening ASEAN options. What Japan and ASEAN should aim for is “collective self-reliance”: the resilience to withstand pressure from any major power or supply disruptions from outside the region.

There were no confirmed deaths or injuries, the park service said in an email.
The flash flood, which began about 2.30pm on Saturday, was caused by rainfall on the Kaibab Plateau, it said.
Torrents of water wiped out footbridges over the creek and significantly altered the landscape, widening the creek bed and creating what appeared to be a new river rapid.

GENEVA, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- A fatal shooting at a rave party in the early hours of Sunday has left one young woman dead and five others injured, as Swiss police are conducting a nationwide manhunt for the unidentified perpetrators.
In a press conference held on Sunday evening, Swiss authorities detailed the latest findings from the deadly shooting. According to the police spokesperson, the incident occurred around 2:30 a.m. local time (0030 GMT) at the Schachen horse racing track in Aarau, capital of Switzerland's northern Aargau canton, where the "Aarau Rave VOL. 7" was concluding.
By the time shots were fired, the event had officially ended at 2:00 a.m., with only about 100 people still on the premises. Witnesses reported hearing what initially sounded like fireworks, with shots ringing out over several minutes as attendees were leaving.
A 22-year-old Italian woman residing in Switzerland died at the scene. Five others - four men and one woman aged 24 to 27, all Swiss residents - were hospitalized, two of whom are also Italian nationals. Police confirmed that none of the injured are in life-threatening condition.
Cantonal Police Commander Michael Leupold told reporters that authorities are pursuing three hypotheses: a terrorist attack, a rampage, or a criminal act such as a settling of accounts in an as-yet-unknown milieu. No motive has been prioritized, and investigators are examining all possibilities.
Ballistic evidence shows shots were fired from two different locations at the scene. Police recovered shell casings of two calibers: pistol ammunition and casings from a long weapon, such as an assault rifle. A "significant number of shots" were reportedly discharged.
A large-scale nationwide manhunt is underway. Police believe the perpetrators have fled the Aarau area and do not currently pose an immediate threat. The operation has mobilized all available Aargau police forces, with support from other cantons, the special unit Argus, the cantonal disaster response element (KKE), and a Swiss Army Super Puma helicopter. German police are also participating in the search as part of routine cross-border cooperation.
As of Sunday evening, police had no concrete leads on the identity or number of the perpetrators, and they ruled out any renewed threat from the shooter(s). ■

Givati soldiers who refused mission over female paramedic sent to military prison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:45:10 UTC
06:45:10 KST

Sixteen soldiers from the forward company of the Rotem Battalion in the Givati Brigade, which also includes yeshiva students serving in the military, were sent to military detention after refusing an order to go on an operational patrol in a Namer armored personnel carrier in Gaza after learning that a female paramedic would be joining them, the IDF announced shortly before midnight on Sunday night. Five soldiers who led the incident were sentenced to 10 days in detention, while 11 others were sentenced to five days.
Two of the five soldiers sentenced to 10 days in detention will meet with an assessment committee before returning to combat duty. The soldiers were tried by the battalion commander, who determined the punishments according to each soldier’s level of involvement in the incident.
Because of the soldiers’ refusal, the operation in Gaza was canceled. According to the IDF, while the force’s commanders agreed to carry out the mission, their soldiers refused to take part because of the female paramedic’s inclusion. In an effort to change their minds, the company commander held a discussion with them in which he explained the importance and urgency of the mission, and the brigade rabbi also ruled that they were permitted to participate. Despite this, the soldiers stood their ground and refused the order.
“These are young soldiers, new to the battalion. They still don’t know how things work,” a soldier in the parallel Tomer Company, which is made up of Haredi troops, told ynet. “During training, everything is separated and clearly defined, and when you arrive at the battalion, you get hit with that reality. Unfortunately, now they’re going to pay for it too.”
Alissa Krant, who serves in the reserves as a paramedic in Brigade 271, told ynet in response to the incident: “I read about this at the height of a reserve deployment with a combat engineering battalion. As a paramedic doing my job and fully invested in the success of our male and female soldiers, it is very frustrating to hear that an order was refused because of the presence of a female paramedic like me.”
Krant added: “When I go out on a mission, I come with medical training. I am a professional, this is my job, and I am responsible for the lives of the people with me. When a soldier is wounded and needs medical treatment, he will not care in that moment whether the person treating him is a man or a woman. Even from the perspective of Jewish law and religion, once it is a matter of saving a life, for life-saving purposes, this should not even be an issue under discussion.
“Since the start of the war, women have entered enemy territory, served alongside men without any special accommodations and done exactly the same work required of them. Hearing something like this does not align with the values of the IDF or with what we bring to the military. Our mission is shared. Our war is not against one another internally — we have enough enemies on the outside,” she added.
Regarding the punishment handed down to the soldiers, Krant said: “I am not happy about any soldier being punished. I am sure what motivated them was belief and not an intention to harm anyone. I am glad the military is taking this issue seriously and putting it on the agenda. In my view, isolated punishment will not bring about change. Change will come through proper explanation and by instilling an understanding of what our role means within the system.”

At least eight die, 17 missing after ferry capsizes off North Cyprus
At least eight people died and 17 were missing after a ferry carrying around 270 passengers and crew capsized off north Cyprus on Aug 30, leaving survivors clinging to its overturned hull.
The privately owned ferry left the port of Kyrenia at 12.30pm local time (5.30pm Singapore time) and immediately started taking on water for an unknown reason, authorities said. It was heading for the Turkish port of Tasucu in the eastern Mediterranean.
Survivors reported the ferry moving erratically, with its last hard impact with the water’s surface breaking the bow of the two-hulled vessel, allowing water to seep in.
The disaster occurred just off the coast of Kyrenia, a popular holiday resort for both locals and tourists. The ferry was one of several shuttle sea services that link north Cyprus, a breakaway unrecognised Turkish Cypriot state, with Turkey daily.
US forces strike two Iranian launchers on Iran’s Larak island, US official says
US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Iran’s Larak island on Aug 30, a US official said, marking the first known American strikes on Iran since late July.
“I can confirm that earlier today US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island. Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into Strait of Hormuz,” the US official said.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said the attack killed and wounded several soldiers and citizens, and would be met with a “response and punishment” from Tehran, Iranian state media reported.
Google Maps will show Lake America in US, not Lake Ontario
Google Maps has changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America for US users to reflect President Donald Trump’s executive order renaming the lake, according to a Google statement.
Trump announced on Aug 27 that he was changing the name of the smallest of the five Great Lakes, part of an escalating trade feud with Canada that has prompted the two countries to impose reciprocal tariffs on billions of dollars in goods.
The president’s order affects the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), which sets the standards for official US maps. It does not have any impact on Canadian naming conventions or how the rest of the world refers to the lake.
Ukraine’s former defence chief seeks US investment for defence tech fund
Ukraine’s former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov is seeking US investment for a defence technology fund, he said in an interview with the Financial Times that was published on Aug 30.
Fedorov is also seeking Western capital to build and manage weapons development companies that he said will help Kyiv resist Moscow, the Financial Times said.
The former defence minister did not say whether he would benefit financially from the fund, nor did he give details on his role overseeing it, according to the FT.

Bruno Fernandes starred with a hat-trick in Manchester United’s 5-2 rout of Ipswich, while Chelsea extended Xabi Alonso’s perfect start with a thrilling 4-3 win against Brighton on Aug 30.
Fernandes shone as he ensured United bounced back from their humiliating 2-0 defeat at Hull on the opening weekend of the Premier League season.

17 farmers killed, over 70 injured in Kherson region since start of war
This was reported by the Rivne Regional Military Administration, citing information presented during a meeting with farmers from the Kherson region, according to Ukrinform.
“A meeting with farmers from the Kherson region was held in the Rivne region. We discussed the challenges currently facing farmers working near the front line, relocation opportunities and further cooperation between the regions,” the statement said.
Farmers from the Kherson region spoke about working under constant Russian attacks. Many farms are located 20–30 kilometers from the front line. Before heading into the fields, farmers coordinate their routes with the military, while some operations are carried out wearing body armor and helmets.
“Due to the hostilities, only about one-third of the agricultural land in our region can currently be used. Russian forces are destroying machinery, crops and businesses. The participants also discussed human losses. It was noted that 17 farmers have been killed and more than 70 injured in the Kherson region since the start of the war.
Despite everything, farmers are not abandoning their farms and continue to work. Some are considering relocation, although this is a difficult process for agricultural businesses: along with machinery, workers and their families must be relocated, while the land and land shares remain in the Kherson region.
According to Deputy Head of the Rivne Regional Military Administration Oleksandr Kokhan, the Rivne region has repeatedly supported the Kherson region during its most difficult moments, providing financial assistance, equipment and personnel. He noted that the Rivne region has business support programs offering compensation for the cost of equipment, part of loan interest, fuel expenses and livestock purchases. Relocated businesses also make use of these opportunities. There are currently 39 such enterprises and institutions operating in the region.

MOSCOW, August 31. /TASS/. Russia is cooperating closely with China and India in the Arctic but has good prospects for cooperation in the area with all BRICS partners, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said in his article, ‘International Cooperation in the Arctic: Challenges and Opportunities,’ published on the arctic.ru portal.
"The countries that cooperate closely with us in the Arctic include, first and foremost, China and India. "We are also ready to develop cooperation with Belarus and other partners and allies in the CIS. South Korea and Singapore should also be mentioned as displaying interest in joint work with Russia in some Arctic projects, notwithstanding their participation in the unfriendly sanction campaign launched by the collective West against our country," Lavrov added.
Lavrov’s article was timed to coincide with a benchmark in the development of Arctic shipping lanes: on August 19, a container ship from China arrived in the port of Murmansk via the Northern Sea Route, a vital part of the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor.
"In collaboration with our international partners, this represents the start of a new phase in the development of Russia’s Arctic region, which accounts for at least 10 percent of the country’s GDP and is home to more than 2.5 million of our citizens," Lavrov said.

Reusable rocket milestone opens a door for Hong Kong’s space ambitions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:30:05 UTC
06:30:05 KST

Reusable rocket milestone opens a door for Hong Kong’s space ambitions
Flurry of commercial activity offers opportunities for Hong Kong’s financial markets, research universities and the Northern Metropolis
On the morning of August 19, LandSpace’s Zhuque-3 Y2 rocket lifted off from the Dongfeng Commercial Space Innovation Test Area. After deploying its second stage and payload into orbit, the rocket’s first stage touched down softly at a recovery site in Gansu province using deployable landing legs.
It was China’s first successful land-based recovery of an orbital-class rocket booster that had just completed an orbital mission – a feat previously achieved only by SpaceX.
The benchmark for reusable rockets remains SpaceX’s Falcon 9, which pioneered vertical landing after launches of this kind and has conducted hundreds of recoveries. Through first-stage reuse, Falcon 9 has driven its launch price down to about US$2,700 per kg (US$1,225 per lb) – a reduction of 85 per cent from an average of US$18,500 in the pre-reusable era. In contrast, China’s commercial launch prices hover at between US$8,000 and US$14,000 per kg, depending on rocket type and mission profile.
The Zhuque-3 is explicitly designed to close that gap. Standing 66 metres tall with a lift-off mass of roughly 570 tonnes, its first stage is powered by nine methane-liquid oxygen engines. Its stainless-steel structure – a deliberate departure from Falcon 9’s aluminium alloy – offers better heat resistance at a lower manufacturing cost. The booster is designed to be reused at least 20 times.

Algeria moves to impose death penalty for setting forest fires after 12 killed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:27:12 UTC
06:27:12 KST

Abbas Mimouni and Tarek Chouiref
31 August 2026•Update: 31 August 2026
Algeria’s president on Sunday ordered the introduction of the death penalty for deliberately setting forest fires after recent blazes across the country killed 12 people.
Abdelmadjid Tebboune issued the directive during a high-level meeting on measures to deal with the aftermath of the fires, attended by senior civilian and military officials, state TV reported.
He instructed the justice minister to submit an amendment to the penal code by Sept. 15 providing for capital punishment for anyone convicted of intentionally setting fire to forested areas.
State television said the sentence would be carried out only after all legal avenues of appeal had been exhausted.
The death penalty remains in Algeria’s criminal code for several offenses, but the country has maintained a de facto moratorium on executions since 1993.
Under current law, deliberately setting forest fires is punishable by up to 30 years in prison or life in prison in certain cases.
Compensation for affected families, plus basic utilities to be restored by weekend
Tebboune also ordered provincial governors to provide security authorities with all available information related to the outbreak of forest fires.
“We saw videos and noticed that a number of fires broke out at the same time, at around 1 am, which raises many questions,” he said.
The president also ordered immediate compensation for affected families, with committees to assess losses and determine the value of damaged property.
He said electricity, gas, water, and telecommunications networks in affected areas should be repaired by next Saturday at the latest, while damaged homes should be restored as quickly as possible.
Tebboune also instructed the housing minister to arrange for construction companies to repair damaged homes within set deadlines, saying life in fire-hit areas should return to normal within a week.
On Wednesday, Algeria’s Interior Ministry said 12 people had been killed in a recent wave of wildfires across several eastern provinces, according to local media.

Import of smart glasses not being considered in this tranche of privacy law changes
An import ban on smart glasses is not being considered by the government at this stage, Attorney-General Michelle Rowland confirms.
The Greens and the crossbench have called for an import ban on the eyewear which can be used to film people without their consent amid an influx of low-cost devices.
Rowland says it's about getting balance right. She says the government doesn't want the glasses used for nefarious purposes but some groups say the technology has had a positive impact.
"We are not specifically in this consultation consulting on an import ban, and as I'm sure you appreciate, an import ban is a matter that would have consequences across government, including across trade, foreign affairs, and other potential legal obligations that can apply internationally," she says.
But the current consultation on changes to privacy laws do not include import restrictions.
"However, we are not ruling anything out in terms of other measures that we can take."
Rowland unveils raft of changes to privacy laws
Attorney-General Michelle Rowland has just unveiled the government's proposed changes to Australia's privacy laws.
They include:
- A test so companies can no longer justify collecting more information than they need, or using it in ways Australians don't expect.
- A right to erasure so Australians can request social media. companies and search engines delete their personal information.
- Measures to stop businesses in trading personal information, such as shopping habits and location data, without clear permissions.
- Bolstering of rules and expectations on how organisations respond to data breaches and manage fraud and financial abuse.
On the issue of smart glasses, Rowland says there are serious concerns and while the Privacy Commissioner is looking into it an import ban won't be addressed in this tranche of changes.

NATO driving the Arctic toward ‘militarization’ – Lavrov (FULL ARTICLE)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:24:30 UTC
06:24:30 KST

Lavrov outlines Arctic ‘challenges and opportunities’ (FULL ARTICLE)
NATO is driving the militarization of the Arctic through intense military preparations that pose a direct threat to Russia’s security and increase the risk of direct armed confrontation, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said.
However, other than the members of the US-led military bloc, the overwhelming majority of countries are willing to engage with Moscow on equal and mutually beneficial terms, the top diplomat wrote in an article for Arctic.ru published on Monday.
The sweeping article touched on Moscow’s plans to develop Arctic shipping and maritime logistics along its Northern Sea Route, upcoming international cooperation, and the steady erosion of previous guardrails for multilateral collaboration in the region.
Read the full text below:
On August 19, a landmark event took place in Arctic shipping. For the first time, a container ship from China arrived at the port of Murmansk via the Northern Sea Route, a vital part of the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor. In collaboration with our international partners, this represents the start of a new phase in the development of Russia’s Arctic region, which accounts for at least 10% of the country’s GDP and is home to more than 2.5 million of our citizens. In this regard, I would like to share a number of considerations on how we assess the current state of affairs in the Arctic and how we plan to develop international cooperation there.
Russia and international partners in the Arctic
The Foundations of the Russian State Policy in the Arctic for the Period up to 2035, approved by President Vladimir Putin, focus the efforts of all government bodies on improving the quality of life for the population of the Arctic zone of the Russian Federation, promoting economic growth in its territories, protecting the environment, and fostering mutually beneficial international cooperation. The latter is of particular importance to the Foreign Ministry, which is entrusted with coordinating functions in relations with foreign countries and intergovernmental organizations. And, I would like to emphasize, the whole range of issues relating to the development of the Arctic zone, maritime logistics and the Northern Sea Route plays an important role in the activities of the Maritime Board of the Russian Federation.
Foreign policy priorities at high latitudes have been enshrined in the currently effective Concept of the Foreign Policy of the Russian Federation of March 31, 2023. In the Arctic, Russia is seeking to preserve peace and stability, reduce the level of threats to national security, and create favorable external conditions for the country’s socio-economic development. We are open to interaction with all constructively minded foreign countries displaying reciprocal readiness to put these ideas into practice. There are quite a few such countries. The vast resource, transport, and logistics potential of the Far North, its unique natural and climatic features, long-standing traditions of regional cooperation, and the rich cultural heritage of its indigenous peoples offer broad opportunities for advantageous partnership.
The countries that cooperate closely with us in the Arctic include, first and foremost, China and India. Substantive discussions on Arctic issues take place with Beijing during regular meetings between the heads of government. The specialized bilateral sub-commission on the Northern Sea Route is operational, as are mechanisms for interministerial consultations and scientific exchanges. The results speak for themselves: they include the launch of regular container shipments across Russia’s northern seas, with plans to increase their frequency, and other achievements, including in polar research.
We are engaged in an active dialogue with New Delhi on issues related to high latitudes. In late August, it was discussed at a meeting of the Russian-Indian Intergovernmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technical, and Cultural Cooperation. Indian corporations are involved in developing the resource potential of Russia’s Arctic region. According to some experts, the Arctic could become a major area of cooperation between Russia and India over the next 20 years.
There are prospects for interaction in the Far North with Brazil, Indonesia, Iran and other BRICS countries. We are also ready to develop cooperation with Belarus and other partners and allies in the CIS. South Korea and Singapore should also be mentioned as showing an interest in joint work with Russia in some Arctic projects, notwithstanding their participation in the unfriendly sanction campaign launched by the collective West against our country.
The interest of non-Arctic countries in establishing cooperation with Russia in the High North is reflected in the active participation of foreign guests in symposia and conferences devoted to Arctic issues. Numerous foreign delegations will take part in discussions during special sessions at the 11th Eastern Economic Forum, which opens on September 1 in Vladivostok. Next March, we look forward to welcoming distinguished guests from abroad to the next major international forum of the Russian Arctic, The Arctic – Territory of Dialogue, which will take place in Murmansk.
Challenges affecting international cooperation in the Arctic
Preserving the Arctic as an area of peace and cooperation meets the interests of the entire international community, and Russia is undoubtedly interested in this as well. However, there are those who do not share this point of view. How else can one explain the fact that NATO countries, as well as the Alliance as a whole, are driving the region towards militarization and creating hotbeds of international tension there?
In February 2026, NATO launched its Arctic Sentry operation, designed to expand its military presence in the High North. Intensive military preparations are underway in close proximity to our northern borders. NATO is conducting large-scale military exercises involving non-regional countries and introducing new components of its command-and-control system.
Such military activity in the Far North poses a direct threat to Russia’s security. It also increases the risk of incidents that could trigger an armed confrontation with potentially disastrous consequences.
This deliberate and systematic effort to foster an atmosphere of mistrust in the military sphere is taking place alongside Western attempts to undermine Russia’s legitimate rights in international cooperation through illegitimate financial and economic sanctions targeting legal entities and individuals from countries of the Global Majority involved in joint projects in the Arctic region.
NATO members and other Western countries make no secret of their true motives, openly declaring their intention to turn the Arctic into a new front for opposing the development of Russia and its like-minded partners.
One manifestation of the West’s anti-Russian policy has been the disruption of previously effective mechanisms of multilateral cooperation in the Far North. Some have ceased to exist altogether, while others have largely lost their relevance without Russia’s participation, after Moscow was forced to suspend its engagement with them in response to hostile actions. The Arctic Council, established almost 30 years ago, on September 19, 1996, remains the only functioning intergovernmental organization.
The Council is approaching its anniversary in a shape that is far from ideal. Since March 2022, as a result of actions by its Western member states, its work has effectively been frozen, leaving the organization in a severe crisis. Ministerial meetings and sessions of its key coordinating body, the Senior Arctic Officials, have been suspended, while its capacity to implement projects has been significantly curtailed. The Council’s activities are now largely confined to expert-level contacts and remote meetings of its working bodies.
Russia is ready to resume the full-fledged work of the Arctic Council, provided that all parties engage in good faith and take into account the legitimate interests of every participant. At the same time, we are prepared for the scenario currently being pursued by NATO countries within the organization as they attempt to discuss Arctic issues among themselves, without Russia, thereby effectively discrediting and marginalizing the Arctic Council. Should this scenario materialize, Russia has the territory, logistics, technology, and reliable partners needed to carry out mutually beneficial projects and confidently implement its plans in the Arctic.
The future of international cooperation in the Arctic
A glance at the world map makes it clear that Russia has been, is, and will remain a leading Arctic state. As climate change continues and the polar ice cover recedes, experts predict that the Arctic will become increasingly accessible for transportation and resource development. The region is already playing an increasingly important role in maintaining stable trade links amid more frequent disruptions to global supply chains, particularly in the straits of the world’s oceans that are of systemic importance to the global economy.
The strategic importance of the Arctic to our country’s national interests and security will also continue to grow. We will pursue the comprehensive development of the High North and further expand the infrastructure of Russia’s Arctic zone in accordance with Russian law and the country’s development priorities.
In our economic activities, we will continue to proceed from the understanding that the Arctic maritime areas form an integral part of the World Ocean. The provisions of the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, which establish special rights and responsibilities for coastal states in the Arctic, apply there in full. Commitment to these rights and responsibilities was reaffirmed in the Ilulissat Declaration, adopted in 2008 by the five Arctic coastal states – Russia, Denmark, Canada, Norway, and the United States. At this stage, we see no need to develop new international legal instruments governing economic and other activities in the High North.
Russia’s foreign policy in the Arctic will remain comprehensive and pragmatic. We support the Arctic’s development as an integral part of the broader Eurasian space of security and cooperation.
Our current opponents should have learned the many lessons of history by now and understood that attempts to speak to Russia in the language of sanctions and threats are futile. Unfriendly and hostile actions have been and will continue to be met with an appropriate response, including asymmetric measures. Russia favors constructive dialogue in all regions of the world, but, when necessary, we will defend our national interests by all available means.
As President of Russia Vladimir Putin has repeatedly emphasized, extensive work is underway in the Arctic, and we are open to cooperation with all partners willing to engage on the basis of equality and mutual benefit. Such partners, beyond the circle of NATO countries pursuing Russophobic policies, constitute the overwhelming majority.Promising areas of cooperation include the development of natural resources and the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor, including its key component, the Northern Sea Route. Priorities also include the development of industrial, transport, and tourism infrastructure.Improving the well-being of people living in the Far North, preserving the Arctic environment, and advancing scientific research will also remain key priorities. In all these areas, we see international cooperation as playing a major role.

The Reason Japan Cannot Commit to Dialogue with North Korea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:24:00 UTC
06:24:00 KST

Only two Japan-North Korea summit meetings have ever been held, both between Japanese Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi and former North Korean leader Kim Jong Il, in September 2002 and May 2004. Since then, an inter-Korean summit was held in October 2007, followed by three more in 2018. U.S.-North Korea summits were held in June 2018, February 2019, and June 2019. Yet Japan and North Korea have not met at the summit level in over two decades.
What makes summit dialogue uniquely difficult for Japan is the abduction issue. From the 1970s through the 1980s, North Korean agents abducted a large number of Japanese citizens. The abduction of Megumi Yokota, a middle school student at the time, especially shocked Japanese society, and resolving the abduction issue has been declared a “high-priority issue” by every successive administration.
Japanese sanctions on North Korea are the heaviest in the world, yet they have not led to the return of a single abductee to Japan since the five abductees came home in October 2002. Japanese public opinion nonetheless persistently calls for heavier sanctions, driven by anger and distrust. This is despite the fact that it was dialogue, not sanctions, that secured Koizumi’s signal achievement: an apology from North Korean leader Kim Jong Il and the return of five abductees and their family members.
The issue is serious and complex. Even if North Korea were to allow Japanese nationals to return, claiming that “new abduction victims have been identified,” that would not produce unqualified satisfaction on the Japanese side. Distrust toward a country that has long insisted “the abductions have been resolved” would only deepen; and even if ten people were to return, the Japanese public would suspect there may be still more abductees. Japan has struggled for years with the question of what would constitute a “resolution” of the abduction issue, but it proved an impossible task given that human lives were at stake.
The key figure who made Koizumi’s historic visit to North Korea possible was Tanaka Hitoshi, the then Director-General of the Asian and Oceanian Affairs Bureau of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. He conducted nearly thirty secret meetings with the North Korean agent known as “Mr. X,” in China and other third countries. The meetings were so secret that even Shinzo Abe, then Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary, was not made aware of them.
After Kim Jong Il admitted to and apologized for the abductions and the five abductees were returned to Japan, public anger fell not only on North Korea but also on Tanaka. Not all abductees had returned, and it emerged that Tanaka had accepted a North Korean suggestion for a “temporary return” of roughly two weeks rather than permanent residency for the five abductees.
Tanaka likewise attracted Abe’s ire. Having taken a strong personal interest in the abduction issue, Abe could not forgive Tanaka for advancing negotiations without informing him. Tanaka was ultimately summoned to Diet deliberations, where he broke down in tears under withering criticism of how the negotiations had been handled. Despite having acted on the prime minister’s instructions, Tanaka received no defense from Koizumi, perhaps because public opinion was too hostile. Koizumi’s diplomacy toward North Korea deserves a more positive assessment than it has received, and it is regrettable that this episode cast such a long shadow. Tanaka was so thoroughly pilloried by Japanese conservatives as a “traitor” that this once-promising diplomatic ace never became vice-minister for foreign affairs or ambassador to the United States.
The affair had lasting consequences. It taught subsequent administrations that even if they were to seriously pursue North Korea diplomacy, public support would be hard to secure given widespread skepticism toward dialogue, and that even partial success, short of a “full resolution” of the abduction issue, would expose them to harsh criticism regardless.
Having witnessed the keelhauling of Tanaka, even the most talented Foreign Ministry officials will not actively pursue North Korea diplomacy. Japanese civil servants are divided from the moment of hiring into elite “career” and specialized “non-career” tracks, with the hierarchy between the two tracks never reversed. Career diplomats rotate postings every two to three years and are guaranteed advancement if they handle North Korea safely without taking risks. The perverse result is that the most capable diplomats are the least likely to actively pursue dialogue with Pyongyang.
This structural problem must be addressed before Japan can make progress on any of its outstanding issues with North Korea. Ultimately, overcoming the problem requires strong political leadership from the prime minister.

The Icelandic parliament will discuss the results of the referendum on joining the EU
Kyiv • UNN
52.8% of Icelanders opposed resuming negotiations with the EU. Parliament will discuss the further fate of the application, which has not been officially withdrawn.
The Icelandic Parliament will discuss the future of the country's application to join the European Union after the majority of citizens opposed resuming negotiations with Brussels. Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir said this, Politico reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to the referendum results, 52.8% of voters opposed resuming EU accession negotiations, while 47.2% supported the proposal. Turnout was 82.5%.
Frostadóttir said that the government would discuss with the parliamentary Foreign Affairs Committee what to do with Iceland's application, which has still not been officially withdrawn.
There will be no EU accession negotiations for now
We will discuss with the parliamentary Foreign Affairs Committee how best to close this chapter. We do not intend to make any final decisions on this matter
Frostadóttir stressed that the referendum results would be respected, meaning that under the current government, negotiations on Iceland's accession to the EU will not resume. At the same time, she said, the issue of membership is likely to become a topic again in the next parliamentary elections.
Iceland began negotiations to join the EU in 2009, but they were suspended in 2013. However, the country has never officially withdrawn its membership application.

Flash floods hit Grand Canyon, at least 20 hikers missing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:17:52 UTC
06:17:52 KST

More than 20 hikers who visited the Grand Canyon in Arizona are missing after flash floods struck the area beginning at around 2:30 p.m. local time, the Daily Mail reported Sunday evening. Authorities are searching for the missing hikers and are asking the public to help identify those who were on the trails they had been hiking.
More than 62 people were evacuated from the area Saturday because of the flooding. All pedestrian bridges crossing Bright Angel Creek were destroyed by the unusual weather after the creek overflowed its banks.
The U.S. National Park Service said in a statement: “Grand Canyon National Park crews, in coordination with the Arizona Department of Public Safety, continue evacuation and incident response efforts and are working to locate individuals who may have been in the affected area.” 
Videos from the scene showed mudslides sweeping through the area as hikers filmed them from a suspension bridge.
There is currently no estimated timetable for reopening the blocked roads, and additional areas in the inner canyon may also have to be closed.
More than 60 people were evacuated from Phantom Ranch, which has a historic canteen and dorms, and is a common spot for rafters to get off and on the river. More evacuations were planned during Sunday, the park said. No injuries have been reported.
Erica Viola said she was at Bright Angel Campground when the rain started Saturday afternoon, and she and about 50 other hikers watched the creek rise and then debris start to flow by, including what looked like a bunkhouse. The group was taken by helicopter to safety, ending her adventure two days early, she said.
About half an inch to 1 inch (1 centimeter to 2.5 centimeters) of rain fell within about 30 minutes in the rocky area where there's a steep drop in elevation, said National Weather Service meteorologist Justin Johndrow in Flagstaff.
"Most of it ran off instantly," Johndrow said.
He said the flooding happened on the north side of the Grand Canyon, where Bright Angel Creek comes from the North Rim down to the Colorado River, dropping around 6,000 feet (1,828 meters).
More rain and thunderstorms were possible for the area into Monday.

US strikes Iranian launchers on Larak Island, marking first attacks in weeks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:12:00 UTC
06:12:00 KST

Yasin Gungor
31 August 2026•Update: 31 August 2026
 
 
US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island on Sunday, marking the first strikes on Iranian territory since late July, an official told Axios.
The operation, which followed a month-long period of relative stagnation in direct military engagements, targeted systems allegedly being prepared to launch rockets carrying sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz, a critical oil transit point.
According to the US official, American forces are “monitoring the area closely and remain prepared to protect the free flow of commerce” through the strategic waterway. The Strait of Hormuz narrows to just 39 kilometers (24 miles) between Larak Island and Oman’s Great Quoin Island.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said several fighters and civilians were killed and injured in the strike and vowed to respond. Iran's Tasnim news agency reported that preliminary information suggested it was a drone attack.
Further details regarding the outcome of the strike were not immediately available.
US President Donald Trump recently said that all mines had been removed from the Strait of Hormuz, and warned of a “zero tolerance policy” on new mine placement. He said Washington was utilizing "Space Force" technology to monitor the area with extreme precision.
Iranian officials have asserted that "no one except Iran knows the location" of the mines in the strategic waterway.
Tensions between Tehran and Washington have remained high since the war began with strikes on Iran in late February. Although a memorandum of understanding was signed in June through Pakistani and Qatari mediation, the US began a two-week bombing campaign and reimposed a naval blockade in July after differences over navigation in the strait.
It has yet to be seen whether the latest strike represents a one-time operation or the start of a sustained new bombing campaign.

Right to question not defiance, every dissent not a threat: SC judge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:10:44 UTC
06:10:44 KST

'In a democracy, the right to question is not an act of defiance.': Justice Bhuyan
NEW DELHI: In a constitutional democracy like India, govt must listen to citizens, give space for dissent, and have institutions that are accountable to society and do not treat every dissent as a threat, Supreme Court judge Ujjal Bhuyan said on Sunday."In a democracy, the right to question is not an act of defiance. It is an essential expression of citizenship, liberty and constitutional responsibility," Justice Bhuyan said at a convocation ceremony at National Law University, Delhi."If we want a democratic society that respects liberty and difference, that culture has to begin somewhere. It can only begin in our universities. A university... should be one of the first places where the habit of thinking freely begins," he said.A university should be a space where an idea is not accepted merely because it is familiar and where students do not hesitate to ask difficult questions simply because the answer may be uncomfortable,” Justice Bhuyan said.He said India’s Constitution guarantees free speech, thinking and believing differently. “Intolerance begins to undermine that framework when disagreement or dissent is no longer treated as a legitimate difference of opinion but as something that must be silenced, rejected or punished.
The ability to live with disagreement is not merely a social virtue. It is the very essence of a liberal constitutional democracy.”Justice Bhuyan said maturity of a democracy is reflected not merely in how it treated opinions that are popular, having the majoritarian mandate, but also in how it responds to opinions that are difficult, unpopular or inconvenient. “The freedom to express an opinion, to disagree with the prevailing view and to participate in public life would be meaningful only when there is space for dissent,” he added.
He quoted Justice O Chinnappa Reddy’s 1986 judgment in Bijoe Emmanuel case, in which the judge had said, “Our tradition teaches tolerance; our philosophy preaches tolerance; our constitution practises tolerance; let us not dilute it.”He pointed out that tolerance under our Constitution does not ask us to surrender our individuality. “It recognises that a free society would contain different opinions, beliefs and ways of looking at the world,” he said.

China's domestic economy continues to weaken

Key Event
What do today's business indicators tell us about Q2 GDP?
Today's release by the ABS Q2 the business indicators have market economists narrowing their focus of the likely outcome of Wednesday's GDP number. But have they changed anything?
While all are waiting for the final pieces of the National Accounts puzzle tomorrow (net exports, terms of trade and public sector spending are still to come), today's numbers don't appear to have shifted the consensus much.
That consensus sits at 0.4% GDP growth over the quarter and 1.9% over the year.
That's a marked slowdown from the 2.5% annual pace in Q1, but a tick up from the 0.3% QoQ growth reported at the end of March.
A big driver in that result is that the solid 1% Q2 growth in 2025 will drop out of the annual calculations.
So, what about today's figures?
NAB has one of the more downbeat forecasts for GDP growth, pencilling 0.2% QoQ, but says even that is now in doubt.
NAB's Jessie Cameron says private non-farm inventories are set to subtract 0.3ppts from Q2 GDP growth.
They also point to some downside risk to the NAB's Q2 GDP forecast, she noted.
However, that comes with a rider that the large fall in inventories is likely, in part, to be driven by the miners destocking, or in other words, shipping their products offshore.
So, the net negative today may well be a positive in net exports tomorrow.
ANZ's head of Australian Economics, Adam Boyton has a more upbeat reading of the figures and says there is a chance that the bank's call of 0.4% growth over the quarter is too conservative.
Company profits rose by 1.8% QoQ rise in company profits (led by the miners) to be 7.4% higher of the year. Wages and salaries rose by 1.4% QoQ and 5.7% YoY.
"The combination of the two points to a robust trend in nominal GDP," Mr Boyton said.
"The sales data in the business indicators release point to a robust print for the production-based measure of GDP and is a source of the upside risk to our preliminary 0.4%q/q Q2 GDP growth forecast."
However, he noted that retail may not be as robust as recent household spending implies.
"A rise in inventories in the retail trade industry, combined with only moderate sales volumes growth of 0.4% q/q (following a 0.1% q/q decline in Q1) and a 5.2% q/q fall in retail profits points to conditions being variable across the economy," Mr Boyton said.
Over at CBA, the bank's economics team is sticking to its forecast for 0.4% GDP growth over the quarter but says there is some downside risk to their forecast.
J.P. Morgan's Tom Kennedy is also sticking with his forecast of a slightly lower than consensus 0.3% growth.
"Australia's business indicators were slightly softer than expected, though not enough to change our 2Q real GDP tracking estimate," Mr Kennedy said.
"Nominal wages and salaries increased 1.4%q/q in 2Q, matching the run rate from the prior quarter and broadly aligning with the most recent Wage Price Index/hours worked data.
"Importantly, this outcome is only marginally above the 10-year average (1.2% q/q) and, in our view, now at levels consistent with the RBA's inflation target."

Key Event
CBA, Colonial First State and Avanteos to pay $249m in banking RC settlement
It's now eight years since the Royal Commission into Misconduct in the Banking, Superannuation and Financial Services Industry started examining some of the the sector's more dubious/illegal operations, but the process of remediation is still slowly rolling along.
In its action against Colonial First State Investments, Avanteos Investments and the Commonwealth Bank, Slater and Gordon Lawyers has finally landed a $249 million in principle settlement of a class action.
The proceedings commenced in 2018 as part of Slater and Gordon's "Get Your Super Back" series of class actions in the wake of the 2018 banking royal commission.
The settlement is still subject to Federal Court approval and was reached without Colonial First State, Avanteos or CBA admitting liability.
Here's more from Slater and Gordon's statement this morning.
"At its heart this case was about the alleged conflict between CFSIL, AIL and CBA's interests in profiting from members' savings, and CFSIL and AIL's duties as trustees to do the best they could for their members. The case alleged CFSIL and AIL failed to properly manage that conflict," said Nathan Rapoport, class actions practice group leader at Slater and Gordon Lawyers.
"Superannuation trustees must prioritise their members' interests over their own. If any superannuation trustees might be at risk of forgetting the lessons from the banking royal commission, the settlement in this case should serve as a reminder."
The case alleged that group members' retirement savings were reduced through the payment of low interest rates on certain cash and deposit investments with CBA offered through Colonial First State superannuation and wrap products, CFS FirstChoice and FirstWrap and Commonwealth Essential Super, between November 2008 and September 2021.
It was alleged that CFSIL and AIL did not act in the best interests of their superannuation fund members when they invested members' retirement savings with their parent bank CBA without trying to obtain the best interest rates available for their members.
It also alleged that CFSIL and AIL received undisclosed payments from CBA which incentivised them to invest members' savings with CBA at lower rates, and that CBA benefited by obtaining access to members' savings at low interest rates.
Slater and Gordon's case alleged that the cash and deposit investments at the centre of the proceeding did not provide members with the returns they were reasonably entitled to expect, and that in total members lost millions in aggregate retirement funding.

US strikes Iranian launchers on Larak island amid strait of Hormuz tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:05:43 UTC
06:05:43 KST

Iran has launched retaliatory strikes on airbases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates after the US attacked Iranian rocket launchers in the strait of Hormuz, the first such hostilities in a month.
Hours later, Iranian state TV later reported that a supertanker had caught fire after hitting two naval mines while attempting to pass through the southern side of the strait. It did not identify the vessel or provide information about its crew.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned that other ships violating its rules would face the same fate and said compliance with its regulations for passage through the strait was mandatory.
The last known US strikes on Iran were in late July and the war has reached a stalemate in recent weeks, with Washington threatening to impose costly sanctions on countries that support Iran.
The latest exchange of fire was sparked late on Sunday by a US attack on Larak Island in the strait. “I can confirm that earlier today US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak island,” a US official said. “Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait of Hormuz.”
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said the US attack killed and wounded several soldiers and citizens and would be met with “punishment” from Tehran, Iranian state media reported.
Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency reported the US attack was a drone strike. The Mehr news agency quoted the IRGC as saying its air defences had shot down a US mq-9 drone over the strait, causing it to crash into Gulf waters.
In response to the attack, the IRGC “targeted technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities, and enemy fighter jet positions at the US-operated King Hussein and al-Azraq airbases in Jordan” with ballistic missiles, causing “heavy damage”, according to state TV.
On Sunday night, Reuters reported a US source as saying that all incoming missiles on US forces in Jordan had been intercepted with no significant impact so far.
Later, Iran’s army said it launched a drone attack on US forces in the United Arab Emirates’ al Minhad airbase early on Monday, Iranian state TV reported. It said the attack was in response to the Larak Island assault.
There was no immediate comment from the UAE on Iran’s claim and the UAE’s defence ministry had not issued a statement on the matter.
Hours after the attacks, US president Donald Trump claimed in a social media post that Iran’s energy hub of Kharg island was being “blown to smithereens” but gave no further details.
The White House and the US defense department did not immediately respond to requests for comment and there was no immediate response from Iran about the Kharg island claim.
Attacking Kharg, which handled 90% of Iran’s oil exports before the war, would severely disrupt the Islamic republic’s energy trade and put huge pressure on its economy.
The US said its earlier attacks on Larak island were aimed at preventing Iran from launching more sea mines into the strait.
Trump said last week that all mines had been detonated or removed from the international waters of the strait of Hormuz and Iran had been told that any ship or boat placing new mines would be destroyed.
The US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February and Iran responded with its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases. The Iran war has now crossed its six-month mark.
Diplomatic efforts, spearheaded by mediators including Pakistan and Qatar, have tried for months to bring an end to the war to no avail.
While a ceasefire was agreed in April and a memorandum of understanding towards a final peace deal was signed in June, no agreement has been forthcoming and Washington has since declared “economic warfare” against Tehran.
US-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed thousands and displaced millions. Eighteen US service members have been killed in the conflict.
The war has led to the blockade of the strait of Hormuz, which before the conflict accounted for the transit of about a fifth of the world’s oil barrels consumed.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

US strikes Iranian launchers in first action in weeks, triggering retaliation
Tehran targets American bases in Jordan after US forces attack launchers on the Strait of Hormuz
US forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz in their first military action in a month on Sunday, breaking a lull in fighting during an intermittent war that has lasted more than six months. Vowing to retaliate for what it called a deadly attack, Iran later said it had launched missiles at US sites in Jordan.
Forces with the Revolutionary Guard Corps were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait, according to Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for the US Central Command. The US military last week completed clearing sea mines from the strait’s international shipping routes.
Semi-official news outlets in Iran reported sounds of explosions near Larak island on the strait. The Guard in a statement carried by Iran’s state broadcaster noted “the martyrdom and injury of several of our fighters and compatriots”.
Later, Iranian state television showed what it said were ballistic missiles being fired by Iran at US bases in Jordan in response to the American strikes. Jordan’s armed forces said they intercepted eight missiles that penetrated the country’s airspace early Monday in the Middle East.
US military officials disputed Iran’s claim that the latest American strikes were an act of aggression, calling them a “limited, precise action” against what they said were minelaying forces.
“In essence, Iran created the threat and the US military eliminated it to protect civilian mariners, commercial shipping, and the free flow of global commerce,” US Central Command said in a statement late Sunday.

File photo: PM Modi being accorded a ceremonial welcome, in Tashkent. Uzbekistan President Shavkat Mirziyoyev is also seen.
India and Uzbekistan upgraded their relations to a comprehensive strategic partnership, set an annual trade target of $ 5 billion and closed in on an agreement for uranium supply to India, as PM Narendra Modi held talks with President Shavkat Mirziyoyev in Tashkent.Modi announced that India would get into a long-term arrangement for supply of uranium from Uzbekistan, a major regional producer and exporter. Both sides agreed to establish a foreign minister-level coordination council to guide all aspects of cooperation under the elevated partnership.Following the talks that focused on expanding cooperation in defence and security, trade and investment, critical minerals, AI, agriculture and health, the 2 sides signed 11 MoUs. Areas covered included culture, education, mining, Ayurveda, tourism and restoration of Buddhist sites in the Central Asian country.Modi also underscored the need for zero tolerance against terrorism and extremism, saying a stronger India-Uzbekistan partnership will be a powerful force for peace, progress and prosperity in Central Asia.The leaders endorsed growing defence cooperation between the 2 countries, including through regular exchanges, capacity-building and joint activities, and expressed their commitment in a joint statement to address common security challenges by further strengthening such cooperation.
Going forward, Modi said, both sides will promote direct linkages, co-production, and co-development between the defense industries of both nations."Close defense and security cooperation between our two countries reflects our deep mutual trust," said the PM.Outlining an ambitious agenda to move forward with “speed and tangible results” in this new phase of our partnership, the PM also said in his media statement that both sides will work systematically on market access, connectivity, banking, and payment systems to achieve the target of $ 5 billion trade by 2030.“We will work together to boost win-win cooperation in infrastructure development. Cooperation in Digital Public Infrastructure, AI, critical minerals, clean energy, space, and nuclear energy is making our relationship future-ready,” said Modi, adding that Uzbekistan is at the heart of Central Asia, and at the heart of India’s engagement with the region.Both sides believe that while India is one of Uzbekistan’s top 10 trading partners, their annual trade of $ 1.32 billion remains significantly below its true potential.In the meeting, the leaders agreed to undertake joint measures to broaden the range of goods traded between the two countries, remove non-tariff barriers, and promote industrial cooperation with a view to further increasing bilateral trade turnover, according to the joint statement. They also decided to create a Joint Working Group to address non-tariff issues and investment barriers.There was focus on Global South cooperation with Modi saying that Uzbekistan’s highest honour for a foreign leader that was conferred on him by the president had left India with the added responsibility of working with Uzbekistan as “Global South partners for the betterment of humanity”.“Both sides agreed to work together to preserve and protect the multilateral trading system with the WTO at its core, especially for the interests of the developing countries,” said the joint statement. Modi and Mirziyoyev discussed a recently concluded jointly feasibility study for Uzbekistan-India Preferential Trade Agreement, directing officials to explore the next steps on a time bound basis.
On international cooperation, the leaders called for comprehensive UN reforms that would reflect contemporary global realities and to make it more representative and effective in dealing with issues of international peace and security, with Uzbekistan reaffirming its support for India’s candidature for permanent membership of the UN Security Council.The leaders explored cooperation in the fields of geology, mining, nuclear energy, industrial cooperation, and critical & strategic minerals, including projects for the processing of mineral resources, according to the joint statement. The 2 sides also announced partnerships between their cities and states, with Modi saying that these arrangements will continuously enhance direct connections in urban management, industry, education, tourism, and culture.

Iran says retaliatory strikes on US bases 'legitimate defence'
Iran's Foreign Ministry on Monday condemned US attacks on Larak Island, and said strikes on US bases in response were "in accordance with the inherent right of legitimate defence."
Iran on Monday said its forces struck US military bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates.
The US bases in Jordan were used in the attacks on the island, which killed and injured Iranian armed forces members and civilians, the Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
In a separate statement on Iranian state media, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two US air bases in Jordan were damaged by ballistic missiles.
Citing Iran's army, Iranian state television reported US forces and helicopters were targeted with drones at the Al Minhad Air Base in the United Arab Emirates.
The US military has not yet commented on the reports of Iranian retaliatory attacks.
Iran says oil tanker hits mines in Strait of Hormuz
Iran's Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) said a "rogue supertanker" struck two naval mines in the southern Strait of Hormuz while attempting to "illegally" traverse the waterway, state television reported on Monday.
The tanker caught fire and was brought to a standstill, the report said, without providing information about the vessel's identity or the condition of crew.
The IRGC warned any ships against not complying with its rules of passage through the Strait of Hormuz.
Earlier, the US military said strikes on Iran's Larak Island targeted IRGC minelaying forces to prevent Iran from further mining the strait.
US military says latest strikes were 'limited, precise action'
The US military's Central Command has rejected Iranian claims that its Sunday strikes were an act of aggression.
"US forces took limited, precise action against IRGC minelaying forces posing an imminent threat in the Strait of Hormuz," it said on social media.
"In essence, Iran created the threat and the US military eliminated it to protect civilian mariners, commercial shipping, and the free flow of global commerce."
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had earlier called the US strikes an "act of aggression" aimed at resolving "domestic problems" and its "diminished credibility."
IRGC attacks US air bases in Jordan, Iranian state media reports
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it retaliated for earlier American strikes on Larak Island by firing ballistic missiles at American positions in Jordan.
The IRGC said it caused "heavy damage" on what it referred to as the King Hussein base and the Al-Azraq base, both in Jordan.
The Jordanian army said it intercepted eight missiles that entered its airspace.
US sources also said that nearly all of the missiles had been intercepted, according to Fox News' chief international correspondent Trey Yingst.
US redirected dozens of ships to enforce Iran blockade
US forces have redirected dozens of ships as part of efforts to enforce a maritime blockade against Iran, the US Central Command said on Sunday night.
The US imposed a naval blockade on Iran in April, after Iran blocked most international shipping in the Strait of Hormuz in late February.
"As of August 30, CENTCOM forces have redirected 83 commercial vessels, disabled 3 and boarded 2 to ensure compliance with the blockade," CENTCOM said on social media.
US forces attack Iran for first time in weeks
US forces reportedly stuck Iranian military sites in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday night — the first US strikes on Iran in over a month.
"Earlier today, US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island," US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins said in a message to the AFP news agency.
"Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz."
Iranian media reported explosions near Larak Island.
The US said last week that it had finished clearing Iranian sea mines from the strait's international shipping routes.
The IRGC said in a statement that the attack on Sunday night "will be answered by the sons of Iran and will result in the punishment of the aggressor."
