Ukraine’s war didn’t go to plan. Its former defense minister’s career did
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
20:58:48 UTC
05:58:48 KST

Ukraine’s war didn’t go to plan. Its former defense minister’s career did
Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mikhail Fedorov has suddenly – and rather unexpectedly – become an adviser to Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto. The news caught many conservative military analysts off guard. Why would Italy want him, and what does Rome hope to gain? Let’s try to make sense of the move without getting carried away.
A manager in khaki, not a marshal
It should be obvious that Fedorov is no military genius, nor does he possess any particular talent as a battlefield commander. That is simply not who he is. He was never a career officer, and he never made his name drawing thick red arrows across maps of future operations. First and foremost, Mikhail Fedorov is an effective IT executive – and a knowledgeable chief customer for the entire defense industry.
His path to that role began as the top digital strategist for Vladimir Zelensky’s presidential campaign, where he built an online campaign network and bet heavily on internet marketing. From there, he went on to create Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation and roll out the Diia digital ecosystem, which changed everyday life across the country. In 2026, Fedorov took over the Defense Ministry amid an urgent need to impose order and bring sweeping digitalization to the armed forces. The timing, it seems, could hardly have been better.
Several major changes in the Ukrainian military were introduced with Fedorov’s involvement:
- Drone procurement for military units was radically overhauled through the launch of a dedicated marketplace designed to minimize red tape. It was a highly unconventional move that significantly shortened the path from manufacturer to frontline unit while opening up a market for many small and relatively young companies. After drones, the same digital approach began spreading to other parts of the defense industry.
- Agile management methods were effectively brought into military life, breaking down long-established systems of multistage approval and allowing new ideas to be tested quickly under real battlefield conditions – directly in the trenches.
- The military opened its doors to software developed by civilian companies. The emphasis shifted toward finding new and unconventional solutions that could be deployed quickly and deliver results immediately, rather than waiting for lengthy testing reports and reviews by specialized military institutes.
Of course, Fedorov’s role in these changes should not be overstated. Many of the initiatives that reshaped the Ukrainian military began before he arrived at the Defense Ministry. What he brought was a fresh, digital perspective that helped cut some corners and speed up the adoption of new ideas.
There were no combat operations or battlefield triumphs involved. He was a digital-solutions manager who put on a military uniform – focused exclusively on digital systems and a project-based approach to reform. And naturally the process was not without its rough edges. Digitalization remains the only clear success he can point to.
Why Rome wants the “Ukraine playbook”
Perhaps that is precisely what Rome needs: not military victories or battlefield credentials, but a fresh, modern approach. That, presumably, is where Italy is placing its hopes. Modern European militaries, including Italy’s, are weighed down by bureaucracy. Decisions on the procurement of new weapons systems and software take years. By the time they are finally approved, technology has already moved on, leaving armed forces to adopt systems that were obsolete before they ever entered service.
Fedorov may well be useful to Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto as a new battering ram against his own conservative military establishment. Rome wants to borrow Ukraine’s experience of rapidly digitalizing military logistics and integrating unmanned systems in real time.
To understand exactly which processes Fedorov may seek to adapt for the Italian military, one need only look inside his “digital briefcase.” It contains no secret missile technology – only commercial software and civilian IT solutions adapted to the needs of a defense ministry.
The Italian military is eager to introduce new digital battle-management systems that combine geospatial tools with hundreds of information sources and a distributed network of users, extending from the General Staff all the way to a frontline commander’s tablet in the trenches. Italy is also naturally interested in digitalizing weapons and military-equipment procurement – and even more so in applying artificial intelligence to military command and control.
It is difficult to judge the results, but on paper Fedorov’s résumé looks highly impressive: experience introducing cutting-edge digital solutions in Europe’s only army currently fighting a major war. That is certainly one way to present it – and why be shy when listing your strengths on a résumé?
What Rome is really buying
A modern army increasingly resembles an IT corporation. Rome does not need Fedorov’s advice on how to defend its coastline or plan an armored offensive. It needs his ability to turn the military into a functioning digital platform.
But let’s take an honest look at the former defense minister’s record. Yes, there was digitalization and digital transformation. It may still be too early to assess the final results, but there have been no major successes on the battlefield – and that, one would think, is what an army is ultimately for and how its performance should be measured.
Then there is the less flattering part of the picture: the image of a petulant child who could not find common ground with career officers and began playing political games in the middle of an ongoing war to increase his own value back home. That hardly seems consistent with the image of a gifted digital manager. Wars, after all, are not won through digitalization alone, but through the coordinated action of different branches and types of forces.
It will be fascinating to see what Fedorov ‘achieves’ in his new job – and whether the spirit of Silicon Valley can take root in the austere offices of the Italian Defense Ministry.
As for the man with the polished résumé and the reputation of a ‘digitalization expert’, a position like this – especially in Rome – offers a splendid opportunity to make a graceful exit from Kiev and trade Ukraine’s brutal political reality for the warm, easygoing comforts of Europe.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

For every 100 laundered, only 1 recovered by authorities: CJI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
20:57:29 UTC
05:57:29 KST

Economic crimes move faster than treaties; global cooperation key to recovery: CJI Surya Kant
NEW DELHI: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said for every Rs 100 laundered, authorities and law enforcement agencies recovered only Re 1, mainly because of the ingenuity of economic offenders, and lack of global cooperation on extraditing fugitives.Money laundered globally in a year was more than enough to buy every single person on earth a modest laptop, CJI said at the 43rd International Symposium on Economic Crime in Cambridge Saturday. "...For every hundred parts of that wealth, ninety-nine are simply referred to in speeches and reports, while only one part is ever actually put right."CJI Surya Kant quoted ancient Indian statesman Kautilya’s Arthashastra, which had recorded that it was impossible for an official to handle the king’s revenue and take nothing from it, and provided for an antidote through audits, cross-verification and confiscation of ill-gotten gain.Referring to India’s layered legislations against economic crimes and its balancing by judicial interventions, the CJI said though India had signed extradition and mutual legal assistance treaties with foreign jurisdictions, “the property we actually recover remains, frankly, underwhelming”.
The CJI said that illicit wealth and economic crimes moved faster than the pace of ratification of treaties and, hence, no jurisdiction, however well resourced or determined, could pursue them alone, despite the existence of provisions for non-conviction based forfeitures, unexplained wealth orders, beneficial ownership registers and financial intelligence sharing.
“None of these tools is missing from our shelves. What is missing, and what each jurisdiction owes the other, is the willingness to use them together rather than one at a time: a forfeiture order in one country acted upon promptly by a registry in another, an intelligence tip followed through to an actual freeze rather than left to gather dust,” he further added.India had initiated processes for extraditions of Vijay Mallya with the UK authorities in 2017 and Nirav Modi with the US in 2018.None of them has fructified in extradition of the two, accused of misappropriating huge sums and fleeing the country.

The Airlink Airlines – the company that organized the flyby – addressed what it called “concerns expressed in various social media and online forums,” insisting that the flights were absolutely safe and coordinated with the relevant authorities.
“The South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval, and support to ensure a safe flyby,” the company said in a statement on Sunday. According to Airlink, both jets were piloted by “highly experienced” crews, each comprised of three senior captains operating as a commander, co-pilot, and a safety officer. The flights were performed within the “approved and rehearsed safety altitude and speed limits for the flypast,” it added.

According to local media, the stadium flybys were part of a South African rugby tradition dating back to the 1995 Rugby World Cup final when a massive South African Airways Boeing 747 flew over Ellis Park Stadium in Johannesburg at low altitude.
Saturday’s feat came ahead of Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry match – part of a special quadrennial tour series between South Africa and New Zealand. South Africans won the game 33-26.

Diabetes impacts men, women differently: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
20:40:49 UTC
05:40:49 KST

Study finds type 2 diabetes complications differ by gender: men face higher heart and kidney risks, women more likely to develop mental health conditions.
NEW DELHI: For men, type 2 diabetes more often sets the stage for heart and kidney disease; for women, the greater threat appears to be mental health problems, a new study tracking nearly 29,000 patients has found.The study, published in PLOS Medicine, followed 28,720 people newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes between 2010 and 2020 using linked primary and secondary healthcare records in the UK. Researchers used a multi-state analysis to track the order and timing of hypertension, cardiovascular disease, end-stage renal disease and mental health conditions over a median follow-up of 6.8 years. Women were more likely than men to be diagnosed with a mental health condition.Women were more likely than men to be diagnosed with a mental health condition, including anxiety, depression or somatoform disorders, after developing diabetes. Such conditions were recorded in 8.1% of women compared with 5.3% of men.Men, meanwhile, were more likely to develop cardiovascular disease or end-stage renal disease, with 8.4% following this trajectory compared with 5.3% of women.
Mental health risks are higher for women with diabetes as compared to men
Senior endocrinologist Prof Ravinder Goswami of All India Institutes of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) said diabetes can affect men and women differently.
Men may develop diabetes at a younger age, while women with diabetes lose the natural protection against heart disease that is usually seen before menopause. The study also found that women with diabetes may have a higher risk of problems related to memory, thinking and mental health.However, he cautioned that these problems may not be caused by diabetes alone, as cognitive and neuropsychiatric problems are generally more common in women. He said doctors should, therefore, watch for these issues while managing diabetes.Hypertension was the most common complication after type-2 diabetes across all age groups and in both sexes. It affected 21.1% of men and 20.2% of women. Men also experienced most complications earlier than women, while women generally had a later onset of events.The study linked diabetes, mental health and mortality, finding that people who developed a mental health condition after diabetes died earlier. Among those with the same disease trajectory, men died on average nine years younger than women.Despite this, women had higher average healthcare utilisation and long-term prescribing than men. The researchers said the lower healthcare use among men in the high-risk mental health trajectory could point to gaps in engagement with healthcare services.
The findings point to the need for sex-specific diabetes care, including routine mental health screening, particularly for younger women, and earlier cardiovascular and kidney monitoring for men.The researchers further added that tracking the sequence and timing of complications could help identify patients at higher risk and enable earlier intervention. However, as an observational study, the findings cannot establish cause and effect, and differences in mental health diagnoses may partly reflect healthcare-seeking behaviour.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

‘Opening a new chapter’: Syria reopens embassy in Libya after talks

‘Opening a new chapter’: Syria reopens embassy in Libya after talks
Syrian foreign minister and Libyan PM agree to cooperation committee and reopening of diplomatic missions closed for 14 years.
Syria and Libya have agreed to reopen Syria’s embassy in Tripoli, which has been closed for 14 years, and reactivate a committee for coordinating bilateral ties during talks between Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah of Libya’s internationally recognised government and Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al-Shaibani.
Al-Shaibani arrived in Tripoli on Sunday to meet with Libyan officials, according to a statement from Libya’s Government of National Unity (GNU).
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Can international diplomacy find a way forward in Libya?
- list 2 of 3Rival Libya factions sign deal to hold national elections within two years
- list 3 of 3Libya factions draft initial election pact amid lingering mistrust
Libya has been split since 2014 between the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity, led by Dbeibah, and an eastern administration, led by Osama Hammad and backed by renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar. Representatives of Libya’s rival governments signed a deal on Sunday to hold national elections within two years.
Cooperation agreement
Damascus and Tripoli signed an agreement to reactivate the Libyan-Syrian Joint Higher Committee, a committee at the prime ministerial level tasked with coordinating political, economic and social ties between the two countries.
Dbeibah and al-Shaibani also agreed to open a Syrian consulate in Benghazi, raising the level of diplomatic representation between the two states.
The talks covered security cooperation and counterterrorism, according to the GNU statement. The two sides also discussed consular services and the status of prisoners, detainees and refugees from both countries.
Economically, they addressed unresolved financial dues between Libyan and Syrian institutions. The Syrian foreign minister also met with Libya’s oil and gas minister and the country’s investment authority chief to discuss energy and investment cooperation.
‘A new chapter’
The Syrian embassy in Libya has been closed since 2012 after Libya’s then-Transitional National Council recognised the Syrian opposition and diplomatic relations between the two countries were severed during then-Syrian President Bashar al-Assad’s rule.
Syrian opposition forces ousted al-Assad in December 2024, ending 61 years of Baath Party rule.
In August 2025, a Syrian delegation raised the post-Assad Syrian flag over the Tripoli embassy, signalling that its reopening was imminent.
Dbeibah called Sunday’s meeting the start of “a new chapter” in their relations, saying it should be “based on shared interests, practical cooperation and addressing outstanding issues”.

manifesta 16 and the past, present, and future of ruhr’s churches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
20:35:29 UTC
05:35:29 KST

Manifest 16, the ‘European Nomadic Biennial,’ found its home in Germany’s Ruhr area. More specifically, it activated twelve churches across the cities of Essen, Gelsenkirchen, Duisburg, and Bochum, transforming them into hybrid exhibition and community places that cheekily spoke to the title of its 30th edition: ‘This is not a church.’ Through contemporary art, walks through these cities, architectural interventions (and a bit of basketball), the event proposes new ways to inhabit the numerous churches in the region that have fallen out of use.
The Ruhr region has a complex history within the European framework because of its natural resources. It sits at the meeting of the Ruhr and the Rhine, making it logistically advantageous as an inland port. To get around from city to city, the Manifesta Guide recommends biking, as the Erzbahntrasse, a former freight line turned bike path, not only exemplifies the infrastructural evolution but is also lined with the foliage of the region and offers a glimpse at the Rhine-Herne Canal.
Each of the twelve churches that make up Manifesta’s program opens with a bit of history that explains how the structure came to be. Bochum’s Gethsemane-Kirche has written that the modest structure, whose entrance is reached only after passing through a small path lined by a dense garden, was designed by architect Otto Bartning for Protestants after World War II. The goal was not to have a grand structure, but a simple place for worship. Because of this, these churches were built close to their parish, earning them the title of ‘pantoffelkirchen,’ or slipper churches, as in the place is so close, you could reach it in your slippers.
Gethsemane-Kirche was shaped by Anda Rottenberg & Krzysztof Kosciuczuk, two of Manifesta 16’s eight ‘creative mediators,’ the term the institution uses to refer to their curator-like organizers who guide the formation of the event. This church was still in use as a place of worship, which was not a given for all of the event’s sites. With that in mind, they decided to create interventions in the space that reflected the active community around the church.
One was the installation of Marina Naprushkina’s inflatable bell-shaped bouncy house that sits in the front lawn of the space. The bell is the ‘advertising symbol of the Bochumer Verein company,’ which had produced rail wheels in the area, with the playful sculpture both inviting people to interact with the work while also opening a dialogue about labor in the region. Inside, Mehtap Baydu’s work, Anali Kazli – With Mothers with Daughters, is a performance-based work that works with eleven women from the city to cook meals for a large audience. In it, she reflects on the pattern within the Turkish language of naming food after women and body parts. Within the piece, she opens a community-oriented discussion on food and language.
North of Essen, there is St. Marien, which, in contrast to Gethsemane-Kirche, has fallen into a state of disrepair and is no longer an active church. The space is a towering brick building almost hiding behind a park. Pieces of the roof are missing, and parts of the stained-glass windows have broken off. Within, works by Alicja Kwade, SUPERFLEX, Jason Dodge, and others fill the unused space. One piece in particular is William Engelen’s Variation on Godspeed in 4/4 (2026), which consists of tubes hanging down into the space, recalling the church organ. Another interpretation of this instrument can also be found in Abbas Zahedi’s work, Ouranophobia 47051 (2026), located in Duisburg’s Kulturkirche Liebrauen.
Making your way to each church requires a grand tour through the Ruhr region. Traveling by bike reveals the dense foliage that seems to touch every corner. Going by public transport exposes the shifting face of western Germany. With every site, a new view of the region comes into view—one that has long been on the precipice of change, yet holds onto relics of the past. By bringing these religious spaces into view, Manifesta 16 reveals the history of this European region through art, participation, and community.
creative mediators: Anda Rottenberg, Krzysztof Kosciuczuk, Josep Bohigas, Gürsoy Doğtaş, René Block, Henry Meyric Hughes, Leonie Herweg, and Michael Kurtz
This article is part of designboom’s MODES OF HABITATION chapter, exploring how the spaces we inhabit can reshape the ways we live together. Discover more stories rethinking domesticity, shared living, and the many forms a home can take here.
from zucchini ballet flats to shoes covered in flowers and dandelion seed heads, the artist turns fleeting plant materials into playful studies of footwear.

Approximately 85 American citizens remain missing in Nepal and China's Tibet region following a massive glacial collapse that triggered catastrophic flash floods on Aug. 26, the US State Department said on Sunday.
"This morning, I can say we now have 85 Americans, approximately, that are unaccounted for," Spokesman Tommy Pigott told ABC News.

The overall death toll from the floods has climbed to more than 800, while nearly 3,300 people remain missing across the border region.

US forces strike Iranian launchers on Larak island in Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
20:27:09 UTC
05:27:09 KST

US forces strike Iranian launchers on Larak island in Strait of Hormuz
US forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz in the first military action in a month, a US official said Sunday. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said the attack on Larak island killed and wounded several Iranian fighters and civilians, and vowed to punish those responsible.
US forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz in the first military action in a month on Sunday, according to a US official, breaking a lull in fighting during an intermittent war that has lasted more than six months.
Forces with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait, according to the official who spoke on condition of anonymity, to detail sensitive military movements.
The US military last week completed clearing sea mines from the strait’s international shipping routes.
Semi-official news outlets in Iran reported sounds of explosions near Larak island on the strait. The IRCG in a statement carried by Iran's state broadcaster noted “the martyrdom and injury of several of our fighters and compatriots.”
The statement said the attack will “result in punishment of the aggressor.”
The fighting comes just days after the Trump administration said it would turn its focus to increasing economic pressure – rather than military action – to try to end its war with Iran. The shifting strategy centers on threats to punish any country or entity that continues to conduct business with Tehran.
The turn to using sanctions as the cudgel of choice comes as the administration weighs diminished munitions stockpiles after months of war, sparking concerns that the prolonged conflict could undermine US military readiness in other parts of the globe.
Read moreTrump says Strait of Hormuz demined, warns of ‘zero tolerance’ for new mines
As the conflict grinds on, Trump’s talk of finding a quick end to the war also appears to be fading. He stressed last week that he’s “not in a hurry” to get Iran back to the negotiating table, and he continues making the case that the Islamic Republic’s leadership is on the ropes.
Appointments to Iran’s senior security leadership in the past month, however, have signaled Tehran’s defiance after weathering decades of sanctions as well as a lack of tolerance for dissent at home.
Trump has consistently emphasised that the US and Israel campaign has been devastating for Iran’s navy and air force. Iranian officials have said the country has suffered $270 billion in direct and indirect damage. Israeli military strikes in the first weeks of the war wiped out much of the theocratic government’s leadership structure.
But Iran has found leverage through its own strikes in the critical Strait of Hormuz where relatively few vessels carrying oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) are risking passage. Iran still has enough drones and missiles to fire at vessels transiting the vital energy waterway, through which 20% of the world's oil normally flows, effectively controlling much of the traffic in the strait.
Tehran continues to assert that even after it works out a management plan for the strait with Oman, its neighbour on the other side of the waterway, the US can't use it until it fulfils its obligations under the memorandum of understanding (MOU) the countries signed in mid-June.
Trump has repeatedly declared that the “Strait of Hormuz is open,” saying 24 vessels passed through last week. But that’s a fraction of the roughly 130 vessels that transited daily before the war began.
Earlier on Sunday, a multinational coalition overseen by the US Navy said commercial traffic through the strait remained at “reduced levels.”
And a monitoring agency run by the British military said an unknown projectile struck a tanker ship on Saturday north of Khasab, Oman, in the strait. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organisation ((UKMTO) said no casualties or environmental impact had been reported, and cited unspecified military authorities. There was no immediate claim of responsibility.
The US military said that as of Sunday, it had redirected 83 commercial vessels and disabled three under its blockade of Iranian ports.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

Wildcard Preston gets first grand slam win outside Australia
Taylah Preston is the first Australian into the second round of the US Open, claiming a straight-sets win over American Alycia Parks.

Storm Hunter and Adam Walton also made early exits on day one at Flushing Meadows as Gibson was unable to disguise her anguish at an opportunity lost.
The 22-year-old rallied from a set and a service break down to look poised to claim her maiden grand slam victory outside Australia before Vekic steadied to post a 6-2, 4-6, 6-3 in two hours and 33 minutes.
The veteran Croat and 2024 Wimbledon semifinalist seemed to be unravelling after blowing a set and 4-1 lead, cursing herself and berating her box as Gibson roared back into the contest.
But Gibson was unable to wrestle back control after failing to convert any of four break-point chances in the second game of the deciding set.
She had Vekic down 0-40 serving at 4-2, only to miss five straight returns to ruefully let the Paris Olympics silver medallist off the hook.
"It's a hard one to swallow," Gibson said.
"Most of the time it's who makes the most unforced errors on the court who comes away with the loss, and today that was me, so it's just something to learn from."
But after starting the year well outside the world's top 100, Gibson has slashed her ranking in half after racking up some 30 match wins, including over former No.1 and dual Australian and US Open champion Naomi Osaka.
"Days like these are really tough. It's hard not to be disappointed. When it comes to the slams, every player wants to do well," said the world No.63.
"But if I'm looking at my entire year so far, I've been able to achieve some things that probably at the start of the year I probably wouldn't have thought I'd be able to do.
"So to still be in the position ranking that I currently have and moving forward to these next tournaments, I don't really have any points to defend, so it's kind of just no pressure and more opportunities."
Aussie qualifier Storm Hunter was defeated by 11th seed Marta Kostyuk in straight sets.
After stumbling at this year's Australian Open, Kostyuk has been in sublime form at the grand slams, making the semifinals of the French Open and Wimbledon to arrive at Flushing Meadows as a genuine contender in the women's draw.
The 11th seed got down to business quickly once the match began, and powered to a 4-1 lead before overcoming a wobble to close out the first set when Hunter produced a double fault on set point.
Kostyuk tightened her grip on the clash in the second set, breaking early and never allowing Hunter a route back as she wrapped up a 6-4, 6-1 victory in 67 minutes.
"I'm very happy to be back to this amazing place," Kostyuk said on court.
"It's not easy to play a qualifier; they've played a whole tournament [already]. I'm very happy with my performance today. I try to keep myself grounded. There's still a long way to go; I'm enjoying my tennis."
Walton also bowed out early, missing two set points in the third set of a tight 7-6 (7-2), 6-2, 7-5 loss to China's Yibing Wu.
World number seven and three-time US Open quarterfinalist Alex de Minaur opens his title quest on Tuesday against Italian qualifier Andrea Guerrieri.
ABC/Reuters/AAP

The U.S. has begun training Polish special forces in drone tactics based on Ukraine’s experience
Kyiv • UNN
American Green Berets are training Polish special forces in Germany to use drones based on Ukrainian experience. The program may be expanded to NATO.
American "Green Berets" in Germany are training Polish special forces in new drone tactics developed based on Ukraine's experience of confronting Russian forces. Poland has become the first U.S. NATO ally to join such training, Associated Press reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
The training is taking place at the Hohenfels training area in Germany. According to the scenario, the Polish special forces must infiltrate through simulated enemy lines, cross several kilometers of territory controlled by the adversary, and use drones against a key target.
We are using the lessons learned in Ukraine. All these consequences that, as we see, either Russia or Ukraine has had to overcome—we are doing everything possible to replicate them
The program was created just a few months ago. It was previously tested twice by U.S. special forces, and now, for the first time, troops from another NATO country have been involved in the training.
Training could be expanded to the entire Alliance
The U.S. military plans to conduct such training several times a year. One officer suggested that, over time, most or even all 32 NATO countries could become interested in participating in the program.
AP notes that the training demonstrates how the United States and its allies are adapting military training to modern methods of drone use, drawing on Ukraine's experience.

Four days of Russian attacks keep Kyiv under near-constant fire. Ukraine is struggling to defend its skies. Ukraine chooses three Western fighters to build its air force around. One of them can fly again from stretch of road in 15 to 20 minutes. The Air Force settled on them after weighing cost, logistics, and repair speed.

Ukraine struck Tu-95 at base Russia launches its cruise missiles on Ukraine's civilians. Satellite image shows third of right wing gone. SBU Alpha struck the strategic bomber at Engels-2.
Kyiv has been under attack for 2 days nonstop. Russia is targeting the capital's civilian supply chains. Russian jet-powered drones have repeatedly struck warehouses, businesses and logistics facilities around the capital, disrupting supplies while rescuers work under threat of further attacks.

Ukraine's intelligence: Russia is running its Nepal, Cuba, Kenya, and India recruitment scheme in Indonesia now. Ukraine's foreign intelligence says it holds documents on at least eight recruited Indonesian citizens.
Partisans say Russian recruiters in occupied Donetsk are taking drunk men from bars straight to enlistment offices. An ATESH agent inside the Dnepr grouping headquarters reports a new scheme.
Russians bought $300 million in body armor, thermal sights, and drone parts on Ozon marketplace Ukraine is bombing. Russians bought 157,700 body armour vests there.

After CIA head's visit to Moscow, Poland's PM warns Russia is preparing to escalate war. He puts critical window at seven or eight months. Poland's prime minister says there are signals of serious Russian preparation.

From the Gripen sale to coast guard boats: Sweden sends 10 vessels to Ukraine. Ukraine's emergency service will use the boats for waterborne rescue work, including clearing mines from river beds. Stockholm's contributions to the US-led PURL programme now total $552 million.

Russia has destroyed 90% of Ukraine's modern commercial storage capacity. Retail logistics are being reshaped. Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi says the country faces no threat of famine, but warns stores could see a narrower range of products.

Iran attacks US bases in Jordan after US strikes Larak Island
The exchange of attacks is the first flare-up in violence between the two sides since late July.
Iran says it launched missiles at two US bases in Jordan following a US attack on Larak Island in southern Iran earlier on Sunday.
In a statement reported by Iranian news agencies on Sunday, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said the combined missile and drone operation, which it called “Punishment of the Aggressor”, hit the King Hussein and Al Azraq bases in Jordan.

The exchange of attacks is the first flare-up in violence between the two sides since late July.
The IRGC said the strikes “destroyed the technical and repair infrastructure, as well as the enemy fighter deployment sites”, inflicting significant damage.
Jordan reported intercepting eight missiles soon after the IRGC announced the attack.
“Air defence systems intercepted eight missiles that breached the Kingdom’s airspace at dawn today, Monday,” the Jordanian military said in a statement.
No injuries were reported at either base.
In a further development on Monday, the IRGC said it shot down a US MQ-9 Reaper drone over the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran’s Fars and Mehr news agencies cited a statement from the IRGC that said that its air defences had intercepted “a long-range American MQ9 drone” over the Strait of Hormuz, which then fell into the Gulf.
In his first comments since the US attack on Iran’s Larak Island, President Masoud Pezeshkian said that Tehran was “not looking for war”, but would “never sit still in the face of any aggression” either.
Pezeshkian made the comments as he was leaving for Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, to attend the summit of the heads of state of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation countries.
Tehran has promised to retaliate for Sunday’s US attack on Larak Island.
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump posted an AI-generated video on his Truth Social platform on Monday, seemingly depicting the bombing of Iran’s Kharg Island.
The footage shows an oil storage tank and an oil tanker exploding, as watched from aircraft above.
“Kharg Island being blown to smithereens!!! President DJT,” the post reads.
There was no other evidence that the Iranian energy hub was under attack.
Before the war started, Kharg Island handled the majority of Iran’s oil exports, making it a vital economic node.
Trump has repeatedly threatened to seize or destroy the island since the start of the war.
The strikes risk renewing the military confrontation as Washington shifts from its bombing campaign to a financial pressure strategy on Tehran, and as the US-Israel war on Iran enters its seventh month.
On Monday, the US military denied that its Sunday attacks were an “act of aggression”.
US Central Command (Centcom) said on X that the US took “limited, precise action” to prevent Iranian forces from laying mines in the Strait of Hormuz and blamed Iran for the attacks.
Iran’s Fars news agency said that the attack by the “American-Zionist enemy” killed and injured soldiers, without providing a figure.
In recent weeks, Washington has been claiming control over the Strait of Hormuz, saying that millions of barrels of oil have passed through the waterway under US military protection despite Tehran’s blockade.
Still, attacks on ships in the strait have been reported almost daily, and Iran has maintained that the waterway is closed.
Sunday’s strikes show that the US is still willing to use military force despite the intensified sanctions to pressure Iran to make concessions over its nuclear programme and claims of control over Hormuz.
Iran has previously responded to similar US attacks by launching missiles and drones at military bases hosting US troops in neighbouring countries.
Last week, the administration of US President Donald Trump announced a push to isolate Iran financially by threatening secondary sanctions against countries and companies that do business with Tehran.
But Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth has warned that the US is prepared to use military force if necessary.
US officials have been touting what they describe as Tehran’s loss of control over the Strait of Hormuz, while arguing that Iran is on the verge of economic collapse due to sanctions and the US Navy’s blockade of its ports.
Tehran, however, has remained defiant, stressing that it is prepared for a long conflict.
On Saturday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed reports that the US is managing to get large amounts of oil through the strait.
“Our intelligence shows major efforts to game energy markets,” Araghchi wrote on X. “US Govt elements use gullible media to influence prices for personal gain and keep [Trump] mired in a losing war. Israel-aligned actors also promote war with rosy assessments. U.S. consumers feel the real bottom line.”
Despite the reports of the US ending – or at least easing – Iran’s control of the strategic waterway, oil prices have remained high amid supply uncertainty.
The average price of one gallon (3.8 litres) of petrol in the US is still more than $4, up from less than $3 when the US and Israel launched the war on Iran in late February.
The skyrocketing energy prices, which are driving up inflation in the US, could hurt Trump’s Republican Party’s chances of maintaining control of Congress in November’s midterm elections.

In Russia’s Kemerovo region, more than 1,700 miners at the Severny Kuzbass company reported nearly a year of unpaid wages. The debt to employees has exceeded 500 million rubles, The Moscow Times reports, according to UNN.
Details

We are not asking for charity; we are demanding what we earned through hard mining labor
In May 2026, Russia’s Investigative Committee reported that the company’s debt had exceeded 256 million rubles. According to the investigation, the company’s head, Stanislav Lupiy, directed funds intended for wages to the accounts of controlled companies and issued bonuses to the management.

Among the causes of the crisis, the Russian authorities cite sanctions, sales problems, and rising production costs and railway tariffs. Kuzbass accounts for about half of all coal production in Russia.

US military attacked IRGC rocket launchers in Iran, senior official confirms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
20:03:52 UTC
05:03:52 KST

A senior U.S. official said Sunday evening that the U.S. military struck two Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps rocket launchers on Larak Island. 
“The two launchers were preparing to fire missiles carrying naval mines toward the Strait of Hormuz,” the official told Reuters and other news outlets. “Our forces have completed clearing mines from international shipping lanes, are closely monitoring the area and are prepared to defend the free flow of commerce through the strait.”
Iran’s Fars news agency reported that an explosion was heard near Larak Island in the strait.
The Tasnim news agency reported that according to "Preliminary, unofficial reports" two people were killed and two others were injured in the American attack.  
Shortly after the attack, the Revolutionary Guards threatened that "the enemy's terrorist act of aggression on Larak Island will be met with a response, and the aggressor will be punished."
"The American-Zionist enemy, once again driven by desperation in solving its internal problems and reducing its credibility among regional countries, seeks to revive its nefarious role and justify public opinion. In a blatant act of aggression, it attacked Larak Island, resulting in the martyrdom and injury of several of our soldiers and fellow citizens," the IRGC also said in a statement.
The Washington Post reported Sunday that senior U.S. military commanders had warned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that large-scale operations against Iran could not be sustained over time, and that continuing to concentrate forces in the Middle East could impair the U.S. military’s ability to deal with threats elsewhere in the world, including defending the United States itself.
According to officials familiar with the classified assessment prepared for Hegseth, the warnings were delivered to the defense secretary by the heads of the Army, Navy and Air Force, as well as commanders of U.S. forces responsible for Europe, Asia and Latin America. They were included in the August 14 edition of the “Secretary of Defense Orders Book,” a classified document detailing the availability of U.S. ships, aircraft, troops and weapons systems around the world that the Pentagon uses in making force-deployment decisions.
The strike in the strait came after about six months of fighting with Iran, as U.S. President Donald Trump pressures Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and accept Washington’s terms for ending the conflict. Trump continues to make clear that all options remain on the table, including renewed strikes, and U.S. Central Command, or CENTCOM, has for months kept more than 50,000 troops on alert in case the president orders further military action.
According to the Post, some of the forces deployed to the Middle East have already been ordered to remain in the region through September, while others are expected to stay into 2027. The Air Force is also preparing for a prolonged presence: According to two officials who saw the document, many of the units sent to the Middle East for bombing missions and round-the-clock operations are expected to remain in the region into 2027.
The possibility that the deployments could be extended again prompted several senior commanders to voice explicit objections. The commanders of U.S. European Command, Indo-Pacific Command and Southern Command, along with the Navy’s top officer, submitted what the Pentagon calls a “non-concur” — meaning they oppose the defense secretary’s decision to extend the allocation of their forces to the campaign, though they would carry out the order if it remains in effect.

What Is Trump’s U.S. Space Academy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
20:00:47 UTC
05:00:47 KST

President Donald Trump last week signed an executive order creating a commission to develop plans for the United States Space Academy, which is intended to “educate and develop the next generation of leaders across the space domain.”
The initiative was first announced when Trump visited the Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas, on Aug. 28 to present the crew of Artemis II with the Congressional Space Medal of Honor. The crew was recognized for their 10-day lunar flyby in April, which took them farther from Earth than any human had ever traveled.
“Given the rapid growth of the Space Force and the commercial space industry and the expansion of our ambitions to the moon and far beyond the moon,” Trump said while giving remarks at the ceremony, “it’s clear we will need to educate and train an entire generation of skilled service members, engineers, and civil operators.”
The proposed academy is envisioned as serving the military, civil government, and broader space industry. However, the exact admissions requirements for Space Academy—which will help characterize who it serves and how—are yet to be determined. Future Space Force officers currently attend the U.S. Air Force Academy.
“The Nation must prepare the next generation of astronauts, scientists, engineers, operators, entrepreneurs, civil servants, and warfighters and ensure that they are capable of advancing American interests in space,” the executive order said. “Achieving this goal requires us to recruit, train, and retain America’s best and brightest from across the Nation.”
At the ceremony, Trump also acknowledged the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, named for one of the forebears of modern space science, which was launched Sunday aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy. With surveying capabilities over 1,000 times faster than its predecessor, the Hubble Space Telescope, Roman seeks to explore dark matter, uncharted corners of the cosmos, and questions about the expansion of the universe.
What do we know so far about the Space Academy?
The first step in establishing the new academy is forming a Presidential Commission to develop recommendations for it. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman will chair the new commission, according to the executive order, and it will also include War Secretary Pete Hegseth and Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink, or their designees, among other federal representatives.
The commission has 120 days from Aug. 28 to submit its report to the President. It must include a governance framework, an academic and leadership curriculum, prerequisites for students, a service obligation for graduates, and a plan of implementation, legislative and otherwise, for all of the included components to take effect.
The White House also released a fact sheet, which described the proposed Space Academy as a “NASA-led federal academy dedicated to combining rigorous technical education with leadership development, discipline, and a durable commitment to public service.”
The fact sheet organized the administration’s case for the academy under three headings.
“Building the Next Generation of American Space Leaders” covered the convening of the commission and how the commission’s subsequent recommendations will be implemented.
“Advancing American Space Superiority” established that intensifying competition in space requires the United States to encourage more students to pursue cutting-edge technical fields.
Finally, “Building American Strength and Driving Achievement” explained Trump’s commitment to the space industry, from signing the legislation that formed the Space Force in 2019 to this month’s National Security Presidential Memorandum, which calls for U.S. ranges to support “more than 1,000 launches and reentries every year” by 2030.
“Access to, from, and within space is a vital national and economic security interest,” the Aug. 20 memorandum stated.
The fact sheet also linked the Space Force to the military’s preparation for future warfare, saying: “The Space Force is critical to preparing the Department of War for evolving warfighting conditions and expanding our capabilities.”
Where will the Space Academy be located?
The future location of the Space Academy has not yet been determined. Trump said that the White House would be accepting proposals. At the Congressional Space Medal of Honor ceremony, he said, “I’m going to be choosing a location very shortly.”
Joking that Sen. Ted Cruz was already interested in hosting the new academy in Texas, Trump continued: “Everybody wants it because it’s the hot thing. Space is the hot thing.”
Trump compared his ambitions for the academy to other prestigious military education institutions.
“So you think of West Point and you think of Annapolis and you think of the Air Force Academy and you think of the Coast Guard Academy. It’s great. They’re all great,” he said. “But we’re going to have now a Space Force [academy].”
Those are based in New York, Maryland, Colorado, and Connecticut, respectively.
“But I said this has to be comparable to [those schools],” he explained. “You know, we don’t want to do it in any other way, and it’s going to be, even architecturally, it’s got to be beautiful. It’s got to be the top. It’s going to be as good as it can get.”

How Palestine is becoming a fault line in French elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
19:56:43 UTC
04:56:43 KST

Breadcrumb
How Palestine is becoming a fault line in France’s 2027 presidential race
France is preparing for its presidential election in eight months, with analysts telling The New Arab that Palestine has become an increasingly important domestic litmus test in the battle for political power.
With President Emmanuel Macron constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive term, the 2027 race is more open than it has been in years.
From left-wing candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon, whose pro-Palestine rhetoric has helped bolster his support, to National Rally (RN) figures seeking closer ties with Israel, analysts said Palestine could emerge as not only a major foreign policy issue but also a defining electoral fault line during the campaign.
The Palestine question has gained greater prominence in French politics following Paris's public response to Israel's genocidal war on Gaza and developments in the occupied West Bank, with Macron's government adopting a more critical stance towards Israeli actions while, at the same time, maintaining diplomatic ties with the country.
This has included France's landmark recognition of Palestine in September 2025 and public condemnation of Israeli officials including far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
"Unlike in 2022, Israel-Palestine can no longer be kept at the margins of French presidential debate. It has repeatedly ranked among French voters' top concerns since October 2023, spiking again with each escalation (Gaza, Lebanon, Iran)," Julia Amoura, a researcher at the French Institute of International Relations (IFRI), told The New Arab.
She argued that the decision to recognise an independent Palestinian state "has turned the issue into a marker of presidential leadership rather than a peripheral foreign-policy question," and predicted that it was likely to become an even bigger foreign-policy dividing line as the campaign advances.
"France's recognition of Palestine has already forced every major candidate to state a clearer position, and the situation on the ground remains volatile: the October 2025 Gaza ceasefire is fragile, with continuing strikes, a US-brokered disarmament plan rejected by Netanyahu, and UN warnings of a possible return to full-scale hostilities," Amoura said. "Any renewed escalation before April 2027 would likely reopen the debate at moments candidates can't control."
Melenchon's polling position
This comes as Mélenchon, leader of La France Insoumise (LFI), has emerged as a serious contender for the second round of the presidential election in several polling scenarios.
He could face the far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen, who is polling at historically high levels and is projected to lead the first round in several potential candidate line-ups next spring.
A recent Harris Interactive–Toluna poll, reported by Politico, put Mélenchon on 16 percent in one scenario, ahead of former prime minister Édouard Philippe on 14 percent and former prime minister Gabriel Attal on 8 percent. Le Pen was well ahead on 35 percent. In scenarios without Attal, Mélenchon and Philippe were tied on 17 percent, underlining that the contest for second place remains open.
Analysts have linked part of Mélenchon’s appeal to his outspoken pro-Palestine stance and his effort to mobilise voters around a vision of a “New France”, centred on younger and more diverse voters who may previously have felt alienated from electoral politics.
LFI has also recorded local breakthroughs, including victories in Saint-Denis, north of Paris, and Roubaix in northern France during the 2026 municipal elections.
"Gaza resonates strongly with younger and urban minority voters, which is why LFI centred its 2024 European campaign on it and why RN has worked to reassure French Jewish voters," Amoura told The New Arab.
"Both communities have also been directly affected by a sharp rise in religiously motivated hate. In 2025, France recorded 1,320 antisemitic acts — a 16 percent year-on-year fall, but still a historically high level — while anti-Muslim acts rose 88 percent to 326 incidents."
She added: “For many French voters, this is not an abstract foreign-policy debate but one intertwined with domestic security and communal anxiety, a combination likely to keep the issue emotionally charged throughout the campaign.”
RN's pro-Israel shift
The issue’s growing prominence is also evident in the RN’s attempt to distance itself from its historic associations with racism and antisemitism while adopting a more openly pro-Israel position.
The party’s promotion of the 28-year-old Jordan Bardella has coincided with a broader rapprochement between Israel and parts of the European far right.
French political analyst François Burgat told The New Arab that growing pro-Israel sentiment in sections of the French far right rests partly on hostility towards Palestinians, whom he said Le Pen views as among the "decolonised" peoples. He linked this to the RN’s longstanding support for restrictive immigration policies and its portrayal of France as threatened by "Islamisation".
"The sympathy the State of Israel garners in France is not directed at the Jewish people as such, but rather at an anti-Muslim people — one with whom those nostalgic for the colonial era easily identify, and one that does not shy away from the extreme violence it is currently deploying in Gaza," he said.
“The question of Palestine will therefore be central to the presidential debate for several reasons, but above all because support for Israel serves as a way to stigmatise France’s Muslim community — a group whose existence and growing assertiveness have come to dominate public discourse.”

'Almost dystopian': Should AI be used to write work emails?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
19:54:38 UTC
04:54:38 KST

Should artificial intelligence be used to write work emails? Australia's workplace tribunal ruled against
The first email was sent in 1971 as an experiment to see if two computers could exchange messages.
Since then, the communication tool has become commonplace in businesses, but with the rise of artificial intelligence (AI), those exchanges have become even less human.
Griffith University's Mai Nguyen said it was now the norm for workers to use AI to sound more professional and use the right grammar.
But the business school senior lecturer warned that using the wrong "prompt" in an AI generator could exaggerate facts and make the text's tone inappropriate.
'Couched in accusatory language'
The widespread use of AI had recently prompted Australia's workplace tribunal to order an employee and their workplace to cease using the technology in all future correspondence.
The order was handed down in a bullying complaint before the Fair Work Commission in late July.
An employee working as a caretaker for a Queensland body corporate submitted to the tribunal that the workplace repeatedly refused to clarify their duties, provided confusing and shifting directions, and made several other allegations.
Commissioner Sarah McKinnon ruled that the employee had been bullied.
But she noted emails from the employee and the workplace and found the caretaker's correspondence was "unhelpful" and appeared to have been prepared with the use of an AI tool.
Commissioner McKinnon described the communication as "lengthy, wide-ranging, replete with generalisations, repetitive, and often couched in accusatory language".
She said it was "unsurprising" that the workplace "eventually chose not to engage" with the employee.
"Unfortunately, its choice to 'disengage and dig in', my description, had the result that it did not engage in any meaningful way with many of the concerns [the employee] was raising," Commissioner McKinnon said.
"This was to the detriment of all parties."
To prevent further bullying of the employee, Commissioner McKinnon ordered all future communication between the parties be "accurate and respectful".
"There is to be no use of artificial intelligence tools in the preparation of correspondence between the parties," she said.
"Parties should endeavour to keep their communications brief and to the point."
The order was to take effect immediately.
Digital communication Professor Daniel Angus said it was an interesting case.
The Queensland University of Technology professor said there was a "natural appeal" to want to use the technology to make text more "forceful or persuasive".
He said someone could use it to overwhelm "an opponent within a debate in this kind of adversarial environment".
Should you disclose an email has been written with AI?
Professor Angus said we need to normalise disclosing the use of AI "a lot more" but conceded it was "a really tricky topic".
"What we're seeing is that there are some folks who are vehemently opposed to the use of AI," he said.
"You can understand why people don't want to be forthcoming about their use of AI."
Law research fellow Guzyal Hill, from the University of Melbourne, said very few organisations had AI policies but said there was a growing push for it.
"It's difficult to avoid AI in terms of large language models in the modern society," she said.
"Australia does not have an AI Act, so each organisation has to develop its own AI Strategy/AI Policy."
The AI Governance Chair at HWLE Lawyers said there wasn't much "harm" in using AI for emails as long as it was used skilfully, in line with legislation and internal work policies.
But she said it should be "discouraged" if private and confidential information was being put into the AI generator.
"The caution is always about the way it's used," Dr Hill said.
Can you tell if AI wrote an email?
Professor Angus said there were "telltale signs" when AI has written texts, but that humans were "notoriously" bad at picking it up.
"I often think about the maligned em-dash (—), which is a real victim of the AI moment," he said.
Professor Angus said the tone of voice was another revealing sign of the AI.
"You could read something and think, 'Well this doesn't sound like them,'" he said.
Professor Angus warned about the increasing outsourcing of emails and other forms of communication to AI agents.
He said that would put workplaces in a "really weird and almost dystopian position" where it is just "a bunch of AI agents talking to each other" while the workers are "seemingly unaware of what they're talking about".
Dr Nguyen reads up to 30 emails each day, and she suspects about 80 per cent of them are AI-generated.
"Especially the long emails, I can predict that [they] come from some sort of AI," she said.
If using the technology for emails, Dr Nguyen advised double-checking that the text is clear, precise, and what you intended to send.
"At the end of the day, the email comes from the name of the sender,"

Fact check: Germany's Merz misstates record in ARD interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
19:53:00 UTC
04:53:00 KST

Fact check: Germany's Merz misstates record in ARD interview
August 30, 2026
As part of an annual tradition, Chancellor Friedrich Merz sat down with public broadcaster ARD on Sunday evening for a wide-ranging summer interview. Amid drooping poll numbers, Merz tried to use the interview to tout his government's work on economic, migration and energy policy.
At the same time, Merz made a number of misleading claims, often overstating his administration's work and misrepresenting climate science.
DW Fact check, in collaboration with colleagues across the ARD fact-checking network, reviewed Merz's interview live.
Did Merz cut asylum numbers by 60%?
Claim: "One of the main issues in the last federal election campaign was the migration crisis, and together with the federal government, we've been able to reduce the numbers by over 60% in just over a year."
Verdict: Misleading
This is misleading for several reasons — it is both questionable what exactly Merz meant by migration, and also not clear to which period he is referring.
The number of asylum-seekers in Germany has fallen significantly, but not to the extent Merz said. According to the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees (BAMF), a total of 56,547 asylum applications were filed in the first half of 2026, including 39,646 first-time applications. Compared with the same period last year, the number of first-time applications fell by 35.4% — significantly less than the figure cited by Merz. Comparing the number of initial asylum applications for the second half of 2025 and the first half of 2026 with the same period of the previous year, the number of initial asylum applications fell from 169,671 to 91,546 – a decrease of 46 percent.
Comparing individual months reveals significant fluctuations: In July 2026, the number of initial asylum applications, at 4,311, was even around 48 percent lower than in the same month of the previous year. A decline of almost 60 percent was recorded only once, inAugust 2025 compared to August 2024, when looking at individual months since Merz took office .
In addition, the downward trend began even before the Merz government took office in May 2025. After the fall of Syrian ruler Bashar Assad in December 2024, the number of asylum-seekers in Germany declined. At the European level, the number of asylum applications also fell in the first half of 2025.
Official statistics also show a decline in general migration. According to the Federal Statistical Office, around 235,000 more people immigrated to Germany in 2025 than emigrated. This means that net immigration was 45% below the previous year's figure of 430,000 people. But that's mostly due to the number of arrivals falling, while the number of departures remained almost stable.
Germany's debt, in context
Claim: "We are still one of the least indebted countries in Europe. We are still a country that has by far the best credit rating of any European nation. No one doubts the debt sustainability of our country or our economy; we are operating within reasonable limits here."
Verdict: Misleading
There are three important ways to measure how much debt EU countries hold: debt-to-GDP ratio, deficit spending and credit rating.
On the first — debt-to-GDP ratio, or how a country's total debt compares to its annual economic output — Germany receives a failing grade. The eurozone requires countries to keep this ratio below 60%. Germany and 11 other countries are above that limit, versus 15 countries which are in compliance, putting Germany smack in the middle of the eurozone.
On the second — government deficits, or a country's net borrowing — Germany is just scraping by. The eurozone asks its members to keep this figure below 3%. Germany's net borrowing is at 2.7%, joining 16 other countries that are also below the limit. Of the 17 countries that meet that requirement, Germany comes the second closest to hitting the 3% limit.
As for credit rating — a grade from investors on how likely a country is to repay its debts — Germany does indeed earn the highest marks possible. But it shares that grade with several other countries. There are only 11 countries in the world with an AAA rating from S&P: Germany joins Denmark, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and Switzerland in earning the grade.
In 2009, Germany amended its constitution by adding a so-called "debt brake," mandating the government to keep deficits to 0.35% of GDP. In 2020, that restriction was suspended to deal with the COVID pandemic and then again in 2022 and 2025 to allow for an increase in defense spending.
Real CO2 balance of electric cars
Claim: "At the European level, the issue with internal combustion engines has nothing to do with CO2 emissions. We want climate-friendly and climate-neutral cars, but we don't want to dictate the technology — it's not up to politicians to decide that. What matters is how much CO2 such a car emits, and the CO2 balance of electric mobility isn't as rosy as it's often portrayed."
Verdict: Misleading
Battery electric vehicles produce, on average, 73% less CO2 emissions than internal combustion engine vehicles, according to the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT), a US-based nonprofit think tank.
Battery electric vehicles do generate about 40% higher production emissions, mostly because of the processes involved in manufacturing the battery, though these are usually offset after about one or two years of driving.
Merz was likely referring to a new paper from researchers at the Technical University of Munich, which right-wing media seized on this week. The paper, which took an average of 19 studies, claimed that battery electric vehicles only reduce CO2 emissions by 41%, compared to traditional cars.
But there's a key issue with the TUM paper: including all those studies means older analyses with outdated electricity mixes are given equal weight. The ICCT analysis, on the other hand, uses a more current estimate.
Either way, there's an overwhelming scientific consensus that electric vehicles are better for the environment than traditional cars.

Fedorov offers drone technology to US in exchange for Patriots, seeks funding for defense tech fund
Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov is seeking U.S. investment for a new defense technology fund and offering to help Washington develop drone capabilities in exchange for Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine, he told the Financial Times in an interview published Aug. 30.
The proposal comes as Fedorov has begun an international trip that has included Italy and the United States after being dismissed by President Volodymyr Zelensky as defense minister.
Fedorov told the FT in Washington that he is seeking backing from venture capitalists, private investors, and U.S. technology companies for a fund that would invest in Ukrainian defense startups and create new companies focused on battlefield technologies.
"This is not exactly a classic venture fund," Fedorov said in an interview. "We're writing a new history of the war."
Fedorov said the fund would initially focus on battlefield robotics, high-speed interceptor drones capable of countering Russia's newer jet-powered attack drones, and low-cost missiles equipped with artificial intelligence.
He also proposed a direct exchange with the United States, saying he would be willing to help Washington "build an army of drones" in return for Patriot interceptors to help Ukraine withstand Russian attacks this winter.
"I'm ready to make that trade," Fedorov told the FT.
Ukraine has faced a critical shortage of Patriot interceptors as Russia has intensified missile and drone attacks against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. The U.S.-made systems are among the few weapons capable of intercepting Russia's ballistic missiles.
Fedorov said Ukraine had already tested high-speed drones designed to bring down Russia's jet-powered attack drones and argued that they could be produced at scale with additional investment.
"We need more jet drones, we need cheap missiles, we need missiles with artificial intelligence," he said. "You can't conduct any kind of dialogue with Putin any other way. He understands only force."
Fedorov served as defense minister from January to July before Zelensky dismissed him in a Cabinet reshuffle. His firing triggered weeks of protests across Ukraine and elevated Fedorov's profile as a potential political rival to Zelensky.
After Zelensky declined to reinstate him as defense minister earlier this month, Fedorov called for wartime elections, a move that divided public opinion.
In an interview with the FT, Fedorov defended his call for elections, saying it was not aimed at replacing Zelensky but at updating the country's governing system.
"This is not against Zelensky, it's not against some specific person," Fedorov said. "It's about the fact that we need to … update the state's operating system."
Fedorov's trip to the U.S. follows a visit to Italy, where he agreed to serve as an unpaid adviser to Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto on modern warfare technologies, his press service told the Kyiv Independent on Aug. 28.
Fedorov's press service said his primary focus would remain on projects in Ukraine and efforts to attract international resources for the country's defense technology sector. During his meeting with Crosetto, the two discussed drones, autonomous systems, air defense, and the development of Ukraine's defense technology ecosystem.
The FT reported that Fedorov was also considering similar advisory roles with other partner countries, potentially including France and the United States. He declined to say whether he planned to meet with officials from the Trump administration during his Washington visit.
Fedorov also said he remained in close contact with U.S. billionaire and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, but declined to comment on whether he planned to meet him in the U.S. Ukraine has relied heavily on Musk's Starlink satellite communications system throughout the war.
Previously, Zelensky awarded Musk Ukraine's Order of Liberty on Aug. 26, as Kyiv seeks his approval to use Starlink on drones operating inside Russia.

Ukraine is testing four new drone interceptors as Russia floods its skies with faster Gerans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

19:49:08 UTC
04:49:08 KST

Ukraine has four potential interceptor systems that could shoot down Russia’s increasingly common jet-powered Geran attack drones, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said on 30 August, according to Suspilne.
Russia has sharply increased its use of the faster drones against Ukrainian cities, causing major damage to civilian infrastructure and many civilian casualties. The attacks are putting near-unprecedented strain on Ukraine’s air defenses.
All four interceptor systems have undergone field testing, Khmara said. Ukraine now aims to bring them to the required level as quickly as possible and scale production to thousands of units.
“The search for countermeasures against jet-powered drones continues,” Khmara told journalists, according to Suspilne. “There are already four potential interceptors that can shoot down jet-powered ‘Shaheds.’ Field tests have already been conducted on them.”
Russia is rapidly expanding Geran attacks
Russia's Gerans are jet-powered adaptations of the Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones that Russia has produced domestically throughout the full-scale war. The faster Geran variants give Ukrainian air defenses less time to detect and engage them.
Ukrainian defense technology adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said Russia used more than 2,500 jet-powered Gerans against Ukraine in August, up from about 1,500 in July.
He also said the drones are being launched against Ukraine almost directly from Russian factories, highlighting the rapid expansion of their production and use.
Zelenskyy calls for faster production
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has made countering the Gerans a priority as Russia sustains repeated attacks on Ukrainian cities.
At a 28 August meeting of Ukraine’s military leadership, Zelenskyy said the country needed to maximize domestic weapons production, with the immediate focus on defending against jet-powered Gerans and increasing Ukraine’s own long-range strikes against Russia.
“[The] main thing is our defense against jet-powered ‘Shaheds,’” Zelenskyy said in his evening address.
He said Russia had adopted a tactic of keeping Kyiv and other cities under repeated air raid alerts, with Gerans reaching the capital as well as cities including Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia.
Four days of Russian attacks keep Kyiv under near-constant fire. Ukraine is struggling to defend its skies
“All our means of countering [them] are already being used,” Zelenskyy said, adding that Ukraine needs a significant acceleration in production of interceptors specifically designed for the jet-powered drones.
Khmara said the four potential interceptors are now at the field-testing stage, with the next step being to bring them into production at a scale of thousands of units.
For Ukraine, that scale is critical. The country must defend a large territory against increasingly large Russian drone barrages while also preserving limited air-defense resources for ballistic and other missiles that require more advanced interceptors.

NHAI has made Automated and Intelligent Machine-Aided Construction compulsory for highway projects longer than 20 km (AI generated image)
NEW DELHI: National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) has made Automated and Intelligent Machine-Aided Construction (AI-MC) compulsory for all highway projects longer than 20 km in length and costing over Rs 500 crore, in what’s a move aimed at addressing quality issues, which have become a major concern for govt.As per an NHAI circular issued on Friday, contractors will have to use the AI-MC system while building the road from the ground up and continuously across the entire spatial footprint of the project. The technology will be used for every major layer of highway, including embankment (raised earth foundation), subgrade (compacted soil base) and Granular Sub-Base (GSB) — the first layer of crushed stone, sand and gravel laid over the compacted soil before the road surface is built.The move is aimed at improving construction quality and ensuring roads are built with greater accuracy and uniformity. AI-MC is a construction technology with on-board computers and sensors on heavy machinery such as graders, pavers, compactors and dozers. Deployment of AI-MC aims to improve the quality, durability and transparency of road construction by replacing manual monitoring with technology-driven, real-time execution and quality control.
TOI has learnt that though AI-MC was first deployed during construction of Lucknow-Kanpur Expressway, it was not used on the entire stretch and at all grades.Officials said the move is designed to minimise human errors, ensure uniform construction standards and generate digital records of every stage of construction, from earthwork to pavement laying. “The new norms make it mandatory to share real-time data with NHAI officials.
This is good for contractors and for us as well. Once the contractor gets real-time data, there will be hardly any scope for sub-contractors to cut corners,” said an official.Some of the industry players in AI-MC segment said that contractors are reluctant to share real-time data with NHAI and other highway construction agencies as this makes them accountable. “Unless NHAI and other agencies get the data in real time, the impact of using the technology will be negligible. It must not be used in a piecemeal way if govt is serious about putting things in order,” said one of them.

Syria reopens embassy in Libya after 14 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
19:44:21 UTC
04:44:21 KST

Omer Asur Cuhadar and Rania Abushamala
30 August 2026•Update: 30 August 2026
Syria reopened its embassy in the Libyan capital Tripoli on Sunday after a closure lasting more than 14 years, according to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA).
Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani officially inaugurated the embassy during a ceremony attended by Arab and foreign diplomats and officials.
The agency said the move is part of a series of successive measures by the Syrian state to reorganize and reactivate its diplomatic missions abroad and attend to the interests of its citizens overseas.
It said the Syrian community in Libya is estimated at around 200,000 people, spread across the country but with significant presence in Tripoli and Benghazi.
Shaibani said the reopening of the embassy reflected the importance and standing of Syrian-Libyan relations, and paved the way for regularizing the status of Syrians in Libya.
Taher Al-Baour, who is responsible for managing Libya’s Foreign Ministry and international cooperation, said reopening the mission was a “positive step” toward returning relations to their normal course and developing them further.
Shaibani also met Libyan Prime Minister Abd al-Hamid Dbeibeh to discuss ways to develop bilateral relations, according to a statement from the media office of Libya’s Government of National Unity.
In August 2025, a Syrian technical and diplomatic delegation to Libya announced that the country’s flag had been raised over the Syrian Embassy building in Tripoli in preparation for its reopening.
The embassy closed in 2012, and relations remained severed during the rule of Bashar al-Assad.
On Dec. 8, 2024, Syrian factions took control of Damascus after capturing other cities, ending 61 years of Baath Party rule and 53 years of rule by the Assad family.

Randy Feenstra, R-Iowa.
"How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given Public Airwaves?" Trump said in a Truth Social post. "Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment."

"THE FAKE POLLS USED BY OUR CROOKED MEDIA ARE OUT OF CONTROL, AND SOMETHING MUST BE DONE ABOUT IT. FCC TO THE RESCUE!" the president said.
The president stormed out of an interview with Welker earlier this year after being pressed on his controversial "weaponization" fund and on evidence of his persistent claims of election fraud.
