18:52:39 UTC
03:52:39 KST

Inside the gift card tampering scam spreading nationally
An ABC investigation has discovered gift cards that have been tampered with are being sold by Australia's biggest supermarkets, with charges even being laid over the issue.
It is leaving shoppers confused and stressed, and raising questions about whether this is linked to a multi-billion-dollar criminal scam.
The packaging felt "kind of funny" in Lavkesh Arora's fingers.
The Melbourne tech worker had gone into Coles that day eager to buy Apple gift cards, lured by a supermarket promotion that gives people extra FlyBuys points when they purchase them.
"I wanted to buy an Apple laptop," he explains.
"Cost-of-living pressure, there was a good promotion on.
"I thought the packaging is good enough, and I shouldn't have to worry."
Once home, Lavkesh tore open the perforated cardboard packaging on his five Apple gift cards, which were worth a total of $2,000.
With the plastic cards inside revealed, he saw one worth $200 and another valued at $500, both had missing digits and redemption codes.
"They were completely scratched out," he says.
Without these crucial codes, Lavkesh could not proceed onto Apple's website and redeem his gift cards.
That knowledge sent him into a panic, wondering if he had been scammed and just thrown $700 down the drain.
"I was anxious and stressed," he says.
"I have my ears and eyes open for scams, so I was surprised."
Lavkesh's experience is not isolated.
Four days after he had bought those Apple cards at a Coles in Melbourne's eastern suburbs, a woman had the same experience at a Coles about 40 kilometres away.
Georgia Perry's story of unknowingly buying not one but four Apple gift cards worth $2,000 with "weird scratching" went viral online.
"They're all f****** fraudulent," she said in an incredulous social media video.
Loading...
Georgia told her story to ABC News at the time this happened to her in May, and it is after this that people contacted the broadcaster with similar claims.
Reports came in from around the country, with the ABC inspecting customers' receipts, gift card photos, and correspondence with companies like Coles, Apple and Australia's gift card distributors.
One person even sent in a video of themselves opening suspicious packaging to reveal a card that had been tampered with.
The earliest reports of a suspect gift card date back to 2024.
In 2024, both a Coles customer in Perth and a Woolworths shopper in Sydney report having a suspect card.
There are more reports during 2025 from puzzled gift card shoppers at Australia's two biggest supermarkets.
And more again this year, with people buying gift cards they couldn't redeem in regional Queensland and Victoria.
Zooming into Melbourne this year, there was a spate of reports to ABC News of strange cards from shoppers in May and June.
This includes those "scratched" Apple cards purchased on opposite sides of the city at Coles supermarkets by Georgia Perry and Lavkesh Arora.
And on the very same day as Georgia Perry, a shopper at Coles's main rival Woolworths also got a suspicious $100 Apple card in the city's eastern suburbs.
"I got home, opened the card and the number was scratched off underneath the opening," Damian Toohey tells ABC News.
"I was really frustrated."
Customers start to unpack the scam
Many people who reported gift card issues to the ABC also experienced frustrating communications with companies involved, with emails raising more questions than answers.
Take Sarah Le Page, who was given a $200 Apple gift card by her husband in September 2025.
The Melbourne-based teacher opened it a few days later and discovered the same "missing digits" on the plastic card as Lavkesh Arora and Georgia Perry.
She went to both Apple and Coles, and ended up in a frustrating back-and-forth about getting a refund.
"This is awful. It was a birthday present. I am not happy," she wrote to an Apple chat representative.
After they submitted extra card data, this chat with Apple led to another curious discovery.
"The gift card is already redeemed," Apple wrote.
So what is happening?
Of the 19 reports of strange gift cards the ABC documented, many were on Apple cards that can be redeemed for the tech giant's electronics.
In an indication of a cat-and-mouse game happening behind the scenes, Apple changed its gift card packaging in Australia in early 2025.
The updated rectangular housing has perforation around the edges that will show signs of tearing.
"Do not sell or buy if package has been tampered with or opened," the new era packaging says in red writing.
So is it possible to get past the safeguards of one of the world's biggest companies? What about credit card companies selling gift cards too?
We asked Adam Parks, who used to be the Australian representative for the US Department of Homeland Security's investigative unit.
Today, he is back in the United States and heads up a Homeland Security taskforce specifically dedicated to investigating gift card fraud.
Project Red Hook was set up in 2024 because there were such widespread reports of tampering.
"All of America's top 20 retailers were being affected," Adam tells ABC News.
In the US, Project Red Hook has found the tampering is happening through a network of people with different roles.
"The only thing that really makes it profitable is to be able to do it at scale," Adam explains.
Adam says the most common method involves people physically going into stores and taking stacks of gift cards.
In the industry, it is dubbed "card draining".
After taking gift cards off shelves, people carefully open the packaging, such as with a razor blade or even by using hair dryers to unstick glue.
The information on the cards that is needed to eventually use the funds is then recorded.
Those details can sometimes be "scratched" off.
The cards are then packaged back up.
"After [taking] card 100, you're probably getting pretty good at taking those apart and putting them back together again," Adam Parks says.
The cards are then returned to the shop floor, waiting for unsuspecting shoppers to buy them.
They are only "activated" for redemption when they are actually paid for.
Adam says there is a "whole infrastructure" that goes on in the syndicate's back end, where people check balances of cards on the codes they stole and whether they have been activated.
Because gift cards are often given as presents, it could be weeks or months before somebody opens them only to discover issues.
"The acquirers [then] spend it before the consumer can spend it," Adam says.
Adam Parkes said it can be lucrative for those operating the scam en masse, with "tens of thousands of victims and billions of dollars" drained.
Besides the obvious inconvenience to consumers, Adam says the real concern is about what activities this "draining" is funding.
In the US, regulators have run busts on warehouses full of electronics and other high-value goods bought with the proceeds of gift card fraud.
They have linked that back to organised Chinese syndicates, funnelling money back to that country.
In two years, they have arrested 250 people, linking the issue to human trafficking, money laundering, even murder. They have identified cases abroad in Canada through to parts of Europe.
"It's really a global phenomenon," Adam says.
"We've obviously seen it in Australia, New Zealand, Singapore.
"We also know that this is tied to the South-East Asian scam compounds down in Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia."
Coles busts gift tamperer in store
ABC News can reveal that last year, Coles worked with police to bust a member of an alleged criminal syndicate that was tampering with gift cards in supermarkets in New South Wales.
Court documents show a man was arrested for placing Apple Gift cards that had been tampered with on the shelves of at least five different Coles stores in Sydney.
Police alleged the man did this with at least $10,200 worth of gift cards, and suspect he was also doing this in Goulburn and the Southern Highlands.
He was sentenced to a two-year community corrections order and a 15-month suspended sentence.
The supermarket's biggest rival also acknowledged the issue.
Gift card scams falling through cracks
It is unclear how much further this crime has spread, or if any authority is collecting wider information.
The Australian Federal Police and the money laundering organisation Austrac both said gift card fraud is not their domain, while the authority that handles complaints about financial products has limited scope over gift cards.
That is because the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) only has jurisdiction over gift cards issued by companies with a financial licence, like Mastercard or Visa. Companies like Apple, Coles and Woolworths do not fall under its remit.
Australian private investigator Ken Gamble took a look at the ABC's investigation.
He said the reports of tampering occurring mostly around capital cities indicated it could be organised crime.
"It's definitely theft, but it would be one law enforcement would give a very low priority to because of the monetary value," he says.
"Unless they join all the dots here and they can see that this is done in great volume, [then] you're not going to get law enforcement to put the resources in.
"And that's the problem. That's why this type of crime is potentially something that could become very prolific in Australia."
What is the industry doing?
Coles and Woolworths both defended the measures they are taking to stop gift card tampering, including reporting suspicious activity to authorities and adopting in-store tactics to thwart scammers.
Woolworths, for instance, is trialling "anti-tamper" hangers for gift cards. It even has manned stations next to their colourful hanging racks in some supermarkets.
"Coles takes the issue extremely seriously," that supermarket said.
"We know that there is no single measure that will eliminate gift card fraud, and this isn't an issue that can be solved by retailers alone, it requires cooperation across retailers, gift card providers and law enforcement."
The ABC found it more difficult to get information out of other parts of the gift card supply chain.
Apple would not disclose who is responsible for producing its packaging; however, it defended its safeguard mechanisms.
Beyond recognisable brand names, there is an entire global industry that helps manufacture and distribute gift cards on behalf of other companies. In Australia, the two biggest are Blackhawk and InComm.
InComm, for instance, manages "His" and "Her" branded gift cards sold in Australian supermarkets that give people credit to shop at retailers like Sportsgirl or Kookai.
The ABC has seen correspondence between stressed customers and the gift card issuers.
For instance, this year a woman secured a $250 replacement gift card from InComm, after a back-and-forth exchange with the company about a Visa "For You" that had clear scratching.
"InComm Payments understands that fraud is an upsetting and stressful experience for consumers," the company said, while defending its packaging and technology.
Blackhawk referred the ABC to the industry association. The Australian Gift and Prepaid Card Association (AGPCA) declined an interview but defended the industry, which it recently estimated is worth almost $21 billion in Australia.
"Gift cards remain a trusted, widely used product, and industry participants continually enhance controls, monitoring and consumer awareness initiatives to protect customers and maintain confidence in the market," its president, David Christie
David Anderson, who runs an Australian fintech pushing digital gift card technology, believes the industry needs to move beyond using gift cards with physical codes on them.
"This [is] old-school technology," he says.
"I think it's quite well known that card draining happens."
Consumers still battling the industry
The biggest losers are consumers.
Many of the more than a dozen people that ABC News spoke to for this investigation described a frustrating and sometimes ad-hoc process to get refunds. Some never got them and gave up.
After discovering his scratched cards, Lavkesh Arora went straight back to his local Coles with his receipts and cards. He was told to go to Apple.
"That was a little surprising for me because the signs of tampering were visible," he says.
Apple eventually gave him a $700 credit.
Georgia Perry did get a refund from her local Coles, after a back-and-forth with the supermarket's customer care team as her story was going viral in May.
"My blood still boils every time I get ads for the Coles and Woolies gift cards," she says today.
Meanwhile, Sarah Le Page ended up doing a charge-back with her credit card company, which she received just as Apple was notifying her that she was also eligible for $200 credit.
"I find it hard to understand why it just keeps happening," she says.
"This needs to be shown to as many people as possible to stop the victim-blaming that is common.
"They need to put themselves in the place of someone receiving a gift and understand the frustration."

Targeted antibiotic gel helps 80% of pilot patients avoid foot amputation, Jerusalem trial finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
18:50:34 UTC
03:50:34 KST

An Israeli-developed technology that delivers antibiotics directly to severe infection sites helped eight out of 10 diabetic patients who had been considered candidates for foot amputation avoid the procedure in a clinical pilot at Jerusalem’s Shaare Zedek Medical Center.
The technology, developed by Israeli biotech company GentaGel, uses a biodegradable polymer to release antibiotics gradually at the site of an infection for up to 60 days, according to information provided by the company.
The small clinical pilot included 10 patients suffering from severe infected diabetic foot ulcers and bone infections who were candidates for either amputation or removal of infected bone. Eight recovered from their infections without requiring amputation, while wound closure and bone regrowth were observed in those eight patients.
The findings are preliminary, and the company is now advancing additional studies in Israel and the United States while pursuing a regulatory pathway with the US Food and Drug Administration.
Diabetic foot infections can be particularly difficult to treat and, in severe cases, can lead to repeated surgery, long hospital stays, and amputation.
GentaGel delivers antibiotics directly to infected areas
Traditional antibiotic treatments are generally administered orally or intravenously, meaning the medication circulates throughout the body while only part of it reaches the infection at the concentration required for treatment.
GentaGel’s approach is designed to deliver the antibiotic directly into the infected area.
Its biodegradable polymer remains at the treatment site and gradually releases the medication, allowing doctors to maintain a high local concentration of antibiotics for an extended period while reducing exposure elsewhere in the body. The technology can release medication for up to 60 days.
The company said the approach could potentially be used for diabetic foot infections, orthopedic infections, chronic wounds, and other localized internal infections.
‘Real potential’ to treat infected bone
The pilot was conducted through a collaboration between GentaGel and Shaare Zedek Medical Center through Madait, the hospital’s innovation arm.
Dr. Mati Nof, director of the Foot and Ankle Surgery Unit at Shaare Zedek and the study’s principal investigator, said the purpose of the trial was to examine whether GentaGel’s treatment could help doctors treat infected bone.
“Based on the findings from the pilot with 10 patients, I became convinced that there is real potential to heal infected bone without the need for amputation,” Nof said.
Dr. Renana Ofan, CEO of Madait, said Shaare Zedek works with start-ups on early-stage validation studies and clinical trials.
“We are proud of the companies participating in our program and pleased to see their technologies progress, and to be part of the process of advancing innovation for the benefit of patients,” she said.
The technology was invented by Prof. Avi Domb, a former chief scientist and former head of the School of Pharmacy and the Institute for Drug Research at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
Domb specializes in controlled drug-delivery systems. GentaGel is led by co-founder and CEO Dr. Ariel Orbach and co-founder and COO Eli Lerner.
The company said severe localized infections represent a major medical and economic burden. It estimated the direct cost of treating such infections in the US at more than $20 billion annually and said the potential markets for applications of its technology are worth tens of billions of dollars.
The results of the 10-patient pilot do not by themselves establish how effective the treatment would be across a larger patient population. GentaGel’s planned follow-up studies in Israel and the US are expected to provide additional data as the company moves toward regulatory review.

Prisons ‘one major event from disaster’ after U-turn on early release scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
18:50:27 UTC
03:50:27 KST

PC Andrew Harper’s killers will remain behind bars after a critical intervention by Andy Burnham, but the move has led to warnings that overcrowded prisons will be left “one major event away from disaster”.
Announcing a U-turn on the early release scheme after weeks of intense pressure, Burnham said he understood “how strongly people feel about this issue”.
The prime minister’s intervention will prevent the early release of offenders guilty of all forms of manslaughter, as well as rapists, child sexual abusers and groomers.
The decision, which affects about 1,400 prisoners, was welcomed by police, victims’ groups and families, including qualified support from Harper’s mother, Debbie Adlam.
But critics said the change could undermine progressive prison reforms in England and Wales. They said the steps Burnham outlined to free up space would take longer to bring into force, putting the orderly management of prisons at risk.
Harper was 28 when he sustained fatal injuries while responding to a quad bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire in August 2019. Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were passengers in the vehicle and both 17 at the time, were sentenced to 13 years in custody for manslaughter.
Speaking to the BBC, which first reported the government U-turn on Sunday, Burnham said he had “heard” Harper’s family.
“I heard, obviously, what Andrew Harper’s family were saying,” he said. “I mean, who couldn’t? Nobody would want a position to arise where those guilty of killing a police officer are let out early from prison.”
Adlam said she was glad and grateful for the change in the new law but felt “a mixed bag of emotions” and campaigning for the change had been traumatic.
“On the one hand we are glad, but we’ve been [put] through the mill and we are only back at where we were to start with,” she told BBC Breakfast. “We’re not making any headway or anything, we are just literally fighting to get back to where we were.”
Harper’s force, Thames Valley police, said the news would be “welcomed by many across policing and our communities”.
Jason Hogg, the chief constable of the force, said: “Today is not about politics. It is about remembering Andrew, recognising the profound impact his death continues to have on those who knew him, the communities he protected and those who serve in policing today.”
Burnham’s 11th-hour intervention will limit the number of places that can be freed up in the prison estate, which ministers have repeatedly warned is on the brink of collapse.
Before the early prison release scheme that had been due to start this week, the prime minister said spaces would be made available by deporting foreign prisoners and releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences.
But critics warned neither measure would free up sufficient space in a system that is operating at 98% capacity in England and Wales.
Up to 6,000 prisoners were due to have their sentences cut short under the new law, but government figures suggest the number will now be about 4,600. With the first batch of prisoners due to be released early in October, prison governor representatives said staff would be put under intense pressure.
“The truth is I wanted to go even further,” said Burnham. “But I’ve pushed the system to the very limits of what’s possible without risking the prison system collapsing within months, putting the public at enormous risk.”
Nicole Jacobs, the domestic abuse commissioner for England and Wales, said Sunday’s announcement would not bring reassurance to domestic abuse victims.
“Victims and survivors will still be forced to take measures to protect themselves from dangerous abusers because the government and our criminal justice system cannot,” she said.
Sources accused the prime minister of making a “politically easy decision” and warned that multiple governments had failed to deport foreign convicts. Burnham admitted the number that could be returned was in the “hundreds”.
The prime minister’s pledge to “end the injustice” of indefinite jail terms (IPPs) in this parliament was hailed as “a day that thousands of families have spent years fighting for”.
But prison experts said it would be complicated, take time and would be unlikely to free up many places in the short term. IPPs were abolished more than a decade ago but still keep more than 2,000 people in England and Wales behind bars.
“The decision to release people on IPPs is extremely welcome, but the government must now deliver it,” said Andrea Coomber, the chief executive of the Howard League, a penal reform charity.
She said Sunday’s announcement left the prison estate “one major incident away from a disaster”.
“All it will take is something like a serious riot or public disturbance and any capacity will be gone,” she added. “It is just too close to the bone and the government will be left with very little room to manoeuvre.”
She said the move threatened to undermine changes to the Sentencing Act, which were brought forward after a review led by David Gauke, a former justice secretary, and were designed to improve rehabilitation rates as well as freeing up spaces for people coming into the system.
“The Sentencing Act changes were based on deep work over a year from the independent sentencing review, the government and civil servants, with parliamentary scrutiny of the legislation,” said Coomber. “Today’s announcement has undone some of that work.”
Pia Sinha, the chief executive of the Prison Reform Trust, said the government should address the number of people on remand awaiting trial, which account for 18% of those in prison.
“If prisons are full they become warehouses – you can’t deliver interventions, self-harm goes up and rehabilitation goes down,” she said.
“The Gauke reforms were not a magic bullet, but they were brave and they were an investment in the future. That progress must not be lost.”
Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary, accused Labour of avoiding parliamentary scrutiny of the changes. “The government must delay the scheme, bring forward emergency primary legislation and exclude the worst offenders properly,” he said.

Hanson says she can smash Labor and message could be resonating
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
18:46:07 UTC
03:46:07 KST

analysis
Why One Nation victory in Western Australian state by-election is a big deal
If you have ever played with dominoes, you will know that once you get the angle right and the first one falls, the subsequent dominoes come down with a speed and ferocity that rip through in a flash.
The so-called "orange tsunami" — the One Nation blitzkrieg raging across the country — feels like it is doing just that.
Once seen as mainly a threat to the Coalition, this weekend One Nation proved it could take seats off the Labor Party.
The damage it inflicts will not just involve shifting votes from one political column to the next on the right-wing side of politics. The damage is coming for the establishment — blue and red.
The Albanese government has not missed the memo coming out of the Secret Harbour loss — if this momentum can be maintained going into the federal election, that could be as soon as next year — the political tsunami is not just hyperbole, it is a reality that must be reckoned with.
Taking the fight to Albo
One Nation winning the Secret Harbour state by-election in Perth's south, with gym owner Luke Herdegen now set to be the party's first representative in Western Australia's lower house, is a very big deal.
Labor's political dominance in the west is fraying. Even after a week when the prime minister visited WA — and was dubbed "WA's daddy" for backing in its clearly unfair GST largesse — the backlash still came to smash Labor.
Even after a week when the One Nation brand was pulled apart due to its messy and contradictory messaging on its Net Overseas Migration target, the party swept to power in Secret Harbour.
Voters did not listen to all the noise; they backed One Nation, and its many contradictions amounted to little. They wanted to smash the establishment regardless.
Pauline Hanson is at the zenith of her political rise, and she is proving she won't play by the rules.
Most political leaders spend by-election evenings at a local RSL, bowls or footy club function room, with two speeches ready — one for a win that usually consists of telling the assembled rank and file the result was a vindication of their world view.
The second, a more subdued tone, is full of gratitude and gently reminds the crowd the wishes of voters must be respected.
Insert some language around learning more from the losses than the wins, thanking the candidate and high-tailing it out of said venue.
Yet on the night One Nation finally came for Labor, Hanson wasn't brushing up on the list of volunteers to thank; she was busy using a mallet to hammer a nail into a coffin marked "net zero".
She later posted online that Labor losing Secret Harbour would show there was "no safe seat in Australia".
She claimed online that One Nation had taken a seat where the Liberals had never been able to challenge Labor.
"We are the only party that can take the fight to Anthony Albanese where the Liberal Party never could," she said.
"We're not splitting the conservative vote. We're taking on the political establishment."
Hanson is now messaging that she can smash Labor and, given the anger in the community, perhaps that messaging is resonating.
Speaking to media on Saturday night, West Australian federal Liberal MP Ben Small described the result as "kicking Labor in the teeth".
He said voters used the by-election to pass judgement on the Cook government, but when pushed on what the result meant for Andrew Hastie, Small quickly shifted the interview to what the results meant for Labor's federal Resources Minister Madeleine King, whose electorate also overlaps Secret Harbour.
He repeated that Labor's primary vote had fallen around three times as much as the Liberal vote.
Labor's primary vote did fall almost three times as far. But the Liberals still went backwards and finished third.
A primary vote of 17.3 per cent is not the kind of result that will see Angus Taylor roll around WA next federal campaign.
The result should send a jolt through Victorian Labor, too.
Loading
Victorian Labor in trouble
Secret Harbour is the exact electorate Labor should be worried about. It is full of young working families, mortgage holders and people with vocational qualifications rather than university degrees.
Loading...
The population has grown, but local services and infrastructure have struggled to keep up.
Redbridge's Kos Samaras says the result should worry Labor in Perth's outer suburbs.
However, he says it should worry Victorian Labor more because "unless something changes, a swag of Melbourne seats with the same profile as Secret Harbour will go the same way".
Samaras argues the profile matters because: "Secret Harbour is outer urban, but it is not diverse. It ranks fourth of WA's 59 electorates for residents nominating British or Australian ancestry.
"Just under 30 per cent of residents were born overseas, below the state figure of 32 per cent, and the overseas born are overwhelmingly from England, New Zealand and South Africa. English ancestry sits at 49.5 per cent against 37.6 per cent statewide, while Chinese and Indian ancestry are under 1 per cent each."
Secret Harbour is a mortgage-belt seat of "young working families, far more vocational qualifications than degrees, and average incomes despite high workforce participation", he says.
"That is the seat One Nation just took off a popular third-term government … given the current mood towards Labor in Victoria, we can almost safely call them lost."
The implications for Hastie are also big and complex. Secret Harbour sits largely inside his federal seat of Canning, which One Nation is openly targeting.
Money and organisers are already being tipped into what will become an ideological arm wrestle over far more than shade cloth.
Hastie is a strong local campaigner and retained Canning with a 6.6 per cent margin last year.
But when One Nation can lift its primary vote by more than 30 points in his political backyard, pretending this is solely Labor's problem is taking optimism a little too far.
Patricia Karvelas is host of ABC News Afternoon Briefing at 4pm weekdays on ABC News Channel, co-host of the weekly Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly and host of politics and news podcast Politics Now.

Oscar Jenkins gives first interview since 13-year sentence in Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30

03:44:16 KST

Australian Oscar Jenkins gives first interview following 13-year prison sentence in Russia
In short:
Australian Oscar Jenkins has given his first interview since he was sentenced in May 2025 to 13 years' imprisonment by Russian authorities for acting as "a mercenary in an armed conflict".
In the interview, Jenkins details why he decided to volunteer as a soldier for Ukraine and how he got there.
The Australian foreign minister described Jenkins's trial last year as a "sham" and called for Russia to follow "international humanitarian law".
An Australian man serving a 13-year prison sentence in Russia after being captured while fighting for Ukraine has given his first interview since being convicted in what the Australian government has slammed as a "sham trial".
Appearing gaunt, with a shaved head and dressed in a prison uniform, in an interview filmed inside a prison in Russian-occupied Luhansk, Oscar Jenkins explained why he decided to join Ukrainian forces in early 2024.
"It felt like the right thing to do; if a country invades another country, why?" he said.
"And if there's not a good reason for that, like Taiwan, then that's something that I should stand up for.
"I'm a young guy. It's not that my life doesn't mean anything to me, but sacrifices might need to be made.
"That's still the attitude I have."
Loading...
Extraordinarily, Jenkins also said he had told his captors he would fight for them too.
"I've written a statement saying that I'd be happy to fight as a soldier for Russia," he said.
"But if they don't trust me or for whatever reason don't want that, then I can understand."
The interview was conducted in the prison over two days by Mark Lowe, an Australian who has been living in Vladivostok for four years and works as an English teacher.
Mr Lowe, who also runs a website that reports sympathetically on Russia and the Putin regime, said he tried for a year to secure permission from authorities to interview Jenkins, which forms the basis of a documentary he plans to release.
"It's geared to a Western audience to enlighten them as to what really goes on in Ukraine," he told the ABC.
"To give them a different perspective."
Mr Lowe said that he used relationships he formed with government officials who had been his English language students to secure permission for the interview, but that Jenkins had no prior knowledge before he arrived.
"I turned up [to the prison] unannounced," he said.
"I said, 'I'm here if you'd like to do an interview with me.' He said, 'Yeah'."
The ABC has been unable to independently verify the circumstances under which the interview was conducted.
However, Mr Lowe claims that no conditions were placed on the interview and also denied he had been pressured to conduct it by Russian authorities.
Asked why they trusted him, Mr Lowe said he believed they approved of the "objective" writing on his website.
Jenkins details his journey to Ukraine
During the interview, Jenkins described his journey to Ukraine, some of the "missions" he was involved with and how he was captured.
Jenkins — who did not have a military background — said that before he decided to fight with Ukrainian forces, he had considered fighting in Myanmar against the military junta and also joining the Israeli defence force.
"I was going to go to Israel. It just felt a little bit too hard for me because I wasn't Israeli or something. But now I think I could have done it," he said.
"I just thought if I were going to go to war, then Israel would be a good bet, but I chose Ukraine because it was easier, I think, just fly in and go there."
He told Mr Lowe that he had been working in China and watching videos on YouTube.
"The video was actually talking about journalism within the Donbas region, but I didn't think that, for whatever reason, I didn't think that journalism was for me.
"I thought, 'No, I'll just go and be a soldier. I want to help, so I'm just going to go be a soldier.'"
He said he bought a ticket from Australia to Poland, then took a bus to the Ukrainian border and approached officials there.
"They asked me, 'What are you going to do'? I said, 'I'm going to volunteer', and that was enough."
After signing up at a recruitment office, Jenkins said he underwent a month of "processing time".
"People didn't like what Russia was doing; they felt Russia was being a bully, and all that while I was prepping for my own position as a machine gunner," he said.
"I was told I was going to be a machine-gunner on the front."
Jenkins said Ukrainian soldiers and American, French and British volunteers trained his group.
He said his "foreign" unit was an official part of the Ukrainian army, "but it felt very unofficial and separate".
"We had a British commanding officer; he was 24 years old, he'd had some experience fighting.
"But things felt a little bit hodgepodge, not a lot of resources to work with, but enough to get to the front and just sort of get yourself in a hole and maybe just hold the line if possible."
He said he went on about nine or 10 missions, including the one during which he was caught.
"Four of us got in the armoured vehicle to go to the position; I was dropped off not knowing that it was essentially Russia, it was a Russian position that I was in already," he said.
Jenkins described digging a trench but then losing touch with the rest of his unit.
"There was a whole bunch of drones, grenades going off from the moment we left that vehicle. There was a lot of chaos."
He said he suffered a broken arm and damage to one leg when a drone dropped a grenade.
After four days in the trench, he was approached by "a guy" who "asked me if I needed a hand".
Loading...
"And then we walked 5 metres forward, 10 metres forward into a blindage [camouflaged dugout], and there were three soldiers there.
"They asked me who I was; I said I was a Ukrainian soldier and then I got captured."
Sentenced to 13 years in alleged 'sham trial'
In May 2025, Jenkins was tried in a court in Luhansk and sentenced to 13 years' imprisonment in a "maximum security penal colony" for participating as "a mercenary in an armed conflict".
Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong described it as a "sham trial".
Ms Wong said that Jenkins was a prisoner of war, so he must be given "the protections afforded to him".
"Russia is obligated to treat him in accordance with international humanitarian law, including humane treatment,"
Russia considers foreigners who have travelled to fight in Ukraine to be mercenaries who are prosecuted under criminal law and not as prisoners of war.
During the interview, Mr Lowe does not ask Jenkins what support he had received from the Australian government.
A Kremlin-aligned, Moscow-based human rights group has previously suggested Jenkins could be released as part of a prisoner swap between Russia and Australia.
It suggested the swap could involve the accused Russian spies Kira and Igor Korolev as well as pro-Putin propagandist Simeon Boikov, known online as the "Aussie Cossack", who is hiding from Australian authorities in the Russian consulate in Sydney.
On Monday, a Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade spokesperson said:
"As a full serving member of the regular Armed Forces of Ukraine captured by Russian Armed Forces, Mr Jenkins is a Ukrainian prisoner of war [PoW].
"We have consistently sought welfare updates from Russia and urged them to grant the [International Committee of the Red Cross] and Mr Jenkins' lawyers access to him.
"We have made clear Australians' expectations that Russia fully complies with its obligations under international law, including with respect to PoWs.
"We continue to request Ukraine prioritise Mr Jenkins' release in a future PoW swap with Russia."

Syria has reopened its embassy in the Libyan capital, Tripoli, after a closure lasting more than 14 years, according to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA).
Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al Shaibani officially inaugurated the embassy on Sunday during a ceremony attended by Arab and foreign diplomats and officials.
In August 2025, a Syrian technical and diplomatic delegation to Libya announced that the country’s flag had been raised over the Syrian Embassy building in Tripoli in preparation for its reopening.
The embassy closed in 2012 after Libya’s then-Transitional Council recognised the Syrian revolution. Relations remained severed during the rule of the Assad regime.
On December 8, 2024, the Syrian revolution succeeded in ending Assad’s regime rule.
Earlier, Libyan Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah and al Shaibani discussed ways to develop bilateral relations and reactivate cooperation frameworks between their countries.
The talks came as Abdulhamid Dbeibah met with al Shaibani in Tripoli following his arrival in the Libyan capital, according to a statement from Libya’s Government of National Unity.
The two sides discussed reactivating Libyan-Syrian cooperation frameworks, raising the level of diplomatic representation and revitalising a joint higher committee, as well as strengthening economic, investment and trade cooperation, the statement said.
They also addressed several financial issues and outstanding dues between institutions in the two countries.
The Libyan-Syrian Joint Higher Committee is an official bilateral cooperation framework intended to strengthen political, economic and social relations. It generally operates at the prime ministerial level and coordinates joint efforts across various fields.
The meeting also covered security cooperation and counterterrorism, the conditions of the two countries’ communities, consular services and issues concerning prisoners, detainees, refugees and displaced people.
Abdulhamid Dbeibah stressed the importance of “opening a new chapter in relations between Libya and Syria based on shared interests, practical cooperation and addressing outstanding issues in a manner that serves the citizens of both countries,” the statement said.
The Syrian foreign ministry said al Shaibani and Dbeibeh discussed bilateral relations and ways to strengthen and advance them in various fields.
The two sides emphasised the importance of broadening cooperation and strengthening communication and coordination between relevant institutions in both countries to serve their shared interests, the ministry added in a statement.
As part of the visit, al Shaibani also met Libyan Oil and Gas Minister Khalifa Abdulsadek and Libyan Investment Authority Chairman and CEO Ali Mahmoud Hassan to discuss bilateral cooperation in energy and investment and ways to expand partnerships and exchange expertise in sectors of mutual interest, the ministry said.
Al Shaibani also met Taher Al-Baour, who is responsible for managing Libya’s foreign ministry and international cooperation, to discuss strengthening relations and expanding bilateral cooperation in various fields.
The two sides signed a cooperation agreement aimed at activating their previous deal regarding the Joint High Committee and amending it in line with political developments in both countries, according to the SANA news agency.

Venezuela's deposed leader Nicolás Maduro said on social media Sunday that he was "standing firm," while sharing photographs from the New York prison where he has been held since his capture by U.S. forces.
Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, were seized in Caracas during a U.S. military operation in January. They are being detained in a Brooklyn, New York, jail on drug trafficking and firearms possession charges, which they deny.
"I am sending these photos as a small gift to all my grandchildren, to the boys and girls, and to all the good people who love us," he wrote on the Telegram messaging service.
"I want you to know that we are standing firm, with our hearts full of your love," he added.
In the two photographs, Maduro is wearing a gray tracksuit and making peace signs with his hands. He appears to have lost weight since his capture.
Although the photographs emerged Sunday, camera data indicates they were taken on June 25, a day after twin deadly earthquakes killed more than 6,500 people and caused widespread destruction in northern Venezuela.
"We will remain strong, calm and confident: God is with us. God will provide. Venezuela will rise again," he concluded.
The message was posted two days after his successor, interim President Delcy Rodriguez, announced a "historic" oil agreement allowing the United States to operate oil fields in Venezuela.
President Trump said Friday that the deal grants the United States majority control of over 60 billion barrels of proven Venezuelan oil reserves. A U.S. official told CBS News that the venture is a "joint project of the U.S. government and an experienced private operator in Venezuela."
"One of the things I am going to do with the Venezuelan Oil is fill up the Strategic National Reserves which, because of Sleepy Joe Biden, has been virtually emptied," Mr. Trump said in a Truth Social post on Sunday. "The 'topping out' process will begin very shortly, and is a Gift from Venezuela to the People of the United States."
The U.S. government will control 55% of the joint venture, split between equity in the venture and the ability to obtain oil from it at cost, the official said.

"This agreement is based on a simple premise: each party contributes what it does best," she said. "Venezuela contributes oil, its industry, and the experience its workers have accumulated over decades. The United States is providing the necessary capital and technology to recover and develop those assets."
Maduro does not have access to newspapers or the internet in prison, but he is allowed to speak by telephone with his family and lawyers for approximately 300 minutes a month, with a maximum of 15 minutes per call, according to a source close to the former leader.

Maduro and his wife's trial in New York will begin on June 1, 2027, a federal court in New York announced in late July. Both have pleaded not guilty. They face potential life prison sentences if a jury agrees that they were part of a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S.

Venezuela says it will retain 'sovereignty' over its oil reserves despite US deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
18:40:18 UTC
03:40:18 KST

Venezuela's acting president says the aim is to turn the country's underground resources into a "source of social and economic well-being for the people of Venezuela."
Venezuela's acting President Delcy Rodríguez said on Saturday that the country would retain "sovereignty" over its oil resources despite a new agreement with the US that grants Washington significant access to the South American nation's reserves.
"One thing must be absolutely clear: Venezuela retains ownership and sovereignty over its resources," Rodríguez said in a speech broadcast on state television.
Under the terms of the agreement, which was announced by US President Donald Trump on Friday, the US is set to take control of 65 billion barrels of Venezuela's oil reserves.
According to Rodríguez, the deal also "calls for the development of 17 strategic fields" and could see investment of "more than $100 billion, and more than $209 billion in taxes for the state."
Rodríguez says the aim is to turn Venezuela's underground resources into a "source of social and economic well-being for the people of Venezuela."
However, some have accused the government of a lack of transparency surrounding the deal, with questions also being raised on social media about whether it will truly benefit Venezuelans.
The agreement comes after more than a decade of struggling to attract investment amid a deep economic crisis in the country.
Some analysts have now welcomed the US' role as a "guarantor" for investments into Venezuela, which has the world's largest proven reserves.
"Without this, these fields would not be developed over the next 10 or 15 years," Oswaldo Felizzola, a professor at the Institute of Advanced Studies in Administration (IESA), told AFP, adding that Venezuela's state-owned energy firm Petróleos de Venezuela "does not have the financial resources to do so."
Oil production in Venezuela rose by 29.8% between January and July, reaching 1.2 million barrels a day, although it remains well below the three million barrels a day recorded 25 years ago.
Rodríguez has introduced reforms in the mining and oil sectors to facilitate the entry of private and foreign capital, while Washington has relaxed sanctions on Venezuela's oil sector.
In a post on X, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio hailed the deal as a "huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people."
"It demonstrates how President Trump's bold foreign policy is driving America First wins: securing stable reserves and low-cost oil in our Hemisphere and lowering gas prices here at home," he wrote.

Watchdog warns insurers are offering insufficient cash settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
18:35:52 UTC
03:35:52 KST

ASIC warns home owners being left short after accepting cash settlements on insurance claims
In short:
At least 63 per cent of final home insurance claims included a cash settlement, according to ASIC.
In many cases, the sum offered by the insurer is not enough to cover the customer's true cost of repairs, raising questions about the "fairness" of these offers.
What's next?
Later this year, a new draft of the General Insurance Code of Practice will be handed to the ASIC, which continues to monitor the issue.
Australia's corporate watchdog is sounding the alarm over insurers' use of cash settlements, concerned they could unfairly short-change home owners dealing with a house insurance claim.
ASIC has been reviewing the industry's use of cash settlements to pay out claims since the impacts of Cyclone Jasper in Far North Queensland in December 2023.
Cash settlements provide customers with a full or part sum of money to independently handle building repairs.
It is an alternative to an insurer overseeing rectification work done by their choice of contractors and covering the cost as required.
ASIC's report found at least 63 per cent of final home insurance claims included a cash settlement, with consumers at risk of insufficient funds that did not cover the true cost of repairs.
ASIC warned cash settlements also risked the home owner experiencing the stress of finding reliable tradespeople, and could leave them with no lifetime repair guarantees.
"These findings are a real concern," ASIC's commissioner Alan Kirkland said.
"There are real questions around the fairness of the offers that are being made to consumers."
Review into five major insurers
ASIC reviewed the policies, procedures, training materials and a sample of claim files from Insurance Australia Group, AAI, QBE, Allianz, and Sure Insurance.
It found most claims involved a cash settlement with little information to determine whether it was in the customer's best interests.
"Insurers ultimately have an obligation to make sure that their cash settlement offers are fair and … they need to communicate with consumers in terms that they understand," said Mr Kirkland.
ASIC's review found that to determine the sum offered, insurers often relied on a single quote from a preferred supplier that was willing to offer discount pricing for the insurers in exchange for repeat business.
"That raises questions around whether the amounts that are being offered to consumers … reflect prices that the consumer could get if they go out to source repairs themselves," Mr Kirkland said.
This is the latest report by the watchdog into insurer conduct, after it conducted reviews in 2023 and 2025 into the handling of flood-related claims.
It comes as home insurance premiums continue to skyrocket, increasing by 51 per cent in the past five years.
Cash settlement offer forced pensioner to sell home
Pensioner Julia Hirning has been forced to sell her Far North Queensland home after discovering the cash settlement from her insurer was not enough to cover the real cost of works.
"It knocks you around physically, mentally, emotionally … and I decided I'm just going to sell it as is, and then look at buying a small home unit,"
Flooding in January 2025 left Ms Hirning's home full of mould.
After more than a year going back and forth with Sure Insurance, she went to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) and her insurer offered her a settlement of $245,800.
"So then I went to a builder that I knew was well known in Townsville; he was well respected and highly recommended," she said.
"He came up and had a look, and his costings were just over $300,000 to do it and do it properly."
Pensioner doing his own repairs
After about a year of discussions with the same insurer, pensioner Leon Wuttrich said he was completing the final repair work himself to finish fixing his home after an insufficient cash settlement.
"I've done a lot of the work, and my wife's obviously helped; I've had builders in too. But it is extremely hard in North Queensland to find builders," he said.
Mr Wuttrich was impacted by the same floods and said Sure Insurance agreed to an initial scope of works quote by one builder for $127,000.
But after the home owner engaged Legal Aid, that amount increased to about $314,000, which he said still was not enough.
"The tiler in the end that came in and did just the two bathrooms was just on $50,000," he said.
He also said the communications from Sure Insurance were "downright non-existent".
"It just confused the crap out of me,"
In a statement to the ABC, Sure Insurance said it "remains focused on responding to our customers' needs in each and every household claim".
An offer without an explanation
The report found insurers often offered cash settlements where claims involved pre-existing maintenance issues.
ASIC said half of the files that it reviewed involved a cash settlement due to the insurers' assessment that the consumer had not adequately maintained their property.
"For the consumer, however, that can mean that they're left in a really complex situation where the insurer is only covering part of the damage and they've then got to coordinate repairs to the other part," Mr Kirkland said.
"We think insurers can do more to help consumers in those circumstances, such as by sourcing quotes for the pre-existing damage and helping to coordinate the overall repairs."
When insurers offer a cash settlement to a home owner, they must provide consumers with a Cash Settlement Fact Sheet so the consumer can make an informed choice on whether to accept the cash settlement.
While all insurers offer a fact sheet, ASIC found most lacked an explanation of the amount.
ASIC found only one insurer could readily extract data on the reason a claim was cash settled. It also found no insurer had processes in place to systematically capture this data.
"They should provide sufficient details for the consumer to understand how the amount of the cash settlement has been calculated and what is included in that cash settlement offer," Mr Kirkland said.
In a statement to the ABC, a spokesperson from the Insurance Council of Australia said: "There has been a significant industry uplift since Tropical Cyclone Jasper, with a focus on making sure cash settlements are clearly explained and understood".
"The review of the General Insurance Code of Practice will set stronger, contractually enforceable obligations on cash settlements and support for customers experiencing vulnerability."
Assistant Treasurer and Financial Services Minister Daniel Mulino said ASIC's findings were an important reminder that insurers "must ensure consumers have all the information they need".
"I would hope the updated General Code of Insurance Practice sees stronger protections in this area."
Public consultation for the redrafted General Insurance Code of Practice closed in July, with the latest draft of the Code expected to be handed to ASIC later this year.

Germany news: Merz warns of 'problems' in Saxony-Anhalt under AfD

Germany: Merz warns of 'problems' in Saxony-Anhalt under AfD
Published August 29, 2026last updated August 31, 2026
What you need to know
- Merz predicts 'significant problems' for Saxony-Anhalt under AfD
- Merkel calls on Germans to 'fight for this democracy'
- German politicians call for ban on radical AfD state branches
This blog is now closed. Thank you for reading.
Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Saturday, August 29, and Sunday, August 30.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Thank you for reading
Thank you for reading this weekend's Germany news blog.
We will back with more news in a fresh blog on Monday. Tschüss!
Gamescom attendance comes close to record high
The international video games trade fair Gamescom came to a close in the western German city of Cologne on Sunday after being attended by an almost record number of visitors.
Around 368,000 gamers attended the event, 11,000 more than in 2025 and 33,000 more than in 2024. The record attendance of 373,000 set in 2019 wasn't quite reached — but Gamescom is getting closer.
Digital reach was once again substantial, with various online formats recording 624 million views worldwide — roughly the same number as before. On the ground in the sprawling halls of Cologne's trade fair, there were 1,743 physical exhibitions — a significant increase on last year (1,568).
"Gamescom has solidified its position as the biggest event in the gaming world," said Felix Falk, Managing Director of the industry association Game.
"At the same time, the unique atmosphere and enthusiasm on site demonstrated how games forge a strong, creative, and diverse community out of people from all walks of life," he added.
Merz: Germany to respond to hybrid threats 'in coming days'
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said that Germany will respond to Russian hybrid threats in the coming week — in coordination with international allies.
"We're largely in agreement within the government as to how to react and we will make this known in the coming days," he told public broadcaster ARD as part of Sunday's summer interview.
The Chancellor's remarks come following the recent drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport. While an explosive-laden drone failed to detonate on August 5, the incident has put Germany's security and defense infrastructure in the spotlight.
Asked whether Germany was in any position to respond to such threats in an appropriate manner, Merz responded: "Let's wait and see what we mean by an appropriate response."
Either way, he continued, any German response will be coordinated with allies. "Our European Union and NATO partners will not be surprised," he said.
Merz predicts 'significant problems' for Saxony-Anhalt under AfD
Election victory for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt next week would do serious damage to the eastern German state, according to Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
"Should it come to that, this state would face significant problems," Merz told public broadcaster ARD in his annual summer interview.
"I cannot imagine that international investors would want to be seen attending the first spades in the ground for new factories or businesses in Saxony-Anhalt alongside an AfD state premier," he said.
According to the latest polls ahead of next Sunday's vote, the AfD maintains a commanding lead with 40% — far ahead of Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) with 23%, the Left Party (13%), the Social Democrats (SPD) (9%) and the Greens (6%).
Merz said he would be appearing twice himself in Saxony-Anhalt over the coming week in order to convince undecided voters (which still make up a good 20% of the electorate, according to polls) not to vote for the far-right.
"We will do everything we can to prevent Saxony-Anhalt falling to extremists," he said, adding: "And that applies to the Left Party, too."
Asked how the CDU intended to form a coalition government in Saxony-Anhalt with such low ratings and while refusing to work with either the AfD or the Left Party, Merz said: "We will look at that once we have the results."
The current state premier, Sven Schulze (CDU), however, has expressed a willingness to form a coalition with the SPD, Greens and the Left Party.
Hockey: Germany's men retain World Cup title
Germany retained their men's field hockey World Cup title with a hard-fought 1-0 victory over Spain in Sunday's final in Wavre, Belgium. The triumph secured Germany's fourth World Cup crown, moving them level with Pakistan as the tournament's joint-record winners.
Michel Struthoff scored the decisive goal in the 44th minute, beating the Spanish goalkeeper to turn the ball into the net and give Germany the lead. Spain pushed for an equalizer, but Germany's disciplined defense held firm through the closing stages.
Goalkeeper Jean-Paul Danneberg was instrumental in preserving the advantage, making several crucial saves and keeping out all four of Spain's penalty corners. Germany, who are also the reigning European champions, absorbed increasing pressure late in the match to see out the victory.
The title adds to Germany's previous World Cup successes in 2002, 2006 and 2023. Argentina secured third place earlier on Sunday with a 2-1 win over co-hosts the Netherlands in the bronze-medal match.
Cologne-Mallorca Eurowings flight forced to land in Paris
A Eurowings plane was forced to make a landing in Paris on Saturday evening after steam was detected in the aircraft's galley, the airline said.
The Boeing 737 with 131 passengers on board was flying from the western German city of Cologne to the Spanish island of Mallorca.
The unscheduled landing at Charles de Gaulle Airport was made as a precaution and under "normal" flight priority status, according to Eurowings.
"The safety of the passengers and crew was at no time at risk," a Eurowings spokesman said on Sunday.
German politicians call for ban on radical AfD state branches
High-ranking German politicians have advocated for proceedings to ban the most radical regional branches of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.
Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and Baden-Württemberg's state premier, Cem Özdemir, called for bans to be initiated swiftly in a joint guest op-ed in the newspaper Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung.
"We once again strongly urge that proceedings to ban the party be initiated as soon as possible, with a particular focus on the AfD's clearly ethno-nationalist state branches in Thuringia, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, and Brandenburg," Pistorius and Özdemir said.
Their comments come just days before the September 6 election in Saxony-Anhalt, where an AfD victory could result in a far-right party leading a German state government for the first time since the end of Nazi rule in 1945.
Pistorius and Özdemir argue that it is important to distinguish between different factions within the AfD.
The two politicians say that the party's more radical, ethnically based wing rejects the constitutional principle. In their view, this wing should be subject to legal scrutiny.
They refer to this faction of the AfD as "völkisch" — a German adjective derived from das Volk, meaning "the people." The völkisch movement was an ethno-nationalist movement and precursor to Nazism. Today, the AfD is often accused of holding völkisch views because its officials repeatedly distinguish between Germans with and without a history of migration.
However, Green Party lawmaker Irene Mihalic warned against a selective ban.
"I see a risk that the idea might eventually take hold that there is an unconstitutional part of the AfD and a constitutional one," she told the Handelsblatt newspaper. "In my view, it is now clear that the entire AfD is at odds with our democratic constitution."
British woman stabbed to death at railway station in Bavaria
A British woman was stabbed to death overnight at a railway station in the southern German state of Bavaria, police said on Sunday.
The 31-year-old was taken to hospital but later died from her injuries.
Police reported that a 27-year-old German man was detained at the scene in Rosenheim — the third-largest city in Upper Bavaria after Munich and Ingolstadt.
Authorities are investigating the circumstances and motive behind the attack and have appealed for witnesses to come forward.
WATCH: AfD and the battle for young voters
For the first time since the end of World War II, a far-right politician could become a state premier in Germany.
In Saxony-Anhalt, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is well ahead of the other parties, with its lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, especially popular among young voters.
Siegmund presents himself as a fresh and positive figure who wants to "get Germany back on its feet."
We speak to young people in Saxony-Anhalt to find out what they like about Siegmund and the AfD.
To what extent are young people being politicized by the right? Or are they simply disillusioned with the established parties?
Three Germans among those missing in Nepal-Tibet flood, China says
Three Germans are among those missing following Wednesday's flash flood in the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China, Chinese authorities said on Sunday.
A total of 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were unaccounted for.
Those missing include:
-

	49 from India

	33 from Latvia

	18 from the United States

"Chinese authorities have notified the respective embassies and consulates of these countries in China," state media CCTV said, citing officials.
The Nepal Tourism Board, however, said eight Germans are missing. It is unclear if the three German nationals reported as unaccounted for by Chinese authorities are included in the number reported by Nepal.
The Foreign Office in Berlin has said "a high single-digit number of German nationals" are missing in the devastating flood.
On Sunday, the combined death toll rose to 750, with more than 3,000 people still missing, local authorities said.
Several scientists believe a glacier collapse high in the Himalayas on Wednesday may have triggered a tsunami-like wall of water which swept away entire villages in the Himalayan region.
Merkel calls on Germans to 'fight for this democracy'
Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel has called on her compatriots to "stand up" for democracy ahead of next weekend's state election in Saxony-Anhalt.
The far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) is leading polls raising questions about what kind of government will be formed.
Despite this, the majority of Germans are not AfD voters, Merkel said at a political event in Berlin on Saturday night.
"I believe that now, once again — something we haven't had to do for many decades — we must really fight for this democracy, simply stand up for it, be a little brave, stand by our word and say that this is a wonderful way to live," she said.
Merkel said the AfD had, to some extent, managed to "dominate all our discussions from morning to night" about politics in Saxony-Anhalt. This meant that many voters no longer knew the policies of the other parties, she said.
But while the AfD has long polled strongest in the eastern states, Merkel — who herself hails from the former East Germany — said the rise of the AfD was not limited to those areas.
"It has become a pan-German phenomenon," she said.
German government expected to hold Moscow responsible for Leipzig drone incident, reports say
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government plans to officially hold Moscow responsible for the Leipzig drone incident in early August, several German news outlets owned by media company Axel Springer SE reported on Saturday.
Berlin is expected to announce the planned move in the coming days, including "extensive" sanctions, three officials familiar with the matter told German newspaper Welt am Sonntag and the media outlet Politico.
However, the three sources did not elaborate on what the specific measures could be. It is also unclear to what extent Berlin plans to hold Russia responsible for the Leipzig incident.
On August 4, a drone loaded with explosives was discovered near Ukrainian cargo planes at Leipzig/Halle Airport, which serves as a hub for military aid shipments to Ukraine for its war against Russia.
Merz told RTL in an interview on Thursday that the federal government would soon identify those responsible for the incident.
Sick leave now costs Germany twice as much as in 2010
The total amount of wages German firms paid in sick and maternity leave has more than doubled over the past 15 years, a study from the Cologne-based German Economic Institute (IW) shows.
IW estimated that German companies paid a record-high €85.6 billion ($111 billion) in wages to employees who were out sick last year. This compares to €36.9 billion in 2010.
Of the larger figure, €72.5 billion represented gross wages, while €13.1 billion was earmarked for social security contributions.
IW said several factors have contributed to the rise, including wage hikes and inflation in other employee costs.
The institute said the total number of employed people has also grown since 2010, meaning more workers are eligible for sick leave.
IW, however, said it had noted a "significant" rise in recorded sick leave since Germany moved to electronic medical certificates in 2022.
Separate research by the Berlin-based IGES Institute in January showed that German workers now take an average of 19.5 working days as sick leave per year, a noticeable increase from about 13 days in 2018.
In an effort to stem the rise, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government will from January ban patients from receiving sick notes from doctors by phone.
In Germany, employers are generally required to pay workers' salaries for up to six weeks before the statutory health insurance fund takes over by paying sickness benefits.
Lower Saxony premier seeks deal on VW restructuring
Volkswagen's second-biggest shareholder has called on all sides to agree on a restructuring plan for the German auto giant in the next few days.
Olaf Lies, state premier of Lower Saxony — which holds 18% of VW's shareholder voting rights — said he was convinced "a viable solution" can be found.
"I strongly urge that we use the time remaining until the next meeting to bring the different positions together," Lies told journalists on Friday.
The state leader noted that VW must face its numerous business challenges head-on, namely costly tariffs, falling demand and intense competition from China.
But he said the group's position in Germany's industrial landscape also had to be considered.
"With its sites in Lower Saxony and across Germany, its tens of thousands of employees and their families, and its suppliers and service providers, Volkswagen also bears an enormous responsibility for the wider economy and society," Lies said.
VW's management now thinks they may need to cut up to 100,000 jobs and that several German factories may face closure.
The supervisory board of Europe's largest automaker is due to meet on September 4 to discuss a turnaround plan.
Survey: Trump's return increased US influence over Germany
Two-thirds of residents think the United States has more influence on Germany since US President Donald Trump returned to the White House.
A poll by the Forsa research institute found that 67% of respondents agreed, while just 11% thought there was less US influence. Around 18% thought it was the same.
The survey for the German-language Internationale Politik (International Politics) magazine found only 2% of 18 to 29-year-olds and 6% of 30 to 44-year-olds think US influence in Germany is lower than before Trump's second term. That's versus 18% of respondents aged 60 and over.
Germany-US ties have soured since Trump's reelection, due to surprise tariffs, talk of seizing Greenland and open sniping over Russia's war in Ukraine and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war.

How to prepare to buy a home while you save a deposit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

The steps first home buyers can take while saving for their deposit
The process of purchasing a home can feel overwhelming.
Beyond putting money aside for a home deposit, it can be hard to know how to prepare.
But there are steps you can take — while you're still saving — that will help you get to the point of signing on the dotted line.
Learn about your options and mistakes to avoid
Mortgage broker Craig Morgan says there is an advantage to being a first home buyer, because it can mean you are aware that there's a lot you don't know a lot, and are willing to learn.
He explains that people buying a second or third property can assume they know everything, but "things change so much" and it might have been a decade since their last purchase.
"Gaining some knowledge and some preparation is the absolute key," Mr Morgan says.
Once you've started saving, Mr Morgan says you could approach a mortgage broker to get a better understanding of your borrowing capacity.
There are online borrowing calculators that can help with this too, but they are not as accurate, he says.
"Your income position is not going to change for most people dramatically over the course of one or two years of saving. Whilst you may not have the deposit yet, you can at least find out what you can afford."
He says there are plenty of loan officers at banks and mortgage brokers that will do this for free (they will be hoping you return later on but you should not feel obliged to).
Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter
Financial educator Natasha Janssens also recommends doing some research and seeking out professional advice before you have your entire deposit saved.
"Twelve months to two years out is a great time … you're going to have so much information to absorb, and you'll have more questions that will arise later."
This will set up your expectations and help you avoid some of those common mistakes people unknowingly make in those crucial final months.
For example, "this is not the time to suddenly be getting a car loan, a credit card [or] quitting your job," she says.
Financial adviser Scott Taylor says taking the time to research first-home buyer incentives "early on your journey" may allow you to utilise the first home super saver scheme.
Put simply, "This is where you can salary sacrifice part of your wage into super or make a one-off contribution to super from your savings and claim it as a tax deduction and then pull that money out when you're ready to purchase a home."
Mr Taylor says you need about three years to "fully maximise" the benefits, so it helps to plan ahead.
Get clear on your own and shared priorities
If you're buying with a partner, you want to really understand each other's priorities, Ms Janssens says.
Taking the time to talk about the significance of a partners' "non-negotiables", "must haves" and "nice to haves" will help when the time comes to negotiate and compromise.
"If you don't understand where each other are coming from and what the significance is of that … conflict can start to arise."
In a couple, we can assume the other person is on the same page, but haven't had those up-front conversations, she says.
Mr Morgan says a couple should have some flexibility during the process, but should be on the "same page" as each other.
"If one person's going in saying, 'it's got to be three bedrooms, it's going to be in the suburbs,' and another person's saying, 'it's got to be a studio and it's got to be on the Yarra', we're not even talking about the same thing," he says.
Before you've bought a home with someone, Ms Janssens also recommends discussing financial backup plans.
It can be "really uncomfortable", but she suggests workshopping how you both plan to pay the mortgage if you decided to have children or one of you became sick, injured or unemployed.
Mr Taylor says it's prudent to think about insurance before you actually go into debt and buy a property.
Income protection insurance could help you afford the mortgage in the event of an illness or injury.
Get (very) familiar with your finances
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC)'s Moneysmart website recommends getting your finances sorted.
This includes creating a budget so you are clear on how much you can afford to put towards your deposit.
Mr Taylor says you need a "clear understanding of your money".
The word "budget" can have a negative connotation, but he says a "cashflow plan" includes understanding your lifestyle and where your money goes, recognising expenses such as holidays and eating out.
"There's normally a disconnect between what a bank says you can borrow versus what impact that would have on your lifestyle," Mr Taylor says.
Before you commit to a mortgage, he says it's important to understand what the repayments would mean.
It's common to overestimate what you might be able to save a month and underestimate other expenses, such as annual insurance premiums, council rates and house repairs.
Mr Taylor also suggests "stress testing" how your finances would look if interest rates rose to seven per cent or someone took maternity leave.
You could map this out on a spreadsheet, seek professional advice to lay out how that could work or trial spending less.
"[If] you can't do it or you're not happy with your lifestyle and it sucks … then buying the house at that level and going into that much debt is not suitable."
Ms Janssens says understanding your finances will also give you an opportunity to change any spending habits that might limit your borrowing capacity.
If you're meeting with a professional (such as a bank employee, financial adviser or mortgage broker) you need a good understanding of any debts, the limits of any credit cards you have, your savings and your living expenses (outside of rent), she says.
"A lot of people don't fully understand how much they get paid," Ms Janssens says.
If you're looking toward buying a home, she says to consider any additional payments, such as overtime, bonuses, loading or salary sacrifice arrangements.
And if you're buying a house with a partner or someone else, it's important to be aware of your joint financial position.
Ms Janssen says this isn't always an easy conversation, but it is an important one.
"If you've been managing things separately, there can be a lot of shame around money."
But accounts with buy now, pay later services (such as Afterpay), credit cards, or having declared bankruptcy can all impact your joint mortgage options, she says. So being transparent with each other can help put you in the best possible position.
This article contains general information only. You should consider obtaining independent professional advice in relation to your particular circumstances.

French presidential race: De Villepin set to run, Faure enters socialist primary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
18:26:25 UTC
03:26:25 KST

With just under eight months to go until the French presidential election, political manoeuvring is in full swing. Several candidates or would-be candidates spoke out this Sunday.
Although he is not yet officially a candidate in France’s 2027 presidential election, Dominique de Villepin is getting very close.
Speaking to BFM TV Sunday, the conservative politician — who formerly served as prime minister under Jacques Chirac and heads the La France Humaniste party — said he would confirm his candidacy "once the election campaign has begun".
He added that he was ruling out taking part in a primary, arguing that "it is not the right way of doing things" but rather "the latest gimmick for the desperate".
Meanwhile, Olivier Faure, the first secretary of the Socialist Party (PS) is due to announce on Sunday evening on TF1 that he will take part in the party’s primary election, after informing MPs from his group of his decision Saturday night. He informed MPs in his group of his decision in a message sent during the night from Saturday to Sunday.
But Dominique de Villepin reserved most of his criticism for Édouard Philippe, arguing that the latter is "playing into the hands" of Marine Le Pen by entering into a form of "one-upmanship" with his proposals to restrict immigration to Mayotte.
The latter, a presidential candidate and leader of the Horizons party, was hosted on Sunday in Tourcoing by Gérald Darmanin for the start-of-season rally of his political movement Populaires. In mid-August, the justice minister officially announced his support for his "friend of twenty years" in the presidential race.
Centrist Gabriel Attal, another former prime minister — who was appointed by French President Emmanuel Macron — and the Renaissance party’s presidential candidate, stated he had "never ruled out a primary".
Attal’s comments come after more 200 elected French politicians signed a column in Le Figaro newspaper on Wednesday, calling for the centrist and right-wing bloc to hold a primary election, as part of a bid to identify a single candidate able to take on the far-left and far-right.
In an interview with France 2 and France Inter, Raphaël Glucksmann, the main rival of Olivier Faure in the social-democratic primary, once again took aim at the leader of France Unbowed (LFI), Jean-Luc Mélenchon, saying that he had "gone beyond all acceptable limits" and that "the democratic left" must "show that it is capable of breaking with those who sow chaos".
