Semicon to put spotlight on CPO, silicon photonics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:43:01 UTC
01:43:01 KST

Silicon photonics and copackaged optics (CPO), technologies seen as critical to meeting the surging bandwidth demands of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, would be among the main themes at the Semicon Taiwan trade show, which opens on Wednesday, event organizer SEMI said yesterday.
The forum runs until Friday at the Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center, with technical forums beginning today.
The event is expected to set a record in terms of the number of participants, SEMI said, projecting more than 1,300 exhibitors from 65 countries across 4,300 booths and more than 100,000 attendees.
Photo: CNA
Optical interconnects underpinning AI infrastructure would be one of the highlights, with contract chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co’s (TSMC, 台積電) compact universal photonics engine (COUPE) platform and the industry’s progress toward mass CPO production expected to draw attention, it said.
With AI chips, high-performance computing processors and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) demanding faster data transmission, conventional electrical interconnects are increasingly giving way to optical communications to boost AI data center efficiency, SEMI said.
The industry is moving beyond chip-level speeds to upgrading rack-to-rack links, as copper interconnects near their limits in bandwidth, power consumption and transmission distance, it said.
Silicon photonics, which uses optical rather than electrical signals, could cut power consumption and data transfer costs, making this a key year for large-scale deployment, SEMI said.
The technology can integrate photonic integrated circuits with electronic integrated circuits, while CPO technology enables optical engines and switches to be packaged together.
In AI and high-performance computing chip systems, advanced packaging technologies can also integrate graphics processing units, AI accelerators, application-specific integrated circuits and HBM, enabling optoelectronic integration with high bandwidth, low latency and low power consumption while overcoming limitations in bandwidth, power consumption and transmission performance.
TSMC has been expanding its COUPE platform and “COUPE on Substrate” CPO solution, with products entering production this year.
AI chip designer Nvidia Corp has partnered with TSMC on COUPE and begun shipping next-generation Spectrum-X switches using CPO technology, with production expected to ramp up in the second half of the year.
TrendForce Corp (集邦科技) in a report last month said Nvidia’s Spectrum-X shipments and Broadcom Inc’s initial deliveries of its 51.2-terabit Bailly CPO switch show that the technology has entered the mass production stage.
Taiwanese firms are also accelerating commercialization, with United Microelectronics Corp (聯電) completing its first mass-produced silicon photonics wafers at its Singapore fab with partner Silith Technology Pte Ltd, the report said.
GlobalWafers Co (環球晶圓) also said some products entered volume production earlier this year, the report added.
Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海精密) expects to begin CPO switch shipments in the third quarter, while affiliate ShunSin Technology Holdings Ltd (訊芯科技) said it has achieved mass production capability for 51.2-terabit and 102.4-terabit CPO products through a collaboration with TSMC.
Powertech Technology Inc (力成科技), which is partnering with Broadcom Inc, plans to begin low-volume production for optical engine components this year before integrating them into CPO switches next year.
Largan Precision Co (大立光) is preparing for a trial production of its first automated CPO line after securing a fiber-array order.
Testing suppliers are expanding, too, with Materials Analysis Technology Inc (閎康科技) installing advanced silicon photonics testing equipment, and ASE Technology Holding Co (日月光投控) building out its CPO ecosystem through subsidiaries and its VIPack packaging platform, the report said.
AM Intelligence, an Indian artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure company, has ordered 9,000 Nvidia Corp Vera Rubin systems, seeking to become one of the first adopters of the advanced computing platform in Asia. Servers equipped with the rack-scale systems are slated to come online next year in southern India, the Hyderabad-based company said in a statement yesterday. Customers include major cloud service providers, AI labs and organizations aiming to develop homegrown Indian AI models, it said. Supplies of high-end Nvidia compute clusters remain tight. Demand from data centers and companies such as Microsoft Corp, Alphabet Inc’s Google and Amazon.com Inc to train AI models

Fuel prices to stay steady for the fifth consecutive week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:43:00 UTC
01:43:00 KST

CPC Corp, Taiwan (CPC, 台灣中油) on Saturday announced that it would leave domestic gasoline and diesel prices unchanged this week, with Formosa Petrochemical Corp (台塑石化) yesterday saying it would do the same.
It is the fifth consecutive week that CPC and Formosa have kept domestic crude oil prices steady under the government’s price stabilization measures.
Retail gasoline prices this week remain at NT$30.5, NT$32 and NT$34 per liter for 92, 95 and 98-octane unleaded gasoline respectively at CPC and Formosa stations.
Prices of premium diesel would stay at NT$29.3 per liter at CPC stations and NT$29.1 per liter at Formosa pumps, they said.
International crude oil prices last week ended lower despite apparent stalling in diplomatic efforts to end the war between the US and Iran, and a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz remaining uncertain.
CPC said its floating price mechanism, based on a weighted average of 70 percent Dubai and 30 percent Brent crude, showed that the average international crude oil price fell to US$91.56 last week from US$93.01 per barrel in the week before.
Additionally, a stronger New Taiwan dollar against the US dollar reduced purchasing costs, it said.
CPC said that as of yesterday, it has absorbed an estimated NT$18.03 billion (US$570.06 million) in losses since the war in the Middle East started in February, by not fully passing on higher international crude oil costs on to consumers and businesses to ease domestic inflationary pressure.

Netanyahu condemns settler raid in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:42:59 UTC
01:42:59 KST

Dozens of Israeli settlers on Saturday attacked the Palestinian village of Qusra in the northern occupied West Bank after nearly three weeks of tension in the area, drawing rare condemnation from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Earlier this month, a group of settlers began blocking supplies from entering Palestinian houses on the outskirts of the village near Nablus, trapping residents inside and drawing unusually strong criticism from the US ambassador.
Weeks later, Israeli forces continue to operate in the area while settlers still roam the surrounding hills.
Photo: AFP
On Saturday, Qusra residents and dozens of settlers had descended on the village, throwing stones at residents and barricading themselves inside a house while Palestinians were inside, the Israeli military said.
In nearby Jalud, NBC News said masked settlers attacked and injured members of its reporting team and a Palestinian woman it had gone to interview.
“I strongly condemn the criminal acts of violence committed in the villages of Qusra and Jalud by a handful of rioters who are violating the law, causing a grave injustice to the law-abiding Jewish community, interfering with the IDF [Israel Defense Forces] in carrying out its missions, and harming Israel’s standing in the world,” Netanyahu said in a statement.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog also condemned the attack in Qusra, while the Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the violence “a disgrace.”
In Qusra, resident Yussef Abdul Kareem Hassan said that a handful of villagers were on Saturday doing work on a house when they were approached by a small group of settlers.
The settlers then called for backup and returned with dozens more, he said, adding that they surrounded the Palestinians inside the house and began throwing stones.
Dozens of Israeli forces were deployed to Qusra on Saturday.
The Israeli military said soldiers and border police forces were dispatched “following reports that Israeli rioters had arrived in the area and that violent clashes had occurred, including stone-hurling toward Palestinians and additional civilians.”
“Upon their arrival, the security forces identified dozens of rioters who had barricaded themselves inside a Palestinian home while Palestinian residents were inside,” the Israeli military said in a statement, adding that it was “aware of reports of Palestinian injuries.”
It said forces had worked to remove the settlers from the house, separate the groups and confiscate vehicles “that were suspected of having been used to reach the area.”
The vehicles would be used as evidence in a police investigation that has been opened, it said, adding that forces continued to operate in the area “to prevent further disturbances and restore order.”
Violence by Israeli settlers toward Palestinians in the West Bank has persisted for years, often with little or no legal consequence, but the past few months have seen a surge in attacks.
More than 500,000 Israelis live in settlements in the Palestinian territory, which are illegal under international law, among about 3 million Palestinians.
Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967.
Israeli forces or settlers have killed at least 1,103 Palestinians in the West Bank, including militants and civilians, since the start of the Gaza war in October 2023, according to an Agence France-Presse tally based on the Palestinian Ministry of Health.

A controversial fenced-in smoking area installed near Taipei’s Gongguan (公館) shopping district was dismantled on Wednesday last week after it was widely ridiculed for looking like a dog cage and for being ineffective at blocking secondhand smoke.
The Gongguan smoking area, which is part of Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) push for a smoke-free city, was removed in less than 10 days after its installation, while six others were removed on the same day.
City councilors have continued to question other designated smoking areas in the city, including open-air spaces enclosed by potted plants, or areas in parking lots marked by only a painted square and sign, mocked by many as the “Emperor’s new smoking area.”
While problematic smoking areas were quickly removed following criticism, the incident is one of a string of controversial public infrastructure projects in Taipei.
Earlier last week, city councilors across party lines questioned why the city spent NT$4.13 million (US$130,580) on two public art bus shelters in Wenshan District (文山), which were reported to be dripping rusty water and leaving a rust stain on the sidewalk below, despite not even being open for public use yet.
In April and June, Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Taipei City councilors Lin Yen-fong (林延鳳) and Chien Shu-pei (簡舒培) questioned the high cost of and long delays in installing eight pedestrian sunshades in Xinyi District (信義), a project that Chiang announced after seeing similar installations on a trip to Seoul in 2024.
Last week, Taipei City Councilor Miao Po-ya (苗博雅) questioned the cost of the eight planned sunshade structures, including NT$49.66 million for construction and NT$9.91 million for design and supervision — an average of about NT$7.44 million each, excluding subsequent maintenance costs. She also asked why the project avoided the council’s prior oversight by splitting the budget into different segments.
Other city councilors across party lines criticized Chiang over the proposal, because the sunshade installations had been slated to be useable by summer this year, but have been so severely delayed that the project is expected to be finished in January next year. Meanwhile, the New Taipei City government was able to install two pedestrian sunshades for about NT$900,000 each in just two months. A difference in quality between the sunshades in Xinyi and the two umbrella-like sunshades that were quickly installed in Taipei’s Ximending (西門町) shopping area last month was also criticized.
The sunshade project also followed controversy last month about the removal of a large number of trees in the past two years, sparking concerns by environmental groups about the impact on urban heat resilience.
While under fire for its public works projects, the Taipei City Government is also facing other major issues.
City councilors last week revealed an alleged delay in putting a 10-year-old girl in protective care after she was allegedly sexually molested by a man they described as one of her mother’s sex-work clients. The city was also criticized for having conducted no benzopyrene tests on cooking oil in the past eight years before a nationwide cooking oil scandal last month.
What is even more concerning is the responses of Chiang and his city government officials when questioned on these important issues. Chiang was accused by the public as dodging questions, giving vague and evasive answers, and even deflecting criticism by blaming the central government or other local administrations led by the DPP.
Asked about the sloppy planning and money wasted on fenced-in smoking areas, Chiang instead asked why the city councilor does not equally question the central and Kaohsiung city governments’ plans which were also modified after public criticism. Regarding the girl, the city’s social welfare department said a professional assessment had initially found that she did not meet the threshold for placement, but launched judicial protective placement after the case was brought to public attention by a city councilor last week; and when asked about the benzopyrene testing, Chiang rallied a protest with Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕) to shift the blame onto the central government.
Chiang, who has continuously appealed to neutral voters by maintaining a mild-mannered, moderate and rational public image, has thrust himself under the spotlight after aggressively attacking the central government at the protest rally. Many voters are starting to question Chiang’s ability govern the city, after seeing his inability to admit to his mistakes and give clear answers to the city’s residents about infrastructure projects and major issues.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has amended its regulations on investment subsidies for businesses investing in countries with which Taiwan has diplomatic relations, raising the maximum subsidy to NT$60 million (US$1.9 million) to encourage investment in diplomatic allies.
The ministry has previously amended the regulations on investment subsidies for businesses investing in countries with which Taiwan maintains diplomatic relations, with the aim of encouraging investment in those countries, creating jobs, raising incomes, promoting economic and social development, and strengthening Taiwan’s economic, trade and diplomatic ties with its allies.
To make the subsidy system more flexible and to better address the diverse needs of businesses as their overseas investments expand, the ministry said it has amended the regulations to broaden the scope of eligible expenses.
Photo: Taipei Times
Under the revised rules, businesses applying for subsidies for the first time may have their expenses for the full year, dating back to Jan. 1, considered for eligibility.
The previous requirement that applicants could claim only one of the following expenses — local employee salaries, factory and equipment costs, office or land rents, or financing interest — has also been relaxed, allowing businesses to apply for subsidies for two or all three applicable categories simultaneously, it said.
Under the revised rules, the maximum cumulative subsidy has been raised to NT$60 million, the ministry said.
Subsidies for employing local workers are calculated at 30 percent of each employee’s monthly salary; subsidies for factory and equipment costs, business premises or land rent are calculated at 30 percent of the rent actually paid; and subsidies for financing interest are calculated at 50 percent of the interest actually paid on loans from financial institutions, it said.

Notes from Central Taiwan: Taiwan cannot engineer its way out of flooding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:42:54 UTC
01:42:54 KST

The flooding in Kaohsiung after the recent torrential rains has become an issue for mayoral candidates of both major parties. Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Kaohsiung mayoral candidate Ko Chih-en (柯志恩) brought in hydraulic-engineering professor Lee Hong-yuan (李鴻源), who called for comprehensive flood control measures on the Dianbao Creek (典寶溪), according to local media. Ko attacked the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) for being behind on flood control measures, but as the city administration observed, there are many weaknesses in how the government can mitigate extreme rainfall. Nor is the river entirely under the management of the city. The low-lying Dianbao River basin has a long history of flooding during heavy rain, and authorities have undertaken extensive channel, embankment, detention and pumping projects, several of which remain incomplete.
Meanwhile the local residents complain that their riverside properties are under a 30-year curse, as the Dianbao’s problems remain unresolved. Economically, the residents are asking the wider public to bear the cost of protecting repeatedly flooded private property. Wouldn’t it be cheaper for the government to simply buy up the land along the river and let it flood?
Exorbitant sums to protect property is not a new thing. A piece from Taiwan Panorama describes Kezailiao (蚵仔寮), a village in Kaohsiung: “were it not for the huge sums spent each year on strengthening the sea walls, Kezailiao would have long ago been swallowed by the sea, and would have disappeared from Taiwan’s map. But the walls have continually been moved inland and have been repaired 27 times, and countless concrete blocks have been laid down to break the force of the waves.” That piece, from 1993, gives a sense of the way water engineering in Taiwan is a perpetual motion machine, perpetually playing whack-a-mole with water issues in Taiwan.
Photo: Lee Hui-chou, Taipei Times
The Taiwan Panorama piece also noted that the flooding downstream, the retreat of the land and widespread land subsidence, result from a multiplicity of factors. Although in most pieces groundwater pumping gets the blame, dam construction in upstream areas traps the silt that might replenish floodplains. Subsidence is often spotlighted, but rising sea levels as humans warm the earth’s climate are also eating away at Taiwan’s coasts (and salting its coastal aquifers). Heritage sites along the southwest coast are at risk from flooding in the next few decades as sea levels rise, as one 2024 paper observed.
GOVERNMENT RESPONSE
In the 1990s the Cabinet, responding to the subsidence problem, developed the Land Subsidence Prevention and Reclamation Plan (地層下陷防治執行方案), which became effective in November 1995. A 2010 assessment in the Taipei Times by aquaculture specialist Peter Sun (孫寧) concluded that the plan had, by then, only marginally reduced subsidence. He proposed spending approximately NT$160 billion over a decade to help operators leave fish farming, seal wells and fill about 10,000 hectares of ponds with dredged sediment. Naturally that sort of common sense was ignored.
Photo: Liu Wang-chun, Taipei Times
In the local media the recent flooding has been treated as a result of torrential rains and, by critics of the administration and locals in Kaohsiung, slow or inept engineering responses. However, as with most of Taiwan’s chronic problems, the heart of the problem is the government’s vast subsidy regime.
A 2023 paper in Nature Scientific Reports on subsidence along the Jhuoshuei River (濁水溪) in Yunlin County observed that in the 1970s the problem of subsidence appeared first on the coast. The government attacked the problem, mitigating it.
“Over the past 10 years, subsidence has slowed in the coastal areas but has continued in inland areas,” the authors observe, continuing: “currently, of all areas of this delta, the central area exhibits the highest subsidence rate.”
How fast is subsidence in the area? A 2024 paper in Remote Sensing says “The InSAR [Satellite-based Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar] results showed a prominent subsidence bowl centered in Yunlin County, with average subsidence velocities around 40 to 60 mm/year.”
The area on the plains around the Jhuoshuei River has over 100,000 wells on farm that mine groundwater to raise crops. Groundwater mining, in turn, is powered by cheap electricity. Taiwan Power Co (Taipower, 台電) monitors electric use and hooks up wells to the grid, but does not inquire whether the pumping is actually legal.
The 2023 paper’s simulations show that decreasing electricity usage decreases subsidence. It seems obvious that the simplest way to do that is to raise the price of electricity, but power prices are subsidized. Another form of subsidy to groundwater pumping is the lack of regulation of water extraction.
Photo: Yeh Yung-chian, Taipei Times
Note that though we blame agriculture, much groundwater pumping occurs for industrial and even recreational use (I used to go to a pool in Changhua that used groundwater). Indeed, there was a period when the Ministry of Education encouraged schools to use groundwater pumps because it was “green.”
CONSEQUENCES OF OVERPRODUCTION
Agricultural products travel through networks of government-run agricultural cooperatives that receive all sorts of funding from local and central governments, from promotion programs to disaster relief. Subsidy regimes encourage overproduction. That is a good thing, if getting cheap food for urban areas is the goal. Yet overproduction has downstream consequences.
Subsidies also help drive the aquaculture output of the Pingtung coastal plain, where subsidence is a critical issue. The aerators in fish ponds going 24 hours a day run on subsidized electricity prices, for example. Naturally, there is a government-subsidized program (what else?) for converting them to greener systems. When the US placed 20 percent tariffs on many goods in August last year, the government sprung into action with an NT$18 billion (US$562.5 million) support program to help the agriculture and fisheries industries, including aquaculture.
A paper in Remote Sensing Applications: Society and Environment on subsidence in Pingtung notes that production has shifted to inland aquaculture as fisheries have gone into decline. Among the factors causing the fisheries decline is of course, massive subsidies to fishing fleets. “As an example”, the authors write, “the 1996-2005 fish yield of the inland aquaculture was 19.8 million tons, compared to 51.3 million tons over 2016-2018.”
Unsurprisingly, land near aquaculture-intensive Linbian Township (林邊) in Pingtung County experienced as much as 3.5m of cumulative subsidence between 1972 and 2019.
Agricultural subsidies are just one form of subsidy. Rivers and their drainage has been badly managed over the years and much land that could be absorbing floods is concreted over, forcing water downstream to more inhabited areas at greater velocities. That program of relentlessly destroying watercourses resulted in part from local and central government programs to subsidize politically connected construction firms. Moreover, extensive channelization and impervious development can reduce floodplain storage, accelerate runoff and diminish groundwater recharge.
For government officials, management of rivers means controlling them via engineering for flood safety, not viewing them as complex ecosystems offering flood control and mitigation services. Nor is their behavior viewed as a consequence of Taiwan’s absurdly generous subsidy programs. But any “comprehensive” approach to managing flooding in Kaohsiung — and elsewhere — long-term means re-engineering not just the nation’s rivers, but its subsidy programs.
Notes from Central Taiwan is a column written by long-term resident Michael Turton, who provides incisive commentary informed by three decades of living in and writing about his adoptive country. The views expressed here are his own.

“Those who allowed this to happen must be held accountable for their decisions... Ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said in a post on social media.
The blast forced hundreds to evacuate and damaged multiple homes, including a care facility for older and disabled people, he added.
At least 37 people were killed, among them the mayor of the nearby town of Dmytrivka, Kyiv region governor Tymur Tkachenko said on social media.
Residents in the area said the explosion was “terrifying.”
“We thought we were being bombed. No one knew it was a detonation,” said Yana Doneli, resident of a nearby town.

Ukrainian prosecutors said they had opened an investigation into criminal negligence.
“On 28 August at around 8:10pm, an unmanned aerial vehicle ... fell on or struck the grounds of an enterprise in the town of Myla,” the office of Ukraine’s prosecutor general said.
Myla is a small town on the outskirts of western Kyiv.
“A large-scale fire broke out on the enterprise’s grounds, and detonation began,” prosecutors added.
The prosecutor’s office said that its investigation would focus on “the legality of the ... storage of explosive objects and materials on the enterprise’s grounds,” as well as whether the owner, whom it did not name, had the “necessary permits and approvals.”
Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky expressed regret that a “lesson” had not been learned following a previous deadly strike on a munitions depot near Kyiv last month.
That investigation revealed serious failings on the part of a state-owned company, which did not comply with regulations regarding the proximity of residential buildings.
“In the fifth year of the full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes over and over is criminal negligence,” Koretsky said on social media. “Everyone responsible, without exception, must face severe punishment so that such situations never happen again.”
Russia launched at least two missiles and 267 drones at Ukraine from late Friday to early Saturday, the Ukrainian Air Force said.

In Russia, Ukrainian strikes killed three people in the Belgorod region and caused a fire at a warehouse belonging to Russian retailer Ozon, officials said.
A strike on the city of Sevastopol in Crimea killed one person, Sevastopol’s Russian-installed governor said.
US-led diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, Europe’s deadliest since World War II, have been at a standstill for months.

‘The river has taken everything’: people return to remains of their homes in Nepal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:39:38 UTC
01:39:38 KST

The bodies continue to wash up. But the morgues have already run out of room.
Since the deadly floods coursed through the Himalayan valleys of Nepal and Tibet, the numbers of people killed have continued to rise. The bodies have surfaced in their hundreds and continue to be pulled from the thick, tar-like mud that engulfed everything after the flood waters receded. By Sunday, the death toll stood at 804 in Nepal and Tibet.
Morgues across Nepal are already overflowing. Authorities say they are overwhelmed with the task of trying to identify the dead, many mangled beyond recognition and turning up miles from home. As places to safely store the victims run out, mass burials have begun in the district of Bharatpur.
DNA samples were taken from each body before it was given a tag and a location number, wrapped in a plastic bag and then placed in a shallow grave. The hope, said the police, was that these bodies would eventually be identified by loved ones through DNA and retrieved for proper funeral rites.
In Chitwan, about 100 miles downstream from the region worst hit by the flash floods and mudslides, more than 250 bodies have washed up along the riverbanks. But they are in such a disfigured state that only nine have been successfully identified. Many will now be buried, at least temporarily, in the forest on the edge of the city.
In an effort to speed up the identification exercise, local officials have adopted a macabre approach of simply asking people to go through pictures of the bodies and look for identifying features: a necklace, a wedding ring, a tattoo, a scar. Photos of those recovered have been placed on to PowerPoint slideshows, for relatives to sit patiently through, and have been uploaded to the Nepal police website. Outside the morgue in the capital, Kathmandu, photographs of the dead inside have been posted on the walls.
Yet with more than 3,000 still reported missing in Nepal and Tibet, there are fears that the numbers of dead may still rise exponentially. Many of the worst-hit areas, where entire villages were wiped away by the tidal wave of mud, water and debris, are still inaccessible except by army helicopter. Speaking on Sunday, the foreign secretary, Amrit Bahadur Rai, said the Nepal government had requested “more than 1,000 freezer units” for safe storage of the dead.
Even in areas lower down the river valley that were decimated by the floods but have remained accessible by road, search and rescue teams have struggled to retrieve all those killed and buried in the mud. On Sunday afternoon in Devighat, a sacred town on the Trishuli River that was left in ruins by the floods, police search and rescue teams prepared to pull another victim from the muddy ruins of a house. All that was visible through the thick mud was their feet.
“It is very tough work. We have retrieved 10 bodies from here so far, maybe there will be more,” said Amabadutta Bhatta, a police superintendent working as part of search and rescue in the city. “The floods destroyed the first and second storey of most homes here. When we finally clear all the mud, which may be many months, who knows what we might find.”
Those who survived the floods in Devighat have slowly come back to see the remains of their houses, many of which were wiped away altogether. Standing next to the carcass of her house, reduced to a few concrete blocks and twisted metal, Usha Nepali, 49, wept for the home where she had raised her four children and then her three grandchildren.
“I invested everything to build this house, so now I don’t know where to go and what to do,” said Nepali. “Nothing is left except this cloth on my back. I haven’t even been able to change clothes since the floods. How can we rebuild this house? This land is no longer safe but it’s the only land we have. The river has taken everything.”
The precariousness of living next to the Trishuli River was underlined on Sunday as the fast-moving waters again swelled dangerously high and rescuers urged people to get to higher ground quickly. Many in Devighat were packing up the few items they could find in their homes, never to return.
Jamuna Magar, 36, said her husband’s family had been living in Devighat for generations. She had come here when she got married and described it as “such a beautiful place”.
In the minutes after they got warning of the flood, she had time to grab her gold but nothing else. As she stood by the ruins of her house, clutching the only thing she had been able to retrieve so far – a plastic vat of vegetable cooking oil – she said she did not see how they could ever live in Devighat again.
“We had experienced flooding before, but we never knew a flood like this could come and take our house,” she said. “Everything we owned was on the ground floor of the house and now it’s all lost. Even our refrigerator washed away. I’m too worried about my life, about my children’s lives to stay here any longer.”
She feared it would take “decades before they can rebuild Devighat again”.

Rival Libya factions sign deal to hold national elections within two years
Signing ceremony takes place at UN mission in Tripoli after initial draft signed by UN-backed committee in Tunis on August 20.
Representatives of Libya’s rival governments have signed a deal to hold national elections within two years after years of political divisions.
The agreement, signed on Sunday, says legislative and presidential elections will be held under a single executive authority within a “period not exceeding 24 months”, according to Walid Ellafi, state minister of political affairs and communications in the internationally recognised Government of National Unity, based in Tripoli.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Libya factions draft initial election pact amid lingering mistrust
- list 2 of 3Qatar pledges support for efforts to end Libya’s political division
- list 3 of 3Libya’s brain drain, 15 years after Tripoli fell
The signing ceremony took place in Tripoli at the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) after the UN-backed “4+4 committee” signed an initial draft in Tunis on August 20.
The committee consisted of four representatives from the House of Representatives, based in eastern Libya, and four representatives from the High Council of State, linked to the Government of National Unity in the west.
Libya has been divided since 2014 between two opposing administrations: the internationally recognised government and an eastern administration backed by renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar.
Shibani AbuHamoud, head of the general delegation of Haftar’s forces, said it would work with UNSMIL on a “framework within one month of the signing of the agreement to follow up on all matters related to its implementation”.
However, the agreement notes that if the House of Representatives and the High Council of State do not approve the deal within a month, it would be adopted nationally by the parties as a constitutional document and would receive international support through the UN Security Council.
Scepticism, however, remains over the success of the agreement, and analysts said the real problem of who governs Libya in the interim remains because they would control the country’s resources and have to deal with a sensitive security environment.
While the UN and other mediators have been trying to unify the country since 2011 after a rebellion toppled and killed leader Muammar Gaddafi, implementation continues to be the biggest challenge. A presidential election has been repeatedly stalled due to political disputes.

NASA launches first telescope named after female scientist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:36:00 UTC
01:36:00 KST

NASA launches first telescope named after female scientist
August 30, 2026
NASA has launched a powerful new telescope designed to explore distant planets, exploding stars and black holes while surveying the universe on an unprecedented scale.
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, named after one of the first women to hold a senior leadership position at NASA, was launched aboard a Falcon Heavy rocket operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on Sunday.
The telescope is expected to reach its destination, approximately 1.6 million kilometers (about one million miles) from Earth, in approximately one month's time.
The mission has a total budget of more than $4 billion (€3.45 billion). The first images are expected back on Earth in early 2027.
What will the Roman telescope do?
Astronomers will use "Roman" to investigate a wide range of cosmic phenomena, including black holes, exoplanets and exploding stars.
"It's going to find thousands of supernovae, tens of thousands of planets, billions of galaxies and tens of billions of stars," said NASA science mission director Nicky Fox. "It's going to be able to do things that we've never been able to do before with its massive field of view."
Roman operates in a similar way to the Hubble Space Telescope, which was launched in 1990 and is now showing signs of age while operating with reduced capabilities.
However, Roman is designed to survey the sky far more quickly and will be capable of completing in just one month observations which would have taken Hubble a century.
Scientists expect Roman to generate more than 500 terabytes of data every year. By way of comparison, Hubble has collected approximately 400 terabytes of data in over three decades in space.
"Roman's vast reach will allow us to find the weird, the rare and the unusual," senior project scientist Julie McEnery said on Saturday. "We'll redefine what it means to find a needle in a haystack."
Who was Nancy Grace Roman?
The James Webb Space Telescope, named after former NASA administrator James Webb, was launched in late 2021 to complement Hubble. Webb observes the universe at different wavelengths, complementing the observations that will be made by Hubble and Roman.
Launching nearly a year ahead of schedule and within budget, Roman is NASA's first space telescope to be named after a woman. Nancy Grace Roman served as NASA's first Chief of Astronomy throughout the 1960s and 1970s, and retired NASA scientist Ed Weiler said the honor was long overdue.
"This is very, very fitting," he said. "I think Nancy would be very proud."

WASHINGTON, August 30. /TASS/. The US administration intends to use oil that would be received as a result of the deal with Venezuela to replenish its Strategic Petroleum Reserve, US President Donald Trump announced.
"One of the things I am going to do with the Venezuelan oil is fill up the strategic national reserves which, because of Sleepy Joe Biden (the 46th US president - TASS), has been virtually emptied. The ‘topping out’ process will begin very shortly, and is a gift from Venezuela to the people of the United States," he wrote on his Truth Social platform.
On August 28, Trump announced a deal with Venezuela that "secured majority US control of more than 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves in Venezuela." According to Venezuela’s authorized President Delcy Rodriguez, the deal provides for the development of 17 oilfields.
The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve was established by a decision of the US Congress in 1975, following the global energy crisis. Currently, underground salt caverns at four major oil storage facilities in the states of Louisiana and Texas hold around 290 million barrels of oil. The total storage capacity is currently set at 714 million barrels. The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve is the largest government-owned reserve in the world.

The Guardian view on the rise of Germany’s AfD: mainstream parties must deliver a bolder response | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:30:02 UTC
01:30:02 KST

The early autumn has become a time of foreboding and angst in German politics. In the eastern states that have become strongholds for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party, it has regularly made headline-grabbing advances in September elections. Only the refusal of mainstream politicians to form coalitions with one of Europe’s most extreme movements has kept it out of power.
This year, the lights are flashing red. Next weekend, when voters in Saxony-Anhalt cast their ballots, the signs are that the traditional firewall may not be enough. In polling, the AfD is currently scoring above 40% in the state, which could win it enough seats to govern on its own. Compared with the last election in 2021, its support has doubled; backing for the closest challenger, the centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), has tumbled by almost 15%.
Those are startling and alarming figures. Since the second world war, none of Germany’s 16 Länder have been governed by the far right, and in office the AfD would exercise substantial powers over education, policing and culture. The Saxony-Anhalt party – which was classified as a threat to democracy by the security services – has pledged to fully exploit them. The party’s manifesto proposes policies such as the segregation of refugee children in separate schools (in violation of EU law), a nationalist curriculum that would shift the focus away from the Nazi period, and the championing of the “normal family” over “sexual deviations and non-reproductive lifestyles”.
Whatever the outcome next weekend, the AfD’s sustained lead in national polls suggests a reckoning is at hand for mainstream parties. Postwar politics in Germany has, for obvious reasons, been founded on a horror of extreme nationalism and a focus on consensus and compromise. But more than one in four voters currently back a party that has discussed a programme of mass “remigration”, which could include passport-carrying citizens deemed to have a “non-German” background.
This stark reality has led to suggestions that the taboo on cooperation with the AfD should be dropped, on the basis that exposing the party to the practical realities of governing would reveal the emptiness of its populist promises. That would be a strategy born of desperation and one carrying great risks, not least for the minorities at the sharp end of the experiment. But there is little doubt that despite attempts to ape the far right’s draconian stance on immigration, the political approach being pursued by Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s coalition government is not working.
As elsewhere in Europe, support for the far right is most concentrated in the ailing industrial regions that were once a source of pride and identity, as well as prosperity. Yet as the country suffers from the double whammy of Chinese competition and US protectionism, Mr Merz’s focus on tax cuts, welfare reform and raising the retirement age is signally failing to address the crisis afflicting Europe’s largest economy.
While campaigning in 2018 to become leader of the CDU, the chancellor pledged to halve the AfD’s vote. Support for it has instead doubled. Mr Merz’s own popularity ratings are at a record low for any chancellor, while his coalition partner, the Social Democratic party, is faring just as badly in the polls. A vote next weekend freighted with ominous symbolism will send yet another message to a failing political class that it needs to rethink its priorities.

The Guardian view on rare earths: it’s common sense to secure essential supply chains | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:30:01 UTC
01:30:01 KST

The alarm sounded 16 years ago. In 2010, China blocked exports of key rare earths to Japan in a row over disputed islands in the East China Sea. The critical minerals are essential to everything from advanced weaponry and iPhones to electric vehicle batteries and wind turbines, so the rest of the world took note. But it didn’t take much action. China still accounts for about 70% of rare-earth mining globally and 90% of separation and processing.
Then, last year, Beijing forced Donald Trump to back away from his trade war – not with its retaliatory tariffs, but the curbing of rare-earth exports. A scramble for new supplies began in earnest. The year-long trade truce is due to expire in November. The price of erbium, an element essential to communications infrastructure, has already jumped because of fears that export controls will soon be renewed.
The 17 metals known as rare earths are far from rare; their name refers to the low concentrations in which they are found. Extraction and processing are costly, complex and often dirty, while returns are low. That’s why the US – which dominated the industry in the 1980s – and others outsourced production to China. Any plan to diversify supply chains must somehow build in predictable demand and pricing to succeed. Even now, US rare earths are reportedly flowing to Asia because of the lack of domestic demand. While “Big shovel” is becoming the new driver of geopolitics, rare earths are a tiny slice of the critical minerals market – worth less than $6bn globally last year.
Efforts to diversify supply chains had already begun. But the US-China standoff accelerated them. Last autumn, the Pentagon became the single largest investor in the US firm MP Minerals. In February, the Trump administration announced that it would spend $12bn to create a critical minerals reserve, focusing initially on rare earths. US officials have reportedly described their plan to create new supply chains as a “Manhattan Project” for rare earths. Others question the strategy behind the splurge of money and projects.
China, which imports rare earths for processing and has seen them affected by the war in Myanmar, also wants to diversify its supplies. Washington and Beijing are looking to South Africa, Greenland and, in particular, Brazil, raising grave concern about the ecological impact. Innovation, particularly in finding ways to recycle rare earths or extract them from mining waste or runoff, could help meet demand and reduce environmental damage. But it will not stop the extraction drive.
Earlier this year, the US launched a critical minerals coalition with 54 partners, including Australia, the European Commission and the UK. A multilateral approach is essential. But Europe and others know it would be extremely risky to count on Washington solely, given the unreliability of the Trump administration, its wild use of trade weapons and its threats to invade Greenland. Stockpiles of essential rare earths, serious investment and stronger partnerships with likeminded allies will be central to a solution. The 2025 European Critical Raw Materials Act set targets for reducing import dependence by 2030. France is already home to the biggest facility outside China to process all 17 rare earths, and a deal for Brazilian minerals is under discussion. But many fear that European countries are moving too slowly. That must change.

Russia has burned millions of Ukrainian books, striking at the infrastructure of Ukrainian culture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:28:23 UTC
01:28:23 KST

Another Russian strike has destroyed tens of thousands of Ukrainian books around Kyiv, adding to a summer of attacks that has wiped out millions of copies and damaged the warehouses, printing plants and markets that keep Ukraine’s publishing industry running.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022, Ukrainian publishers, printers, bookstores, warehouses and other parts of the literature industry have repeatedly been hit by Russian attacks.
The destruction has drawn comparisons to earlier Russian and Soviet efforts to suppress the Ukrainian language, culture and national identity, with publishers and cultural figures warning that the current attacks are damaging not only businesses and infrastructure but the means through which Ukrainian culture is produced and preserved.
The latest loss came on 28 August, when a Russian drone struck a Nova Post fulfillment and sorting center in Sviatopetrivske, Kyiv Oblast. More than 60,000 books stored there were destroyed, including books belonging to Ukrainian publishers and retailers such as Vivat, A-BA-BA-HA-LA-MA-HA, Osnovy, Readeat and Book.ua.
The destruction is taking a growing toll on Ukrainian culture
Nova Post director Yevhen Tafiichuk said the strike destroyed the company's most modern robotic fulfillment center, along with books from several publishers and stores. He said the company is working with affected partners to compensate their losses and is moving toward a decentralized fulfillment system to reduce the risk of losing large inventories in a single strike.
“For centuries, the enemy has tried to destroy the Ukrainian language, culture and memory. Once, it burned libraries and banned printing; today, it launches missiles at printing plants and warehouses filled with books,” Tafiichuk said.
The latest destruction comes after the Ukrainian publishing industry estimated that Russian attacks had already destroyed about 13 million books in July and August – nearly a third of the number of books Ukrainian publishers printed during all of 2025.
Russia has burned 13 million Ukrainian books in three months, nearly third of everything country printed in 2025
Another warehouse full of books goes up in flames
The Sviatopetrivske strike hit a logistics facility rather than a publishing house itself, but the consequences spread across much of the book market.
Readeat founder Dmytro Feliksov said more than 60,000 physical books were destroyed and estimated his company's losses at more than UAH 23 million. The warehouse held stock for several publishers and booksellers.
Vivat CEO Yuliia Orlova said the publisher also lost books stored at the Kyiv warehouse in the attack. The company had already begun moving some print runs to other parts of Ukraine, including Lviv, after earlier Russian strikes destroyed publishing infrastructure. But many new releases and books by Ukrainian authors remained in Kyiv.
The same attack destroyed a warehouse used by A-BA-BA-HA-LA-MA-HA to fulfill direct orders. The losses came as publishers were already trying to spread their inventories across multiple locations to reduce the risk posed by Russian strikes.
Millions of books destroyed across Ukraine, publishers hit again and again
On 1 August, a Russian strike on the warehouses of RNK-Ranok destroyed nearly 8 million books, including hundreds of thousands of school textbooks. The Ukrainian Book Institute said the loss from that strike alone was equivalent to about 30% of the country's annual book production.
A separate Russian strike on 19 July destroyed the Konvi printing facility and about 250,000 books belonging to Knyholav, along with print runs and materials belonging to numerous other publishers.
BookChef has suffered some of the largest losses around Kyiv. A Russian strike in July destroyed about 800,000 books at its main warehouse. A second strike in August hit a backup warehouse opened after the first loss, destroying more than 100,000 additional books, Interfax-Ukraine reported.
The attacks have also damaged publishing offices and warehouses. On 16 August, Russian strikes near Kyiv’s Pochaina metro station damaged the offices and warehouses of BookChef and RM, including areas where books were stored.
Kyiv’s Pochaina market also burned
The damage is not limited to modern distribution centers.
On 16 August, a Russian strike set fire to Kyiv’s Pochaina book market, one of the capital’s best-known places to buy new, used and second-hand books. Much of the market burned, with the fire covering more than 2,000 square meters of commercial space.
The market, formerly known as Petrivka, had operated for about 30 years and was a major hub for second-hand books and other goods. Dozens of thousands of books were destroyed, according to local reporting.
The destruction was extensive enough that 60–70% of the market's commercial space was lost. The surviving Bukinist section began reopening later in August, with booksellers returning to trade where their stock had survived, RBC reported.
The market's destruction also meant the loss of a part of Kyiv's book culture that cannot simply be replaced by reprinting new editions. Second-hand books, older editions and used collections had been traded there for generations.
The losses are hitting an already fragile industry
The Ukrainian publishing sector had been growing before Russia's latest attacks, helped in part by rising demand for Ukrainian-language books during the full-scale invasion.
But publishers now face the repeated cost of replacing destroyed print runs, warehouses and equipment while also trying to keep books moving to stores and readers.
Olesia Ostrovska-Liuta, director general of Mystetskyi Arsenal, said the Ukrainian book industry had only recently begun to grow, making the latest losses especially painful.
“Losses are accumulating, while the tools to minimize them are being built extremely slowly,” she said. “Culture will not disappear, but it will once again be drained of its strength.”
Publishers seek help to rebuild and protect a supply chain under attack
The Ukrainian Publishing Association has called for additional support, including war-risk insurance for book stocks, affordable financing to rebuild printing capacity and the restoration of state purchases of books for libraries.
The Ukrainian Book Institute has also appealed for international support for the publishing sector, saying Russia has systematically targeted publishing houses, bookstores, printing facilities and warehouses since the start of the full-scale invasion.
For publishers, the latest strikes show that moving books from a printer to a reader has itself become a wartime vulnerability. A single warehouse can contain the output of dozens of publishers, and losing it can erase months of work and leave books unavailable even when the companies themselves survive.
Nova Post says it is responding by distributing inventory across more locations rather than relying on large centralized facilities. The strategy may help reduce future losses, but it also reflects how deeply Russia’s ongoing attacks have altered the basic infrastructure through which Ukrainians produce, store and buy books.

Cleverly to run ‘classically Conservative’ campaign to be next London mayor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:25:02 UTC
01:25:02 KST

James Cleverly has pledged to run a “classically Conservative” campaign to become the mayor of London, insisting that his victory in the capital would be a stepping stone for Kemi Badenoch to become prime minister.
The former home and foreign secretary denied he had resigned from the shadow cabinet to run for mayor following a shift to the right under Badenoch’s leadership.
However, in a series of interviews on Sunday he avoided speaking about culture war issues, which have been a focus for the Conservative leader.
“I am going to put forward a classic Conservative case to be the mayor of London, and it’s about enterprise, it’s about opportunity,” Cleverly told Times Radio.
“That is a classically Conservative vision, and it will run in parallel to and supportive of Kemi’s plans for the country as a whole.”
If he wins his party’s nomination, Cleverly is expected to run a more moderate campaign than the last Tory candidate, Susan Hall. She drew criticism for claiming there was a “problem with crime” in the black community and was forced to apologise for liking a tweet in 2020 that had a picture of Enoch Powell captioned: “It’s never too late to get London back.” Hall lost to Labour’s Sadiq Khan in 2024, who won with 43.8% of the vote.
Cleverly, who lost the Conservative leadership race to Badenoch, is considered a more moderate voice in a party that has moved to the right as support for Nigel Farage’s rightwing Reform UK has grown.
Giles Dilnot, the editor of Conservative Home, who has worked closely with Cleverly in the past, denied a rift and said he thought it unlikely the MP for Braintree was using his attempt to become mayor as a route to become the next Conservative leader. “There is not a hidden side order of ‘what’s next’ here,” he said.
Asked if Cleverly was likely to seek to put distance between himself and the Tory leader to attract more centre-left voters in the capital, he pointed to Cleverly’s 2024 speech during the Conservative leadership contest in which he called for his party to be “more normal”.
“Mayoral campaigns are often focused on the person – the personality is that extra 10% rather than just the rosette,” Dilnot said. “James is gloriously normal and I wouldn’t be surprised if he’s selling what he is: a normal Londoner who wants the city to succeed.”
Prof Tony Travers, of the London School of Economics, said the restoration of the supplementary vote system in the 2028 London mayoral election – where voters have a preferred first and second choice, with the second choice counted if no one wins more than 50% of the vote – meant Cleverly had to win over voters whose first choice was the Liberal Democrats.
“The last thing Cleverly would want to do is put off Liberal Democrats, whose party has been the main beneficiaries of the Conservatives’ shift to the right in the south of England,” Travers said. “I think we are likely to see him adopt a pre-Brexit traditional, centrist Conservative position.”
The entrance of a Conservative big-hitter into the May 2028 contest will raise further questions about whether Khan, who was first elected in 2016, will run for a fourth term, a question he has thus far avoided.
A YouGov survey this month found that 56% of Londoners thought he should step down and allow a different Labour candidate to stand.
A recent poll for the Mile End Institute, Queen Mary University of London, found that Khan would win a fourth term if he stood despite a surge in support for the Greens. The Savanta survey put Labour on 33%, Reform on 20%, the Conservatives on 18%, the Greens on 14% and the Liberal Democrats on 10%.
If Khan steps out of the running, Dawn Butler, Labour MP for Brent East, is expected to stand, while other potential candidates in the Labour ranks include Rosena Allin-Khan and David Lammy, the former justice secretary.
Cleverly told LBC he thought Khan had “really lost passion for the job”, adding that as a Londoner he wanted to stand against “very anti-London” Andy Burnham.
“Andy Burnham just doesn’t get it,” he said. “He’s got a war with London, and London needs someone to fight its corner.”

Vance, Rubio, or Hegseth? Trump's inner circle quietly prepares for fierce US 2028 race - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:23:11 UTC
01:23:11 KST

Who in US President Donald Trump’s inner circle will succeed him as president in 2028?
That appears to be the question on much of his cabinet’s mind, as Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Vice President JD Vance, and now Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth each weigh presidential runs.
However, voters this November may cut one, or all, of the three men’s political ambitions short.
Trump is placing a significant amount of pressure on Republicans to win the upcoming November midterms to maintain the party’s congressional majority.
Notably, the president is currently polling at a 33% approval rating, an August Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
Trump pressures Republicans to win midterms to maintain congressional majority
Trump has repeatedly said that Republicans have “got to win the midterms,” and has implied that losing them would lead to “very bad things” for US voters.
"I'm here because I love Iowa, but I'm here because we're starting the campaign to win the midterms. Got to win the midterms," Trump said in a January speech in Iowa.
"If we lose the midterms, you'll lose so many of the things that we're talking about, so many of the assets that we're talking about, so many of the tax cuts that we're talking about – and it would lead to very bad things.”
In a separate interview in January with Reuters, Trump expressed frustration that the GOP could lose control of the House of Representatives or the Senate, and cited historical trends that have seen the party in power lose seats in the second year of a presidency.
“It's some deep psychological thing, but when you win the presidency, you don't win the midterms,” Trump said. He boasted that he had accomplished so much that “when you think of it, we shouldn't even have an election.”
But even Trump, though he has tried before, cannot stop an election.
So the question remains: who will his successor be?
Trump has not directly endorsed anyone yet, though he has said he will when the time is right and has privately shared his preferences.
Trump has publicly egged on a contest for his endorsement between Vance and Rubio, and has said that the two running on the same ticket would be his “dream team.”
“By the way, I do believe that’s a dream team. But these are minor details. That does not mean you have my endorsement under any circumstance. But you know … I think it sounds like presidential candidate and vice presidential candidate,” he said in May.
Vance: MAGA heir apparent or Trump's whipping boy?
Trump has praised and disparaged Vance in front of audiences, at times making him seem more like a whipping boy than an heir apparent. In one instance, he notably said he would blame Vance if a deal with Iran fails.
But Vance is still largely seen as the frontrunner to inherit the GOP, and Trump has reportedly said as much in private conversations.
Notably, The Washington Post reported in August that Trump privately told investors in the Oval Office that “at the end of the day, we need to elect JD.”
Some White House sources told the Washington Post that Trump will not endorse any candidate until much later, and that his mind is constantly changing on who to endorse.
Trump later denied the report, saying: “I think he’s great, but we’re way too early to even be thinking about that.”
A March Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 79% of Republicans held a favorable view of Vance, while 19% held a negative view. Some 71% viewed Rubio positively, while 15% viewed him unfavorably.
Vance is associated with MAGA’s younger wing, which helped get Trump into office in 2024 but is reportedly eroding over issues like rising inflation. He courted several Silicon Valley businesspeople for their support in the 2024 election and has continued to court business moguls to help fundraise for the Republican Party.
Additionally, he could attract more working-class voters, given his roots in Ohio and his familial ties to rural Appalachia.
Although his deal with Iran fell through, Vance told his advisers that he believed his role in the talks put him at a political advantage because he helped create a popular agreement to end an unpopular war, according to the Washington Post.
However, some voters have said that Vance is unlikeable and too much of a yes-man for his current role as vice president.
He notoriously called Trump “America’s Hitler” during the president’s 2016 run, before he became his political ally.
Rubio: Tenured international policy hawk who polls better than Vance
Marco Rubio, as previously mentioned, is besting Vance in some hypothetical matchups against Democrats. A May Emerson College survey put Vance with 36% of conservative voter support, with Rubio at 35%.
If Rubio decides to run, he could point to the myriad of global crises that he managed as proof of his leadership skills. In the first half of the term alone, Rubio has managed diplomatic relations regarding Iran and the US’s allies, assisted in rebuilding Venezuela after devastating earthquakes and the ousting of former authoritarian president Nicholas Maduro, and explicitly redefined the US’s foreign aid strategy.
According to the May Emerson College survey, he tends to receive support from older, more educated Republicans and Hispanic voters.
In terms of polls, conservative voters appear to prefer Rubio to Vance in hypothetical head-to-head races against Democrats. In a survey done by Emerson College, Rubio beat Vance in all but one hypothetical race.
Rubio defeated both former vice president Kamala Harris and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in hypothetical races by the same margin, 48% to 43%. Vance, by comparison, narrowly defeats Ocasio-Cortez, 46% to 44%, but loses to Harris by four percentage points.
However, Rubio legally cannot run for president while serving as secretary of state or as a national security adviser.
He has indicated that he intends to finish out the rest of his term in the role; sources close to him told the Washington Post that he has no political campaign waiting in the wings.
Sources close to the secretary of state told the Washington Post that he had reduced his speaking availability to avoid talking about the 2028 election.
Wild card or Liability? Hegseth weighs presidential run
And then, there’s the administration’s current wild card: former Fox News anchor and current Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
NBC reported on Friday that Hegseth has floated the idea to his close associates within the past few months. He reportedly believes that he has attributes that made Trump popular with his core voter base, like his tough-guy attitude and conservative stance on social issues.
“Pete Hegseth should consider running for president,” Chairman of the American Conservative Union Matt Schlapp told NBC. “He’s an impressive guy and has a tremendous amount of energy.”
However, his handling of the conflict with Iran, Signalgate, and conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln could potentially affect his polling with voters. Hegseth hasn't been mentioned in any recent polls about the 2028 elections, since the NBC report came out on Friday.
“MAGA really loves Hegseth because they love the cut of his jib. But you’ve got to deliver the goods. If you want to be secretary of war, you’ve got to win wars,” one pro-Trump operative close to the White House told NBC.
Hegseth, along with Pentagon and White House officials, has discredited the rumors that he is weighing a presidential bid.
The secretary said on Friday that any reports of him weighing a presidential bid were "100% false," adding that his "only job" was making the Department of Defense great.
Be that as it may, he is currently mobilized on the campaign trail during the middle of the US’s conflict with Iran, something that former defense secretaries have abstained from.
Three former defense secretaries, Leon Panetta, Chuck Hagel, and William Cohen, told NBC that Hegseth’s partisan political appearances are something that they deliberately abstained from in the past.
“My God, we’re at war. We’ve got a huge problem,” Hagel, Obama’s defense secretary and former Nebraska senator, told NBC.
“We’ve got a global issue here that we’ve gotten ourselves into with this mess, and what are you doing going to Iowa and campaigning when you should be paying attention to your job?”
It is also worth noting that no defense secretary has ever been president, while several vice presidents and secretaries of state have later made the jump to be commander in chief.
Additionally, Hegseth had several scandals before he was confirmed as secretary of defense, including his drinking habits.
What comes next?
For now, all three men appear to be shrugging off any questions about their candidacy. Rubio has repeatedly downplayed his presidential ambitions despite his previous run against Trump, and has said that he will not run in 2028 if Vance does.
Vance has said he would wait until after the midterm results, and that he doesn’t make decisions “until I absolutely must.”
Hegseth said that reports of him weighing a presidential run were “100% false,” but then campaigned for Republicans in Iowa and Kentucky during an active conflict.
Trump’s popularity has also taken hits for incidents that the three men were directly involved in. Most specifically, the White House’s handling of the war with Iran.
The war has rapidly reshaped the midterms and has affected thousands of Americans’ bank accounts because of the rising cost of gas.
One Reuters/Ipsos poll found that only 31% of US voters approve of the Pentagon’s handling of the war, which has not technically ended.
Another Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 69% of Americans believe Trump had not clearly explained the goals of US military involvement in Iran.
Whoever inherits the mantle will not only have to answer for their role in the conflict, but also accept responsibility for others’ perceived mistakes in the administration. While Vance, Rubio, and Hegseth all successfully tied themselves closely to Trump in 2024, it might hurt their chances of running as individual candidates.
The midterms will help clarify which of these three men can effectively communicate to voters what the GOP looks like post-Trump, and who can distance themselves from the administration’s shortcomings or spin their mistakes in a marketable way.
The race to be the 2028 GOP nominee doesn’t technically start until after the midterms, but in effect, it already has.
Trump’s endorsement will have an enormous impact on the race, but it won’t come anytime soon. In the meantime, the president who remade the GOP in his image may discover that choosing who inherits it is more difficult than choosing who serves beneath him.
Idan Kweller and Reuters contributed to this report.

The Durban Conference 25 years later: A blueprint for anti-Israel demonization - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:22:26 UTC
01:22:26 KST

“Durban was the restarting of the Zionism is Racism campaign. It was the blueprint for accusing Israel of genocide and starvation and war crimes,” Gerald Steinberg, founder and president of NGO Monitor, told The Jerusalem Post on Sunday.
Monday marks 25 years since the “Durban” Conference, officially the UN World Conference Against Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance, held in South Africa from August 31 to September 8, 2001.
Over 12,000 representatives came together to forge a common strategy against discrimination.
However, ironically, the conference has become synonymous with discrimination of the anti-Zionist kind, and is considered by many the birthplace of modern anti-Israel rhetoric.
Preceding the conference was the NGO Forum, which had over 7,000 participants gather to create a pre-planned and coordinated anti-Israel strategy. It was here that the intentional use of words such as “genocide,” “war crimes,” and “apartheid” entered the scene.
UN Resolution 3379 equated Zionism with racism
Six months before Durban, a preparatory conference had taken place in Tehran, although the Islamic Republic of Iran had refused to grant permission to Israeli and Jewish organizations.
In their absence, the delegates drafted a summary document accusing Israel of “ethnic cleansing,” of implementing “a new kind of apartheid” and “a crime against humanity,” and saying Zionism was “based on race superiority” – a document that formed the basis for the NGO declaration at the main conference in Durban.
Ahead of Durban, Secretary of State Colin Powell warned the UN officials that the US would not participate if the agenda was used to restart the Zionism is racism campaign.
The UN high commissioner at the time, Mary Robinson, promised them that this would not happen, but when they arrived, they found no change. The US and Israel ultimately walked out of the conference.
The final NGO declaration called for the restoration of UN Resolution 3379 equating Zionism with racism and demanded the application of all measures used against apartheid South Africa to Israel.
Steinberg told the Post that Durban was the restarting of the Zionism is Racism campaign that had been run 26 years earlier in 1975 by the Soviet Union and the Arab League.
The language itself can actually be traced back to 1948, and the use of the term Nakba and “Israel is doing to the Palestinians what Germans did to the Jews.” However, this did not gain so much traction outside of Palestinian spheres.
The difference at Durban, Steinberg continued, was that it became legitimate, mostly due to the commandeering of non-governmental organizations under the label of human rights.
“And that has been the engine that has driven the demonization of Israel and language like genocide, starvation, deliberate killing of children, war crimes,” Steinberg told the Post.
Steinberg said the specific strategies developed during Durban have been refined and expanded over the last 25 years, and that NGOs keep coming back to the same language and the same processes that were first used at Durban.
“At the Durban NGO forum there was no debate – they adopted a plan of action naming Israel specifically and repeatedly as a genocidal state, committing war crimes, ethnic cleansing, apartheid, and then they established mechanisms for the complete isolation of Israel. Nothing there was incidental or accidental.”
Durban is also where the BDS movement began, and where the International Criminal Court was chosen as the appropriate body to label Israel as the “world’s biggest violator of international law,” Steinberg continued.
Implementation of strategy
Steinberg said the first time NGOs rolled out the new strategy was six months after the Durban conference with the Jenin Massacre myth.
In April 2002, multiple international media outlets and NGOs spread unverified claims that the Israeli military deliberately killed hundreds of civilians during the Battle of Jenin. Rumors claimed 500 people had been massacred and buried in mass graves.
Amnesty International and Christian Aid were instrumental in spreading the rumor.
However, subsequent investigations by human rights organizations (including Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International) found no evidence of a massacre.
“It was obviously a lie, but it got a lot of traction. Journalists picked it up. NGOs spoke of Israeli war crimes, and they repeated that all the way through the last 25 years,” said Steinberg.
“Durban was a blueprint which went beyond calling Zionism racism, but added genocide, starvation, war crimes, and all those other elements.”
The same thing has happened time and time again, he continued.
“Every single time there was a military clash or a terrorist clash, and Israel responded – the 2006 Lebanon war, the 2008-2009 first Gaza war, Operation Cast Lead, the Goldstone Report, Operation Protective Edge – all those mechanisms were trotted out.
“The condemnation of Israel, the fact-finding commissions, the NGO reports, social media.
“Then, when October 7 started, they had already practiced all of the elements of the Durban strategy. It just exploded in a much greater magnitude, but it was all there in all of the years before.”
Launching NGO Monitor
In response to what he was seeing and the bastardization of the role of NGOs, Steinberg launched NGO Monitor.
“Having watched this process take place and expressing my concerns and seeing the amount of power and influence of NGOs, and how the UN went along with it, I thought I could do a project and document the political role of NGOs, and particularly the manipulation of the language of human rights and the mechanisms of human rights,” he told the Post.
“I thought, ‘I can do that for a few years as an academic, write a couple of articles, maybe a book, and have some graduate students.’
“It was supposed to be a three-year project at a university, and it turned into NGO Monitor, because the deeper that I dug in understanding the NGO industry, and I began to see it as an industry, the more I realized how much power and influence they have, and how little attention was being paid.
“There are huge amounts of money going into these organizations which have no accountability, no democratic frameworks; all of their decisions are made in secret, behind closed doors.”
Antisemitism at Durban
Another key part of the Durban conference, aside from the targeting of Israel, was the shocking and overt displays of antisemitism.
At the forum, NGOs sold copies of The Protocols of the Elders of Zion.
Pamphlets were also distributed showing Hitler’s photograph with text reading: “What if I had won? The good thing is there would have been no Israel and no Palestinian’s [sic] bloodshed.”
There were multiple reported examples of Holocaust revisionism and Jewish members being told: “Blood was on their hands.”
Holocaust survivor and US Congressman Tom Lantos called the Durban Conference “the most sickening display of hate for Jews I have seen since the Nazi period.”
Former minister of justice and attorney-general of Canada Irwin Cotler said, “If 9/11 was the Kristallnacht of terror, then Durban was the Mein Kampf.”
There was one notable outcome of this Jew-hatred: the gradual writing of what’s now called the Working Definition of Antisemitism of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA).
In the immediate aftermath of Durban, Steinberg said many Jewish leaders came together and discussed the urgency of developing a modern definition of antisemitism to reflect what they saw at the forum.
The definition was first published in 2005 by the European Monitoring Center on Racism and Xenophobia. It was then officially adopted by the IHRA in 2016.
