HOW CHINA’S 12345 HOTLINE IS REWIRING CITIZEN SERVICES
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:00:16 UTC
01:00:16 KST

HOW CHINA’S 12345 HOTLINE IS REWIRING CITIZEN SERVICES
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
In cities around the world, the mechanics of local government often grind slowly: a pothole reported but not repaired, a noise complaint logged but unanswered, a maze of departments passing responsibility from one counter to another. Yet across China, a simple five-digit number—12345—is reshaping how governments respond to citizens and, increasingly, how they anticipate problems before they arise.
What began decades ago as a basic telephone hotline has evolved into one of the most citizen-centric and innovative public sector projects in urban governance. For Professor Alfred Tat-Kei HO, Dean of the College of Liberal Arts and Social Sciences (CLASS) at City University of Hong Kong (CityUHK), the system represents something rare: a smart-city vision that has moved from rhetoric to reality.
“The dream, the vision was there. Everybody talked about that globally,” says Ho. “Citizen service should be easy, should be convenient, should be accountable, should be participatory, should be transparent. But who has been able to implement that vision and really carry it out effectively? Not many cities in the world, and yet Chinese cities are now leading the way.”
From Fragmentation to One-stop Governance
The intellectual roots of 12345 hotline lie in earlier reforms abroad. The US led the early stage of e-government reform in the world. Also, emergency hotlines such as 911 were eventually complemented by 311 call and web-based systems for non-emergency complaints such as barking dogs and garbage collection. The idea was to create a single access point for everyday civic concerns.
Ho himself wrote in 2002 about the possibility of “one-stop shopping” for city services, envisioning an integrated platform where citizens could file complaints online and departments would coordinate behind the scenes. The promise was greater responsiveness and accountability.
But implementation proved difficult. Governments needed technical capacity to standardise complaints, route them accurately, track progress and close cases. They also needed political will and cross-departmental cooperation. Without that, complaints languished, citizens grew frustrated and agencies retreated into silos. “It is a good vision, but it’s not easy to implement,” Ho notes. Governments require “a lot of capacity … a lot of IT investment … cross-departmental coordination”.
Building the Infrastructure for Responsiveness
China’s 12345 system, first launched in Shenyang more than 40 years ago, was transformed roughly 15 years ago through e-government reforms. Today it operates as a multi-channel platform: citizens can call, use smartphone apps, submit requests via websites, or visit civic centres in person.
Behind the scenes, complaints are converted into standardised digital work orders and routed automatically to the relevant department. Response times are monitored, often with expectations of resolution within 48 hours. In many cities, officials call or email residents to confirm that issues have been resolved.
The scale is formidable. In Beijing alone, the system handles more than 25 million calls annually. At the city’s civic centre, a room-sized dashboard displays real-time data: number of incoming calls, categories of complaints, geographic hotspots. The information is visible to policymakers, managers, frontline workers and community stakeholders.
“With that kind of data, you can track the issues and allocate internal resources to address those problems more effectively,” says Ho.
This is not simply a customer service improvement. It is an administrative redesign that integrates citizen input directly into the machinery of government.
The latest evolution of 12345 hotline pushes the model beyond reactive complaint handling toward predictive governance. Cities are combining hotline data with other datasets—including traffic flows from ride-hailing platforms—to identify patterns before they become crises.
For example, if congestion on a particular street steadily worsens at rush hour, planners can consider expanding the road or building parking nearby. “Through analytics, you not only address issues proactively, but even prevent those issues,” says Ho.
Some cities have extended monitoring to publicly available social media posts. In one widely reported case, an elderly resident posted online about a dangerous pavement in her neighbourhood. Officials detected the post, contacted her directly and dispatched a repair team the same day. “They don’t even need to wait for citizens to pick up a phone to complain,” Ho says.
A Cultural Shift in Public Service
Aside from technology, Ho emphasises a parallel cultural shift—moving away from narrow departmental mandates toward collaborative problem-solving.
In one Beijing case, an elderly woman living in a fifth-floor walk-up requested help installing an elevator. Since it is technically not a standard government responsibility, instead of rejecting the request, hotline staff and district officials spent nearly a year mediating among apartment owners. The elevator was eventually installed.
“The 12345 system essentially says: ‘You know what? I notice you have a problem. Let me see how we can rally different people to help you solve that problem’,” Ho explains. 
This cross-sectoral approach brings together government departments, neighbourhood associations, private actors and residents themselves. It requires an elaborate IT backbone and a mindset change.
“It’s a cultural shift to: we are here to help,” Ho says.
Implications Beyond Mainland China
The implications extend beyond the mainland. In Hong Kong, the 1823 hotline functions largely as a referral system, with fragmented authority across departments. Ho argues that while Hong Kong’s “small government” model differs from mainland cities, it could develop its own version of integrated service delivery by leveraging NGOs and community organisations more systematically.
“The challenge for Hong Kong is to build a system that is unique, grounded in the Hong Kong context,” he says, emphasising cross-sector partnerships.
As cities worldwide confront aging populations, infrastructure strain and climate pressures, the lesson of 12345 hotline is not merely technological. It is institutional. By integrating citizen voices into data systems, aligning departments under shared accountability, and shifting from reactive fixes to predictive planning, governments can transform complaints into a feedback engine for continuous improvement.
In that sense, 12345 is more than a hotline. It is a blueprint for how public governance can evolve from bureaucratic fragmentation toward coordinated, data-driven and citizen-centred innovation.

Brain stimulation helps socially anxious individuals control avoidance behaviors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:00:16 UTC
01:00:16 KST

Researchers have found that applying a specific pattern of mild electrical stimulation to the brain can help individuals with high social anxiety better control their automatic avoidance behaviors. By synchronizing the rhythmic activity between the brain’s cognitive control and movement centers, the treatment improved participants’ ability to override their immediate emotional impulses. The findings from this small study were published in The Journal of Neuroscience.
Social anxiety disorder is characterized by an intense fear of social judgment and a strong urge to avoid situations that might cause distress. This behavioral avoidance brings immediate, temporary relief. However, this same avoidance ultimately maintains the psychological condition by preventing individuals from experiencing the situations and learning that they are actually safe.
Standard treatments like exposure therapy require patients to confront their fears directly. People with severe social anxiety often struggle to override their automatic urge to flee, which can limit the effectiveness of such therapies. Overcoming this pattern requires a psychological mechanism called emotional action control, which is the brain’s ability to suppress automatic reactions and execute a different planned response.
Brain regions coordinate this kind of control by communicating through rhythmic electrical impulses, commonly known as brainwaves. When a person needs to override an automatic behavior, an area responsible for cognitive control called the lateral prefrontal cortex must sync its low-frequency rhythms with the high-frequency rhythms of the sensorimotor cortex. The sensorimotor cortex is the brain region that ultimately plans and executes physical movements.
Prior studies demonstrated that artificially enhancing this synchronization could improve emotional control in people without anxiety. A team of researchers from Radboud University in the Netherlands, led by Sjoerd Meijer and Bob Bramson, wanted to test if this intervention could be adapted for a clinical population. They designed an experiment to see if rhythmic stimulation could help individuals who struggle with intense social anxiety.
The researchers recruited 49 adults who were screened using the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale, a standard clinical questionnaire. Because the participant count was less than 50, this is considered a small study. The research team focused entirely on individuals whose anxiety scores indicated a high likelihood of experiencing daily social anxiety disorder symptoms.
During the experiment, participants lay inside a functional magnetic resonance imaging scanner. This machine tracks blood oxygen levels in the brain to measure dynamic changes in neural activity. Participants held a joystick on their abdomen and viewed images of happy and angry faces on a computer screen.
In the standard version of the task, participants were instructed to pull the joystick toward themselves when they saw a happy face and push it away when they saw an angry face. This instruction aligns with natural human tendencies to approach positive stimuli and avoid negative ones.
In the challenging version of the task, the rules were reversed. Participants had to push the joystick away for happy faces and pull it toward themselves for angry faces. This specific setup forced the participants to exert mental effort to override their automatic emotional impulses to pull away from perceived threats.
While the participants performed these tasks, the researchers applied a technique called dual-site transcranial alternating current stimulation. This noninvasive intervention uses specialized, ring-shaped electrodes placed directly on the scalp. The device delivers weak, oscillating electrical currents designed to mimic and influence the brain’s natural internal rhythms.
The researchers tested three different stimulation conditions. The first was an in-phase condition designed to synchronize the lateral prefrontal cortex and the sensorimotor cortex. The second was an anti-phase condition designed to disrupt their synchronization. The third was a sham condition where the stimulation was turned off almost immediately, serving as a placebo baseline to compare against.
The three stimulation conditions alternated in short blocks of about one minute each. Between blocks, the researchers included pause periods to allow the effects of the previous stimulation to wash out. This ensured that each testing block remained independent of the others.
The researchers found that participants performed better at the task during the in-phase stimulation. They made fewer errors on the challenging, reversed-rule task compared to the baseline sham condition. The anti-phase stimulation did not produce statistically significant performance benefits.
The brain imaging data revealed that the in-phase stimulation successfully strengthened the functional connection between the targeted prefrontal and sensorimotor regions. The electrical intervention also altered the activity of the amygdala, a deep and evolutionarily older brain structure that processes raw emotions like fear and generates automatic defensive reactions.
During in-phase stimulation, the amygdala exerted less influence over the participants’ physical joystick movements. The researchers noted that the intervention seemed to strengthen the brain’s goal-directed pathways. This allowed the prefrontal cortex to successfully compete with the emotional signals coming from the amygdala at the level of physical execution.
The behavioral benefits varied from person to person. The improvements were largest in individuals whose prefrontal cortex showed the strongest physiological response to the electrical stimulation. Participants with the highest self-reported trait anxiety tended to show the strongest neural responses to the intervention.
The brain scans also revealed a difference in how highly anxious participants process control compared to general populations. Rather than using the frontal pole to integrate emotions and goals, the anxious participants relied heavily on the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. This specific subregion is known for strict rule-based processing, suggesting that anxious individuals must rely on rigid rules to bypass their easily overwhelmed emotional centers.
The study relies on functional magnetic resonance imaging, which tracks blood oxygen levels rather than direct electrical brainwaves. While the researchers manipulated the electrical phases at the scalp, they could not directly measure the resulting changes in the participants’ actual brainwaves during the task.
There was high individual variation in how strongly the participants’ brains reacted to the stimulation. Standardized stimulation protocols may not work equally well for everyone. Individual differences in head anatomy and natural brain activity alter how the electrical currents travel through the skull and interact with neural tissue.
Future research might use individualized computer models to adjust the electrical currents based on a person’s specific brain structure. Scientists also need to investigate whether this type of intervention can produce lasting changes in avoidance behavior in real-world social settings. This might eventually involve testing the stimulation as a tool to enhance traditional exposure therapy.
The study, “Improving Emotion Control in Social Anxiety by Targeting Rhythmic Brain Circuits,” was authored by Sjoerd Meijer, Bob Bramson, Ivan Toni, and Karin Roelofs.

Rohingya crisis: Aid falls and hope fades
UNHCR’s Bangladesh representative, Ivo Freisen, warns that dwindling aid is driving hope down among Rohingya refugees.
Nine years after the mass exodus of Rohingya refugees from Myanmar, more than one million stateless people remain in overcrowded camps in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar. The crisis is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain as humanitarian funding declines; refugee numbers grow and living conditions deteriorate.
In this discussion, UNHCR representative in Bangladesh, Ivo Freisen, says hope is fading as desperation grows, with about 95 percent of mainly Muslim Rohingya refugees relying fully or largely on humanitarian assistance. He warns that limited education and opportunities are pushing some young Rohingya to risk dangerous sea journeys in search of a better life.
Freijsen says a lasting solution depends on creating conditions for a safe, voluntary and sustainable return to Myanmar, including addressing discrimination, citizenship and freedom of movement.

Remains exhumed in Volyn villages of Ostrivky and Volia Ostrovetska reburied
This was reported by Suspilne Lutsk, according to Ukrinform.
“Over a hundred people gathered for the reburial. Representatives from both the Polish and Ukrainian sides arrived to pay their last respects to the deceased,” the report states.
A burial pit was dug on the grounds of the former village of Ostrivky, at the entrance to the memorial. It contains 55 wooden coffins. Polish and Ukrainian priests recited prayers for the repose of the souls of those who died during World War II.
Numerous representatives of Polish and Ukrainian authorities, as well as descendants of residents of the former villages of Ostrivky and Volia Ostrovetska, took part in the ceremony. According to RMF24, those present included Piotr Zgorzelski, Deputy Speaker of the Polish Sejm; Marta Chenkovska, Minister of Culture and National Heritage; and Karol Polejowski, Deputy Director of the Institute of National Remembrance. Also in attendance were former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki and Paweł Kowal, Chair of the Sejm Committee on Foreign Affairs. The Ukrainian side was represented, among others, by Deputy Minister of Culture Ivan Verbytskyi.
As reported by Ukrinform, during exhumation investigations that took place from July 14 to August 7, the remains of 48 people were found on the territory of the former village of Volia Ostrovetska, and the remains of six people were found in the village of Ostrivky. The remains of one person were exhumed in the village of Ostrivky near the cemetery across from the memorial; however, the date of burial is still being determined.
The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance reported that the remains of men, women, and children were exhumed. Samples were collected during the work for DNA analysis.

Germany's Christian Churches take a stand against far right

Germany's Christian Churches take a stand against far right
August 30, 2026
Flags flutter in the wind outside Magdeburg's Catholic cathedral. "Love thy neighbor, dialogue, human dignity, solidarity. VOTE CONSCIOUSLY!", they proclaim. Just a few minutes' walk away, a sign on the building of the Protestant Cathedral Congregation reads: "DIVERSITY IS DIVINE." Other Protestant churches across the region display banners reading "Heart Instead of Hate."
For many months now, warnings about the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is particularly strong in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, have been part of everyday church life. During a sermon at a pilgrimage event in September 2025, Magdeburg Bishop Gerhard Feige remarked almost in passing that pilgrims of hope do not cast their votes on a whim, "into the blue." He was interrupted by prolonged applause — blue is the AfD's party color.
The AfD holds a commanding lead in the polls ahead of the state election on September 6. The prospect of a government led by the party alone appears increasingly plausible. At the same time, Germany's domestic intelligence agency has classified the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt branch as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organization.
Churches speak out against AfD
In Saxony-Anhalt, 10% of the population is Protestant and 3% is Catholic; only a few thousand people belong to the Muslim or Jewish faiths.
More than 85% of the state's 2.1 million residents have no religious affiliation, compared with a national average of 47%. Nevertheless, the churches play an important role as defenders of democracy — and that, apparently, is precisely what troubles the AfD.
With its so-called government program, adopted at a state party conference in April, the party launched a broadside against both the Protestant and Catholic churches. The program calls for an end to all state payments to the two churches and for the abolition of church tax collection by public authorities, a service for which the churches themselves pay.
In cases of so-called church asylum, where refugees seek shelter on church premises for fear of renewed persecution in their countries of origin, the AfD is calling for churches to be held financially accountable on a "permanent" basis.
The Protestant Academy of Saxony-Anhalt should also no longer receive any state funding whatsoever. The reason, according to the AfD, is its "political agitation in line with the established parties: climate dogma, gender ideology, and the rainbow cult." The academy is said to advocate "unchecked mass immigration." Yet in scarcely any German federal state is the proportion of foreign nationals as low as it is in Saxony-Anhalt.
From estrangement to open confrontation
The sharpness of the criticism goes far beyond anything typically heard from other regional branches of the Alternative for Germany or from the party's national leadership. Long gone are the days when representatives of the then-emerging party complained about not being invited to church congresses or Catholic conventions.
In February 2024, the plenary assembly of the German Catholic Bishops' Conference unanimously adopted a declaration entitled "Ethnic Nationalism and Christianity are Incompatible." In it, the bishops identified an ethnonationalist mindset within the AfD and spoke of a "genuine right-wing extremism." The document was prompted by the state elections scheduled to take place later that year in the eastern German states of Thuringia, Saxony, and Brandenburg. Now, in September 2026, elections are due to follow in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.
At present, the confrontation between the AfD and the churches is nowhere more intense than in Saxony-Anhalt.
For Bishop Feige, the AfD's current direction is "without question" an expression of ethnonationalism. "Until now, Saxony-Anhalt's motto has been 'Thinking Modern'. The AfD wants to replace it with 'Thinking German'," he told DW. "The AfD's election posters speak a very clear language: 'Save your country', 'Take your country back', 'Deport from day one!' What else could that be but ethnonationalism?"
The 74-year-old said he "could never have imagined that so many people today could once again be so easily led astray, or that arsonists, pied pipers and respectable-looking agitators could emerge, and that so many would fall for them."
As an example, Feige cited the so-called flag assembly that the AfD wants to reintroduce in the state's schools: the raising of the flag and the singing of the national anthem. "This existed during the Nazi era and was later adopted by the GDR," he said, referring to the former East Germany. "And now it is supposed to return? I find that inconceivable."
Both major Christian churches emphasize they are speaking out not against a particular party, but in defense of a Christian view of humanity. Whether the issue is climate protection and the safeguarding of creation or the treatment of strangers, the churches' interventions are "primarily not political messages, but Christian ones, and should not be interpreted as an endorsement of any particular political party," Friedrich Kramer, bishop of the Protestant Church in central Germany, recently told the online magazine Die Eule.
Religious freedom, according to the AfD
Jews and Jewish life, incidentally, are never mentioned in the government program. By contrast, Islam appears repeatedly. According to the AfD, it will "restore religious freedom to appropriate limits." Islam is described as a "religion alien to our culture." Freedom of religion, the party argues, does not oblige Germans to "fulfill every demand of the Islamic lobby."
Representatives of the state's Jewish association, which includes the synagogue of the Jewish community of Halle targeted in a 2019 right-wing extremist attack, as well as representatives of the largest mosque congregation in the state, declined to comment when asked.
Notably, the AfD's platform speaks of a "Christian mission" that, in its view, the churches supported by church tax, which it labels the "church-tax churches," no longer fulfill. This evokes the support that US President Donald Trump receives from influential evangelical and conservative Christian groups in the United States. In Saxony-Anhalt, however, there is only a limited presence of comparable religious milieus.
Why bishops are sounding the alarm
"A government involving the AfD would have devastating consequences," Kramer said. That is why, he added, cultural institutions and civil society organizations are joining forces to warn against the AfD.
His Catholic counterpart, Feige, likewise cautioned against "downplaying" the prospect of an AfD-led government. During the election campaign, he said, the party is presenting itself "with messianic ideas" and promoting slogans such as "Everything will be fine" or "Anything is possible."
Because the AfD's lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, "comes across as highly polished and enthusiastic," some people ask what could possibly be "right-wing extremist or dangerous" about him. "But behind him stand forces that give cause for concern," said Feige. "If an AfD single-party government comes to power here, it will be a pilot project. Then Saxony-Anhalt will become a gateway to national politics."
This article was originally written in German.

Germany's Christian Churches take a stand against far right
August 30, 2026

Ukrainian drones destroy Russian air defense, radar systems at Yeysk, Millerovo airfields
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
15:54:07 UTC

Ukrainian drones destroy Russian air defense, radar systems at Yeysk, Millerovo airfields
Ukraine conducted overnight long-range strikes on Russian military infrastructure, destroying air defense and radar systems at two military airfields, Unmanned Systems Forces Commander Robert "Madyar" Brovdi said Aug. 30.
Madyar said Ukrainian drones targeted the Yeysk airfield in Russia's Krasnodar Krai and the Millerovo airfield in Rostov Oblast.
According to Madyar, Ukrainian forces destroyed a Russian Pantsir-S1 air defense system, a Sopka-2 radar, and an aviation weapons depot at the Yeysk airfield. They also destroyed Kasta 2E2, RSP-27, and Nebo-SV radar systems, as well as aviation facilities and a depot at the Millerovo airfield, he said.
The destruction of the Russian air defense and radar systems was confirmed by additional reconnaissance, Madyar said.
He said the main target of the operation was a DRL-27 module of Russia's RSP-27 aircraft landing radar system at Millerovo. The radar is used both to detect aerial targets and to control air traffic at the airfield, working together with a PRL-27 landing radar.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claims.
The strikes are part of Ukraine's intensifying campaign against the Russian military and energy infrastructure. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Aug. 28 that Ukraine should significantly increase the frequency of its long-range drone strikes against Russia, setting a goal of launching 1,000 such drones a day.
Ukraine currently launches more than 300 long-range drones on average each day, Zelensky said, arguing that the number needs to rise as Russia intensifies its aerial attacks against Ukrainian cities.
Ukraine has increasingly used long-range drones to strike Russian military and energy infrastructure far behind the front line, while Russia continues to launch large-scale drone and missile attacks against Ukrainian cities.

Venezuela oil 'gift' to refill American reserves; Canadian businesses 'pour into' US: Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
15:53:25 UTC
00:53:25 KST

US President Donald Trump has said that oil from a recently struck deal with Venezuela would be used to replenish the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which has been drawn down sharply in recent years in response to global supply disruptions and high fuel prices and that Canadian businesses are rapidly relocating to the US.
Trump said in a social media post on Sunday that the “topping up" process would begin shortly, describing the Venezuelan oil as a "gift from Venezuela to the people of the United States".
It remains unclear how quickly the deal could supply oil to the reserve or provide any near-term benefit to US motorists.
The agreement, announced by Trump on Friday, aims to revive Venezuela’s battered oil industry. However, significant investment and infrastructure work will be needed before production can rise substantially.
The reserve held about 290 million barrels as of August 21, near a 44-year low, after the US drew down its stockpile under both the Biden and Trump administrations in response to global supply disruptions, including the Russia-Ukraine war and the war with Iran.
On Canada
Trump also stated that Canadian businesses are rapidly relocating to the US as trade hostilities between the two neighbouring nations intensify.
“Canadian businesses are pouring into the United States. We want to make our own cars, etc. That’s what’s going to happen,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
He asserted that Canada has been “ripping us off for years” and vowed that the current economic relationship would be fundamentally altered.
It remains unknown exactly which Canadian firms have initiated relocation plans or how much capital is moving across the border.
The US president’s remarks follow the imposition of 50 percent US tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods on August 22 and his recent directive to impose a 50 percent tariff on all Canadian cars, trucks, and steel starting Jan. 1, 2027.
Trump maintains that these measures are necessary to address a trade deficit exceeding $60 billion. He has repeatedly urged manufacturers to move their operations to American soil to secure "zero tariffs".
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has rejected the US approach, labelling the new levies a "miscalculation" and an attempt to "hurt and divide" Canada. Carney recently stated that the country is "at war" over trade and announced that Ottawa will implement reciprocal tariffs on $20 billion worth of US imports beginning September 8.

Trump says US will refill its petroleum reserves using Venezuelan oil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
15:50:45 UTC
00:50:45 KST

Trump says US will refill its petroleum reserves using Venezuelan oil
President Donald Trump says in a post that the 'topping out' process will begin shortly.
United States President Donald Trump has said on social media that oil from a recently struck deal with Venezuela will be used to replenish the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, an oil stockpile that the country keeps for emergencies and that has been drawn down sharply in recent years to respond to global supply disruptions and high fuel prices.
The US president wrote on Truth Social, the social media platform he owns, that the reserve had been made “virtually” empty, while blaming former US President Joe Biden.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3What’s behind the US deal to seize control of Venezuelan oil reserves?
- list 2 of 3Venezuela says it retains ‘sovereignty’ following US oil deal
- list 3 of 3Delcy Rodriguez says Venezuela ‘retains sovereignty’ despite US oil deal
Trump said in the post that the “topping out” process will begin shortly, describing the Venezuelan oil as a “Gift from Venezuela to the People of the United States”.
It is unclear how quickly the Venezuela deal could provide oil for the reserve or deliver any near-term benefit to US motorists. The agreement Trump announced on Friday is aimed at reviving Venezuela’s battered oil industry, but it will require significant investment and infrastructure work before production can rise substantially.
The US reserve held about 290 million barrels as of August 21, near a 44-year low, after the US drew down its stockpile under both the Biden and Trump administrations in response to global supply disruptions, including Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the current US-Israel war on Iran.
The “historic” deal with Washington to hand over 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil will last 25 years and allow Venezuela to develop its oil industry while preserving “ownership of and sovereignty” of its resources, Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez said in a televised address on Saturday.
The project envisages the development of 17 strategic oilfields with an initial production target of 1.5 million barrels per day, she said.
The broader plan also includes the development of eight greenfield oil blocks as part of a wider expansion of the country’s energy sector.
Under the deal, $19 from every barrel of oil produced and sold to the US will flow to Caracas, an arrangement that could be worth $209bn per year to Venezuela, depending on oil prices, Rodriguez said.
Venezuela will keep ownership of its natural resources “while leveraging capital, technology and operational expertise to support the recovery of a strategic industry that has been severely affected by sanctions”, she said.
Caracas has been under pressure to act in line with Washington’s demands since January, after US special forces abducted then-Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and Venezuela’s Supreme Court handed leadership over to his vice president, Rodriguez.

Relief and sorrow in Iceland after EU membership talks referendum fails
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
15:49:09 UTC
00:49:09 KST

The result of the referendum has also been hailed by right-wing figures from across the UK and France.
A mix of relief and dejection spread across Iceland on Sunday after the country narrowly voted "No" to resuming talks with the European Union on potential membership.
Many Icelanders had gathered in the capital Reykjavík to follow the results as they came in overnight, with both supporters and opponents of accession negotiations celebrating as the count progressed.
In Saturday's vote, 52.8% rejected resuming EU entry talks, while 47.2% voted "Yes," according to public broadcaster RÚV.
Speaking from Reykjavík after the result was called, Skuli Olafsson Skuli, a pastor, said he was "a little bit relieved."
"It has been quite aggressive, this discussion," he said. "But now I hope the opposing parties will find a way to make this community here in Iceland a little bit better just by using our own methods and, of course, those relations we have with Europe, America, and Asia."
Anna Maria Bogadottir, an artist, said the outcome of the vote had left her "in a kind of denial."
"It's hard to grasp that it's a no," she added.
Iceland's centre-left prime minister, Kristrún Frostadóttir, has pledged to "respect" the result while also praising the high voter turnout.
"It's obvious that close to half of the country wanted to continue these negotiations, but over half of the population did not. We will respect that result," Frostadóttir told a press conference on Sunday.
"The fact that we got people to the table on a matter like this is extremely important for us," she continued. "It gives us a stronger mandate to make a decision on this matter."
Writing on X, former Icelandic President Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson - who had backed the "No" campaign - said the "nation has spoken."
The result of the referendum has also been hailed by right-wing figures from across the UK and France.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage - who was a key supporter of Brexit - congratulated Iceland on "voting to keep their independence."
France's Marine Le Pen added: "At a time when some are pushing for greater federalism and the transfer of sovereignty to the European Commission, this vote serves as a reminder that another Europe is possible – a Europe of free, sovereign nations cooperating voluntarily on matters of common interest."
For its part, the European Commission offered a short statement on the result, saying it "takes note of the outcome" and that it "respects the choice of the Icelandic people."
Iceland first applied for EU membership in 2009 in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, with the Commission issuing a favourable opinion in February 2010. A new Eurosceptic government ended talks in 2013.

NHS doctor denies posting social media support for Hamas in London court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
15:47:10 UTC
00:47:10 KST

A doctor working in Britain’s state-funded National Health Service (NHS) has denied posting social media content supporting Hamas during a court appearance at London’s Central Criminal Court, the Old Bailey, on Friday.
According to local news outlets, Dr. Rahmeh Aladwan, 32, pleaded not guilty to four counts of expressing support for a proscribed organization.
She also denied one count of stirring up racial hatred in written material and a further count of using words that were threatening or abusive.
According to the charge sheet, the disputed social media posts were published between July and December last year.
The court previously heard that Aladwan allegedly wrote, “I don’t condemn Hamas. I don’t condemn October 7,” alongside “I condemn the existence of Israel” in a post in July.
'Free thr world from Jewish supremacy,' 'Glory to the Palestinian resistance'
Further charges allege that in December last year, she posted, “Free the world from Jewish supremacy.”
The court was also previously told that around the anniversary of the October 7 attack, she allegedly posted an image of a bulldozer accompanied by text reading, “Glory to the Palestinian resistance.”
Aladwan was arrested at her home in Pilning, South Gloucestershire, and formally charged with the six offenses in March. Appearing via video link for Friday’s hearing, she entered her not-guilty pleas before the court.
The defendant was granted continued bail and will face trial at Bristol Crown Court beginning in March next year.
The criminal prosecution follows a series of disciplinary actions initiated against Aladwan by British medical regulators.
In November 2025, the Medical Practitioners Tribunal Service suspended her medical license for 15 months after concluding that her online conduct fell well below professional standards. During the tribunal proceedings,
General Medical Council proceedings detailed that Aladwan had published material promoting antisemitic tropes, justifying terrorism, and targeting colleagues, following formal complaints and evidence packages submitted by advocacy groups including UK Lawyers for Israel (UKLFI) and the Campaign Against Antisemitism (CAA) that raised alarms over patient safety and workplace inclusion.
UKLFI submitted evidence packages regarding Aladwan’s social media posts to the General Medical Council, which prompted her regulatory referral and subsequent 15-month suspension starting in November 2025 pending a full hearing.
Social media posts repeatedly crossed into terror support, antisemitism
Detailing their intervention, UKLFI shared a statement with The Jerusalem Post: “Our report detailed multiple instances where her public social media posts appeared to cross the line from political expression into unlawful support for terrorism or antisemitism.
“She repeatedly posted narratives framing the events of October 7, 2023, as acts of ‘resistance,’ arguing that the conflict did not start on that date and that all Israelis were complicit settlers, effectively attempting to justify Hamas’s massacres.
“She also aggressively denied and minimized the verified atrocities, systematic rapes, and hostage-taking committed by Hamas. Her posts appeared to defend and support the terrorist group’s propaganda.”
The statement continued, noting that she “spread harmful conspiracy theories, promoting debunked claims such as that Israel funded ISIS and that the Israeli military targeted its own citizens at the Nova music festival.
“She also published posts comparing Israeli actions to Nazi crimes and the Holocaust, which would likely stir up racial and religious hatred.”
Concluding their assessment, UKLFI noted, “We believed at the time, and continue to believe, that such conduct fundamentally undermines public confidence in the medical profession and violates the professional duties expected of registered doctors.
“Dr. Aladwan is one of a number of doctors in the UK who are being investigated by their regulator for similar conduct.”
Reacting to the court proceedings, Stephen Silverman, director of Investigations and Enforcement at the CAA, said in a statement to the Post, “It’s about time this doctor was in the dock.
“Far from being an isolated case, these sentiments and rhetoric are at risk of becoming normalized in our healthcare system. Part of the reason is the lack of repercussions.”
“A tribunal was happy for this doctor to keep working while her regulator investigated her, only to reverse its decision after pressure, including by us,” Silverman added.
“Meanwhile, the investigation itself has been ongoing for years now, and she is now in court on terrorism charges.
“This is just the tip of the iceberg: there are many more practitioners under investigation that go on forever by regulators that are plainly failing to uphold professional standards in our hospitals.”

Transcript: Rep. John James on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Aug. 30, 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
15:47:07 UTC
00:47:07 KST

Transcript: Rep. John James on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Aug. 30, 2026
The following is the transcript of the interview with Rep. John James, Republican of Michigan, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Aug. 30, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And we're back with Michigan Congressman John James, who is also the Republican nominee for governor in his state. He joins us from Rockford, Michigan. Good morning to you, Congressman.
REP. JOHN JAMES: Hey, Margaret. Good morning. Thank you so much for having me on. I'm really excited because in a state like Michigan, we have the most extreme ticket running with Abdel Al Sayed and Jocelyn Benson campaigning with people who said that we deserve 9/11, I say never forget.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Wow, I want to ask you about some issues with your platform and the like, but never forget. Of course, I'm sorry. Did you just accuse Senate candidates of something to do with terrorism? I'm not clear on what you just said.
REP. JAMES: Yeah, they're- they're campaigning with extremists who say that America deserved 9/11, and I think that coming up on the 25th anniversary of 9/11, these are statements that are way out of bounds and should definitely be clarified. Michigan is ground zero for this republic in this next election, and we need to make sure that we stop socialism and that we save the state of Michigan, because we don't do it here, it's going to go to the rest of the country.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, I think you're talking about a supporter of a Senate candidate that that Senate candidate has started to distance himself from, and that influencer Hassan Piker has disavowed those past comments he made, but let's put that aside because I don't want to get into that. I want to talk about you. You are an Iraq war vet, and we are now given your time in uniform and your service to this country. I wonder what you think that we're now at the six-month mark of the war with Iran. We were told it was going to be four to six weeks. As you know, it's unpopular. 61% of Americans, according to our polling, disapprove of it. It's driven up gas prices. It's affecting America's role in the world. I wonder if you agree with what appears to be a switch away from military force towards economic sanctions. And do you think your constituents deserve more of an explanation from the administration as to what they're doing?
REP. JAMES: I believe very strongly when people say "death to America," we should take them at their word. I graduated West Point in the class of 2004, and we took our oath of affirmation, knowing that we would go to war. And as a result, the class of 2004 suffered the most casualties of any service academy since Vietnam. We understand the cost of war. We hate war, and we want to use every method, diplomatic or economic, to make sure that we keep Americans safe and we keep our young military members out of war. I applaud the administration's effort to make sure that Iran has no nukes, so they cannot threaten America and our allies. I applaud the administration's efforts to use every resource at their disposal to pursue peace, and these are the types of things that- that- that our people want. But we also have a number of things in the state of Michigan that we can do to lower the cost of living, to increase affordability, and these are the types of things that I'm running to do as governor to reduce harmful regulations that will lower gas prices and will lower the cost of groceries. These are the types of things that Michiganders are talking about: increasing affordability, particularly with energy and housing and healthcare. And I'm excited to be able to do that here at home.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay. Well, Michigan, in particular, has a major reliance on trade with Canada, your neighbor to the north. Their prime minister said he's going to match the U.S. tariffs on Canada dollar for dollar, starting September 8. Do you have any idea what this trade war is going to cost Michigan?
REP. JAMES: Absolutely. I am somebody who actually understands the automotive industry. I'm an automotive supplier. I have actually created jobs in the state of Michigan, and I recognize how important and crucial our partnership with our friends and family in Canada is. But I also recognize how crucial it is that the status quo not continue. Michigan has lost over 300,000 manufacturing jobs since the 90s, and that cannot continue. But at the same time, we need the negotiators to go back to the table, stop acting like children, and negotiate a fair, mutually beneficial, reciprocal deal that will benefit the United States of America and the state of Michigan. As a governor, I will be able to work with the president, be able to work with the prime minister to make sure that we can do this. Hopefully, it doesn't take that long, but I stand ready and willing to assist to make sure that we have an economy that works for Michiganders and one that will continue to create prosperity in the state of Michigan.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, if you win, you would be Michigan's chief executive here. So, January 1st, when you would be sworn in, is the very same date President Trump says he'll hit Canada with a 50% tariff on cars, trucks, auto parts, and steel. Canada's prime minister said workers in your state rely on Canadian demand since they are the largest customer for autos. This is going to be a big blow on the first day of your administration. Would you ask the White House not to do this?
REP. JAMES: Well, we're already talking with with members of the trade team and we're going to be continuing to engage with them so that we can avoid those things. Look, tariffs are not the objective. The objective is to protect Michigan jobs. The objective is to make sure that we deepen and continue our relationship with Canada. Wanted: Leaders for Israel’s next generation - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
15:46:26 UTC
00:46:26 KST

Wanted: leaders for a country of 10 million. Requirements include leading by example, taking responsibility, representing everyone, including those who voted against you, and describing what you are building, not who you are fighting. Must inspire trust. Must make a path for new leadership. Willingness to make difficult decisions is a plus. Humility and empathy preferred. Courage required.
Sound reasonable? It should. Twenty of us wrote this list at the start of the Argov honors program in leadership and diplomacy at Reichman University. Our program head asked one question: What do we expect from our country’s leaders? She hoped the exercise might become an op-ed. It took a year. You are reading it.
We started the exercise a few weeks after the last living hostages came home. The Israel-Hamas War was not over, and some of us were still serving or waiting to hear about reserve duty. But the weight had lifted just enough to ask what comes next. And if we are being honest, the assignment seemed a little ambitious. Twenty students, 20 opinions, one op-ed? Good luck.
Somehow, the foundations practically settled themselves. Most Israelis, we suspect, are like this, too. From any camp, who would actually cross out “take responsibility”? Or “put your country before your personal interests”? We agree on the job description. Our politics rarely rewards it.
“Take responsibility” means exactly what it says. Blame is everywhere in our public life. Ownership is almost nowhere. A leader who cannot say “I failed, and here is what I will do about it” should not ask a 19-year-old to cross a border fence.
“Serve everyone” means the campaign ends when the counting does. Once elected, you represent the people who voted against you and the ones who protest outside your window. A government that treats half the country as an internal enemy is at war with its own reserves.
“A positive vision” means telling us what you are for. Every party in Israel can recite what it is against. Few can describe the Israel of 2026 that they want to build – one where war is no longer the organizing principle of its politics. Fear may mobilize voters, but it does not lower the cost of living or fix a broken education system.
“Compromise” means courage, of a specific kind. The test of leadership is the willingness to make decisions your own supporters might not all like, and to stand in front of them and explain why.
“Make room for the next leaders” means treating succession as a duty. A generation that refuses to prepare its successors, then wonders why talented young people build start-ups instead of parties, has answered its own question.
Roles of leadership
WHY DOES a job this reasonable attract so few good applicants? Everything around it warns them away. The loudest voices drown out a quiet majority, and the media business model rewards the split. And people are tired – five national elections in four years, then years of war and reserve duty. A tired public stops demanding, and a politics that benefits from exhaustion has every reason to keep the public exhausted.
We know how a job posting written by students reads. Easy to write, brutal to live. We are not claiming to speak for everyone our age, but this generation has a particular experience of war, service, and political instability, and with it a particular stake in what leadership demands.
Over the past year we took courses on diplomacy and public speaking, great power competition, entrepreneurship, and the future of technology. We met politicians, officers, founders, educators, and diplomats. The lessons accumulated on their own: leadership comes in many shapes and sizes, and Israel can be served from almost any of them.
But the list from that first exercise never changed. It held in every room we entered, in Israel, the US, or Taiwan, which convinced us of its claim on the one room it was written for.
It also convinced us of its claim on us. We cannot demand a political culture we refuse to practice. If we want leaders who listen to people who disagree with them, we must keep doing it ourselves. If we want leaders who put the country before their personal interests, then some of us might eventually have to make that trade too.
On October 27, thousands of young Israelis who saw battle before they ever saw a ballot will choose the leaders who send them. Our generation proudly gave what the moment asked of us. But we do not need gratitude. We are owed a standard. Demanding it is a right we have earned and an obligation we intend to keep on election day and beyond.
Our program head spent the year believing in us more than we believed in ourselves. She has a dream we all know about: that one day there will be an Argov party in the Knesset. And no, this is not an announcement of one. Although, in fairness, she does tend to be right.
We will all be building the country from different rooms. But the posting is public now, and the requirements are too. The country is hiring. And whoever applies should know that a generation with every reason to be tired has decided to keep demanding anyway.
The writers are the 2026 class of the Argov honors program in leadership and diplomacy at Reichman University.

Plea filed in Supreme Court ahead of CJP protest
NEW DELHI: A plea has been filed in the Supreme Court seeking directions that no march or procession be taken out in Lutyens’ Delhi without prior police permission.This comes ahead of the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) proposed September 5 protest march, led by families of students who died by suicide following the cancellation of the NEET exam and subsequent re-test, as well as those who allegedly faced police excesses during the July agitation.The march was announced to protest what it alleges is the Centre’s failure to honour assurances made on July 25 that had led the group to withdraw its 36-day agitation over examination irregularities.
Delhi Police had earlier said it had received no request for a procession from India Gate to the Delhi Police Headquarters, despite the CJP announcing plans for the march.
The petition, filed by retired Delhi Police officer Rajendra Singh, seeks directions that large-scale mobilisation, marches or organised demonstrations in security-sensitive areas, including India Gate, Central Vista and adjoining zones, should not be held without requisite permissions.It also seeks regulation, postponement or modification of any proposed mobilisation in Lutyens’ Delhi until after the BRICS Summit scheduled for September 12-13.The plea further asks that no procession or march be allowed to cross authorised limits except in accordance with permissions and the applicable regulatory framework.

In Kyiv and the region, “phantom patrols” will operate again — how the control system will work
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
18:43:16 EEST
00:43:16 KST

In Kyiv and the region, “phantom patrols” will operate again — how the control system will work
Kyiv • UNN
Starting August 31, three unmarked patrol cars will monitor speed in Kyiv and the region. Violations will be recorded automatically.
Starting August 31, three "phantom patrol cars" will begin operating in Kyiv and the Kyiv region. Their main goal is to reduce the number of people injured and killed on the roads. Oleksii Biloshytskyi, head of the Patrol Police Department, reported this on Facebook, UNN writes.
Details
It is noted that later the "phantoms" will also appear in other regions. Their number will also increase in the future, Biloshytskyi said.
What are "phantoms"?
These are special vehicles that are almost indistinguishable in appearance from ordinary cars.
These vehicles are equipped with systems for monitoring the speed of moving vehicles, which make it possible to measure speed both while the "phantom" itself is moving and when it is stationary in a particular location. After an offense is recorded, license plates are read and recognized, followed by checks against databases
After that, metadata containing the relevant information is sent to the automated enforcement system, which processes it and automatically issues a ruling on an administrative offense. Nearly all speeding violations will be recorded automatically, without stopping the offending vehicle.
The system can record speeding violations in both the same and opposite directions of travel.
Is it possible to record offenses other than automatically?
Yes. In non-automatic mode, traffic violations will be recorded by the special vehicle using the two video cameras with which it is equipped. They can record traffic violations occurring both in front of and behind the service vehicle. If the most blatant violations are recorded (for example, creating an emergency situation), the inspectors inside the "phantom" may stop the offender in accordance with the requirements of Article 35 of the Law of Ukraine "On the National Police" and consider the case of an administrative offense

SEN. BLUMENTHAL: This trip was exhilarating because Ukraine is clearly making progress. It's turning the tide, but it was also heartbreaking to see the toll that this war is taking. MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
SEN. BLUMENTHAL: --sites with Starlink that will really send a message to Putin that the United States and Europe means business. But they sense a danger of escalation that can't be met by just words, and in fact--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay.

MARGARET BRENNAN: You mentioned Russia sanctions. SEN. BLUMENTHAL: First and foremost, this bill was the result of painstaking, sometimes painful negotiations with the U.S. Trade Representative, the White House, my colleagues in the House and Senate on both sides of the aisle. It passed the Senate 86 to 11. Not many measures doing that kind of successful passage these days, and it has increased authority for the president to impose scorching sanctions on the oligarchs, the financial institutions. It has measures to crack down on the shadow fleet, and it has tariff authority, but narrowly constrained to the five largest purchasers of Russian oil and gas.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
SEN. BLUMENTHAL: None of our European allies would be tariffed. And here's the main point, it is a moment of extreme urgency, for the reason that Putin may try to escalate, but also because Putin is on his heels economically. His economy is on the verge of major crisis. He has a deficit looming of $125 billion, 5% of his GDP, an interest rate of 14% on his national debt, and this kind of sanctions bill, throttling the flow of revenue to his war machine, could undercut completely his ability to wage this--
MARGARET BRENNAN: So you think--
SEN. BLUMENTHAL: --brutal murderous war.

SEN. BLUMENTHAL: I'm very hopeful--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

MARGARET BRENNAN: I want to ask you about what's happening in the state of Connecticut. Nationwide, ICE arrests have increased significantly in June and in July. MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

The head of a French LGBTQ rights association was hospitalised after a nighttime attack in Paris, activists and prosecutors said on Sunday.
Pierre Picavet, a police officer and LGBTQ rights campaigner, was injured in an assault in the French capital overnight from Saturday to Sunday.
Picavet is president of FLAG!, a Paris-based association that brings together employees of France's interior and justice ministries and works to combat discrimination against LGBTQ people.
As he left a bar in the historic Marais district in central Paris, Picavet was struck with a bottle and sustained multiple injuries, including internal bleeding and a head wound, according to the prosecutor's office.
The association STOP Homophobie denounced what it described as a "homophobic attack" and shared photographs of Picavet's injuries.
"STOP Homophobie condemns this attack in the strongest possible terms and stresses that anti-LGBT+ violence remains a reality," the group said.
Prosecutors said, citing Picavet, that the attacker repeatedly directed a homophobic slur at him.
"He immediately identified himself as a police officer and showed his police ID, but this did not deter the suspect from attacking him," prosecutors added.
The suspected attacker was taken into custody. Prosecutors said he had no previous criminal record and was intoxicated at the time of the assault.
Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire condemned what he called "this despicable homophobic attack" in a message in French posted on X.
"We will never surrender our streets to hatred," Grégoire said. "Paris will remain a refuge, a bulwark and a city of freedom for everyone."

TRIPOLI, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- Libyan Acting Foreign Minister Taher Al-Baour on Sunday met with visiting Syrian foreign affairs chief Asaad Hassan al-Shibani in Tripoli to discuss bilateral relations, according to the Libyan Foreign Ministry.
During the talk, the two sides discussed issues of common interest, ways to advance Libyan-Syrian relations, and means of strengthening bilateral coordination and consultation, the ministry said in a statement.
They also discussed arrangements for reopening the Syrian embassy in Tripoli, which resumed operations on Sunday after 14 years and is expected to strengthen diplomatic communication and facilitate consular services, the statement read.
The talks also covered finalizing procedures to activate the Libyan-Syrian Joint Higher Committee and signing an agreement to regulate its work, which would open broader prospects for cooperation in economic, development, and other areas of mutual interest, it added.

Al-Shibani's visit is the first by a senior Syrian official to Libya in 14 years, following the fall of Bashar al-Assad's government, as both countries move to restore diplomatic ties and expand political, economic and security cooperation.
The Syrian Embassy in Tripoli was closed in 2012, after Libya's then-ruling National Transitional Council recognized the opposition Syrian National Council as the legitimate representative of the Syrian people. ■

China Focus: AI cooperation with China brings hope to Pakistan's small farmers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
23:38:35 CST
00:38:35 KST

GUIYANG, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- For many small farmers in Pakistan's Punjab province, the country's most populous province, farming has always felt like a roll of the dice against the whims of the weather. But local farmers may soon see their fortunes change.
Syed Muhammad Ashiq Hussain Shah, Punjab's agriculture minister, is attending the 2026 China International Big Data Industry Expo, which runs through Sunday, in Guiyang, capital of southwest China's Guizhou Province. He said his delegation has a clear mission: to find Chinese partners who can help bring AI-powered farming tools to millions of smallholders back home.
According to the Pakistani official, many small farmers in Punjab province lack access to reliable, timely information. Meanwhile, climate change is making weather patterns increasingly erratic, with sudden downpours, prolonged droughts and scorching heat waves adding new risks to agricultural production
Punjab's agricultural authorities are now developing an AI-powered digital monitoring network designed to deliver weather forecasts, crop monitoring and real-time data on soil, water and pest control directly to farmers.
"We want to use AI to monitor the weather, soil and water, and to digitally track crops as well," Shah said. "We also want to use AI for pest control, so that a farmer can simply send a picture of a plant and get help identifying the problem. "
"If farmers can receive this information through a digital platform, they can make better decisions and reduce losses. That is why we see AI as an important tool for improving agricultural productivity and supporting farmers in Punjab," he said.
"That is exactly why we are here -- to find partners and learn from China's experience," he added.
In fact, China and Pakistan, including Punjab, have already shared a solid foundation in agricultural cooperation. Shah said Punjab signed at least six memorandums of understanding following previous visits to China and has been actively following through on them.
Chinese companies have also played a significant role in Punjab's high-tech farm mechanization program. Shah estimated that about 90 percent of the machinery acquired under the program -- including harvesters and tractors -- came from China. Now, this partnership is evolving beyond hardware to include smart technologies and intelligence.
Ali Mustafa Dar, adviser to the chief minister of Punjab on artificial intelligence and special initiatives, observed that China does not treat AI as something separate from economic development, but integrates it across manufacturing, logistics, cities, agriculture, transport and public services.
"China thinks long term. It builds the infrastructure. It experiments and learns. And when something works, it has the capacity to take it to extraordinary scale," he said.
As China's first national comprehensive big data pilot zone, Guizhou offers precisely the kind of experience Punjab is looking for. Dar said Guizhou is particularly interesting because it demonstrates that AI begins with strong data foundations.
Guizhou is a key hub for China's national "East Data, West Computing" project. This national strategy operates similarly to a power grid, shifting the heavy data processing demands of China's economically bustling eastern coast to resource-rich western regions. Crucially, the project utilizes the western region's abundant green energy such as wind and hydropower, making it a major milestone in green technology and carbon reduction.
By late July 2026, Guizhou housed 50 key data centers, with total computing capacity reaching 176.57 EFLOPS. Nearly 98.4 percent of this capacity was dedicated specifically to AI-related computing.
Dar said he is keen to understand how Guizhou has built its data ecosystem -- from infrastructure, data centers and standards to governance, industry and the applications built on top.
Meanwhile, Dar emphasized that their goal is not simply to import technology. His vision of the next stage of cooperation is to deliver concrete results: better public services, stronger local technology companies, and more jobs for young people. "That is what AI cooperation should ultimately achieve," he said.
He expressed hope that such collaboration could eventually provide useful models not only for Pakistan and China, but for other developing countries facing similar challenges.
Shah echoed that the expo offers a great opportunity for the delegation to showcase Punjab, meet potential Chinese partners and explore new areas of cooperation, particularly in AI and digital technologies.
Themed "Token: A New Path to Value of Data Elements," the 2026 China International Big Data Industry Expo has attracted 372 domestic and international companies and over 16,000 registered guests. It showcased new technologies, products, and applications in areas including the token economy, computing power, large model innovation, and data element circulation. ■

Prof Jason Arday’s accuser Nathan Cofnas has been barred from teaching on Ghent University campus for three months but has been allowed to continue his research position.
Cofnas, an American academic, was suspended from his postdoctoral research position at the Belgian institution earlier this month pending a “preliminary investigation” launched after Arday’s death.
Ghent did not name Cofnas but has since confirmed that it has “imposed a disciplinary measure” on a staff member for three months, under which they were “required to work remotely and may not carry out any teaching”. Cofnas’s research activities in the role have been “strictly limited to the research topics for which the appointment was made”.
In a post on X, Cofnas said he was grateful to Ghent’s rector, Petra De Sutter, “for allowing me to stay”.
The US ambassador to Belgium, Bill White, who had criticised Cofnas’s suspension, claimed on his official X account that the university and Cofnas had “amicably reached an agreement” to lift the suspension, enabling the academic to complete his one-year appointment.
In a statement, Ghent said an inquiry was under way “to determine if further disciplinary action is warranted”. The university later confirmed it had been in contact with the US ambassador, who “provided further context regarding his statements on X”.
Cofnas’s role at Ghent has been controversial. In May, the university’s philosophy department alleged to the institution’s leaders that Cofnas had “very limited expertise” for his role researching “the future of liberalism” and that he had a “far-right agenda”.
In July Cofnas accused Arday, a University of Cambridge sociologist, of plagiarism, alleging also that there were “serious questions” about his biographical claims. Arday was found dead on 14 August.
White, a Donald Trump supporter, donor and fundraiser, had called Cofnas’s suspension “truly unacceptable”, calling earlier this month for De Sutter to rescind it immediately.
On Friday, White wrote on his personal X account: “I just saved Belgium from a complete global media meltdown and well deserved spanking by @elonmusk and everyone by resolving the UGHENT Cofnas matter – quite quickly.”
The previous night, Cofnas thanked White and the US state department for “defending American values” on X, adding: “It was beyond my imagination that such a person would take an interest in the fate of a postdoc. The Ambassador responded with great support which helped to bring about a just outcome.”
Cofnas has been accused of promoting pseudoscientific ideas of racial difference in his online writings, and was reportedly among bloggers recommended to the Palantir founder Peter Thiel by a “race science” researcher.
Cofnas has also hit out at Trump and Maga in his writing, while claiming the US president’s executive orders against diversity, equity and inclusion in the US were a “cause for celebration”.
In a piece in April last year he said the Republican party had “degenerated into a low-IQ cult of personality”.
Hitting out at Trump’s tariffs, he said the effect “will be to halt the American economic juggernaut, discredit the anti-woke movement, pave the way for a leftwing populist … [and] stop the right’s momentum in other countries”.
In October, he wrote: “The right simply does not have the human capital to retake the institutions and run them effectively. The vast majority of intelligent, psychologically stable, and public-spirited Americans remain left and woke. The Trump administration’s war on universities, science, and data has only reinforced smart people’s identity as leftists.”
Asked by the Guardian if he stood by previous criticisms of Trump and Maga, Cofnas said: “I voted for Trump three times and I am still a registered Republican. I strongly criticised some Maga policies, particularly tariffs. There are other Maga policies that I support, such as interventions on behalf of free speech.”
Ghent University said it did “not wish to comment further on the controversy surrounding this matter … ongoing preliminary disciplinary inquiries must be allowed to proceed calmly, independently and with full respect for the rights of all those involved”.

Libya political parties set 2-year elections roadmap at UN-led talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
15:35:00 UTC
00:35:00 KST

Representatives of Libya's rival political factions signed an agreement Sunday to hold long-delayed national elections within two years, aiming to resolve disputes over electoral laws and reform the country's election authority.
The political process to resolve more than a decade of conflict in Libya has been stalled since an election scheduled for December 2021 collapsed following disputes over the eligibility of the main candidates.
Sunday's signing ceremony was held at the United Nations Support Mission in Libya, UNSMIL, in the Libyan capital Tripoli.
It followed talks in a smaller format, known as the 4+4, that involved two representatives of each of Libya's four main institutions: the Government of National Unity (GNU), the High Council of State, the House of Representatives and the Libyan National Army.
Walid Ellafi, state minister of political affairs and communications in the GNU, said legislative and presidential elections should be held "within a period not exceeding 24 months" under a single executive authority and unified national institutions.
Shibani AbuHamoud, head of the army's general command delegation, said the 4+4 would work with UNSMIL "to develop a framework within one month of the signing of the agreement to follow up on all matters related to its implementation."
The agreement says that if Libya's House of Representatives and High Council of State fail to approve the deal within a month, the parties will seek to adopt it nationally as a constitutional document through broad national mechanisms and secure international backing through the U.N. Security Council.
Libya has had little stability or security since a 2011 NATO-backed uprising.
It split in 2014 between warring eastern and western factions but there has been little major warfare since a 2020 cease-fire.
All Libya's major political players have repeatedly called for elections, but many Libyan people have voiced doubts that they would want a vote that could push most of them from positions of authority.

New UK PM Burnham’s honeymoon ends as Trump, first budget loom large

Andy Burnham has enjoyed a honeymoon first month as UK prime minister, but the hard trade-offs involved in governing are about to get real as parliament returns from its summer break in the coming days.
Since succeeding Keir Starmer on July 20, Burnham has pleased voters with several low-cost sweeteners, including cutting electricity bills and bus fares, while burnishing his casual man-of-the-people vibes.
He has poured pints of beer with his finance minister, played guitar in Ukraine, and kept up a prolific output of slick social media videos during a self-styled “listening tour” of Britain.

A YouGov survey published on August 18 found that 46 per cent of Britons view him favourably, up 12 points from when he first arrived at Downing Street.
With lawmakers on holiday, the new prime minister has largely been able to avoid thornier issues during his first weeks in office.

Brad Lander, the Jewish progressive Democratic candidate for the US House of Representatives in New York’s 10th Congressional District, was targeted with insults and calls to leave over allegations of being a Zionist while attending a protest outside Madison Square Garden on Saturday.
"You look like a scrotum, you filthy ballsack!" one protester shouted at him. "F*** you, ballsack Zionist!"
He was further accused of being "another paid Zionist" and was told to "get out of here."
The confrontation took place during a protest against an event organized by the Hindu nationalist RSS movement. Lander attempted to explain to protesters that he had come to join their cause, but some made clear that, in their view, there was no place at the demonstration for a Zionist, even one who opposes the policies of the Israeli government.
The confrontation was particularly notable given Lander’s own views on Israel. Over the past year, he has become one of the most prominent Jewish critics of Israel within the progressive wing of the Democratic Party. He has described the war in Gaza as “genocide,” called for an end to “American complicity” in the conflict, and said he would not support additional military aid to Israel at the time.
Despite those positions, Lander continues to describe himself as a “liberal Zionist.” He supports Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state and opposes the boycott movement against Israel.
Lander tried to explain his position during the confrontation. “I am Brad Lander, the Democratic candidate for Congress in New York’s 10th District, and I came here today to join others and say no to RSS,” he said.
Lander criticizes Madison Square Garden for hosting 'fascist and hateful rally'
He criticized Madison Square Garden for hosting what he described as a “fascist and hateful rally,” comparing the decision to host the event to the infamous pro-Nazi rally held at the venue in 1939.
Not all protesters joined the confrontation. Several attempted to intervene between Lander and those confronting him, urging them to stop. “Brad, please, we are all here for the same cause,” one protester said, while another told Lander that they were trying to protect him.
Lander said he understood their efforts to help him, but he would not accept the demands. “They are making it very difficult for me to leave. They have no right to tell me where to stand.”
Lander, a former New York City comptroller, defeated Rep. Dan Goldman in the June Democratic primary, winning 66% to 34%. Goldman is considered one of the Democratic Party’s most prominent supporters of Israel. Lander received the active backing of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who during the campaign criticized Goldman, among other issues, for supporting military aid to Israel.
Hindu nationalist movement RSS accused of incitement against minorities
The Madison Square Garden event drew thousands of attendees, with RSS leader Mohan Bhagwat serving as the keynote speaker. The Hindu nationalist movement is considered the ideological home of India’s ruling BJP party. Critics accuse the group of extreme nationalism and incitement against minorities, allegations the movement rejects.
The confrontation with Lander highlights growing tensions within the progressive movement over Israel. Even a Jewish politician who adopted much of the left’s harsh criticism of the Gaza war arrived to protest alongside progressive activists and called for a “free Palestine,” yet was still targeted with insults solely because he continues to define himself as a Zionist.

Ukraine Hits Russia’s Refineries So Bad Moscow Is Now Importing Fuel for Its Warplanes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
15:24:49 UTC
00:24:49 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits Russia’s Refineries So Bad Moscow Is Now Importing Fuel for Its Warplanes
Systematic Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries have sharply reduced the country’s aviation fuel production, forcing Moscow to import Jet A-1 from South Korea and Egypt to support both military and civilian aviation, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence said on August 29.
According to HUR, Russia has also temporarily banned exports of its own aviation fuel as it attempts to preserve domestic supplies.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“To meet the needs of combat and civilian aviation, Russia, which for decades positioned itself as an energy superpower, has officially introduced a temporary ban on exports of its own aviation fuel and is forced to seek ways to import foreign Jet A-1 aviation fuel,” Ukrainian intelligence said.
Jet A-1 is broadly comparable to the Soviet- and Russian-standard TS-1 and RT kerosene fuels used in gas-turbine aircraft engines, allowing it to be used by a wide range of aircraft operated by the Russian military.
HUR said the imported fuel is suitable for aircraft including the MiG-29, Su-34, Su-35S, Su-30SM, Su-57 and Su-24M, as well as Tu-95MS strategic bombers.
The fuel could also be used by Russia’s newer jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 attack drones, which employ Telefly TJ2000A turbojet engines or Russian-made equivalents designated TRD-2000.
Ukrainian intelligence said three tankers linked to Russia’s shadow fleet have already delivered approximately 70,000 metric tons of Jet A-1 from South Korea and Egypt to Russian ports in St. Petersburg and Vladivostok.
The shipments were reportedly arranged for Russia’s Independent Oil and Gas Company, which supplies large quantities of fuel to TZK-AERO.
TZK-AERO, in turn, provides fuel under government contracts to the Russian military, the Federal Security Service and other Russian security formations, according to HUR.
Ukrainian intelligence said the supply chain for South Korean aviation fuel involved UAE-based Caliph Energy Trading FZE.
The Egyptian supply route reportedly involved the Middle East Oil Refinery, known as MIDOR, the Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation and UAE-based trading company Vernal Overseas FZE.
Earlier, reports emerged that Russia was considering easing aviation fuel standards in an effort to increase production following Ukrainian strikes on the country’s oil refineries.
Russia’s Transport Ministry has proposed allowing aviation fuel with a freezing point of up to minus 50 degrees Celsius, compared with the current requirement of minus 60 degrees Celsius.
