6 issues that will shape Ursula von der Leyen’s legacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

6 issues that will shape Ursula von der Leyen’s legacy
With 3 years left in her term, the Commission boss must revive Europe’s industry, defend its rules, bolster security, support Ukraine, expand the bloc — and pay for it all.
Ursula von der Leyen has three years left to cement her legacy, but it’ll be far from easy.
Von der Leyen’s second term ends in 2029, by which time she’ll have been at the helm of the European Commission for a decade. If, as Brussels Playbook reported earlier this summer, the EU executive chief won’t seek a third term, then she’s in the final stretch of her career in Brussels.
Her time in office has been dominated by crisis management — Covid-19, Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, sky-high energy prices, war in Gaza. In the years to come, the challenges will likely keep mounting, including competition from China and the United States, and upcoming elections in France, Spain, Italy and Poland that could reshape the EU.
Advertisement
In the Commission’s Berlaymont HQ, von der Leyen and her team are feverishly working on her State of the EU speech, to be delivered on Sept. 16. It’s when she will set out her plan for the years to come. After that, she’ll have to deliver.
“Speeches are important. But it’s the actions that create legacy,” said Martin Hojsík, a vice president of the European Parliament from the Renew Europe group.
“Europe has become more vulnerable economically, competitiveness remains a major challenge, social and regional inequalities persist, and too often her Commission has reacted to crises rather than anticipated them,” said Victor Negrescu, a Parliament vice president from the Socialists and Democrats group. “I expect her to use this moment to defend her record, but also to explain how Europe can deliver more on growth, investment, social cohesion and strategic autonomy. For me, the real question is not how her legacy is presented, but what concrete results Europeans will see by the end of this mandate.”
Here are six potential headaches likely to define von der Leyen’s remaining time in office.
1. Reversing Europe’s decline
Will von der Leyen be able to stem the Continent’s economic decline … or oversee the death of its industrial heartlands?
It was von der Leyen who asked former Italian PM and European Central Bank chief Mario Draghi to draw up a report into the continent’s competitiveness. He was brutal in his assessment, saying that “without action, we will have to either compromise our welfare, our environment or our freedom.” He called on Europe to invest an additional €800 billion a year to drag itself out of a trough of low productivity and feeble growth that’s pushing it behind the U.S. and China in the international pecking order.
Advertisement
Von der Leyen promised to turn Draghi’s warning into an industrial strategy, but the headwinds are strong. European companies face high energy prices, fragmented capital markets, complex regulation and intensifying competition from abroad.
And while European companies need Chinese markets and supply chains, that dependency comes at a high cost. State subsidies have allowed Chinese firms to build capacity that far exceeds domestic demand, and their EVs, batteries, solar panels and steel are putting pressure on EU rivals. Meanwhile, Beijing’s stranglehold over critical minerals used in the green transition and high-tech sectors creates vast danger.
“What you have seen with the EU position on relations with China is the status quo is far too heavily tilted in China’s favor and cannot endure,” said a Commission official, granted anonymity to speak freely. “At EU level, there’s now near-total agreement on diagnosing the problems. There is near-total agreement on what the solutions are to address those problems. The only remaining question is how robust are member states willing to be in their follow-through.”
Mario Draghi smiles after he was awarded the 2026 International Charlemagne Prize of Aachen, on May 14, 2026. | Sascha Schuermann/AFP via Getty Images
Von der Leyen’s dilemma is how to keep the Chinese market open while preventing overcapacity from hollowing out EU industry.
The Commission is overseeing a reset in China relations, while considering stronger trade-defense tools and measures to reduce supply-chain dependence. It’s a delicate balance: too much confrontation could trigger a damaging trade war; too little could leave Europe without a viable industrial base.
Brussels and Beijing are engaged in talks to resolve the issue. Trade chief Maroš Šefčovič has set an October deadline to make progress. Failure could mean that China becomes the next front in the trade war.
Advertisement
2. Protecting EU regulations from Trump
Can von der Leyen rein in Big Tech without every European decision on competition, data, digital sovereignty or child safety becoming a transatlantic confrontation?
The Digital Markets Act and Digital Services Act are in their enforcement phase, and the EU’s fines against Apple, Meta and Google have already infuriated Washington. Von der Leyen is pushing ahead with plans to restrict children under 13 from using social media, which could provoke Donald Trump further.
“We would not presume to tell the U.S. how to regulate on their sovereign territory. And that is the very fair and coherent thing we ask for in return,” said the Commission official quoted above.
3. Addressing the climate crisis while slashing green rules
The Green Deal was the defining project of von der Leyen’s first term. But with far-right forces surging around the EU and an outcry that green rules are adding to Europe’s industrial strain, von der Leyen is now being forced to undo the very policies she implemented.
If von der Leyen weakens the Green Deal too much, she risks losing credibility with citizens and her coalition partners. If she insists on ambitious rules, she could provoke more political backlash.
Advertisement
“Some environmental policies were adopted without thinking about the social issues,” acknowledged Marie Toussaint, a French Green MEP. “How to heat your home? For some people the bills are already impossible to pay. So we need to ensure that in every sector we have this social concern and we refrain from adopting anything that would worsen people’s lives.”
4. Defending Europe and Ukraine
Europe’s security debate has moved from speeches about “strategic autonomy” to the urgent question of where to get weapons and deter Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The EU is increasing defense spending, backing joint procurement and trying to expand industrial capacity through initiatives such as the €150 billion SAFE program. But national governments still disagree over how much to spend and how to spend it.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, flanked by Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky, delivers a speech during a ceremony to mark the Day of Ukrainian Statehood, in Kyiv on July 15, 2026. | Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP via Getty Images
The test is whether Europe can build a defense industry that can stand on its own, given the Trump administration’s repeated undermining of NATO.
Von der Leyen will also need to ensure that Ukraine enters any potential peace negotiations with Russia in the best position possible.
“We know exactly how to talk to Russians,” said Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna. “Pressure, no compromises, and only from [a position of] strength.”
Advertisement
That means von der Leyen must ensure Ukraine gets financial and military support as well as credible long-term security guarantees, while keeping the Trump administration onside.
But while in Brussels support for Ukraine remains high, more Kremlin-friendly governments have won power around the EU, with the potential for others to join them after a series of elections in 2027, including in France and Italy.
“We operate in the real world. We have to take political reality and political developments into account in the work we do,” said the Commission official. Regardless, they added, “President von der Leyen will continue to make the case for Ukraine because that’s clearly in Europe’s best interest.”
5. Expanding the EU
Ukraine, Moldova and countries in the Western Balkans have moved closer to the EU, but political support for enlargement is not the same as readiness to admit new members.
Candidate countries must still complete difficult reforms on the rule of law, corruption and judicial independence. Current EU members worry about the cost of enlargement, future funding needs and whether the institutions can function with more than 30 members.
But von der Leyen needs to show that accession is still a credible process rather than a permanently postponed promise, before the countries in the EU’s waiting room run out of patience and look elsewhere for alliances.
Advertisement
“We deserve to be in a much more advanced position than we are right now,” North Macedonia’s Foreign Minister Timčo Mucunski said about his country’s stalled bid to join the EU. “To say that we have been treated unfairly is an understatement.”
6. Paying for it all
The EU’s next long-term budget will determine which of these headaches von der Leyen can actually treat.
The Commission proposed an almost €2 trillion budget for 2028–2034, but two entrenched camps are battling over the plan.
The so-called Friends of Cohesion — among them Italy, Greece, Poland and Spain — want more money for traditional spending areas, particularly cohesion policy and the Common Agricultural Policy, and want those funds delivered through familiar national and regional channels.
The other camp, made up of frugal countries including Germany, Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands, wants less spending and a different allocation of cash: more for innovation, defense and European industrial capacity.
The fight collides with the political calendar.
Advertisement
A cadre of the EU’s biggest countries will hold elections in 2027, including France, Italy, Spain and Poland. Some politicians will be reluctant to explain to voters why they should send more money to Brussels; others why traditional funding should be reduced.
Yet the new EU budget (known as the Multiannual Financial Framework) must take effect on Jan. 1, 2028. That means the deal needs to be negotiated well in advance.
Von der Leyen’s second term ends in 2029. | Olivier Matthys/EPA
The closer it gets to 2027, the more domestic politics will dominate the talks — and the harder it will be to secure unanimity in the Council and consent from the European Parliament.
“When it comes to MFF negotiations, endgame negotiations are always tough, but it always gets done,” said the Commission official. “Those exact motivations [2027 elections] are fantastic factors to get the job done now.”
Eliza Gkritsi, Seb Starcevic, Max Griera and Mathieu Pollet contributed to this story.

The Third World War may be fought with weapons built in garages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
14:57:13 UTC
23:57:13 KST

The Third World War may be fought with weapons built in garages
“And out of the smoke locusts came down on the earth and were given power like that of scorpions of the earth…” – Revelation 9:3-5.
NATO has reportedly drawn up a plan for war with Russia in the event of a Russian attack on the Baltic states. At first glance, the document might seem unremarkable given the most senior officer involved in preparing it holds the rank of major, because every year, Russian and American military academies produce hundreds of officers capable of writing plans of this sort.
But two things make it worth paying attention to. The first is that modern military science is undergoing a profound crisis and the old methods of warfare are becoming increasingly difficult to use. Tank breakthroughs, deep encirclements and prolonged artillery barrages are all far more dangerous than they were even a decade ago because the battlefield is saturated with unmanned aerial vehicles.
The second is more surprising as military plans for a potential war aren’t usually made public, therefore NATO appears to be sending a message that we understand how warfare has changed, and we’re preparing for it.
The outlines of a possible non-nuclear Third World War can already be seen in such planning, but that assumes, of course, that nuclear powers could become involved in a global confrontation without crossing the nuclear threshold, instead fighting through local allies and proxies. What stands out in the NATO concept is the central role given to robotic and autonomous systems.
Fully autonomous warfare still belongs partly to the future, but even remotely controlled systems have already changed tactics more dramatically than almost any military innovation of the modern era. The closest historical comparison may be the arrival of rifled weapons, when massed column attacks became suicidal.
Only a few years ago, tanks were still regarded as the decisive instrument of land warfare, yet today a tank may struggle even to reach its firing position because the approaches are covered by drones, including so-called ‘waiters’ that land, remain concealed, and take off only when ordered to attack.
Technology has changed the battlefield with extraordinary speed and now NATO has published a defense concept for the three small Baltic states that appears to acknowledge this new reality. The importance of the document lies less in the rank of the officers who drafted it than in the fact that the alliance is publicly demonstrating its readiness for a different kind of war.I suspect that was the main reason for publishing it and the message is directed at an adversary that already has four years of intensive combat experience. The contours of a future non-nuclear world war are therefore becoming clearer. I’m not a military specialist, so I will speak only in broad terms. Human soldiers may increasingly be concentrated in elite formations and special forces, while much of the conventional battlefield is handed over to machines.
Back in the late 1980s, a special forces officer once told me that such units were becoming less useful when employed in support of large conventional armies and he predicted a gradual decline in the importance of elite formations, but history may now be turning in the opposite direction.
Perhaps the armies of the future will consist largely of small groups of highly trained soldiers operating in support of vast numbers of robotic systems. Drones have already transformed warfare and artificial intelligence and autonomous platforms may transform it far more radically.If that happens, enormous armies could become obsolete and inflicting strategic damage on an enemy may no longer require columns of armored vehicles or millions of soldiers. Nor would it necessarily require the gigantic defense-industrial complexes familiar from the 20th century as much of the equipment could be cheap and rapidly replaceable.
Even today, effective drones can be assembled in a garage, but of course, future combat systems will require increasingly sophisticated electronics, although it’s not yet clear how different many of those components will be from technologies already used in smartphones and consumer electronics.
This would also change the nature of military targets, for why attack an enemy’s tanks if you can disable the electricity that allows its entire military system to function?
Power stations will inevitably become heavily protected, but transmission networks are much more difficult to defend and it’s impossible to guard every kilometer of high-voltage cable. This could lead to a new emphasis on dispersed electricity generation and the Soviet Union already experimented with unconventional solutions in remote northern regions, including the use of nuclear technology originally developed for submarines. The economics of war would change as well given that drones are operated by small teams – or eventually by autonomous systems – and are cheap compared to the industrial machinery of traditional warfare.
 They also reduce the enormous logistical burden associated with artillery, where a shell must be manufactured, transported by rail, moved again by truck and finally delivered to a gun. Even then, dozens or hundreds may need to be fired to destroy a single target. The scale of traditional warfare is difficult to comprehend. During one offensive in the First World War, the Entente fired roughly 25 million artillery shells, while the Central Powers mobilized about the same number of men over the entire conflict.
Modern precision weapons are far more effective, but they are also increasingly expensive, and massed artillery itself is becoming vulnerable to drones and counter-battery systems. That’s why the Third World War, if it comes, may look nothing like the previous two.It may not begin with millions of soldiers crossing borders or vast tank armies moving across Europe. Instead, it could consist of many simultaneous regional conflicts fought by smaller allies of nuclear powers, while the great powers themselves remain protected beneath their nuclear umbrellas.
A future world war may therefore not be one enormous battlefield but dozens of smaller ones, connected by drones, satellites, artificial intelligence, and the political interests of states that can’t afford to fight one another directly.

Ukraine offers invaluable lessons to NATO, from new technologies to national resilience – expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
14:57:00 UTC
23:57:00 KST

Ukraine offers invaluable lessons to NATO, from new technologies to national resilience – expert
Can Kasapoğlu, Senior Fellow and Defense Analyst at Hudson Institute, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“Ukraine offers invaluable lessons to NATO. The first one is pennies versus dollars. Affordable, scalable, sustainable mass can outperform exquisite systems in combat,” Kasapoğlu said.
According to the expert, comparing the cost of Ukrainian drones with the value of the Russian equipment they destroy showed how defense-economics asymmetry can systematically impose attrition.
In his view, the second important lesson is the need to assess “red lines” rather than mythologize them.
“Ukraine sank the Moskva, struck Moscow, attacked Crimea and Alabuga, damaged energy infrastructure, and hit strategic-bomber bases through Operation Spiderweb. Before the war, Western analyses portrayed such actions as possible thresholds for Russian tactical nuclear use. That escalation did not occur. The risk remains, but deterrence requires empirical judgment, not paralysis,” Kasapoğlu said.
The expert identified national resilience as the third lesson.
“Few expected Ukraine to withstand a war of this scale, making national resilience-building as important as weapons procurement,” he stressed.
In addition, Kasapoğlu said, NATO must prepare for protracted interstate wars.
As reported by Ukrinform, peace requires pressure on every member of the coalition supporting Russia until continuing the war forces them into a serious dilemma and a settlement begins to offer them benefits.

Canada erects giant ‘Lake Ontario’ sign as spat with Trump over name escalates

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
14:55:55 UTC
23:55:55 KST

Donald Trump and Canada continued a verbal duel on Saturday over the US government’s administrative renaming of Lake Ontario, with the Ontario premier erecting a giant sign saying “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” – and the American president posting a video of him tearing down an avatar of that sign, erecting a replacement saying Lake America, and dancing to YMCA.
Rhetoric over the naming of Lake Ontario is the public face of an escalating trade dispute between the US and its northern neighbor involving a 50% US tariff on Canadian steel and retaliatory tariffs from Ottawa.
Trump’s order for the US government to refer to Lake Ontario as Lake America by Sunday had at least one prominent impact. Google Maps had changed Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America for US users to reflect the president’s executive renaming order.
Canada’s prime minister Mark Carney has flat-out rejected the renaming, explaining that Lake Ontario derives from an Indigenous Wendat word meaning “the lake is beautiful, the lake is great” that dates back more than 400 years.
With talks to resolve the trade dispute stalled, Trump issued an executive order on Thursday directing US agencies that the lake was now Lake America.
It revived memories of a dispute earlier in his second presidency with Mexico, which saw Trump direct US agencies to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.
“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America,” Trump told reporters before he signed an executive order renaming the body of water among US federal agencies.
In a statement explaining why it was acquiescing to Trump’s desired name for Lake Ontario, Google said its practice is to “reflect name changes in official government sources”. Trump’s order affects the US’s federal Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), “which sets the standard for official US maps”, the tech company said.
Lake Ontario’s name change “does not have any impact on Canadian naming conventions or how the rest of the world refers to the lake”, Google said in a statement. And it said “those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario’” on Google Maps, “and those outside … the US and Canada will see both names”.
Google had done similarly in Trump’s executive order for the US government to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America. Google Map users in the US for now see that body of water named as the “Gulf of America”.
Meanwhile, on Saturday, the US president raised the volume again by resorting to the kind of AI-generated imagery for which he has shown a penchant.
He posted one such video of an army of Canada geese with Trump-like blond hair firing rifles in protection of Lake America. He published another of himself kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with Lake America while he danced in his distinctive way to a soundtrack of the Village People hit YMCA, which he has incorporated into his public appearances for years.
Across the US’s northern border, Ontario’s premier, Doug Ford, replied with a two-stories-high billboard declaring “Lake Ontario. Now and Always,” near Grimsby, Ontario. Ford said Trump was trying to rename the lake because Ontario and Canada were “standing up for ourselves”, and he argued the name would outlast the president.
“Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario,” Ford said in a video posted on social media.
He appeared on Sunday on the ABC News program This Week and remarked that Trump’s Lake Ontario renaming order was like “something out of Saturday Night Live,’” the famous NBC sketch comedy show.
“No one’s going to call it Lake of America,” Ford said. “It’s been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It’s going to continue being Lake Ontario.”
In an interview with the Associated Press earlier, Ford said the late Ronald Reagan would be “throwing up” over Trump’s tariff policies.
Meanwhile, Manitoba’s premier, Wab Kinew, said Trump’s Lake America provocation was akin to an aging rock band trying to revive an old hit.
“You know when, like, a rock band is really over the hill and you see them like in a casino playing some song from like 50 years ago, I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now,” Kinew said. “Like he thought he had a real hit, a real golden oldie, with the Gulf of Mexico.
“He’s trying to bring back that, and he’s trying to play the hits for his base. But I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad, and it’s not his best work.”
Wendat Nation grand chief Pierre Picard called Trump’s move an attempt to erase Indigenous history. “I want to tell him that it is unacceptable for us, as a nation, to have a president who can eradicate our history, our culture and our identity,” Picard said.
Trump on Sunday afternoon published a social media post declaring “Canada to be the worst”.
“I don’t want Canadian anything. They’ve been ripping us off for decades, and it’s going to stop,” Trump also wrote, referring to the ongoing US-Canada trade war.
Lake Ontario is one of North America’s five Great Lakes, alongside Superior, Michigan, Huron and Erie. At 7,340 sq miles, Lake Ontario is the smallest of those in terms of surface area.

The fish win: Iceland voted in a referendum against joining the European Union
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
14:54:42 UTC
23:54:42 KST

Icelanders voted by a narrow majority over the weekend against their country joining the European Union, according to referendum results published Sunday, dealing a disappointment to Brussels, which had hoped for a victory by the “yes” camp amid growing Euroskepticism in other countries across the continent. In the referendum, Icelanders decided by a small margin that preserving the island nation’s full independence and complete freedom of action in its fishing waters was too important to put at risk.
Iceland, an Arctic island nation of about 400,000 people, began talks on joining the European Union as early as 2009, after the severe economic crisis it experienced. But in 2013, following the rise to power of a Euroskeptic right-wing government, those talks were suspended. 
In the referendum held over the weekend, Icelanders were asked by the incumbent center-left government whether to renew those negotiations. A victory for the “yes” camp would not have meant that Iceland would definitely join the EU, because it would first have had to reach an agreement on the terms of accession and then put that agreement to another referendum. The victory of the “no” camp, however, closes the door to any such accession for the foreseeable future and certainly until a new government is formed, currently expected in 2028.
The vote count overnight kept the country in suspense, as the “yes” camp took an early lead before the trend shifted in favor of opponents. By dawn, only a few hundred votes separated the two camps, before the gap widened as ballots came in from areas of the country where opposition was stronger. By morning, Iceland’s public broadcaster reported that final results showed 52.8% of those who took part in the referendum voted against the government’s proposal to open negotiations with the European Union, while 47.2% supported it. Voter turnout was 82.5%.
Iceland’s government presented EU membership as a step that would protect the country from trade wars and rivalries in the Arctic and described the referendum as a “now or never” moment. Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir said a “no” vote would end the debate for as long as her center-left coalition remained in power.
Senior officials at EU institutions in Brussels had expressed hope that an Icelandic vote in favor of accession talks could ease skepticism toward further EU enlargement and strengthen the bloc strategically at a time when Arctic security has become an increasingly urgent issue. The vote took place against the backdrop of repeated threats by U.S. President Donald Trump to take control of neighboring Greenland, threats that prompted some voters to support the idea of European solidarity. Although Iceland is already a NATO member, supporters of the proposal argued that EU membership would give Iceland greater protection from its neighbors if Trump were to make similar threats against the volcanic island.
90% of fishing industry opposed: Dutch boats will not fish here
In any case, the debate within Iceland over joining the EU focused on interest rates, fishing rights and the cost of living rather than security issues. Iceland is grappling with high inflation and interest rates that have made mortgages expensive, and supporters of a “yes” vote argued that EU membership, and perhaps even adoption of the euro, could bring relief. The Icelandic central bank’s interest rate stands at 8%, compared with 2.25% at the European Central Bank.
“It won’t solve Iceland’s structural flaws, but it could become a catalyst for a healthier economy,” said chief economist Vilhjálmur Hilmarsson of the Viska union, one of Iceland’s largest labor organizations.
Opposition leader Guðrún Hafsteinsdóttir, who led the “no” campaign, argued in response that the economic case was overstated.
“These are not problems Brussels will solve for us. These are problems Icelandic politicians must solve,” she stressed.
A leading force in the “no” campaign was Iceland’s influential fishing industry, which feared that the EU’s Common Fisheries Policy would allow Spanish, Dutch and other fishing vessels into its economic waters and reduce fish stocks. According to polls, 90% of workers in the fishing industry oppose joining the European Union.
The descendants of the Vikings who settled Iceland have made their living from the sea for hundreds of years, and the abundant catch of cod and squid is not only a major pillar of Iceland’s economy but also a central part of its national identity. Iceland gained independence from Denmark in 1944 and has a proud history of refusing to allow larger and wealthier European countries to exploit it. One example is the “Cod Wars” it fought with Britain in the 1970s, during which it insisted on preventing British fishing boats from operating in its waters and even sabotaged them. At the height of the confrontation, Iceland also threatened to withdraw from NATO.
Under EU rules, fishing quotas are based in part on historical fishing patterns. For that reason, some Icelandic officials said that even if the country joined the EU it would retain control over its waters, since no EU country has fished there for decades. Opposition leader Hafsteinsdóttir was unconvinced.
“I know the European Union will come with certain promises of flexibility, especially at the beginning, but we know that won’t last forever,” she said.
Brussels’ hopes for an 'Arctic arm' dashed
Opponents of EU membership pointed not only to the fishing issue but also to the fact that Iceland already enjoys partial integration into European agreements, such as membership in the European Economic Area and the Schengen free-travel zone, without giving up sovereignty as it inevitably would under full membership. They also argued that Iceland’s voice would be swallowed up in the vast European Parliament and that it would be better off signing its own trade agreements, such as its agreement with China.
For the European Union itself, the referendum result is a bitter disappointment. For a bloc that has not admitted any wealthy country since 1995, but only relatively poorer states such as Bulgaria and Romania, Iceland’s accession would have been seen as a sign of success for the EU’s enlargement policy while also strengthening its presence in the Arctic, which is becoming an increasingly important arena of economic and security competition.
A “yes” vote in Iceland could also have helped reignite debate over accession in Norway, its oil-rich neighbor, which has likewise remained consistent over the years in rejecting EU membership. In recent weeks, senior EU officials had sounded willing to make compromises to bring Iceland into the bloc, including recognition of the “unique conditions” of Icelandic fishing.

Guinea-Bissau votes in referendum to rewrite constitution and boost presidential powers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
14:53:16 UTC
23:53:16 KST

Voters in military-ruled Guinea-Bissau, after a coup, vote on Sunday in a referendum to boost presidential powers before elections to restore civilian rule, a process mired in controversy.
Voting got off to a slow start in some areas when the polling stations opened at 08:00 CET. According to media correspondents, security was stepped up at strategic points in the capital, with members of the National Guard and the police deployed at key locations.
This referendum is taking place against a backdrop of political instability and is being challenged by the opposition, not only because it has already been approved and published in the Official Gazette of the Republic -before the people had been ‘heard’- but also because it was drafted by the military junta, that is, by a transitional government without prior consultation.
"No one was consulted, neither political parties nor civil-society organisations, let alone traditional and religious leaders, and so on. So everything was done in secret," said the head of the Guinea-Bissau Human Rights League, Bubacar Turé, last week, speaking to Euronews.
Turé also stressed that campaigners for a "no" vote in the referendum were not authorised to campaign. "This is not an environment of freedom," he added, which is another reason why the opposition has called for a boycott of today’s vote.
Some analysts say the military government lacks legitimacy to change the constitution, which has fuelled discontent among citizens.
"The fundamental question is: who drafted this constitution, and on whose behalf? To protect which interests or institutions? Who stands to gain from this constitution?" said Guinea-Bissau political analyst Paulino Quadé, speaking to the Associated Press.
A military government seized power in November 2025 following disputed elections in which both the former president, Umaro Sissoco Embaló, and the opposition candidate, Fernando Dias, claimed victory.
After the military junta took power, it appointed General Horta N'Tam as transitional president under a temporary constitutional charter that bars him from standing in elections.
If it goes ahead, the new constitution drafted by the self-styled National Transitional Council will give the president more powers and reduce parliamentary representation, among other changes.
The military junta currently in power unanimously approved a constitutional amendment to shift the country from a parliamentary to a presidential system, and the public is now being asked to endorse it. The new text proposes scrapping the previous system, under which the prime minister came from the parliamentary majority, leading to complex power-sharing arrangements. It would also allow the head of state to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and cabinet members, as well as to dissolve parliament.
Measures the opposition contests, arguing that they downgrade political parties and the popular will.
"This constitution significantly weakens the prime minister and the government, subordinates the National People’s Assembly and the political parties, and undermines, or even ignores, the popular will expressed at the ballot box, bringing all the inherent risks of division and political and social tensions," said Muniro Conté, spokesperson for the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), to the Associated Press.
The military authorities argue that a smaller parliament, reduced from 102 to 65 seats, would allow for easier and more substantive debates, while the new presidential powers would underscore the president’s higher authority over the prime minister, which they say has been a source of political instability in the country.
Coup after coup
Since winning independence from Portugal in 1973, West Africa’s only Portuguese-speaking country has been rocked by several coups and attempted coups. Indeed, last year’s coup in Guinea-Bissau deepened West Africa’s democratic crisis, adding to the growing number of countries in the region under military rule.
In November 2025, the army seized power a few days after the presidential elections, toppling then president Umaro Sissoco Embaló and suspending the electoral process as the vote count neared its end and it was becoming clear who the new president-elect would be.
Several African leaders described the situation as a "staged" power grab after the military allowed the former president to hold a press conference to announce that he was being removed from office and that he was allowed to leave the country in seemingly favourable circumstances. The most sceptical observers say Embaló handed power to the military after realising he was losing the election.
During the 2023 legislative elections, Embaló himself dissolved parliament, which was dominated by the opposition, in response to what he described as an attempted coup, and then ruled by decree until he was deposed by the army.
This referendum follows a series of similar moves in other African countries, including Zimbabwe and Chad, which have amended their constitutions in recent years to extend presidential terms, remove age limits or strengthen executive powers.
With around 2.2 million inhabitants, Guinea-Bissau has suffered five coups and a series of attempted coups since 1974. The country has the highest ratio of natural wealth per capita, according to the World Bank, yet more than half the population lives in poverty.
Of the more than 2 million inhabitants, around 915,000 are eligible to vote today.
Sunday’s voting ends at 17:00 GMT, and the first provisional results are expected on Tuesday.

Feature: Chinese firm helps rural Egyptian women improve livelihoods through poultry raising
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
22:52:11 CST
23:52:11 KST

A robotic arm stacks bags of feed at New Hope Alexandria Co., Ltd. in Beheira Governorate, Egypt, July 27, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Haobo)
by Mahmoud Fouly
CAIRO, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- In a training room in Egypt's northern Beheira Governorate, rural women listened closely as Chinese and Egyptian specialists explained poultry-raising techniques, from temperature control and ventilation to weight monitoring and disease prevention.
Held at the Family and Child Development Center in Dimisna village, the session was part of the China-Egypt "New Hope" initiative, which empowers low-income rural women by helping them establish small poultry-raising projects at home.
The initiative is implemented by Chinese agribusiness New Hope Liuhe Co., Ltd. in cooperation with Egypt's National Alliance for Civil Development Work (NACDW) and its member foundation, Sonaa El-Kheir (Good Makers) for Development.
Each participating family has received 55 chicks, along with feed, medicines and other necessary supplies. With the roughly 60-day cycle now nearing completion, veterinarians make regular household visits and stay in touch with the women via a WhatsApp group.
For Amal Ahmed, a housewife from Dimisna, the project offers rural women a chance to improve their income without leaving home.
"Dr. Suhaila, New Hope's vet, has been following up with us since the first day we received the chicks," Ahmed said. "We weigh the chicks to monitor their growth, and whenever there is something unusual, we consult her."
"We already raise poultry at home, but this cycle involves much closer attention. We follow their instructions continuously, day by day," she added.
The current program is the second phase of New Hope's poultry-farming technical training in Egypt, involving five subsidiaries and covering about 600 rural households, according to the company.
In Beheira, the project covers 100 families across four villages, including Dimisna, with 25 families from each village.
In its first phase last year, participants increased their income by an average of about 8,900 Egyptian pounds (about 175 U.S. dollars), with a poultry survival rate above 95 percent, the company said.
Mohamed Abdel-Maboud, manager of the "New Hope" project and Sonaa El-Kheir's Family and Child Development Centers project, said the initiative combines economic empowerment with practical training for rural women.
"The project has benefited everyone here. It provided rural women with an excellent economic empowerment opportunity, and they are particularly pleased with New Hope's technical support," Abdel-Maboud said.
Suhaila El-Shazly, a veterinarian with New Hope, said the women receive regular technical guidance on temperature, ventilation, humidity, and disease prevention.
She said many of the women had previously raised poultry only on a small household scale and were unfamiliar with the management practices used on larger farms.
"We explain to them how a large-scale system operates so that they can apply the same methods and raise their 55 chicks according to the same standards used on farms with 10,000 birds," she said.
Another beneficiary, Hind Saeed, said families will receive the proceeds after the birds are sold at the end of the cycle, adding that many hope to join a second or third round.
"The project makes a major contribution to providing families with a decent life," Saeed said. "I hope they continue doing this."
New Hope said the project aims not only to provide immediate economic support but also to transfer practical poultry-raising skills for more sustainable income.
Wu Jun, a senior sales manager at New Hope Alexandria Co., Ltd., one of New Hope Liuhe's subsidiaries in Egypt, said the project's core goal is to adapt China's rural revitalization experience to local conditions in Egypt and help rural households increase their incomes through better farming practices.
Wu said Beheira's location in the Nile Delta, with favorable conditions for poultry farming and a large number of family farms, makes it well-suited to the project.
He said New Hope has about 20 veterinarians in Egypt who provide technical services to farmers, including farm visits, feeding and health checks, vaccination guidance and on-site training.
"We do not merely sell feed. We provide a complete system of services, including guidance on equipment use and animal-raising techniques," Wu told Xinhua. ■

NASA's Roman Space Telescope, set to probe universe with JPL tech, launches on SpaceX rocket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
14:52:07 UTC
23:52:07 KST

NASA’s Roman Space Telescope, set to probe universe with JPL tech, launches on SpaceX rocket
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope — a $4.3-billion sister to the Hubble and James Webb telescopes — launched into space Sunday morning on a SpaceX rocket with space enthusiasts and scientists from around the world looking on.
Once fully operational, the observatory is expected to vastly expand scientists’ inventory of planets outside our solar system, increasing it from about 6,300 planets to more than 100,000. Scientists aim to find some of those with a cutting-edge instrument built by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in La Cañada Flintridge.
“It’s a little bit like having a kid go off to college,” said Vanessa Bailey, JPL instrument scientist for the planet-hunter, called a coronagraph. “You’re used to having it around, being able to go visit it when you want, and now, it’s out in the world.”
Roman will also complete detailed surveys of the sky to help physicists better understand “dark matter,” which pulls the universe together, and “dark energy,” which pushes it apart.
Caltech will play a leading role in managing Roman’s scientific operations.
A SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket carrying Roman lifted off from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida at 4:26 a.m. Pacific. As the rocket rumbled along the Space Coast, nerves turned into catharsis for JPL scientists and engineers looking on.
“I had my hands over the rails, white knuckles, as we were counting down — and then, just, tears streaming down my face as she went up,” said Alina Kiessling, a JPL research scientist who studies dark matter and dark energy.
She watched alongside her husband, JPL Roman project scientist Jason Rhodes, from the space center. Shortly after launch, their nanny at a nearby Airbnb shared a video of their two children, ages 5 and 1, watching, too.
The rocket successfully deployed the 18,000-pound telescope about 31 minutes after launch. Roman then opened its array of solar panels and sunshades, which power the craft and keep its sensitive instruments cool.
In the middle of a post-launch news conference, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman’s phone began to ring. “The president is excited about Roman,” he said.
“I just want to thank everybody and congratulate you. It looked beautiful on television,” President Trump (who proposed killing the project multiple times) said on speakerphone. “You are doing a fantastic job.”
Roman was initially projected to come in over budget, but a significant course correction helped the telescope launch on budget and ahead of schedule.
While JPLers are already planning their celebrations, Roman coronagraph project manager Feng Zhao said the team wouldn’t truly be able to relax “anytime soon.”
Over the next three months, Roman will deploy its antenna, adjust its course, and power on its two instruments: JPL’s planet hunter and a night-sky surveyor called the Wide Field Instrument.
Roman’s final destination is the same cosmic parking lot where the James Webb Space Telescope resides: a million miles from Earth, far past the moon. At this spot, Earth’s and the sun’s gravity create a stable point, allowing the spacecraft to better conserve fuel.
Then, it’s time for some “very cool science,” Zhao said.
The Roman Space Telescope, equipped with JPL tech, may shed some light on the greatest mysteries of the universe.
Once in operation, the Coronagraph Instrument will attempt to observe planets that are 100 million times dimmer than their host star, a significant improvement over James Webb. To do it, the instrument can maneuver a flexible mirror with near-atomic-scale precision to focus the bright starlight into a pinprick, then block it with a mask so it can observe the dim planet.
Those observations will inform an aspirational future mission — the Habitable Worlds Observatory, which aims to view Earth-like planets more than 1 billion times dimmer than their host stars.
The Wide Field Instrument will focus on observing the night sky with the clarity of Hubble, but cover a vastly greater area than the 36-year-old observatory. With this, scientists hope to better understand dark matter and dark energy, which are invisible but make up 95% of the universe.
Scientists do not yet know whether dark matter is made up of ancient black holes lurking throughout space, undiscovered heavy and slow particles, or unknown lighter and faster particles. The different theories provide different answers for how dark matter should clump. By looking at how dark matter’s gravity bends the light of galaxies, Roman will be able to measure this clumping.
As for dark energy, scientists long thought its strength has remained constant throughout the universe’s history. However, recent observations suggest it is weakening — potentially jeopardizing Einstein’s so far unblemished theory of general relativity and calling into question the leading description for how the universe will die.
Scientists hope Roman’s observations, paired with other cutting-edge space and ground-based telescopes, will help settle whether dark energy is constant, or if the recent measurements point to deeper problems in our understanding of the universe.
The cosmos is riddled with evidence that the universe began with an exotic, unfathomably rapid expansion, but scientists don’t know why it happened. NASA JPL’s SPHEREx mission will seek answers to the mystery of cosmic ‘inflation.’
NASA anticipates the telescope’s first images will come in early 2027.
“Doing things like this — launching a telescope into space to uncover the mysteries of the universe — this is the best of humanity. This is what we can aspire to as a species,” Rhodes said shortly after launch. “So, I’m on top of the world.”

Thailand beats China to win at Asian Women's Volleyball Championship, earns first-ever Olympic berth
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
22:51:48 CST
23:51:48 KST

Team Thailand celebrate after the final match between Thailand and China at AVC Women's Volleyball Continental Championship in Tianjin, China, Aug. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Sun Fanyue)
TIANJIN, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- Thailand edged China 3-2 in a back-and-forth final of the 2026 Asian Women's Volleyball Championship here on Sunday, claiming the continental title and securing the country's first-ever Olympic berth in women's volleyball.
Thailand took the opening set 25-20 before China hit back to win the next two 25-11 and 25-23. Thailand then forced a decider with a 25-18 fourth-set win and held its nerve in the fifth to seal the match 15-10.
The victory gave Thailand its fourth Asian Championship title. Its previous triumph came in 2023, when it also defeated China in the final. China remains the most successful team in tournament history with 13 titles.
Thailand had never previously qualified for the Olympic women's volleyball tournament. The result also made it the second team to qualify for Los Angeles 2028 through continental competition, after Canada beat host Dominican Republic 3-1 in the final of the NORCECA Women's Continental Olympic Qualifier on Saturday.
China recovered strongly after losing the opening set, dominating the second with five blocks and rallying from 22-19 down to take a tense third set 25-23. But Thailand regained control in the fourth and pulled away late in the decider. A crucial block put Thailand 9-7 ahead before two aggressive jump serves forced China into consecutive reception errors, effectively putting the match beyond the host.
China, a three-time Olympic champion, has competed at every Games since making its Olympic debut at Los Angeles 1984, but Sunday's defeat denied the host an early ticket to Los Angeles 2028. ■

Libyan rival factions sign agreement on reshaping election commission, electoral laws
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
22:51:27 CST
23:51:27 KST

TRIPOLI, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- Libya's "4+4" Committee on Sunday signed an agreement in Tripoli on reshaping the board of the High National Elections Commission (HNEC) and addressing disputes over presidential and parliamentary election laws.
The "4+4" Committee, comprising four representatives from eastern Libya and four from the west, was launched by the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) as an alternative mechanism to overcome the political impasse after Libya's House of Representatives and the High Council of State failed to agree on amending electoral laws and appointing a new board for the HNEC.
Under the agreement, which was signed at the headquarters of UNSMIL, Dhou Al-Hamali was recommended as chairman of the HNEC board, while Sana Al-Lishani was named deputy chairperson. Ali Al-Tayea, Haitham Al-Tabouli, Ali Abu Salah, Badiwi Mohamed, and Ali Al-Mabrouk were named members of the commission's board.
Regarding the presidential and parliamentary elections, the committee agreed to separate the results of the presidential election from those of the legislative elections.
The agreement stipulated that the elections should be held under a single executive authority and unified national institutions, including sovereign institutions and the military.
It further stipulated that a second round of the presidential election would not be mandatory if a candidate obtains more than 50 percent plus one vote of the ballots cast.
Under the agreement, presidential and legislative elections must be held within 24 months, with both civilians and military personnel eligible to run.
The agreement was signed against the backdrop of Libya's ongoing political and institutional divisions, as the country seeks to end years of transitional periods through presidential and parliamentary elections. ■

====================================================================================================

Xinhua Headlines: China promotes coordinated development of data industry, artificial intelligence
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
22:51:22 CST
23:51:22 KST

*Riding the wave of digital industry growth, traditional industries are receiving a fresh boost from data and artificial intelligence, a transformation on full display at the 2026 China International Big Data Industry Expo.
*The interplay between data and AI is doing far more than just upgrading traditional industries; it is also catalyzing the emergence of new business models and employment categories.
*As an international event, the expo has attracted enterprises from multiple countries, including Singapore, Morocco and Canada, seeking new cooperation opportunities in the data and AI industries.
GUIYANG, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- China's data industry hit 6.78 trillion yuan (about 1 trillion U.S. dollars) last year. Now, as the 2026 China International Big Data Industry Expo gets underway, one question emerges: how does data become the "new oil" of the AI era?
"Wherever AI advances, we push forward the construction and application of high-quality datasets," Liu Liehong, head of China's National Data Administration, told the expo's opening ceremony in Guiyang, capital of southwest China's Guizhou Province.
Yang Jie, secretary-general of the World Data Organization, added that the richness, purity, authenticity and professionalism of data directly determine the cognitive depth, knowledge accuracy, and capabilities of large models.
Themed "Token: A New Path to Value of Data Elements," the expo was held from Friday through Sunday and has attracted 372 domestic and international companies and over 16,000 registered guests. It showcased new technologies, products, and applications in areas including the token economy, computing power, large model innovation, and data element circulation.
ENERGIZING TRADITIONAL INDUSTRIES
Riding the wave of digital industry growth, traditional industries are receiving a fresh boost from data and artificial intelligence, a transformation on full display at the expo. In the host province, hydropower stations, wind farms and solar plants along the Wujiang River are now connected through a unified digital system -- a vivid example of how data technology is transforming conventional industries.
"We're bringing together hydropower, wind and solar into one smart dispatch platform," said Fan Sheng, deputy general manager of Guizhou Wujiang Hydropower Development Co., Ltd., at the expo.
According to Fan, a long-standing challenge for the power industry is that changing wind, cloud and rain conditions cause large swings in renewable energy generation. Accurately forecasting these fluctuations and coordinating a mix of power sources has become essential for maintaining grid stability and making the most of clean energy.
The company cleaned, integrated and standardized data from meteorological, hydrological, new energy station and grid operations, then established data exchange with the grid dispatch system so that forecast results could be directly applied to actual power generation planning.
Using years of local data, technical teams trained multiple models that can now predict conditions up to 15 days ahead, giving operators more time to make informed decisions, Fan said.
The results are promising. Company test data shows wind forecast accuracy at 91.95 percent, solar forecast accuracy at 94.54 percent, and cascade hydropower inflow forecast accuracy at 94.1 percent -- an improvement of about 4 percentage points year on year.
"AI's edge in industrial upgrading goes beyond technology -- it lies in its reach as a foundational infrastructure," said Duan Zhongxian, a professor at Guizhou University.
Duan advocated for integrating computing power with industry, agriculture and cultural tourism -- turning computing power into a powerful driver for upgrading traditional industries.
"The real strength of computing power is in enabling businesses to undergo digital transformation," Duan said.
FOSTERING NEW BUSINESS FORMS
The interplay between data and AI is doing far more than just upgrading traditional industries; it is also catalyzing the emergence of new business models and employment categories.
While many worry about jobs being replaced by AI, others are discovering new opportunities emerging from the technology's rapid advancement.
Take embodied intelligence -- a field that gives AI a "physical body" to perceive, decide and act like humans in the real world. To make robots as dexterous as people, massive amounts of high-quality real-world data are essential.
In a residential apartment in Guiyang, 21-year-old Wang Junbao, a recent graduate from Guizhou Tongren Data Vocational College, moves through daily household chores -- tidying up, washing dishes -- while wearing a panoramic data collection headset.
As an embodied intelligence data collector, his task is to record human movements from a first-person perspective: how to grasp, how to exert force, how to navigate obstacles. The behavioral data, once processed, serve as "fuel" for training robots.
"This industry has great potential, and it's deeply rewarding to contribute to the progress of embodied intelligence," said Wang, who joined Shanghai Benyuan Digital Technology Co., Ltd. in June after a three-month internship. "Five or six of my classmates stayed with the company after their internships."
Duan Annan, general manager of the company's Guiyang branch, said the company has spent over a decade in AI data, specializing in four core areas: multimodal large models, world models, embodied intelligence and autonomous driving.
"Real-world scenes, real interactions, and real action data are the core bottlenecks constraining model deployment," Duan noted.
Duan said the Guiyang base currently employs 400 on-site staff, alongside 800 collectors across the country. With over 100,000 hours of effective collection, it has supplied high-quality data for domestic embodied intelligence models and boosted local digital employment.
Beyond the rise of new job roles, data and AI are also reshaping how businesses operate. Many exhibitors at the expo are micro-enterprises with just three to five employees, or even "one-person companies," a sign of new entrepreneurial vitality fueled by data and AI.
"AI is not simply taking away jobs. It is reshaping existing work and creating entirely new professions," said Qin Yongbin, vice president of Guizhou Minzu University.
"While AI will replace routine and repetitive tasks, it will also generate more roles that demand creativity, decision-making, emotional intelligence and complex teamwork. The future is about human-machine symbiosis, where humans direct and machines assist. The essence lies in collaboration," Qin said.
BOOSTING INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION
As an international event, the expo has attracted enterprises from multiple countries, including Singapore, Morocco and Canada, seeking new cooperation opportunities in the data and AI industries.
Dubuya Thulani, a Zimbabwean entrepreneur, launched his blockchain-based data platform two years ago. Named Wazisana, which means "very transparent" in Swahili, the platform connects African agricultural exporters with Chinese buyers.
"Chinese buyers want to buy African agricultural products, and African farmers want to sell to China. They need a bridge like this," Thulani said. The platform requires African farmers to upload videos of their entire production process -- from planting to fertilization -- for products such as coffee. AI then processes the data to generate comprehensive, readable descriptions for potential Chinese clients, detailing fertilizer and pesticide usage.
"We have already exported coffee, red wine and avocados successfully, and we are already profitable," Thulani said. "Next, we want to expand our business and contribute to win-win cooperation between China and Africa through data and AI. This is also what technological progress truly means -- sharing and advancing together, so that the benefits of AI can reach all of humanity."
When talking about the delegation's trip to northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region and Guizhou, which brought nearly 30 officials from Pakistan's Punjab province to study China's smart agriculture and AI expertise, Syed Muhammad Ashiq Hussain Shah, Punjab's agriculture minister, said his province is actively building an AI-powered digital monitoring network for farming.
"We are focusing on finding partners in China and learning from China's experience," he said, "The big data expo is a great opportunity for us to showcase Punjab, meet potential partners and explore new areas of cooperation."
Cristian Davis Acosta, consul general of Chile in Chengdu, shared his country's AI ambitions. "In Chile, we are trying to develop our own AI tool called Latam-GPT," he said. "It is similar to ChatGPT, but it is designed for Latin America. China already has very advanced AI tools, so perhaps we can establish cooperation between institutions on both sides and exchange experiences. We may even be able to develop new tools together."
He noted that Guizhou is an important hub for data centers and the digital economy in China. "It is a very strong and interesting partner for us, so we see considerable potential for cooperation in this field."
During the speech at the expo's opening ceremony, Muhammadou M.O. Kah, former chair and current vice-chair of the United Nations Commission on Science and Technology for Development, urged fostering open and inclusive international cooperation.
"Expanding access to digital public goods, open AI methodologies, and capacity building, so that every nation can actively participate in the data economy," he said.
"If we act together, with courage, data will create more value, and innovation will bring a better future," he added. ■

Trump says US to use Venezuelan oil to replenish US Strategic Petroleum Reserve
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
14:50:26 UTC
23:50:26 KST

Yasin Gungor
30 August 2026•Update: 30 August 2026
US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that Washington will utilize its newly secured control over Venezuelan oil to refill the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), the nation's emergency crude oil supply stored in underground salt caverns in Texas and Louisiana.
“One of the things I am going to do with the Venezuelan oil is fill up the Strategic National Reserves which, because of Sleepy Joe Biden, has been virtually emptied,” Trump wrote on his social media platform Truth Social.
He characterized the Friday deal between Washington and Caracas as a “gift from Venezuela to the people of the United States” and that the “topping out” process will commence shortly.
The current inventory of the SPR stands at 289.7 million barrels as of Aug. 21, significantly below its total authorized capacity of 714 million barrels. The reserve experienced its largest-ever drawdown in 2022 when the previous administration released 1 million barrels per day for six months to counter rising prices, eventually selling off 45% of the stockpile by late 2023.
The Department of Energy has not yet issued technical guidelines for the upcoming transfers.
Venezuela agreement
Trump's plan follows a transaction on Friday, in which Washington secured majority control over 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves in Venezuela.
Venezuelan Interim President Delcy Rodriguez, who assumed power in January following a US military operation that captured Nicolas Maduro, confirmed the pact will remain in effect for 25 years.
Rodriguez said the agreement involves developing 17 strategic fields, expecting over $100 billion in private investment and more than $209 billion in tax revenue for the South American nation.
The strategic pivot toward Venezuelan oil arrives as the Strait of Hormuz, the world’s most important oil transit point, is stranded amid the war with Iran that began on Feb. 28 and is said to have reached a stalemate.

UAE investment push incentivizes Lebanon to break from Iran, Hezbollah, analyst tells 'Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
14:49:50 UTC
23:49:50 KST

The United Arab Emirates’ recent investment push in Lebanon will help incentivize Beirut to “steer away from” Iranian and Hezbollah influence, Middle Eastern political analyst Dr. Ahmed Alkhuzaie told The Jerusalem Post on Sunday.
The UAE’s Foreign Trade Minister Thani bin Ahmed al-Zeyoudi led a delegation of more than 80 prominent figures to Lebanon last week, where an intergovernmental memorandum of understanding was signed to strengthen bilateral relations, the two countries’ foreign ministries confirmed.
During the high-profile visit, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun and Zeyoudi reportedly focused on advancing bilateral economic cooperation, with plans for the UAE to expand trade and investment in Lebanon’s private sector.
The countries signed the intergovernmental memorandum of understanding on Thursday, following the opening of the Lebanon-UAE Economic Forum on Wednesday, where five additional agreements were also initialed.
“Lebanon is pursuing a new phase of economic renewal, and the UAE stands ready to be a partner in that journey,” Zeyoudi said. “By strengthening trade flows, encouraging investment partnerships, and formalizing channels of business-to-business engagement, we are beginning a new chapter in bilateral relations and building a solid foundation for sustainable growth that will benefit both nations.”
Though the countries already enjoy a degree of economic cooperation, with non-oil trade reaching $4.2 billion in 2025, a 35.6% increase compared to 2024, the timing of the agreement is significant as it comes at a key juncture for Beirut.
Trade, investment expansion encourages Lebanon to seek alternatives to Iran
Having been dragged into multiple wars by Iran-backed Hezbollah, an expansion of trade and investment while Lebanon is still rebuilding after the latest conflict could help encourage Beirut to continue to seek alternatives to Iranian support.
“Security and investment go hand in hand, but as long as there is will and genuine intent, challenges will not be an obstacle,” Aoun told Zeyoudi, according to the UAE’s Foreign Ministry.
Notably, the UAE recently cut financial ties with Iran, ending all trade, commerce, and money transfers with Tehran in response to months of aerial attacks launched by Iran against the UAE.
“It is a good incentive for the Lebanese government, as well as a good drive for them to steer away from Iran’s and Hezbollah’s influence and work on the disarmament process,” Alkhuzaie told the Post.
“If it’s part of a new strategy, or a continuation of an existing one that will make things faster, then it makes total sense on both the economic and political sides.”
Security concerns behind UAE investment push
Members of the delegation have also told international media that security concerns were among the factors behind the investment push.
Mohamed Yusuf Adam, vice president of the National Pulse investment conglomerate in the UAE and a member of the delegation, told The National that business leaders were encouraged “to focus on the economic aspects, to focus on improving the situation more than focusing on waiting until the crisis is resolved or waiting on other ideas.”
Members of the economic forum also told the site that they were reassured by the fact that Beirut had “regained its sovereignty” by banning Hezbollah from holding arms.
Though Alkhuzaie stressed that Israel had not been striking areas likely to be of interest to UAE investors, he acknowledged that fewer or no Israeli attacks would help safeguard investments in the short term.

====================================================================================================

Nepal begins mass burials of unidentified flood victims as families seek missing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
14:49:49 UTC
23:49:49 KST

Nepal's scenic Chitwan district, known for its forests and rivers, has become the site of mass burials for hundreds of unidentified victims whose bodies were swept away by the torrent that devastated the Himalayan region days ago.
In the plains, nearly 200 kilometers from the flood-ravaged valleys of Rasuwa where the disaster struck on Wednesday, authorities have dug hundreds of graves in Chitwan's Devghat forest.
Until recently, the forest trails were a popular spot for morning walks. They now serve as a temporary burial ground for bodies too badly decomposed to be identified.
"We were left with no other option and had to take this step. Our concern was the risk to public health posed by the rapid decomposition of the bodies," said Ganesh Aryal, chief district officer of Baratpur, Chitwan.
Authorities buried 96 unidentified bodies in the forest on Saturday and planned to bury more than 100 others on Sunday, as recovery teams continue to retrieve victims from rivers and piles of debris.
About 780 people have been killed, and more than 3,000 are reported missing after a flash flood triggered by a glacial collapse swept through valleys along Nepal's border with China, causing catastrophic damage.
Around 100 rescue workers, police officers and other officials were helping to document the dead, photographing remains, helping relatives with identification and preparing bodies for burial.
Authorities said they carefully recorded every burial site, placing identification markers both above and below ground and logging precise location data.
DNA samples were collected from the unidentified dead by the Nepali authorities, allowing them to locate and exhume remains if victims are identified later through family claims, official records, or genetic testing.
India has already sent a forensic team that will be working with their Nepali counterparts to support the analysis of DNA samples. Nepal is also liaising with a team from China.
Temporary morgue set up to process unidentified remains
At Bharatpur Hospital, the stench of decomposition began at the gate, about 200 meters from a temporary morgue where around 50 police officers and hospital workers handled recovered bodies, most wearing only basic surgical masks.
Officials briefly allowed a Reuters reporter to view the facility from the entrance.
About 125 bodies lay inside on the floor, with many showing advanced decomposition after days in floodwaters, overwhelming a mortuary designed to handle just 50 bodies.
"The bodies are decaying fast," said Inspector Anil Thapa, who is overseeing one of several facilities handling the dead in the disaster-stricken district.
"Of the bodies we have recovered so far, more than half are beyond recognition," Thapa told Reuters. "Many have no visible faces."
A few hundred meters away, the Chitwan Expo Center has become the focal point for grieving families searching for missing relatives.
More than 200 people gathered outside a hall where photographs of recovered bodies were expected to be displayed to allow visual identification. Many in the crowd carried backpacks and luggage, suggesting they had traveled from distant districts.
Several families said they had arrived the previous day but had still not been allowed inside the hall.
Nearby, an aging single-story house has been converted into a temporary storage facility for bodies awaiting identification.
Three tents stood outside the building, including a Nepal Red Cross helpdesk and a police registration point. Incense burned beneath the desks but provided little relief from the odor.
As the Reuters reporter approached, a police officer handed over a mask, while another instructed colleagues to replenish mask supplies if they ran low.
The dark interior contained rooms filled with body bags stacked on bunk beds. Dry ice sat near the entrances while air conditioners and an industrial cooling unit ran continuously in an effort to slow decomposition.
Recovery operations in full swing
As recovery operations continued, a vehicle carrying 13 bodies arrived at the facility. By 10 a.m. local time, six ambulances were parked outside while another vehicle waited for space so it could unload.
Families waited outside for a chance to learn whether their loved ones were among those recovered.
The constant arrival of bodies underscored the scale of the disaster and the challenge facing authorities to identify the dead and provide answers to families still searching for missing relatives.
The toll was evident on those handling the bodies.
"Once I come here to work, I am unable to think about food," Thapa said, his uniform drenched with sweat. "Forget eating, I don't even feel like drinking water."

Chinese fighter jet based on Israeli design sold to Muslim-majority Uzbekistan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
14:49:31 UTC
23:49:31 KST

Another Muslim country is receiving the legacy of a previous Israeli aircraft project as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu instructs the defense establishment to prepare for the development of a new Israeli fighter jet in an effort to maintain Israel’s defense independence.
A video broadcast on Uzbek television confirmed that Uzbekistan will become the second customer of China’s J-10C fighter jet, after Pakistan became the first country to purchase the aircraft.
The J-10 bears a strong resemblance to Israel’s Lavi fighter jet, developed by Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI), whose production was canceled after a government decision in 1988.
According to foreign reports, China later bought the Lavi's plans to accelerate the development of a domestically produced fourth-generation fighter jet and modernize its air force. The funds China paid helped cover the costs of ending the project in Israel.
The Chinese fighter has already been used in combat, participating in aerial clashes between Pakistan and India last year. The aircraft was reportedly used to shoot down Indian Air Force Rafale fighter jets while carrying the advanced PL-15 radar-guided missile.
Uzbekistan's order reflects increasing Chinese influence in Central Asia
Uzbekistan has ordered 24 J-10 aircraft in the export configuration, a move that reflects China’s growing influence in Central Asia, where countries were previously under Russian influence.
The aircraft, which originated in Lod, is now serving a second Muslim country, although one that maintains diplomatic relations with Israel.
According to assessments, Muslim-majority Bangladesh could also become the next customer for the J-10. The aircraft is cheaper than the American F-16 and is marketed to countries that are not interested in purchasing US-made fighter jets.

This was reported by the Center for Countering Disinformation at the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine, according to UNN.
Details
According to the CCD, one of the targets of the attack was the Norwegian Agency for Public and Digitalization. The cyberattack caused a three-day disruption to the operation of dozens of government services. In addition, information related to Norway’s state budget was leaked in parallel.
The Center noted that the pro-Russian hacker group Server Killers, which has been operating since 2023, claimed responsibility for the attack. Previously, the hackers had attacked resources in Romania and Canada.
The attackers themselves allegedly linked the cyberattack to Oslo’s policy toward Ukraine. In particular, they cited as their motive revenge for Norway’s conclusion of a strategic partnership agreement with Ukraine and its decision to continue financial support for Kyiv until 2027.
The CCD considers such cyberattacks to be an element of Russia’s hybrid pressure on states that support Ukraine.
The use of cyberattacks as a direct response to the diplomatic and financial steps of European states is a classic manifestation of the Russian Federation’s hybrid war. The main goal of such operations is to exert pressure on Ukraine’s allies
The CCD emphasized the need to strengthen the joint cyber defense of partner states and introduce additional sanctions against pro-Russian hacker networks.
We remind you
Earlier, UNN reported that Europe is recording an increase in Russia-linked acts of sabotage, espionage, and cyberattacks. However, there is no evidence of preparations for a direct attack on NATO.

Google Maps will show Lake America in US, not Lake Ontario
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
14:46:00 UTC
23:46:00 KST

Google Maps will show Lake America in US, not Lake Ontario
- Google Maps renamed Lake Ontario to Lake America for US users following President Donald Trump's executive order amid a trade dispute with Canada.
- The name change applies only to US maps via the Geographic Names Information System and does not affect Canadian or international naming.
- Canadian officials and governors strongly rejected the change, affirming the lake will always be called Lake Ontario outside the US.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Google Maps has changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America for US users to reflect President Donald Trump’s executive order renaming the lake, according to a Google statement.
Trump announced on Aug 27 that he was changing the name of the smallest of the five Great Lakes, part of an escalating trade feud with Canada that has prompted the two countries to impose reciprocal tariffs on billions of dollars in goods.
The president’s order affects the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), which sets the standards for official US maps. It does not have any impact on Canadian naming conventions or how the rest of the world refers to the lake.
“Since we update Google Maps to reflect name changes in official government sources, which is GNIS for the US, people using Maps in the US will see Lake America, those in Canada will continue to see Lake Ontario, and those outside of the US and Canada will see both names,” Google said in a blog post issued on Aug 29.
The White House, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s office and Ford’s office did not immediately comment on Aug 30 on Google’s decision.
Google Maps made a similar change to the Gulf of Mexico in 2025, labelling it the Gulf of America following Trump’s executive order on his first day in office renaming the body of water.
Carney immediately rejected the lake’s name change on Aug 27. Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul of New York, which shares a long border with Canada, declared that “New York won’t be calling it that”, while Phil Scott, the Republican governor of neighbouring Vermont, called Trump’s decision “petty and disappointing” on social media.
The premier of Ontario, Doug Ford, on Aug 29 unveiled a large lakeside sign that reads, Lake Ontario: Now And Always, in both English and French.
“President Trump can call it whatever he wants, but I can tell you, the rest of the world will always call it Lake Ontario,” Ford said.
On the evening of Aug 30, an Ontario minister, Stephen Crawford, said the province was reviewing its websites after Lake America appeared on sites like the Liquor Control Board of Ontario.
The LCBO, a major global buyer, is not stocking US alcohol due to the trade war.
“Some Ontario government agency websites pull map data directly from Google Maps,” Crawford said on the social media site X.
“Following recent changes by Google, we’re actively reviewing our websites to make sure they all identify Lake Ontario by its correct name: Lake Ontario”. REUTERS
