South Africa urges ICJ to act on Israel's ongoing Gaza violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
12:47:52 UTC
21:47:52 KST

Breadcrumb
South Africa urges ICJ action over Israel's non-compliance with Gaza orders
South Africa has submitted a dossier to the International Court of Justice (ICJ), accusing Israel of continuing to disregard court orders intended to protect Palestinians amid the Gaza conflict, which is set to enter its third year.
The South African Foreign Ministry said on Friday that the dossier was submitted on 25 August to assist a committee of judges responsible for monitoring the implementation of provisional measures and recommending possible action to the court.
Pretoria said it presented the evidence after concluding that Israel had failed to comply with three legally binding provisional measures issued by the ICJ to protect the rights of Palestinians under the Genocide Convention.
South Africa launched legal proceedings against Israel at the ICJ on 29 December 2023, alleging violations of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The court subsequently issued three separate provisional measures orders on 26 January, 28 March and 24 May 2024, after South Africa requested urgent intervention over the humanitarian situation in Gaza.
The rulings required Israel to take all necessary measures to prevent acts prohibited under the convention.
The court also ordered Israel to implement safeguards against potential genocidal acts, halt military operations in the southern Gaza city of Rafah where such operations could cause physical destruction to the Palestinian population, and provide regular reports on its compliance with the measures.
In its latest statement, South Africa said it would continue pursuing “all avenues available” to seek Israel’s full and immediate compliance with the court’s orders.
“Regrettably, Israel has not complied with the Orders,” Pretoria stated in the filing.
South Africa warned that the rights of Palestinians in the Gaza Strip could be “destroyed before [the ICJ] renders its final decision”, a situation it said threatened the "legitimacy of the ICJ itself".
The dossier stated that, as of August, at least 73,407 Palestinians had been killed and 174,335 injured, together representing "over 10% of the Palestinian population" of the Gaza Strip.
It also said that, since the announcement of a "so-called ‘ceasefire" in October 2025 the Israeli military had killed an average of one Palestinian child per day.
The submission further stated that miscarriage rates among Palestinian women had "increased more than three-fold" in 2026.
South Africa also said that Israel had “arbitrarily detained and deported Palestinians” who were subsequently “tortured, subjected to sexual and gender-based violence, and to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment”.
The department additionally accused Israel of killing local journalists and preventing foreign journalists and UN-mandated investigative bodies from entering Gaza.
Israel has repeatedly rejected allegations that it is committing genocide in Gaza, despite rights groups warning that the scale and nature of its violence, including killings, restrictions on humanitarian aid, mass displacement and the destruction of medical services, could amount to genocidal acts.
Rights groups have also pointed to statements by Israeli officials that they say indicate genocidal intent.
Despite a ceasefire in Gaza that has been in place since October 2025, Israeli attacks have continued across the devastated Palestinian enclave. Israel's military has killed at least 1,313 Palestinians since then, according to Gaza's health ministry.

Spain announces €165m emergency package for Ceuta as migrant returns continue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
12:45:44 UTC
21:45:44 KST

The Council of Ministers will on Tuesday approve an emergency package to revive the economy and strengthen public services in Ceuta, one month after the mass arrival of migrants.
Spain's government plans to allocate €165 million to Ceuta's recovery, an emergency package of measures that will be approved this Tuesday by the Council of Ministers, one month after the mass arrival of migrants in the autonomous city.
The sum will be added to the medium-term recovery plan worth €180 million, according to local media, in a move previously announced by First Deputy Prime Minister and Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo.
The new package aims to revive the local economy and strengthen public services after a crisis that has disrupted activity in the autonomous city and shaped the start of the new political year. Of the total, €80 million will be channelled into Ceuta's economy over the next four months, and another €70 million is earmarked for 2027.
In all, €150 million will go into direct economic support over the next year and a half. Of that, €35 million will be devoted to direct aid for small and medium-sized enterprises and the self-employed, while another €15 million will be used to boost trade and tourism, sectors that were particularly hard hit in August.
The Council of Ministers also plans to allocate 15 million to strengthen education, healthcare and the justice system in Ceuta — three of the areas that have been at the centre of public demands in recent weeks.
One month on from the crisis
The migration situation continues to shape the city's recovery. One month after the events of 30 and 31 July, around 5,000 of the roughly 72,000 people who entered irregularly remain in Ceuta, while efforts continue to open new reception facilities and speed up return procedures.
In that context, the Minister for Territorial Policy and Democratic Memory, Ángel Víctor Torres, who heads the single command created by the government of Pedro Sánchez to deal with the crisis, has pledged that all migrants who entered the country irregularly will be returned to Morocco.
"Our intention is that all of them are returned, everyone who entered between the 30th and 31st, in accordance with the law," Torres said in remarks broadcast by RTVE, referring to the "approximately" migrants who, he said, "remain on the streets" of Ceuta.
The government considers the emergency package separate from the 180 million euro plan, which is structural in nature and currently being negotiated with business organisations, trade unions and representatives of different sectors of the city.

NEW DELHI: RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav on Sunday took a jibe at the BJP and RSS, saying, “guḍ khaye, gulgule se parhez”, amid the spat between NDA allies Chirag Paswan and Jitan Ram Manjhi over reservation.The leader of opposition in Bihar assembly also accused the two Union ministers of acting on the “instructions” of the RSS and alleged that the BJP-RSS was “anti-reservation”.He also challenged Chirag and Manjhi to resign from their posts and contest elections from unreserved seats if they opposed reservation.Taking a dig at the two leaders on X, Tejashwi said, “Guḍ khaye, gulgule se parhez!” He alleged that Chirag and Manjhi were speaking in different voices on the issue of sub-categorisation of SC/ST reservations while allegedly acting on the directions of the RSS.“Two Union Ministers, Shri Jitan Ram Manjhi and Chirag Paswan, are speaking in opposite directions on the instructions of RSS, diverting attention from the original objective of BJP-RSS to end reservations, and want to gauge the sentiments of reservation supporters,” he said.

Chirag-Manjhi lock horns over quota within quotaTejashwi's remarks came a day after differences within the NDA over sub-categorisation of SC/ST reservations became public, with Chirag Paswan and Jitan Ram Manjhi taking opposing positions.The row began after Manjhi and his son, Bihar minister Santosh Kumar Suman, supported the idea of sub-categorisation to ensure that the most deprived Dalit communities receive a greater share of reservation benefits.Chirag, who heads the Lok Janshakti Party (Ram Vilas), strongly opposed any move to review reservation and demanded that Manjhi and his son resign if they supported such a measure.“The constitutional provision of SC/ST reservation is based on social discrimination and not economic status. If they want to change the Constitution, then debate the issue in Parliament. Those who talk or think about reviewing reservation should first resign, as they actually want to completely end it and reduce its scope,” Chirag said.He also asserted that reservation was in place in the past, remains in place today and would continue in the future.Responding to Chirag's demand, Suman said he was ready to resign, but challenged Chirag to take the first step.“As far as resignations go, we are ready. My younger brother’s party is the bigger one; they have more numbers than us and are politically third-generation too, so let them take the lead. Let him step forward by resigning and we are prepared to resign alongside him,” Suman said.Tejashwi invokes Bhagwat's 2015 remarkTejashwi also targeted RSS chief over his earlier remarks on reviewing reservation, saying, “Mohan Bhagwat had also spoken earlier about reviewing reservations”, adding that Bihar “ne unke kaan pakad kar achhe se uthak-baithak karwa di thi. ====================================================================================================

Andy Burnham pledge to end indefinite prison terms ‘a step towards healing’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
12:36:46 UTC
21:36:46 KST

Campaigners have hailed Andy Burnham’s pledge to bring an end to indefinite jail terms as “a day that thousands of families have spent years fighting for”.
The prime minister has said he will “end the injustice” of imprisonment for public protection (IPP) sentences during this parliament, meaning people will no longer be trapped indefinitely under a sentence abolished more than a decade ago.
The IPP sentence was a form of indeterminate sentence in which offenders were given a minimum jail tariff but no maximum for a range of crimes.
Introduced in 2005, IPPs were designed for the indefinite detention of serious offenders who were perceived to be a risk to the public, but were used much more widely than intended and issued to offenders who committed low-level crimes. The sentence was scrapped in 2012 but its abolition was not retrospective.
Those given an IPP sentence were, in addition, placed on licence indefinitely after release, and were only eligible to have their licence removed after 10 years. The 10-year period was overturned last year and IPP prisoners may now seek termination of their licence after two years in the community, and it ends automatically after four years.
Statistics from the Ministry of Justice and HM Prison and Probation Service show that as of 30 June this year 856 people remained behind bars after being given IPP sentences. Eight out of 10 of those have been jailed for at least 10 years beyond the minimum term at which they could apply for parole.
A further 1,415 IPP prisoners were recalled to custody after being released on licence, the data shows.
Responding to Burnham’s announcement on Sunday, Marc Conway, a former IPP prisoner who now leads a campaign group against the sentencing regime called Ungripp, said the move was a long overdue step towards justice.
Conway, who was handed an IPP sentence for armed robbery, was one of three released offenders who tackled the Fishmongers’ Hall terrorist Usman Khan in 2019 on London Bridge. Conway has previously spoken of his fear that tackling the terrorist might have landed him back in jail under the terms of his IPP.
“This is a day that thousands of families have spent years fighting for,” Conway said. “For too long, their loved ones have been trapped by a sentence that was acknowledged as flawed over a decade ago.
“While we welcome this critical action by the government, we do so with heavy hearts for those who did not live to see this day, and for the families torn apart by years of endless uncertainty. Legislation alone cannot undo 20 years of damage, but it is the essential first step toward healing.”
Ungripp urged the Ministry of Justice and the probation services to ensure that the implementation of the decision was swift, transparent and accompanied by comprehensive community and mental health support for all those transitioning off IPP licences and out of custody.
Among those to have suffered from the impact of IPP sentences was Tommy Nicol, who took his own life while serving under the now abolished regime.
He was handed a minimum tariff of four years for robbery. After six years in prison, he was told he would not be eligible for another parole hearing for at least another two years. His mental health deteriorated and he died a few months after that decision.
Nine months before his death, Nicol described the sentence in a handwritten formal complaint as “psychological torture of a person who is doing 99 years”.
Responding to Sunday’s announcement, his sister, Donna, who has been a prominent campaigner against the IPP sentence, said: “When I heard the announcement today, my heart instantly split in two. Half of me felt a profound sense of relief for the thousands of families who have spent years living in the same horrific limbo that destroyed my family. The other half of me was crushed by the absolute, unbearable pain that this decision comes 10 years too late for my brother, Tommy.
“While I welcome the commitment to finally bring legislation to terminate these sentences and provide an endpoint to this nightmare, my message to the government today is clear: words are not enough. Implementation must be swift, clear and compassionate. Every day this takes to enact is another day someone’s son, brother or father is driven to the brink of despair.
“Nothing will ever bring Tommy back through our front door. Nothing will undo the trauma my family suffered watching him lose his life to a sentence that should never have existed. But if this announcement means that no other sister has to stand where I am standing today, then Tommy’s legacy, and the fight of every IPP family who refused to give up, will finally have achieved the justice he was denied.”
Speaking on BBC Breakfast, Burnham said he had made the “judgment” that the public would prefer offenders who have served their time being freed before those who have not, and that he had “longstanding concerns” about IPP sentences, which had caused “a sense of unfairness” in some cases.
He promised to apply a “commonsense” approach and said legislation would be brought forward to end such sentences by the end of the parliament.
He told BBC Breakfast: “Many of the people in this position have more than served their time. But on the scheme that I inherited, they would have remained in prison, while others who committed serious offences would have been let out early.
“And we will set up a cross-party oversight group to look at how this is done, because there are still individuals who will pose a risk to communities. It does need to be done in a very careful way with regard to public safety, national security and all of those issues.”

‘Without us, no wheel would turn’: the unsung heroes keeping England’s transport moving
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
12:35:40 UTC
21:35:40 KST

Not many people get to park their car here – bang in the middle of Heathrow airport, on the taxiway just a stretch of grass away from where a line of passenger planes is coming in to land.
It’s close enough to see the shimmering air and smoke as nose tyres hit the tarmac. “An A380 will put down as much rubber as a car’s entire tyre,” Jack Quantick-Thorne says. He knows – part of his job is to ensure the runway team scrapes it off and patches things up overnight. And it is all recycled, he adds.
The airfield operations officer is not in the limelight much, but is one of a host of unsung workers keeping transport moving. And some jobs far from the public eye turn out to be not only essential, but surprisingly challenging.
Jack Quantick-Thorne, airfield operations officer, Heathrow
Passengers might only catch a glimpse of Quantick-Thorne from a window seat on landing, if he grabs the paddles to marshal a plane into the exact designated spot at the stand. “People just think you’re that person with the table tennis bats,” he grimaces slightly, as the Guardian requests a demonstration. “That’s like 5% of my job.”
In fact, most planes are now brought to the stand via laser-guided electronic displays. But human marshalling remains a crucial backup. Brandishing the paddles, Quantick-Thorne beckons in a taxiing British Airways arrival, the pilot peering down from the cockpit and steering 50 tonnes of plane straight towards him. The nosewheel travels bang on the guideline, stopping exactly in position for the airbridge to swing in and allow passengers to disembark.
Nerve-racking? “No. When you’ve got a really big plane, an A380, you need a second marshal right by the wheel to check it’s stopped in the right place,” he says.
Back in the car, the job continues: “I’m patrolling, I’m looking around, scanning everything – is the refueller doing his job properly, has the aircraft got chocks under its wheels?”
That includes monitoring the road system under Heathrow’s airfields, recognising every vehicle and checking any infringement: drivers here can also clock up points on their licence, if he spots them.
Officers also need to look out for wildlife – particularly birds, a serious danger for jet planes (and vice versa). How does he deal with them? “We’ve got methods of dispersal,” says the airfield operations officer.
These, marvellously, turn out to be speakers on the roof of the van, which play a range of bird sounds: “If I saw a flock of starlings, if I played a starling noise, the starling would think, ‘Oh, maybe there’s a predator nearby,’ and they fly off.”
And, he demonstrates, “I’ve got common gull. Black-headed gull. I’ve got a falcon”.
Are there falcons? “No,” he explains patiently. “So you think about it from a bird’s point of view. If there’s a pigeon over there, best play a falcon so it will fly off.”
If he now knows birds, it’s the planes that drew him here. He was previously at Nats, the air traffic control centre in Swanwick, managing the planes, but never up close. There is more to it than the paddles – but, he confesses, he takes every opportunity to use them, and records each plane that he has marshalled, including every aircraft in BA’s short-haul fleet.
Being a pilot is the dream, he admits, but the prohibitive training costs – £100,000 or more – put it out of reach. For an enthusiast, he reckons the job is the next best thing. Last year he had to tow the Concorde that still stands at the edge of the airfield across for an exhibition: “It was the first time one had moved in years – incredible to see in the rear-view mirror.”
Chris Thackaberry, network traffic controller, Transport for London
The day starts in Victoria Station House overlooking the bus terminus, a grand old building that looks considerably less so inside, where Chris’s desk is surrounded by hundreds of cardboard diversion signs.
About 500 of the capital’s 19,000 bus stops are on his patch in Westminster – home to some of Britain’s most congested streets, where dozens of bus routes cross. Roadworks are the bane of the bus and Thackaberry’s job is to keep them moving – armed with a van, pliers and zip ties.
Sometimes he can plan for roadworks months ahead. But other days are less predictable, when life suddenly blocks a route: “It could be a broken-down vehicle or a burst water main, but I’ve had windows falling out of buildings, I’ve had a collapsed horse on a bridge. I had an upside down Lamborghini in Piccadilly … I don’t know if it was sticking to the 20mph limit.”
His incident response van contains an orderly standing desk area and even a printer to rustle up more signs if needed, as well as spill dry sacks, ready to suck up any diesel or oil leaked over the road.
It also has two cylinders affixed to the wall containing “spit kits” – swabs to pick up any saliva aimed at staff, with clear bags to seal, ready to take the evidence to the police. “It’s just part and parcel of when you’re working in London, for anyone in uniform.”
In a sweltering Trafalgar Square, as he hunts in the midst of four lanes of traffic to hitch his cardboard signs to any available piece of spare street furniture, the complexity of the puzzle becomes clearer.
“There’s so many routes go through here, we’re fighting with ourselves for space.”
Sarah, railway signaller, York
Gone are most of the signal boxes of old: these days, Britain’s railway is mostly controlled from one of 12 remote centres. From a windowless room in York, trains right down the East Coast mainline are guided on their way.
“In the old days, it was lever pulling,” says Sarah. “Now it’s a click of the mouse instead. Like a computer game scenario, but it’s real track, real trains, real people. We have to manually click, signal to signal, for every train that comes through our patch.”
Signallers have five screens at eye level showing the railway, and five above with timetables and traffic management information.
“When you first start the job, it feels so far removed. There’s no windows, it’s like a black hole in the middle of the building, but you are signalling trains from York all the way into King’s Cross. I remember thinking: ‘How many hundreds of people are on that train we’re signalling?’”
Anything from a circuit failure to a trespasser to a sick passenger on a train can hold up the lines. “Our job initially in any incident is to make the area safe – that’s first and foremost. And then we look for a workaround, to keep trains moving. The days when there are serious incidents are few and far between. But every day there’s something.”
Jamie *, public service vehicle engineer, Manchester
At Jamie’s bus depot, servicing the Bee Network, the first shift starts at 5am and the last ends at 1am, but engineers might stay through the night with a breakdown.
“In the daytime it’s routine: vehicles are inspected by law on a monthly basis,” he says. “But engineers have bus driving licences too, if a bus was to break down, often we’d take another one out to the driver to keep the service running.”
With city buses that stop and start frequently, there is typically more treatment and maintenance. And newer vehicles don’t necessarily mean less work, he says: “They bring a lot of new issues and we’re constantly learning, going back to college on courses to learn the tech.
“Electric buses haven’t made the job easier – but they and the new diesel engines are clean. Working back in the day, it was a hell of a lot dirtier, especially in depots indoors or undercover,” says the vehicle engineer.
He will check each bus’s brakes, emissions tests and inspect the nuts and bolts everywhere from the underside to the driver’s cab. “We see a lot in the press about the conditions in the cab, but we’re cleaning those buses: it’s like a greenhouse, and the heat from the engines also comes into our workshop.
“Even the drivers don’t understand what engineers do – I always say we are the forgotten people. But without us, no wheel would turn.”
Frankie *, baggage handler, Gatwick
The thing people don’t understand, explains Frankie, is that the placement of bags in the hold is not random. “It’s all done on weight distribution. You have to put baggage where you’re told – it is a very specific job, you do not deviate.”
At many airports, larger aircraft such as long-haul planes are loaded with bags already in large crates, lifted into position by machine. But short-haul flights at Gatwick are loaded manually. “An average bag is about 20kg and the average load is 90 bags off, 90 on, for three or four people. If you do eight turns a day, that’s nearly 30 tonnes your team is lifting. You get fitter – it’s like going to the gym, you end up lifting heavier and heavier bags.”
Passengers who fear for their luggage often make the job harder: “The worst thing is shrink-wrapped bags. It’s slippery, harder to hold on to, and less grip for the belt to pull up. And those straps around bags, they can get jammed in the belts and break them.
“People don’t realise how damaging it can be – and pointless. If you’re on a flight where customs do spot checks, they go for the bags that are wrapped. And there is so much CCTV and security. If I get caught opening a bag, I’d lose my job – why would I risk that?”
There are, says Frankie, more women doing the job now: “It’s getting more female-friendly. A lot of people choose this type of job to get into aviation: they want to be pilots or crew eventually, and just want to be around planes any way they can.”
* Names have been changed

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Japanese City Pop pioneer Onuki Taeko made her Taiwan debut Sunday, performing on the closing night of the Jam Jam Asia music festival at the Taipei Music Center.
Onuki, who has been active in music for more than five decades, reflected on her career during the performance and became emotional as she thanked fans for their continued support. She said she had considered whether to continue performing, but the unwavering support of her fans had allowed her to keep singing, according to MNews.
Onuki has expanded her overseas performances in recent years, including appearances in Los Angeles and South Korea. For her first JJA performance, she selected songs that had proved popular with audiences during her overseas performances.
“I’m really happy to meet everyone,” she told the audience before leaving the stage. She also reminded fans to “stay healthy” and thanked them again for their support.
Onuki's appearance was one of the highlights of JJA, which brought more than 80 Taiwanese and international acts to seven stages at the Taipei Music Center on Aug. 29-30. The lineup included Accusefive, Yang Nai-wen (楊乃文), LINION, Asian Dub Foundation, Le Petit Soldat, and DJ Krush, among others, per a press release.
Born in Tokyo in 1953, Onuki formed Sugar Babe with Tatsuro Yamashita and other musicians in 1973. The group released the album “SONGS” in 1975 before disbanding in 1976, when Onuki launched her solo career with “Grey Skies.” She has released 27 original albums.
Her music has incorporated pop, electronic, and Brazilian influences, as well as acoustic and orchestral arrangements. She also collaborated with Sakamoto Ryuichi on the album “UTAU.” Her music production for the 1997 film “Tokyo Biyori” won the Japan Academy Film Prize for Best Music.
Onuki's earlier recordings have gained a new international audience amid the global resurgence of City Pop. Her 1977 album “SUNSHOWER,” in particular, has been rediscovered by younger listeners and reissued on vinyl.
JJA was held as part of the Taipei Music Expo, which ran from Thursday to Sunday at the Taipei Music Center. TMEX focused this year on technology and sustainability and included exhibitions, international forums, industry matchmaking, and performances.
Organizers said TMEX brought together more than 60 international and domestic music brands and industry organizations, along with more than 100 international industry professionals and creators, to strengthen connections between Taiwan's music industry and overseas markets.

Icelanders reject reopening talks to join the EU despite Trump's Greenland threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
12:32:44 UTC
21:32:44 KST

Icelanders voted to reject resuming talks to join the European Union, as issues such as domestic control over fishing appeared to override geopolitical security concerns.
Broadcaster RUV reported that 52.8% of voters rejected the government's push to reopen EU membership negotiations, while 47.2% voted in favor.
The question put to the Nordic nation of nearly 400,000 was whether Iceland should resume accession negotiations with the European Union.
A majority "yes" vote would have led to a negotiated agreement being put to a second referendum for Icelanders to accept or reject.
The debate has taken on deeper significance in the wake of U.S. President Donald Trump's Arctic saber-rattling.
But in the end, concern over the potential loss of control over its fishing industry and an erosion of national identity won out over how Iceland might be affected by geopolitical rivalries.
"The 'No' side succeeded because it tapped into the most fundamental driver of Icelandic national identity: the demand for absolute self-governance. This is inextricably linked to control over natural resources and fisheries, which forms the very heart of the Icelandic understanding of sovereignty," said Eiríkur Bergmann, professor of politics at Iceland's Bifröst University.
Fishing's share of Iceland's broader economy has declined over the decades, even as seafood remains a major export industry.
Marine products and farmed fish made up nearly 47% of the country's exports in the August 2025-July 2026 period, according to Statistics Iceland.
But production halved from a peak of 2.2 million tons in 1997 to 1.1 million tons in 2024, World Bank data show. Agriculture, forestry and fishing contributed 9.1% of Iceland's gross domestic product in 1995, but only 3.7% by 2025, as manufacturing and services grew in importance.
Greenland or Iceland?
The U.S. president has long advocated for control over neighboring Greenland on national security grounds. Notably, Trump appeared to repeatedly mix up Greenland and Iceland during a special address at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland earlier in the year.
Iceland, a founding member of NATO, is the only ally without its own military forces. The country also sits astride the so-called GIUK Gap, a naval choke point between Greenland, Iceland and the U.K. that links the Arctic to the Atlantic Ocean.
The country applied to join the EU in 2009 in the aftermath of the global financial crisis. A euroskeptic government suspended negotiations in 2013, and the accession process was formally ended in 2015.
It's already deeply integrated into the European framework, partly through its membership of the European Economic Area, which gives the volcanic island access to the EU's single market without requiring full membership.
It's also a member of the Schengen Area, which allows passport-free travel between it and other participating European countries.
At the start of the year, Iceland's Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Gunnarsdottir said that deeper dialogue and collaboration with the EU would be a key factor in shoring up the country's interests.
"It is clear that the international system we have lived in since the end of World War II is in turmoil," Gunnarsdottir said in an article for Icelandic newspaper Visir, according to a Google translation.
"What is perhaps most striking about this referendum is that despite the profound geopolitical upheaval around us – including rapidly shifting security paradigms in the North Atlantic – these global realities never really filtered properly through into the public debate," Bifröst University's Bergmann said.
"The 'Yes' side lost because they ran a highly technical and, frankly, passionless campaign."
—CNBC's Sam Meredith contributed to this story.

Istanbul to host 1st Mecca Pact meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
12:31:08 UTC
21:31:08 KST

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan speaks with his Saudi Arabian counterpart, Faisal bin Farhan, ahead of a meeting.
Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan will hold the first meeting of a committee established under a joint defense pact in Istanbul on Aug. 31, as the three countries seek to deepen military cooperation and coordinate on regional security.
The Strategic Political and Defense Committee’s inaugural meeting is expected to bring together the foreign and defense ministers and military chiefs of the three countries, according to Turkish diplomatic sources.
Türkiye is expected to be represented by Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Defense Minister Yaşar Güler and Chief of General Staff Selçuk Bayraktaroğlu.
Pakistan’s delegation is expected to include Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Federal Defense Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif and Army Chief Asim Munir. Saudi Arabia is expected to send Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan, Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman and Chief of General Staff Fayyadh bin Hamed Al-Ruwaili.
The committee was established to provide strategic direction for activities under the Mecca Joint Defense Pact, signed by the leaders of the three countries earlier this month.
The meeting is expected to address international security issues and efforts to strengthen the defense capabilities of the three countries and improve interoperability among their armed forces, the sources said.
Participants are also expected to discuss deeper cooperation in the defense industry, including joint production and research and development, as well as stronger joint counterterrorism efforts.
The committee is expected to establish a framework for a secretariat and other mechanisms to coordinate work in areas of joint activity. It will also seek to draw up a roadmap for implementing the pact in the coming period, according to the sources.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shahbaz Sharif signed the pact in Mecca on Aug. 7.
The agreement was signed amid what officials described as growing instability in the countries’ regions and internationally. It seeks to promote security, peace, stability and prosperity while strengthening the three countries’ joint deterrence capabilities.
The pact stipulates that “an attack against any one of the parties will be considered an attack against all parties.”
The three countries have sought to expand defense ties in recent years, including through military exercises, defense industry cooperation and diplomatic coordination.
Ankara slams Israeli statement
Meanwhile, Türkiye on Aug. 29 rejected an Israeli Foreign Ministry statement targeting Erdoğan, saying the “lies and slanders” in it reflected the mentality of officials serving in the Israeli government.
“The statement issued by the Israeli Foreign Ministry reflects the cowardly and rotten mentality of the criminals serving in the Israeli government, particularly [Benjamin] Netanyahu,” Ankara said.
The statement accused Erdoğan of being antisemitic and of inciting hostility toward Israel.
Türkiye’s Foreign Ministry said Netanyahu and his “criminal network” had brought “historic shame” on the Israeli people through what it described as genocide in Gaza.
“The immunities enjoyed by Netanyahu and his criminal network are disappearing both legally and politically,” it added.

Boat with around 270 people on board capsizes off North Cyprus; one dead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
12:30:31 UTC
21:30:31 KST

At least eight die, 17 missing after ferry capsizes off North Cyprus
NICOSIA - At least eight people died and 17 were missing after a ferry carrying around 270 passengers and crew capsized off north Cyprus on Aug 30, leaving survivors clinging to its overturned hull.
The privately owned ferry left the port of Kyrenia at 12.30pm local time (5.30pm Singapore time) and immediately started taking on water for an unknown reason, authorities said. It was heading for the Turkish port of Tasucu in the eastern Mediterranean.
Survivors reported the ferry moving erratically, with its last hard impact with the water’s surface breaking the bow of the two-hulled vessel, allowing water to seep in.
The disaster occurred just off the coast of Kyrenia, a popular holiday resort for both locals and tourists. The ferry was one of several shuttle sea services that link north Cyprus, a breakaway unrecognised Turkish Cypriot state, with Turkey daily.
Turkish Cypriot leader Tufan Erhurman told CNN Turk he was “deeply saddened” by the incident.
Video footage showed people in red life jackets sitting or standing on top of the overturned vessel as authorities scrambled coastguard and private vessels for assistance to bring them to shore.
“The vessel had been moving very badly. It was constantly lifting out of the water and slamming back down. It was shaking violently,” survivor Efe Multici told CNN Turk.
“Three or four minutes later, the ferry leapt high into the air, then came crashing down. The front left side burst open and water started pouring in.”
Turkish Cypriot authorities said the captain of the vessel and seven crew had been detained for questioning. By late afternoon, the ship had sank, settling on the seabed at a depth of 514 metres. Divers from Turkey would be assisting the search, they said.
“If there are people still inside the vessel, reaching them does not appear easy at the moment,” Erhurman said. “Efforts are being made using other technologies to reach them as well.”
Major rescue operation underway
Cyprus was battered by fierce storms on Aug 29, with one person dying after his sailboat crashed onto rocks in rough seas in the island’s south-east.
Asked about the cause of the capsize, Erhurman noted the storm on Aug 29, but said the weather on Aug 30 was considered suitable for travel.
“There is a great sense of shock here. This is not something we have experienced before,” he said, speaking from the crisis centre set up in the area.
North Cyprus is a breakaway state recognised only by Turkey, which supports the area economically and militarily.
In Turkey, President Tayyip Erdogan extended his condolences to the families affected.
Expressions of condolence and offers of assistance also came from Cyprus’s internationally recognised government. Cyprus has been split down Greek and Turkish Cypriot lines since 1974, when Turkey invaded in response to a brief Greek inspired coup.
“Efforts to reach those who are still missing continue uninterrupted,” Erdogan said. “God willing, we hope to receive positive news from these efforts.”
The Turkish Cypriot Interior Ministry said the passenger ferry ‘FILOJET’ was carrying 259 passengers and eight crew, and it began taking on water about four nautical miles off Kyrenia while sailing from Kyrenia to Tasucu in Turkey.
Four Turkish Cypriot coast guard vessels and a civilian passenger boat were deployed to the scene, along with five Turkish coastguard vessels and two helicopters, the ministry statement said. REUTERS

Will US threats over Iran be the last straw for Beijing?

Opinion
Will US threats over Iran be the last straw for Beijing?
China’s measured stance since the Xi-Trump summit in May is reaching a tipping point as US pressure mounts
3-MIN READ3-MIN
15
 Listen
Zhou Xiaoming is a senior fellow at the Centre for China and Globalisation in Beijing and a former deputy representative of China’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office in Geneva. 
Earlier this month, when US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent threatened sanctions against any nation continuing to purchase Iranian crude oil, he did not name China. He did not need to. China, the Islamic Republic’s largest oil customer, is squarely in Washington’s crosshairs.
The US has already unveiled new sanctions against 60 individuals, companies and vessels linked to Iranian trade, including some in mainland China and Hong Kong. Just three months after the May summit between President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump appeared to stabilise bilateral trade relations, the fragile calm is being tested again.
So far, China has signalled it will not be coerced. The stand-off sets the stage for what could be the next major rupture in an already fraught relationship.
Washington has not been idle since May. In June, the Pentagon added dozens of companies – including Alibaba, Baidu and BYD – to its list of “Chinese military companies”, a designation that can restrict these companies’ access to US capital and market. In July, it announced a 10-12.5 per cent tariff on goods from 60 economies, including China, following its Section 301 investigation into forced labour.
This was followed by a ban on imports of Chinese robots and power inverters (July) and a 15 per cent tariff on polysilicon (August). The cumulative message is clear: Washington is tightening the screws on multiple fronts, and Iran is merely the latest lever.
Beijing’s response to this onslaught has been deliberate and calibrated. Gone are the days of blanket tariff retaliation. Instead, China has preferred to hold its fire where the cost of escalation outweighs the benefits, striking back with precision when core interests are threatened.

12:30:00 UTC
21:30:00 KST

I was born and raised in Jerusalem, and I still live here. Growing up, I do not remember my generation or my father’s sorting friends and neighbors by religion. I never thought of Issam, my friend, as “the Christian,” or Nizar, my next-door neighbor, as “the Muslim.”
At some point, however, a strange new phrase entered our vocabulary: “our Christian brothers, our partners in the homeland.” I never liked it. Why “partners”? They were never anything other than an indigenous part of this country — milh hadha al-ard, or “the salt of the earth,” as we say in Arabic.
I feel the same discomfort with slogans such as “we seek national unity between Palestinian Muslims and Christians.” Such slogans often end up proving the opposite of what they intend — as though we first have to establish that people who have lived together for centuries are, in fact, one people.
This matters because the decline of the Palestinian Christian presence is real, serious, and accelerating — and the response remains largely stuck at the level of warning. Every few months, church leaders, activists, and the Palestinian media return to the same message: Christians are disappearing. But there is no plan to confront that decline.
Today, roughly 47,000 to 50,000 Christians remain in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, according to Palestinian Bureau of Statistics figures from 2017, and probably fewer today. Gaza had close to 1,500 Christians before the war; fewer than 500 are believed to remain, though no precise figure is possible amid displacement, killing, and the destruction of institutions and records.
This decline does not happen all at once. It happens quietly: a young Christian Palestinian from Jerusalem leaves to study and does not return; a couple builds a life in Chile rather than Bethlehem; a family in Ramallah moves to Houston, having concluded that building a future at home has simply become too difficult. The reasons are clear to all: occupation, the permit regime, expanding settlements, escalating settler violence, severe restrictions on movement, fragmented territory, economic pressure, and the absence of political prospects. This is the cage — the open prison — in which Palestinians live. But explaining Christian emigration only through that prism is no longer enough.
Before going further, it is important to acknowledge what has already been done. More than 15 years ago, Kairos Palestine offered a different vision, beginning with its 2009 document and developing into a theological and political movement and an international advocacy platform. Its message was clear: Palestinian Christians are not a separate minority waiting to be rescued from outside. They are an indigenous, deeply rooted part of the Palestinian people. Remaining on the land and resisting its dispossession, Kairos Palestine argued, are both political and theological responsibilities. With that voice, Kairos took Palestine into churches and Christian communities abroad, calling for advocacy, political pressure, and boycott, while insisting that emigration should not become an inevitable fate.
The problem, then, is not a lack of vision. There is a language of steadfastness and an international advocacy network. What is missing is the institutional and economic infrastructure that makes staying possible. It is easy to tell a young Palestinian: “Stay on your land.” The harder part is answering the questions that follow: Where will I work? Can I afford a home? How will I educate my children, start a business, and what happens when my home is demolished, or when I cannot reach my university or workplace?
This is where the churches have a particular responsibility. They possess resources most Palestinian civil-society organizations do not: valuable land and properties, schools, hospitals, guesthouses, financial resources, and international networks. Church property cannot be treated simply as an internal administrative matter. The battles over historic properties around Jaffa Gate in Jerusalem demonstrated the consequences of losing strategically important Palestinian Christian land. The lesson should be clear: the wider community cannot be called upon only after a property has been lost. Major sales and long-term leases of Palestinian Christian property should be subject to independent local review involving community representatives and Palestinian experts in law, finance, and real estate. Palestinian Orthodox Arabs have demanded a greater role in church affairs for generations — that the reform is difficult is not a reason to avoid it.
The same principle should apply to church-run schools, hospitals, and vocational institutions. Scholarships could prioritize fields needed by the Palestinian economy, and vocational programs could equip young people to earn a living without leaving. Churches connected to the pilgrimage and religious tourism industry could work deliberately to keep more of that revenue in the local economy — supporting Palestinian tourist guides, guesthouses, restaurants, transport providers, and small businesses.
No one should overstate what churches can accomplish. A scholarship does not create a job, and a training certificate does not remove a checkpoint. Churches cannot end the occupation or create a Palestinian state. But they can decide whether the resources they control remain disconnected services or become part of a coherent strategy for community survival.
The thirteen church denominations in Palestine do not need to merge, and that is clearly not realistic. They need to coordinate and divide responsibilities according to their strengths. The Orthodox Patriarchate, because of its property holdings, has a particular responsibility for defending church-owned land. Catholic institutions can do more in education and vocational training. Anglican and Protestant churches, with their international networks, can take a stronger role in legal advocacy, residency, family reunification, and international pressure.
The diaspora is another largely untapped resource. Palestinian Christians in the Americas, Europe, and the Arab world possess capital, expertise, and business networks. The question is where they are when it comes to providing small-business loans, housing assistance, youth projects, and investment in Palestinian Christian communities — in Bethlehem, Beit Jala, Beit Sahour, Jerusalem, Taybeh, Zababdeh, and elsewhere. Perhaps more urgently: where are they when it comes to the rapidly disappearing Palestinian Christian community in Gaza? What is required is capital, competent management, transparency, and will.
Palestinian civil society, business associations, professional bodies, political leaders, and Muslim institutions should also be part of a national effort to protect the Christian presence. The decline of Christians is part of the wider Palestinian crisis of land, movement, employment, and demographics. There should be practical Muslim-Christian mechanisms to defend families facing displacement, support local businesses, and advocate for threatened communities.
Western solidarity also needs to change. “Save the Christians of the Holy Land” is an emotionally powerful message, but it can obscure the larger reality: Palestinians — Muslim and Christian — are being pushed to leave by occupation and the conditions it creates. The better message is: help Palestinians remain on their land, and help Palestinian Christians build a future there. That means supporting housing, vocational education, small businesses, legal defense, land protection, and community institutions — not simply producing another report documenting how many Christians have left.
It is time for Palestinian churches to measure their role and impact differently: How many families did they help stay? How many homes were restored? How many young people were trained and helped to find work? How much land was protected? These are the real markers.
The demographic decline of Palestinian Christians is real and painful. Occupation is the cause, and while churches cannot end it, that does not absolve them of responsibility for what they can do. They have land, institutions, money, schools, international networks, and a diaspora. Kairos Palestine gave Palestinian Christian steadfastness a language and a political voice. What is needed now is to turn that message into an institutional and economic project that makes staying in the birthplace of Jesus a viable choice.
For years, we have asked: how many Christians are left? How many have left? The right question is different: what have we done to ensure that the Palestinian Christian family can remain rooted in its home, its land, and its homeland?

America lost its longest war five years ago. This is what victory looks like for the Taliban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
12:29:11 UTC
21:29:11 KST

America lost its longest war five years ago. This is what victory looks like for the Taliban
“When Ashraf Ghani goes, we’ll go with him. And he’ll go when the Americans do.”
The conversation took place on the balcony of a luxury high-rise in Shahr-e Naw, central Kabul. The man speaking to me was a young government employee, and Ashraf Ghani was serving his second term as president of the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan. It was May 2017. The republic had four years and three months left.
A city living on borrowed time
Afghanistan at the time could best be described with a line from Dickens: “It was the best of times, it was the worst of times… we had everything before us, we had nothing before us.” Kabul was both deeply Westernized and full of contradictions. The former was fueled by the abundance of foreigners and foreign aid; the latter by the unending fighting and terrorist attacks.
Downtown, you could find nightclubs throwing Valentine’s Day and Halloween parties, modeling agencies, coffee shops serving cheesecake, bowling alleys, and tattoo parlors. On the outskirts, tent camps were expanding to accommodate internally displaced people – refugees from the provinces, mostly in the south, whose homes had been destroyed by the war. Street boys begged in English: “Give me one hundred dollars!” Artists painted murals warning about domestic violence, fashionable women wore jeans and bright makeup, and Western NGOs taught Afghan children to skateboard.
At the same time, some places – including the park in Shahr-e Naw itself – were unsafe even in broad daylight because of the number of drug addicts, while robberies and kidnappings had become routine. After sunset, the city shut down. Several years later, The New York Times would call Kabul a city of hope and despair – an apt metaphor.
To protect itself from the constant bombings, Kabul grew a shell of concrete walls and checkpoints. There seemed to be as many police officers and soldiers on the streets as civilians, while American surveillance balloons hovered continuously over the city. None of it helped much. That same May, while I was there, a tanker truck packed with explosives detonated in the diplomatic quarter, killing more than 90 people and wounding around 400. Smaller incidents had long since ceased to qualify as news. One of my editors gave me a simple rule:
“If there’s a terrorist attack in Kabul and fewer than ten people are killed, don’t write about it. That’s not news.”
Politics and public life were no less remarkable. Afghanistan’s parliament had as many women as the US Congress, yet in the center of the capital a mob lynched Farkhunda Malikzada, a young Afghan woman, after a mullah falsely accused her of burning the Quran. Corruption broke every record, and the central government was weak. Hamid Karzai, the republic’s first president, had been dubbed the “president of Kabul.” Ashraf Ghani was already merely the “president of the presidential palace.” A provincial governor removed from office could simply declare that the president had no authority over him and remain at his post. Drug production reached unprecedented levels: according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, 84% of the opiates on the global market in 2017 originated in Afghanistan.
This was what years of NATO’s military presence had made of the country and its capital. Once the troops withdrew, the existing order was bound to collapse.
The war that kept changing uniforms
The arrival of the United States and its allies in Afghanistan opened a new chapter in a civil war that, with varying degrees of intensity, had already been raging for 23 years.
Pandora’s box was opened in 1978, when the left came to power. The United States, Pakistan, China, and the Gulf states began actively arming the opposition, while the new government asked the Soviet Union for help. From 1979 to 1989, the Limited Contingent of Soviet Forces carried out what Moscow called its “internationalist duty” in Afghanistan, supporting a friendly government and controlling the major cities and some of the roads – the most any foreign army could hope to hold in the country’s mountainous terrain.
After the Soviet withdrawal, Mohammad Najibullah’s pro-Soviet government survived for roughly four years before being overthrown by the mujahideen: warlords who had first fought the shuravi – “Soviets” in Dari – and then turned their guns on one another in a struggle for power. The Taliban entered Kabul in 1996, bringing down the mujahideen government everywhere except the Panjshir Valley. The international community then forgot about Afghanistan for five years. It remembered the country only after the September 11, 2001 attacks, because Osama bin Laden was hiding there.
Immediately after the attacks came an episode recounted in ethnography classes to every student specializing in Afghanistan. George W. Bush issued the Taliban an ultimatum: hand over bin Laden. They refused. The official explanation was that there was no evidence linking him to the attacks. But there was an unofficial reason as well: bin Laden was a guest in Afghanistan. For the Pashtuns – the country’s largest ethnic group, to which the Taliban also belong – the rules of hospitality are sacred, and surrendering a guest to his enemy would bring shame for generations.
Uninterested in the finer points of the local mindset, Bush spent a month bombing Afghanistan and destroying the Taliban’s air force and air defenses. Then came the ground operation, first carried out with the help of allied forces – the same mujahideen – and later by US Marines under Operation Enduring Freedom. The United States had entered the longest war in its history and, at the same time, decided to build a democracy in Afghanistan – a bold idea for a country still living, in many respects, in the Middle Ages, with only a third of its population able to read and write. American filmmakers would later explore the absurdity of the situation and Washington’s profound failure to understand the country in War Machine, starring Brad Pitt.
For the first several years, things went reasonably well. Hamid Karzai, mentioned above, was elected president, a parliament was elected, and the United Nations and other international organizations threw themselves into reconstruction. While much of the money ended up in officials’ pockets, life did improve in some respects: child mortality declined, and the number of young women attending universities rose.
By 2005, however, the Taliban had recovered from their defeat and launched a guerrilla war in the south, where they found no shortage of supporters. Again, I think back to those university ethnography classes. We were taught that Afghans prefer something of their own, even if it is bad, to something good imposed by outsiders. In other words, Afghans have always hated occupiers. NATO troops – who periodically stormed into the women’s quarters of homes during raids or killed civilians, whether by mistake or out of fear – were no exception. The Taliban, for all their conservatism and radical methods, were still their own. Their values did not clash with those of Afghanistan’s rural heartland. I still remember how Taliban fighters were welcomed in Kabul during a three-day ceasefire in 2018: people gave them flowers, took selfies with them, brought them food, hugged them, and wept.
During the years of the American presence, much of the resentment toward the Soviet Union had faded.
”Yes, you fought us, but you fought well, like men,” former mujahideen told me again and again in different parts of the country. “You were brave: face to face, and the stronger man won. But these people? They bomb us from airplanes.”
The runway at the end of the world
On August 15, 2021, a message from Kabul woke me. It was from an Afghan journalist I knew.
”They’re here.”
“Who?”
“The Taliban. They’ve taken the city. It’s over.”
I had flown out of Kabul in February, and that assignment had been my bleakest: three or four explosions a day, activists and politicians being assassinated, Taliban patrols operating barely 12 miles from the capital. Kabul was practically under siege. Intense localized fighting raged in the south, official figures put the death toll at a hundred people a day, and provincial capitals kept changing hands.
Biden had announced that American troops would leave Afghanistan by September 11 – the irony was hard to miss – but analysts remained fairly optimistic. After all, Najibullah had held on for several years. Why couldn’t Ghani? Operation Enduring Freedom had long since been replaced by the noncombat Resolute Support mission, with alliance troops training and advising their Afghan counterparts so they could stand up to the Taliban on their own. Depending on the forecast, the republic was expected to survive anywhere from two to six months.
The Afghan armed forces did, in fact, have plenty of combat-ready units: Special Forces and commando brigades, as well as the Grom and Gardez regional army corps based in Khost and Kandahar. But every conversation I had with the military left me with the same heavy feeling. Many complained that both their allies and their commanders were indifferent to their fate, while morale in more remote areas was catastrophically low. The commander of a checkpoint in Kunar Province told me he had gone several months without food, ammunition, or pay. Of the eight soldiers under his command, three were suffering from depression. One no longer got out of bed and was preparing to die, even though his wound was not serious; he was also using drugs. Two others were planning to defect to the Taliban. Every evening, the militants used loudspeakers to urge them to surrender, promising to spare their lives – a common practice at the time, and the Taliban generally kept their word. The commander himself, though “tired to death,” as he put it, had no intention of giving up. He had killed too many of them to expect mercy.
”No one will fight for the president. Nobody likes him,” he told me as we said goodbye. “And the president wouldn’t fight for us, either. The Americans deceived him, and he’ll deceive us.”
His words about the president proved prophetic: Ashraf Ghani fled to Uzbekistan before Kabul had even fallen fully under Taliban control. But the checkpoint commander was wrong about his own future. He survived the fall of the government and became a taxi driver. Tens of thousands of his former comrades found work as security guards, construction workers, shopkeepers, or day laborers. The new government granted them amnesty but did not trust them enough to keep them in the army.
But back to the morning of August 15. Mass panic gripped Kabul. A crowd rushed to the airport – the only place still under coalition control – tore down the barriers, and flooded the tarmac. Terrified people tried to force their way onto American planes, and their fear was entirely understandable: many remembered the public executions and ethnic cleansing of the Taliban’s first period in power. Photographs from Kabul in August 2021 bore an uncanny resemblance to those from Saigon in April 1975, when the Americans were also evacuating their allies. History does, after all, have a way of moving in circles. Kabul itself, incidentally, fell without a fight. Among those who spent weeks waiting for a flight and sleeping on the runways were many former members of the security forces who had gone home without firing a shot and hidden their uniforms.
”American troops cannot and should not be fighting in a war and dying in a war that Afghan forces are not willing to fight for themselves,” US President Joe Biden said in summing up the debacle.
”We were betrayed,” General Sami Sadat, a deputy commander of the Afghan army, told The New York Times.
Analysts now expected mass reprisals and another round of civil war. But Afghanistan – now the Islamic Emirate – was quiet.
A different kind of silence
A teapot filled with green tea sits on the desk of a Taliban official at the Ministry of Information. My hospitable host diligently keeps my cup full, pushes a dish of chewy candies toward me, and asks what I think of the new government. A month and a half has passed since the fall of the republic – or the “victory,” as the Taliban themselves call it.
”Have you been to our country before?”
“Yes.”
“And when was it better – then or now?”
“It’s much safer now,” I say. It is clearly the answer he expects, and one I can give with a clear conscience.
This time I arrived in Kabul from the north, after a 12-hour drive from Mazar-i-Sharif through the Salang Pass. Under the republic, such a journey would have been unthinkable. Fighting had raged all along the road. The reminders were everywhere: burned-out army vehicles stacked in pyramids, the walls of homes blown away by explosions, and the road itself, pocked with craters from mines and shelling. You can now walk at night in any part of Kabul, though few Afghans take advantage of the opportunity. No one yet understands what to expect from the new rulers. People fear them, despite all the leaders’ talk of peace and brotherhood. Yet after events that many Afghans experienced as the end of the world, life slipped back into its familiar rhythms with surprising speed. Government offices and banks were operating, stores were open, and there were no fewer women on the streets – and not all of them were wrapped in the famous blue burqas. The worst fears had not come true, at least not at that point.
”Just give us time,” the Taliban official says with a smile. “After the revolution, the Bolsheviks needed time to accomplish something, too.” He calls them “the Communists.” “Come back in five years, and everything will be different.”
And now, almost five years later, I do see Afghanistan again.
It is still quiet here, despite the conflict with Pakistan and divisions within the leadership. But it is a different kind of quiet.
The Emirate has many enemies, and its security services are exceptionally vigilant. To the Taliban, every foreigner is a potential spy. Tourists, reporters, and the staff of the humanitarian missions still operating in the country are kept under constant surveillance, while Afghans who speak with them can face trouble, up to and including arrest. The religious police, meanwhile, enforce compliance with Sharia. The sticks in the officers’ hands may be mostly for show, but people still try not to attract their attention.
Music is banned. There are many prohibitions, and a good number of them concern perfectly innocent things such as chess, which is now considered a form of gambling. The craters left by explosions have long since been patched. Restaurants that look far more like Dubai than Kabul are opening in Shahr-e Naw. The drug addicts were forcibly removed from the park long ago and sent to treatment centers that have almost no medicine. Girls still have not returned to school since the takeover, and working women are almost nowhere to be seen. No, unlike the republic, the Islamic Emirate is not a place of contradictions, and Kabul stopped being a city of despair long ago. But there is little hope left in it, either.
Downtown, the concrete walls are being dismantled. They are no longer needed now that the bombings have stopped. The republic-era murals have faded so badly that the words “We Want Peace” are barely legible. And Afghanistan has, indeed, enjoyed its longest stretch of peace in 40 years.

Scientists discover a massive heat anomaly deep inside Mars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
12:27:59 UTC
21:27:59 KST

Scientists discover a massive heat anomaly deep inside Mars
- Date:
- August 30, 2026
- Source:
- Caltech
- Summary:
- Mars has a hidden temperature divide, with its southern interior potentially hundreds of degrees hotter than the north and partially molten. The discovery could help explain several long-standing Martian mysteries, including unusual magnetism, seismic behavior, and clues to the planet’s ancient water history.
- Share:
Researchers have uncovered a major temperature imbalance deep inside Mars, with the planet's southern interior appearing significantly hotter than its northern half.
Gravity measurements suggest that the interior beneath Mars's southern hemisphere is about 200 to 400 degrees Celsius warmer than the north and may be partially molten. The finding offers a new window into the Red Planet's geologic history, including periods when Mars may have had environments capable of supporting life.
The study was led by Caltech alumnus Alexander Berne (PhD '26), now a postdoctoral associate at the University of Arizona. The results were published August 27 in Nature.
Mapping Mars From Gravity
While completing his graduate work at Caltech, Berne developed a model that uses subtle variations in gravity to estimate the internal structure of a planetary body. He and his colleagues later applied that approach to Mars.
The researchers analyzed decades of observations from three Mars missions: Mars Global Surveyor, Mars Odyssey, and Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. By tracking extremely small changes in the spacecrafts' velocities, the team was able to reconstruct the gravitational field surrounding Mars.
The Sun's gravitational pull on Mars changes over the course of the planet's seasons because Mars travels along a slightly elliptical orbit and rotates on a tilted axis. The researchers used a method known as tidal tomography to study how these gravitational signatures change over time and to build a model of the planet's interior.
"Scientists usually assume that the interiors of planetary bodies are generally spherically symmetric, but this is not necessarily true," Berne says. "As we get more gravity data, we can determine the three-dimensional intricacies of a planet's interior structure. These inferences in turn give us a blueprint for designing future missions and scientific exploration of these worlds. Understanding the interior structure of planetary bodies helps us unravel the processes that shaped their formation and evolution."
A Deep North-South Divide
Mars has long been known to look very different across its two hemispheres. The southern surface is dominated by tall mountains and heavily cratered terrain, while the northern hemisphere consists largely of broad, low-lying plains.
The new results show that this contrast may extend far below the surface. Researchers were surprised to find that Mars is also thermally uneven inside, with the southern interior hundreds of degrees hotter than the north.
That hidden heat could help explain several other puzzling features of Mars.
Scientists have detected unusual magnetic signatures in iron-rich minerals in the southern hemisphere. A hotter southern mantle could indicate that Mars once had a magnetic field strong enough to produce differences in magnetism between the two hemispheres.
NASA's InSight mission also previously found that seismic waves lose energy more quickly in the south. Higher temperatures in the region could help account for that behavior.
Clues to Mars's Watery Past
"The dichotomy that we see between north and south is important to understand because it gives information about processes that may have influenced the hydrology of Mars, including the formation of basins that may have held water," says Amirhossein Bagheri, a postdoctoral scholar at Caltech and co-author on the paper. Bagheri is also a former member of the InSight team.
Understanding the temperature difference could therefore provide new clues about how Mars evolved and how its landscape developed during periods when liquid water may have existed on the surface.
Researchers do not yet know what caused the thermal anomaly. Several possibilities remain under consideration.
One hypothesis is that a giant impact released heat from the north. Another suggests that spontaneous convection may once have occurred within the southern Martian mantle. A third possibility is that thick geological structures in the south trapped heat and prevented it from escaping efficiently.
A New View of Mars's Interior
The paper is titled "Tidal Tomography Reveals a Thermal Anomaly Beneath Mars's Crustal Dichotomy."
In addition to Berne and Bagheri, co-authors include Nicholas Wagner and Harriet Lau of Brown University, Isamu Matsuyama and Angela Marusiak of the University of Arizona, Sander Goossens of NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Karwai Cheng of the Institute of Astronomy and Astrophysics at Academia Sinica in Taiwan, Antonio Genova of the University of Rome in Italy, Marc Rovira-Navarro of the Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands, Chuan Qin of UCLA, Douglas Hemingway of the University of Texas at Austin, Shijie Zhong of the University of Colorado Boulder, and Francis Nimmo of UC Santa Cruz.
The research was funded by NASA.
Journal Reference:
- Alexander Berne, Nicholas Wagner, Isamu Matsuyama, Sander Goossens, Antonio Genova, Marc Rovira-Navarro, Amirhossein Bagheri, Chuan Qin, Angela Marusiak, Douglas Hemingway, Harriet C. P. Lau, Kar Wai Cheng, Shijie Zhong, Francis Nimmo. Tidal tomography reveals a thermal anomaly beneath Mars’s crustal dichotomy. Nature, 2026; 656 (8129): 848 DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10893-x

EU needs Russia as ‘external enemy’ to collect more taxes — Kremlin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
12:22:56 UTC
21:22:56 KST

MOSCOW, August 30. /TASS/. European authorities are trying to portray Russia as an "external enemy" in order to collect more taxes from their populations for their defense capabilities, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told journalist Pavel Zarubin.

Incidents of AI going rogue double – Guardian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
12:22:35 UTC
21:22:35 KST

Incidents of AI going rogue double – Guardian
A record number of instances of artificial intelligence (AI) lying, ignoring users’ commands or acting in harmful ways to achieve its goals were registered last month, The Guardian has reported, citing a monitoring group.
Concerns about the safety of AI are on the rise after advanced models by OpenAI and Anthropic exhibited rogue behavior during testing this summer, with calls made to halt their development and introduce stricter government oversight of the process.
There were more than 300 incidents of real-world loss of control involving AI models employed by actual businesses and private individuals in July, which is almost double the number in June, an article in the paper said on Saturday.
The data came from the Loss of Control Observatory, which was set up by the UK government’s AI Security Institute (AISI) last November to track complaints about issues with AI made by users on X, it said.
As the monitor only gathers reports from a single social media platform, the true number of incidents must be higher, The Guardian noted.
A majority out of the 1,600 complaints on X in 2026 were made by software developers using AI bots in their work, according to AISI.
The monitor said that despite the fact that most real-world loss of control incidents did not cause significant harm, it has registered an increase in severity of AI’s deceptiveness and neglect of human commands.
Reports by users “evidence AI systems’ willingness to disregard direct instructions, circumvent safeguards, lie to users and single-mindedly pursue a goal in harmful ways,” AISI warned.
Tommy Shaffer-Shane, the senior policy manager at the Centre for Long Term Resilience, which operates the observatory, told The Guardian that it is wrong to suggest that AI only misbehaves during testing.
“We need to not be complacent that these things won’t happen in the real world and there is evidence that they already are,” he said.
The monitor has called on the British government to oblige AI companies to report loss of control incidents and to introduce emergency powers, including temporary restrictions on artificial intelligence, in order to deal with the more severe cases.

Ahead of the new school year, Anna Panna highlights one of the simplest skills of children’s independence – being able to prepare their own meal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
12:22:09 UTC
21:22:09 KST

Marking Riga’s 825th anniversary and the approaching start of the new school year, families attending the international kite festival “Fantadroms” yesterday, 29 August, were encouraged to think about a seemingly simple yet important everyday skill – a child’s ability to prepare their own meal. At the “Rīgas Miesnieks” picnic area, cookbook author and content creator Anna Panna joined the initiative by preparing 825 sandwiches – symbolically matching Riga’s 825th anniversary – which she and the “Rīgas Miesnieks” team handed out to festival visitors.
As 1 September approaches, families are returning to the familiar rhythm of the school year – earlier mornings, school, work, extracurricular activities, sports practices and other daily commitments. At this time of year, one question becomes particularly relevant: when children come home from school or head off to afternoon activities, are they able to prepare something simple to eat on their own? Being able to take care of one’s own meal is an everyday independence skill that can benefit a child throughout life.
It does not necessarily have to be a complicated hot meal. What matters most is giving children the confidence that the kitchen is not a place reserved only for adults and that they can prepare something to eat themselves using just a few everyday ingredients. There is no need to start with complicated recipes – even an ordinary sandwich can be a child’s first step towards independence in the kitchen.
The latest publicly available data on the health behaviour of Latvian schoolchildren also show why greater attention should be paid to pupils’ eating habits. According to the Centre for Disease Prevention and Control of Latvia’s Health Behaviour in School-aged Children study for the 2022/2023 school year, only 49.3% of surveyed 11-, 13- and 15-year-olds ate breakfast every weekday. By comparison, the figure was 74.5% in 2002. The study shows that fewer than half of the surveyed adolescents eat breakfast regularly and that the proportion has declined significantly since 2002.
The study also highlights that eating breakfast regularly is associated with healthier dietary habits – including greater consumption of fruit and vegetables and lower consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages – as well as better academic performance. Moreover, the habit of eating breakfast regularly when established in childhood tends to continue into adulthood.
Anna Panna: The Most Important Thing Is Not to Be Afraid of Doing Things Yourself in the Kitchen
Anna Panna, author of four cookbooks, content creator and co-owner of “Mr. Bunny Kitchen”, not only develops recipes in her everyday work but also encourages parents to involve their children in preparing food.
“Sandwiches are often unfairly underestimated, as if they were something so obvious that everyone automatically knows how to make one. But for a child, it is precisely these simple things that can mark the beginning of independence in the kitchen. I think it is very important for children not to be afraid of the kitchen and to know: if I’m hungry, I can make something for myself. It doesn’t have to start with complicated recipes. Take some bread, choose what you like, add vegetables and create your own combination. For a child, it is both a practical skill and a small sense of independence – I can do this myself. When school starts and family life becomes much busier again, these very simple skills become especially useful,” says Anna Panna.
A symbolic number was chosen for the event – 825 sandwiches in honour of Riga’s 825th anniversary. In this way, one of the simplest everyday meals also became part of the city’s birthday celebrations.
“Every day, we work to ensure that quality products reach family tables, but what people do with these products at home is just as important. Before 1 September, we talk a lot about school bags, notebooks, clothes and extracurricular activities, but there are also very simple everyday skills that children will use throughout their lives. One of them is being able to prepare something to eat for themselves. Our idea is very simple – let’s start with a sandwich. If a child can choose the ingredients and prepare a simple meal independently, that is already a small step towards greater independence. For parents, meanwhile, it is a good reminder to let children not only watch in the kitchen but actually do things themselves. It really is that simple – the bread is already sliced, the Doktordesa sausage is already sliced too; all you need to do is put the two together and a great breakfast is ready,” says Sindija Prīse, Head of Marketing and Product Development at “Rīgas Miesnieks”.
The company emphasises that a sandwich should not be seen as one fixed recipe – its ingredients can be adapted to individual tastes by adding fresh vegetables and other products. The key is to show children the basic principle: a simple meal can be prepared quickly and independently.
The Centre for Disease Prevention and Control of Latvia’s recommendations for promoting healthy eating in schools also encourage involving children in practical activities, including food preparation, thereby helping them develop a better understanding of healthy eating habits.
825 Sandwiches for Riga’s 825th Anniversary
The “Rīgas Miesnieks” picnic area was part of the international kite festival “Fantadroms”, held on 29 August at the Riga Passenger Port. Taking place in Riga for the first time, the festival brought together kite artists from several countries around the world, with large-scale flying sculptures and demonstrations of sport kites filling the skies above the Daugava throughout the day.
The festival programme also included kiteboarding competitions, creative workshops, a stone-balancing performance by artist Bridget Polk, activities for families, a picnic area and an end-of-summer party. “Fantadroms” concluded a month of celebrations dedicated to Riga’s 825th anniversary.
The anniversary number itself inspired the initiative to prepare and distribute 825 sandwiches to festival visitors, while also delivering a simple reminder ahead of the new school year: sometimes one of the most valuable things we can teach a child begins with a very simple question – “Can you make yourself a sandwich?”
