Apart from the joyous hyperactivity that comes with suddenly making it to No 10, there are good reasons why Andy Burnham seems to be a prime minister in a hurry. If he decides that his first term is going to run to its maximum length, he has three years, which is a maddening time-frame: too long for him to just tinker here and there, set out his long-term vision and then ask the electorate for permission to do more, but probably too short to start and finish many of his key projects. His chosen solution, it seems, is a mixture of the strategies he would use for each approach, which includes running at some issues at breakneck pace.
So it is with his specialist subject: devolution for England. The huge changes now afoot actually began under Keir Starmer, with the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act passed earlier this year. Areas that previously had two tiers of local government will see them replaced with new unitary councils. But the most historic move centres on regional mayors – what the government calls “strategic authorities” – and a shift that the Whitehall PR machine is hyping up as a “fundamental rewiring of the way our country works, surrendering power that for too long has been held in Westminster and Whitehall”. In principle, this is unquestionably worth celebrating. But it also gives rise to a whole range of increasingly urgent and awkward questions.
One change became clear earlier this year, and now looks like it will be turbocharged. By April 2027, regional and metro mayors will be able to keep as-yet-unspecified quantities of the business rates generated in their areas, and from the following year onwards, they will retain a share – also yet to be announced, presumably because the Treasury and No 10 North are wrestling with it – of local income tax receipts.
These revenue streams will replace existing Whitehall grants rather than being additional money. But Burnham’s announcements have, among the more established and confident mayors, triggered visions of even greater liberation from Westminster and Whitehall, and possible command of schools, GP services, childcare and much more. There are also welcome predictions of loans being taken out against mayoral authorities’ projected income to fund long-overdue projects, most promisingly in housing and public transport.
England’s 14 regional and metro mayors are right to see a growing opportunity for a civic political renaissance. Burnham and his people are equally correct in their conviction that improving public services and infrastructure, and firing up growth, demands a leading role for these mayors. But whatever the PM’s insistence that he intends to foster “good growth in every postcode”, the core of the vision is undeniably city-based. As the London School of Economics’ local government expert Tony Travers told me last week: “The whole idea of this version of economic change, which is very embedded, is that the only way to make the economies of city regions work is by letting the central part of the city develop fast, and hope that people will commute in and out to take advantage of it.”
And at that point, we should pause for thought. I write this from Somerset, which sits just outside the West of England mayoral combined authority (containing Bristol, South Gloucestershire, and Bath and North East Somerset) and therefore has no regional leader, nor yet plays any part in a strategic authority. Together with its neighbouring county of Wiltshire, it contains the sort of places that almost no one talks about: towns ringed by countryside or on the coast – Melksham, Bridgwater, Calne, Minehead, Trowbridge – that have experienced serious decline, and have been denied a voice for far too long.
Too many places, in fact, are now years behind parts of the country whose devolution journeys began a long time ago. The best thing to be by far is an established mayoral strategic authority – which, according to a House of Commons library briefing, qualify for the widest range of powers and integrated multi-year funding settlements, and include Greater London, Greater Manchester, the Liverpool city region, the West Midlands and such recently elevated territories as Cambridgeshire and Peterborough and the aforementioned West of England.
A second tier is reserved for such “mayoral strategic authorities” as Tees Valley, Greater Lincolnshire – led by Reform UK’s Andrea Jenkyns – and Hull and East Yorkshire, which have to wait at least 18 months after their foundation to join the top rank, and have more restricted or ringfenced funding. They will probably soon include areas that the government is still in the arduous process of getting on board, including Kent and Medway, and “Wessex”: a giant territory that will include Wiltshire, Dorset, Bournemouth and – oh joy! – Somerset. And beneath them, you find foundation authorities such as Lancashire and Devon and Torbay, which have no elected mayor yet and are run by local politicians.
When we spoke, Travers asked me a rhetorical question: “What happens to all the places that are not in high-performing areas that can build up their tax base?” We do not really know the answer yet, because so many of those areas are barely on the first devolutionary rung. Stoke-on-Trent, for instance, which needs every shred of help and local empowerment it can get, only took its first steps to joining a foundation authority in March this year. Cornwall, to which the same applies in spades, finally agreed to become a single-foundation authority at the end of last month. The story of devolution up to now, all told, is replete with delays and procrastination: in late 2025, for instance, the Starmer government postponed mayoral elections in Greater Essex, Sussex and Brighton, Hampshire and the Solent, and Norfolk and Suffolk from 2026 until 2028.
And then everything changed. On 31 July, the new government put out a statement titled Re-wiring the State, setting out its ambition to make central government “smaller and more strategic” and “to ensure every area in England has, or is in the process of establishing, a strategic authority by the end of 2027, with strategic authorities in place everywhere by the end of 2028”. Given that most councils and public services are hopelessly cash-strapped and overburdened, that is a remarkable timetable, particularly in the midst of other devolution headaches. The weekend brought news that plans for new, larger police forces are being delayed because their proposed boundaries don’t match up with those of some mayoral authorities. The reports also mentioned the PM’s unwieldy-looking proposals for reconfigured fire and rescue services and integrated care boards to fit with devolution areas in the same way: there are slight shades of lines and shapes being drawn on maps, and messy reality being hurriedly squeezed into them.
There is another potential problem: the whole programme threatens a system with not nearly enough accountability. Even if an elected mayor is in place – and remember, some of them will probably be from Reform, with all that may entail – proper scrutiny will be in short supply. The only area with an elected assembly that can properly monitor the mayor will still be London: the rest will have “scrutiny committees” that do not sound very convincing at all.
Note also a plain fact about those established, pre-eminent mayoral strategic authorities: most of them are in the north of England and the Midlands, which might avenge years of southern dominance, but seems to threaten answering one story of unfairness with another. As a resident of the south-west, I know we have an immense amount to contribute to the devolution drive, which needs to feed ideas upwards to Whitehall as well as down from central government to the social grassroots. If the past 15 years have taught us anything, it is that the worst thing to be, politically speaking, is left behind: as fast as he and his senior mayoral mates move, Burnham has to be sure that speed and zeal do not have very damaging consequences, and that he takes absolutely all of us with him.
- 
  John Harris is a Guardian columnist

Trump the renamer-in-chief keen to leave his mark – or his stain – on world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
11:00:55 UTC
20:00:55 KST

Is it a key policy move which will “recognize the extraordinary contributions of the American people”? Or “real foolishness”?
Whatever the impact of Donald Trump unusual decision to retitle Lake Ontario as Lake America, days after Canada’s prime minister refused to be cowed by Trump’s punitive tariffs, it has certainly divided opinion – but perhaps it shouldn’t have come as a surprise.
Trump, after all, is a president who in his second term has proved himself to be the renamer-in-chief, with arguably his biggest successes coming in the area of rebranding buildings and entities, frequently after himself.
There was the United States Institute of Peace being renamed the Donald J Trump United States Institute of Peace last December. The introduction of so-called “Trump accounts” to encourage people to save money. The establishment of “TrumpRx” pharmaceutical sales. And, perhaps most hubristically, the plan to introduce “Trump-class” battleships – the largest battleships the US has created since the second world war.
Given the naming pattern, perhaps Americans can be thankful that Lake Ontario wasn’t renamed Lake Trump. The title Lake America, announced in an executive order on Thursday, strikes as a little unimaginative, a little on the nose.
That’s because the president has already done this: unilaterally and, some might say, unsuccessfully, renaming the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America on the first day of his second term. (Eighteen months on, few serious media outlets use the term “Gulf of America”, with Trump’s order effectively only applying to the federal government, although that didn’t stop the White House from banning the Associated Press from the Oval Office in February 2025 when the news agency declined to use the term.)
In his Lake America order, Trump didn’t mention the trade spat with Canada that prompted the renaming. Instead, the president claimed: “It is the policy of my Administration to recognize the extraordinary contributions of the American people and the rich heritage of our history by naming great natural landmarks for our shared achievements.”
Trump went on to claim that the US “claims most of the Lake’s volume”, because the deepest part of the lake lies within US territory. “This is official, effective immediately,” he said after signing the order, although, as the Associated Press noted, the order actually says the changes must be made within 30 days.
Whether that will convince people to use the new term remains to be seen, because Trump certainly can’t force other countries to use it, and even his order is limited in scope. It directs Doug Burgum, the secretary of the interior, to “update the Geographic Names Information System” – basically a sort of grand online map – to “remove all references to Lake Ontario” from government materials, but it’s unclear how the government will force businesses – and states – to follow up.
While we wait to see who adopts Lake America, Trump is embroiled in an ongoing battle in his attempt to rename the Kennedy Center, in Washington. Trump fired the center’s existing board last year and appointed a group of lackeys that voted to add his name to the center.
The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts thus became the Donald J Trump and the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, but, after a judge ruled Trump’s name was added illegally, went back to the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in May. (Trump’s board is now attempting to rename the center the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J Trump. Members also want to rename a plaza in front of the building after Trump.)
There are also rumblings that the Trump administration wants to rename New York City’s Penn Station after the president – a move unlikely to go down well in a city where Trump is deeply unpopular.
In the meantime, the response to the newly rebranded Lake America has been tepid.
“New York won’t be calling it that,” Kathy Hochul, the state’s governor, responded to a White House social media post announcing the change. Given Lake Ontario’s only US border is the state of New York, Hochul’s opposition could cause a problem, although it will surely be welcomed by New York-based cruise companies whose marketing materials use the term Lake Ontario.
Canadians are also unimpressed.
Asked about Trump’s move during a press conference on Thursday, Wab Kinew, the premier of Manitoba, was withering in his assessment.
“You know when a rock band is really over the hill and you see them in a casino playing some song from like 50 years ago? I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now,” Kinew said.
“He thought he had a real hit, a real golden oldie with the Gulf of Mexico, and he’s trying to bring back that, and he’s trying to play the hits for his base. But I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad and it’s not his best work.”

Dining across the divide: ‘He says he feels pride about being English, but I don’t’

Finley, 23, London
Occupation Planetary scientist
Voting record Labour before the last election, where he voted Green, and will stick to Green “if Andy Burnham goes ahead with North Sea oil drilling”
Amuse bouche During university, he worked on a project with Nasa on Europa, one of Jupiter’s moons. He loved it so much he got a tattoo of Europa on his right shoulder
Gavin, 54, London
Occupation Retired software engineer
Voting record Tory “out of habit and upbringing” until Brexit; ever since then, Lib Dem and sometimes Green
Amuse bouche He and his wife went on holiday to Australia in 2003 and met the actor Rob Lowe at their hotel, but had never seen him in anything so didn’t recognise him. When they later asked for a photo, his “jokey condition” was that they watch The West Wing when they got home
For starters
Gavin We got on very well. I wouldn’t normally go to a vegan restaurant, but my daughter is vegan and I’ve told her she should go there.
Finley It was extremely enjoyable – my nerves melted away quickly. The food was fantastic, and Gavin and I got along better than I expected.
Gavin I started with roti with three sauces. Then I had chickpea curry with greens, and a beer. It was all very nice.
Finley I started with amazing deep-fried dumplings. Then I had plant-based fish with coconut, lentils and braised tomatoes, and some pineapple and kimchi pholourie, which were almost like pakoras. Fantastic.
The big beef
Gavin I don’t think the state should try to compete with the open market; the open market is always going to be cheaper, as they will always try to reduce costs.
Finley If you give power to the state to control, for example, utility companies, the service will be provided for the constituents’ benefit, not the shareholders’ benefit.
Gavin We did talk about Thames Water. I think in the case of utilities, state-run companies actually could do a better job than the free market – but they will also be somewhat hamstrung by unions.
Finley We talked about how privatisation essentially ruined a lot of utility companies, because there was no motivation for the shareholders to provide a good service. They just want profits, which is why the CEOs at water companies have been reporting record-high wages as the service worsens.
Sharing plate
Gavin I would be in favour of legalising drugs. The tax could provide another revenue stream for the government – plus, it takes away the incentive for crime. I think people should be allowed to do whatever they want as long as they don’t hurt anyone else.
Finley I think if we decriminalise drugs and treat addiction like a healthcare problem, the symptoms suffered by wider society will also be treated – as we’ve seen in Portugal. Instead of spending millions on drug policing, spend it on rehabilitation and healthcare programmes that will target the issue in a more humane manner.
For afters
Gavin I don’t find flags hung from lamp-posts intimidating – a lot of flags give a positive message, such as the Ukraine flag when the war started, LGBTQ flags – but context matters. During the World Cup, when I saw St George’s flags, I’m annoyed that I had to stop and think: “Wait, what does that mean?” because the England flag has been purloined by the far right.
Finley When you’re putting flags in a public place where communities are diverse, it has the connotation of division. Gavin says he feels some pride about being English, but I don’t. There seems to be something about Englishness that’s violent and divisive. I don’t really want to see the English flag wherever I go – even during the World Cup, knowing domestic abuse rates go up when England lose.
Takeaways
Gavin Finley gave me hope. I think part of the problem with politics is it pushes people into pigeonholes: left wing or right wing. And actually, if you have a proper conversation, you realise everyone wants broadly the same thing.
Finley I think people from older generations need to be more optimistic. If we lean in to cynicism, nothing will get done. But Gavin was also really climate positive, and that was so refreshing to hear. I think this type of conversation should be had more often, and food is a fantastic way to facilitate that.
Additional reporting: Kitty Drake
Gavin and Finley ate at Jam Delish in London.

UK asks banks for feelgood stories about keeping out dirty money
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
11:00:54 UTC
20:00:54 KST

The government is asking bankers and lawyers to provide feelgood stories about how they blocked dirty money from entering the UK, as ministers try to prove the UK’s money-laundering controls are working.
The Treasury’s call for evidence is meant to illustrate that the UK has upped its game when it comes to preventing financial crime, particularly since its last dismal assessment by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) global crime watchdog in 2018, which fuelled allegations that London had become a hub for “dirty money”.
“To build the strongest possible picture of system-wide effectiveness,” the government call for evidence said, “we are looking for real-life examples with clear, demonstrable results that illustrate how the UK’s anti-money laundering, counter-terrorist financing and sanctions frameworks operate effectively in practice.”
The government is rushing to collect those examples before it submits its own evidence packet to the taskforce in October. The watchdog’s assessment team will then visit the UK for an on-the-ground review next summer.
But the UK faces an uphill battle to prove the City has made substantial changes, and are staying alert to new threats including a surge in AI-fuelled investment fraud and the growing popularity of cryptocurrencies, which can help shield the source of transactions.
Last year, the National Crime Agency estimated that £100bn is being laundered through or within the UK every single year, with City firms providing legal and financial services for fraudsters, human traffickers, the illegal drug trade and other types of organised crime. The UK’s national risk assessment on money laundering and terrorist financing has also classed the UK legal sector as “high risk” for every one of its assessments since 2017.
“As the UK approaches its next FATF mutual evaluation in 2027, the pressure on its anti-money laundering (AML) regime is intensifying,” the rating agency Moody’s said in a report published earlier this year. “Billions are spent each year in the UK on supervision with hundreds of firms refused entry to the financial system following due diligence, yet an estimated £100bn is still laundered annually.”
Moody’s added: “When FATF examiners arrive in the UK, they may ask how much of that risk is really being reduced by the UK’s controls, intelligence and enforcement, and how quickly.”
The first phase of the next FATF review will allow the UK government to submit its own evidence, outlining how effectively the country handles and prevents money laundering and other financial crime.
The Treasury is asking City firms to share any cases, from 2022 onward, showing how they dumped, or refused to take on, potentially high-risk clients. That is on top of cases where a company’s intervention later led to a state investigation or prosecution.
The government has also asked companies for any examples where they discovered red flags for financial crime in customer profiles, and how this ended up changing the types of clients the firm was willing to take on.
A Treasury spokesperson said: “We take firm and coordinated action across government and industry to crack down on economic crime. We have introduced new strategies, enhanced enforcement capabilities and increased funding designed to disrupt those seeking to abuse the UK economy.
“As you would expect, the government regularly engages with industry on this - and preparations for the FATF assessment in 2027 are no different.”

If Chen is promoted to a more senior role in Beijing, a move that would be in keeping with the precedent set over the past two decades, it would create vacancies at the top of Shanghai’s leadership.
Zhu, 54, is a career finance official who spent much of his working life in his native province of Zhejiang, where he is believed to have crossed paths with Premier Li Qiang during the latter’s spell as governor.

‘A warning saved my life’: can Hongkongers trust smartwatches, or are they being misled?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

‘A warning saved my life’: can Hongkongers trust smartwatches, or are they being misled?
Medical practitioners and fitness experts say wearable tech could support personalised, proactive healthcare as adoption hits 63 per cent among Hongkongers
Alice Wong had little idea how seriously ill she might become until unusual patterns on her smartwatch prompted her to seek medical advice.
A year ago, Wong, who was still in her twenties, had bought the device but paid little attention to it. That changed when she received an unusual notification warning her of an irregular heart rhythm.
What followed was a health scare and a visit to a local doctor, who diagnosed her with atrial fibrillation, or AF – an irregular heart rhythm in which the atria, the heart’s upper chambers, beat chaotically. The condition can reduce the heart’s efficiency and significantly increase the risk of blood clots, stroke and heart failure.
“I am a young and fit adult. I exercise regularly and have never previously had a serious medical episode. I don’t go for medical check-ups often, so I dread to think what could have happened if my device had not picked this up,” said Wong, who has since begun taking medication and expects to make a full recovery.
While medical practitioners, fitness experts and technology developers told the South China Morning Post that wearable devices had significant potential to support personalised and proactive healthcare, some also warned against misusing the technology or treating wearables as substitutes for doctors.
Commercial wearable technology differs from medical-grade wearables and diagnostic tools. It generally focuses on health and lifestyle tracking, monitoring metrics such as exercise, heart rate and sleep.

How attention deficit hyperactivity disorder shapes sexual experiences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
11:00:01 UTC
20:00:01 KST

Adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder often face distinct challenges in maintaining sexual satisfaction and connection with their partners. A recent analysis of personal accounts from people with the condition revealed that characteristics such as a heightened need for novelty and difficulty regulating focus can deeply influence their intimate lives. The findings were published in the journal Archives of Sexual Behavior.
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by differences in executive functioning. This term refers to the mental skills involved in working memory, flexible thinking, and self-control. People with the condition often experience variations in how their brains produce and respond to dopamine. Dopamine is a chemical messenger involved in reward processing, motivation, and physical arousal.
Because of these neurological differences, the condition frequently manifests as distractibility, impulsivity, and a heightened drive to seek out new experiences. These traits can create friction in social settings and intimate partnerships. Previous assessments have indicated that this population generally reports lower levels of sexual satisfaction compared to those without the diagnosis. Yet few investigations have explored exactly how these individuals perceive and navigate their own intimate encounters.
To understand the lived experiences behind these statistics, researchers Annelil E. Desille of the Institute for Social Neuroscience in Australia and Beatrice Alba of Deakin University gathered personal testimonies. They wanted to identify the specific ways that neurological differences shape both sexual satisfaction and the interactions that follow sexual activity. Understanding these perspectives could eventually help mental health professionals provide better guidance for patients facing relationship difficulties.
The researchers recruited 98 adults who reported having a formal diagnosis of the condition from a health practitioner. The participants ranged in age from 18 to 64, with the majority residing in Australia or the United States. To confirm the presence and severity of their symptoms, all participants completed a standard self-report screening questionnaire. The study group included 72 women, 17 men, and eight non-binary individuals.
Through an anonymous online survey, the respondents answered five open-ended questions about their consensual sexual experiences. They were prompted to describe their overall satisfaction, their motivations, and how they communicate with partners. They were also asked to identify specific factors that affect their satisfaction and detail how they act immediately after sex. The researchers chose a written format to reduce social pressure, allowing participants to answer sensitive questions honestly.
Desille and Alba analyzed the written responses by looking for recurring patterns and underlying ideas. They organized the data into three primary themes that capture the varied ways participants experience intimacy.
The first theme highlighted a tension between cooperation and disconnection within relationships. Some participants described highly satisfying experiences rooted in teamwork. In these cases, mutual effort, open communication, and a shared emotional connection fostered intimacy. Respondents noted that having a partner who accommodated their needs or shared their diagnosis helped them feel secure and sexually fulfilled.
Conversely, other respondents reported deep dissatisfaction stemming from a loss of sexual interest in their partners. Some described a habit of suppressing their own needs to please someone else out of a fear of rejection. Others expressed frustration over an inability to maintain interest in a partner after the initial excitement of a new relationship faded. These participants often felt bored or unfulfilled when their specific relational needs were not met.
A second theme centered on how individuals behave after sexual activity concludes. The responses revealed a split in how participants seek a sense of security during this vulnerable time. Many described a strong desire to connect through physical affection, cuddling, and conversation. These individuals reported that discussing what they enjoyed about the encounter helped them feel grounded and present.
On the other hand, a portion of the group detailed an urge to withdraw immediately after intimacy. Some respondents dealt with insecurity or sensory overload by independently focusing on daily tasks, showering, or looking at their phones. These opposing reactions highlight how the condition can amplify a person’s need to either intensely seek out reassurance or abruptly distance themselves to regain emotional balance.
The final theme captured the direct impact of cognitive and behavioral traits on sexual encounters. Participants frequently mentioned how a need for novelty and experimentation shaped their desires. They expressed a preference for trying new things to keep their brains engaged during intimacy.
They also described the challenge of staying present in the moment. Respondents noted that distractibility, sensory overload, and everyday stress often disrupted their focus and diminished their enjoyment. One participant expressed the need to “somehow keep my attention on the task at hand and not having it drift off into space, and being able to push through the sensory overload to climax.” Overcoming these cognitive hurdles required immense mental energy, which occasionally turned intimacy into a source of stress rather than pleasure.
The study relies on subjective, self-reported accounts, which provide insight into personal experiences but cannot establish the prevalence of these challenges across the broader population. The researchers also noted that their participant group was heavily skewed toward women. Future research would benefit from a more balanced demographic sample to see if these themes hold true across different genders.
The analysis did not account for whether participants were taking medication at the time of the survey. Pharmacological treatments are a common approach to managing the condition and could alter a person’s focus and emotional regulation during intimate encounters. Medications can also cause physical side effects that independently affect sexual functioning and satisfaction.
The researchers also did not track the presence of other mental health conditions, such as anxiety or depression. These conditions frequently co-occur with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and can influence a person’s sexual satisfaction and relationship dynamics. Documenting these concurrent conditions in future studies could help isolate which relationship challenges are specifically tied to executive functioning differences.
The study, “It’s Not You, “It’s Me”: Sexual Experiences and Sexual Satisfaction in an ADHD Sample,” was authored by Annelil E. Desille and Beatrice Alba.

Taiwan marks International Whale Shark Day with traveling exhibition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
10:54:15 UTC
19:54:15 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ocean Conservation Administration on Sunday launched a traveling whale shark exhibition in Kaohsiung to mark International Whale Shark Day and promote marine conservation, per CNA.
The “Starry Giant by the Sea” whale shark exhibition opened at KW2 in Kaohsiung Harbor, featuring two 20-foot shipping containers transformed into an immersive marine space. It will tour Tainan, Taichung, Hualien, and Taipei after its Kaohsiung run.
OCA Director-General Lu Hsiao-yun (陸曉筠) said whale sharks are the world’s largest fish. They are generally gentle and feed primarily on plankton and small fish. The distinctive white spots covering whale sharks are unique to each individual, resembling an identification card and providing scientists with an important tool for identifying individual animals and tracking their movements, Lu said.
The exhibition features four sections covering whale shark specimens, scientific research, interactive experiences, and picture-book stories. A juvenile whale shark specimen donated by the National Museum of Marine Biology and Aquarium is also on display.
The two containers are designed around changing ocean landscapes and use lighting, sound, and interactive technology to create an immersive environment. The displays introduce whale shark biology and feeding habits while highlighting Taiwan’s research and conservation efforts.
Three Ocean Conservation Administration mascots — a white dolphin, whale shark, and green sea turtle — made their first joint public appearance at Sunday’s opening ceremony.
The administration reminded the public that whale sharks are protected marine wildlife in Taiwan. People who encounter one should maintain a safe distance and avoid chasing, surrounding, obstructing, or touching the animal, as such actions could violate the Wildlife Conservation Act, per CNA.
The Kaohsiung exhibition runs through Oct. 28. It will subsequently move to the Tainan Cultural and Creative Industries Park, the National Museum of Natural Science in Taichung, Taiwan Cement’s DAKA Park in Hualien, and Taipei Zoo.

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
10:54:02 UTC
19:54:02 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Torrential rain hit Changhua County on Sunday afternoon, causing flooding in several areas and forcing the closure of two underpasses in Changhua City.
The Minsheng and Xiaoyang underpasses were flooded and closed in both directions after rainfall, according to the Changhua County Police Bureau. Police began traffic controls at about 3 p.m., placing traffic cones and using police vehicles to block both entrances. Drivers were advised to take alternative routes, per CNA.
The Central Weather Administration issued an extremely heavy rain advisory for Changhua and Yunlin counties, citing the influence of a low-pressure system and strong afternoon convection that could produce short-duration, intense rainfall. Hsinchu, Chiayi, Pingtung, and Taitung also faced the chance of localized rain.
A Yuanlin City resident surnamed Wu (吳) said that when the rain arrived, the water accumulated along both sides of Jingxiu Road. Some residents were able to move parked scooters and motorcycles, while others were not able to move their vehicles before they were submerged.
Flooding was also reported near Qingshan Elementary School in Yuanlin, where muddy water flowed through the area. Parts of Nanping Street were flooded to about half the height of a vehicle tire, while sections of Yuying Road were cordoned off, per CNA.
Residents in Xiushui Township described the rainfall as sudden, with people using social media to warn one another to exercise caution when traveling. Police urged drivers not to attempt to cross flooded roads or underpasses and to follow traffic-control measures until conditions improve.

UK seeks £37m support deal for helicopter forces
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
11:53:30 BST
19:53:30 KST

The Ministry of Defence is preparing a contract worth an estimated £37 million to provide additional engineering, logistics and support personnel for the UK’s Support Helicopter Force and Commando Helicopter Force at RAF Odiham, RAF Benson and RNAS Yeovilton, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The pipeline notice published on 28 August sets out an enduring requirement for contracted personnel across aviation engineering, logistics information systems, airworthiness records, supply and other enabling functions where the MOD says military capacity is constrained.
The planned contract is expected to run from 1 November 2027 until 31 October 2032, with an option to extend the arrangement for a further two years to October 2034. Its estimated value is £37 million excluding VAT, or £44.4 million including VAT.
The MOD intends to use a competitive flexible procedure, with publication of the formal tender notice currently expected on 1 December 2026.
The requirement is explicitly linked to pressure on the Service workforce across engineering and logistics functions. The procurement notice states: “There is an enduring requirement for contracted labour and personnel support across aviation engineering, logistics information systems, airworthiness records, supply and enabling functions at RAF Odiham, RAF Benson and RNAS Yeovilton.”
It adds that the contractor will be required to provide suitably qualified and experienced personnel to supplement Service personnel where military capacity is constrained.
The contract is being structured around outputs rather than a fixed number of posts. The MOD says workforce gap information may be used to guide priorities, but the figures will not amount to a guaranteed staffing requirement or workload for the successful supplier.
According to the notice: “This is an output-based personnel support requirement; it does not prescribe fixed posts or transfer the Authority’s responsibility for directing and assuring Defence outputs.”
The work will support both the Support Helicopter Force and Commando Helicopter Force, covering aircraft availability, maintenance throughput, logistics resilience, airworthiness assurance and the wider generation of operational capability.
The Support Helicopter Force includes the RAF’s heavy and medium battlefield lift capability, centred on aircraft operating from bases including RAF Odiham and RAF Benson. The Commando Helicopter Force, based at RNAS Yeovilton, provides aviation support to the Royal Marines and wider littoral operations.
The MOD says the planned contractor support will help it move scarce engineering and logistics resources between requirements as flying programmes, maintenance activity and readiness demands change.
The notice states: “Support shall remain responsive to flying programme requirements, maintenance activity, emergent tasking, readiness cycles, future capability transition and changes in workload across output groups, functions, locations and time.”
No fixed quantity of work is being guaranteed under the proposed arrangement. Historic workload figures and planning assumptions will instead be used as guidance while the contractor responds to changing requirements across the three sites.
The MOD makes that point explicitly in the notice, stating: “The Authority does not guarantee a fixed volume of tasking. Activity assumptions, historic data and annexed output schedules are indicative and shall not be interpreted as guaranteed workload, fixed workforce demand or a prescriptive staffing schedule.”
The procurement covers engineering support services, helicopter repair and maintenance support and wider air transport support services. The notice also identifies the competition as particularly suitable for small and medium-sized enterprises and voluntary, community and social enterprises.

'Uzbekistan is at heart of Central Asia': PM Modi announces new roadmap, $5 billion trade target - top quotes
Edited by: Kanchan Yadav / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 30, 2026, 18:51 IST

The two sides  discussed cooperation in digital public infrastructure, artificial intelligence and nuclear energy.
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday said India and Uzbekistan have decided to elevate their relationship to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, setting a target of $5 billion in bilateral trade by 2030.Addressing a joint press meet with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, PM Modi said the two countries share common aspirations and are looking to expand cooperation across trade, technology, defence, energy, infrastructure and other strategic sectors.“Uzbekistan is at the heart of Central Asia and at the heart of India's engagement with the region,” the Prime Minister said.He noted that 2026 marks 15 years of the India-Uzbekistan strategic partnership and said the two countries were now looking to give their relationship a broader and more ambitious framework.“India and Uzbekistan have deep similarities in their thinking and aspirations. Youth, innovation, inclusive growth and modern technology are at the core of both Young Uzbekistan and Developed India 2047. Following this shared vision, we are continuously working for the welfare of the people of both countries. This year marks 15 years of our strategic partnership. On this special occasion, we have decided to elevate our relations to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership,” PM Modi said.
“Our bilateral trade has crossed $1 billion. Now, we have set a target of $5 billion in trade by 2030,” he added.During delegation-level talks at the Kuksaroy Presidential Palace, the PM announced a long-term arrangement for uranium supplies from Uzbekistan.“We will also establish a long-term arrangement for the supply of uranium. Today, we are formalising three sister-city and sister-state arrangements. We should create a roadmap to fully realise their potential,” PM Modi said.The two sides also discussed cooperation in digital public infrastructure, artificial intelligence, critical minerals, clean energy, space and nuclear energy.“We will work together to enhance win-win cooperation in infrastructure development. Collaboration in areas such as digital public infrastructure, AI, critical minerals, clean energy, space, and nuclear energy is making our relationship future-ready,” PM Modi said.Defence and securityPM Modi said defence and security cooperation would be expanded through direct linkages, co-production and co-development between the defence industries of the two countries.“The close defence and security cooperation between our two countries reflects our deep mutual trust. In the future, we will promote direct linkages, co-production, and co-development between the defense industries of both nations,” he said.PM Modi said India and Uzbekistan shared a commitment to combating terrorism, extremism and separatism.“We believe that terrorism, extremism, and separatism pose serious challenges to the entire region. Maintaining a policy of zero tolerance against these threats has been, and will continue to be, our shared resolve,” he said.The prime minister also highlighted cooperation in agriculture, healthcare and traditional medicine, saying the strengths of the two countries could complement each other.“By combining Uzbekistan's experience in horticulture with India's modern agricultural practices, we will contribute to the food security of both nations. Uzbekistan's medicinal herbs and India's expertise in Ayurveda form a natural combination,” PM said.Sister-city, state partnershipsPM Modi also announced that India and Uzbekistan would establish three sister-city and sister-state arrangements to expand cooperation beyond the national capitals.“We aim to ensure that our partnership is not limited merely to our national capitals; therefore, we are establishing partnerships between our cities and states,” he said.He also highlighted the potential for cooperation between Uzbekistan's New Tashkent project and India's GIFT City.“Mega-projects like 'New Tashkent' are underway in your country, while in India, we have developed GIFT City in Gujarat. We would be delighted to welcome a delegation from your country to study best practices and the use of technology in these developments,” PM Modi said.Mirziyoyev outlines new areas of cooperationMirziyoyev said the talks had identified several new areas where India and Uzbekistan could expand cooperation, including energy, culture, critical minerals, pharmaceuticals, jewellery and agriculture.“During our discussions, we identified new areas where we can realize our existing potential. We aim to advance cooperation in sectors such as energy, culture, critical minerals, pharmaceuticals, jewelry, and agriculture,” he said.“We will prepare roadmaps for each of these sectors; specific teams from India will visit here, and our teams will travel to India, enabling us to clearly define our objectives in these fields,” Mirziyoyev added.The Uzbek president said the two countries would continue to coordinate on global issues and support each other at international platforms including the United Nations, BRICS and the Non-Aligned Movement.He also highlighted growing educational and cultural ties, noting that four Indian universities are currently operating in Uzbekistan. Mirziyoyev said a 30-day visa-free regime and efforts to promote direct flights would further boost people-to-people exchanges.“Our partnership has ascended to a new level of quality, emerging as a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership,” Mirziyoyev said.PM Modi receives Uzbekistan's highest honourDuring his visit, Mirziyoyev conferred Uzbekistan's highest state honour, the Order of “Oliy Darajali Dustlik”, on PM Modi. Calling it a moment of “immense pride”, PM said the award reflected the longstanding friendship between the two countries.
“'Dostlik' means friendship. This single word exquisitely captures and expresses the sentiment that lies at the very core of relations between India and Uzbekistan,” PM Modi said.He dedicated the honour to the people of India and the shared heritage of the two countries.“This honour does not belong to just one individual; it belongs to 1.4 billion people of India,”PM Modi said.“From this historic land of Uzbekistan, I want to reassure the people of Uzbekistan today that India will never step back from its responsibilities. We will honour this friendship in every way,” he added.
“Uzbekistan loves Yoga!” PM Modi said in a post on X, highlighting the country's participation in the first World Yogasana Championship held in Ahmedabad earlier this year.“Uzbekistan was a proud participant in the first-ever World Yogasana Championship held in Ahmedabad earlier this year. Some of the medalists were also present today. They came back with great memories of India and the Championship,” he said.PM Modi also commended the Yoga Federation of Uzbekistan for promoting yoga in the country.The prime minister is on a two-nation visit to Uzbekistan and the Kyrgyz Republic. From Tashkent, he will travel to Bishkek to attend the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit on August 31 and September 1.

RAF Envoy support extended after Phase 2 competition fails
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
11:49:29 BST
19:49:29 KST

The Ministry of Defence is extending support for the RAF’s two Envoy IV business jets by two years at a cost of up to £26 million after the competition intended to deliver their longer-term support and military modification produced only one bid, which was deemed unaffordable, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The contract modification published on 28 August provides further context to the continuing pause in work intended to allow the two Dassault Falcon 900LX aircraft to operate in non-benign airspace, which the UK Defence Journal reported in June has no definitive date for resumption.
The aircraft, known in RAF service as Envoy IV, currently operate from RAF Northolt on the Civil Aircraft Register using a combination of civilian and military pilots. Their existing Phase 1 support contract with Centreline Aviation Limited had been due to expire on 31 March 2027.
Under the original Command Support Air Transport programme, a second phase was intended to provide enduring in-service support and military modifications, alongside transferring the aircraft from the Civil Aircraft Register to the Military Aircraft Register.
The latest procurement notice confirms that the MOD competed that Phase 2 requirement but abandoned the process in late 2025.
The department states: “The CSAT Phase 2 requirement, for enduring in-service support and military modification under the Military Aircraft Register (MAR), was competed under Contract Notice Ref: 2023/S 000-036566. The Invitation to Negotiate was withdrawn on 14 November 2025 due to receipt of only one tender, which was deemed unaffordable.”
The disclosure does not establish that the failed competition was itself the reason the separate work to enable operations in non-benign airspace was paused. It does, however, show that the wider procurement intended to move Envoy IV onto a more enduring military footing had failed before ministers subsequently confirmed that elements of the military modification programme were on hold.
As the UK Defence Journal reported in June, Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty asked the MOD how long work to enable Envoy IV operations in non-benign airspace would remain paused.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard replied: “The work to enable Envoy IV aircraft operations in non-benign airspace has been paused, and there is currently no definitive date for when this activity will recommence. The Department’s programme priorities are kept under regular review to ensure alignment with operational requirements and available resources.”
Pollard had previously told Parliament that several options were being considered to expand the future capability of the aircraft, including military modifications, but said the work was “currently paused whilst other activity has been prioritised.”
The military modification programme was intended to provide capabilities required for operations in more demanding threat environments, including defensive aids, secure communications and the certification necessary for the aircraft to operate under military arrangements. Rather than proceeding with the original Phase 2 procurement, the MOD will now extend the existing Centreline arrangement until 31 March 2029 while preparing another competition.
The department states: “Due to the failure of the Phase 2 competition, the UK MOD intends to modify the existing Phase 1 Contract with Centreline Aviation Limited pursuant to Regulation 72(1)(b) of the Public Contract Regulations 2015.”
The modified contract will provide continued operation and in-service support for both Envoy aircraft, while also covering what the MOD describes as “preparatory and enabling activity associated with potential transition from the CAR to the MAR”. It will maintain airworthiness management, safety case ownership, crew qualifications and operational approvals while the longer-term arrangement is reconsidered.
The wording is significant because the modification provides for preparations associated with a potential transition to military registration rather than announcing the resumption or completion of the military modification programme itself.
The MOD says the extension is required to give it enough time to hold another competition for enduring support through to the aircraft’s planned out-of-service date in April 2037, while allowing at least six months for any new contractor to transition into government-provided facilities at RAF Northolt. According to the notice, the measure is intended to avoid “an interruption to this essential military capability at a time of rising global tension.”
The MOD adds: “The modification will extend the duration of the contract for 2 years and is intended solely as an interim measure. The anticipated maximum value of the modification is £26M.”
The change raises the stated value of the current contract from £80 million to £106 million excluding VAT. The modified arrangement will also become a Qualifying Defence Contract under the Defence Reform Act 2014 and Single Source Contract Regulations.
The Envoy IV aircraft were acquired to replace the RAF’s BAe 146 fleet and entered service in 2022. The original procurement envisaged the Falcons initially operating under civilian registration and contractor airworthiness responsibility before a subsequent military phase moved them onto the Military Aircraft Register and established their enduring support model.
For now, Centreline will continue operating and maintaining the two aircraft through March 2029 while the MOD reruns the competition, with the separate work required to enable Envoy IV operations in non-benign airspace remaining without a publicly stated restart date.

Iceland votes against restarting talks on joining EU
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
11:49:11 BST
19:49:11 KST

Iceland votes against restarting EU membership talks
- Published
Iceland has voted against resuming talks on joining the European Union 13 years after they were broken off.
Public broadcaster RUV reported that 52.8% of the more than 225,000 people who voted had rejected the government's proposal, while 47.2% had backed it. Some 12,600 votes separated them.
Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir's centre-left government promised to hold a referendum by 2027, but brought it forward because of international tensions, including US President Donald Trump's threats against Greenland.
However, debate in this island nation of almost 400,000 people centred more on its fishing industry rather than security concerns.
With some 270,000 people eligible to vote, RUV reported the turnout of 82.5% was the highest in any Icelandic election since 2009.
Already part of the EU's single market and Schengen border-free zone, full EU membership would bring Iceland into the customs union and eventually the eurozone currency union.
Iceland began its application to join the EU in 2009 in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis and the collapse of Iceland's banking system.
Its application was already well advanced when a eurosceptic government came to power in 2013 and put those talks on hold.
Fishing rights were the biggest obstacle to Icelandic accession then - as they remain today.
Iceland fought successfully to protect its fisheries from foreign fishermen during the Cod Wars with the UK in the 1970s - shortly after gaining independence from Denmark - and the country's fish and marine industries still account for almost 40% of its exports.
Many No voters feared EU membership would mean ceding some control of these lucrative fishing grounds under the bloc's policies, which control how much a member state can catch.
"The No side was much more skillful in sort of tapping into the political national identity in Iceland, which emphasises formal independence, coming out of a long independence struggle coming out of Denmark," Eirikur Bergmann, a professor of politics at Bifröst University, told the BBC.
"And so they were able to appeal to people's very fundamental feelings."
On the other hand, the Yes campaign "ran an overtly technical campaign, never really explaining the purpose or the passion in why Iceland join the EU", he said.
Iceland's EU referendum results
Votes cast: 225,031
The referendum campaign fuelled debate about Iceland's place in the world, Kristrún said after casting her ballot in the capital on Saturday.
She told a news conference on Sunday afternoon that the issue of EU membership would not be revisited while her government was in office.
One of her ministers denied that the result had been a setback for the government, pointing to the high turnout for the vote.
There was a significant geographical divide in which way people voted, with the capital, Reykjavík, backing EU accession talks and rural areas being more in against them.
The question on the ballot was: "Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?"
A Yes vote would not have been a final decision on joining the EU, but a move towards an accession agreement, which would then have to be approved by a second referendum.
Equally, the No vote does not rule out the chance of Iceland resuming talks at some point in the future.
While economic concerns dominated the referendum campaigns, security issues also featured.
Iceland is a founder member of Nato but has no military and relies on its allies for defence. Being a part of the EU would have granted it full access to the bloc's joint defence infrastructure.
The country has backed Ukraine during Russia's full-scale invasion and officials have also been alarmed by Russia's increased maritime manoeuvres near the island.
But Trump's expressed interest in subsuming another Arctic island, Greenland, into the US has raised concerns more recently.
Iceland's Foreign Minister Katrín Gunnarsdóttir told Sunday's news conference that she would seek to strengthen the country's defence relations with other countries following the referendum.
However, Bergmann said: "The debate was firmly domestic, it was called prior to the second term of Donald Trump, and the tumults of the world didn't really penetrate into the debate."
Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, a senior fellow at the European think tank Bruegel, told RUV that the EU had failed in "selling itself" even though it "clearly would like to see itself as also a security actor, particularly in the Arctic".
He said the result "will be viewed as a missed opportunity - certainly for Iceland, but also the EU".
An unnamed EU diplomat appeared to agree with this assessment, telling news agency Reuters that the outcome was "a clear setback for Brussels" while noting that issues of fishing and independence had been decisive.
The win for the No camp was met with applause from eurosceptics elsewhere.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, one of the main proponents of the UK's exit from the EU, said Icelanders had voted "to keep their independence".
Marine Le Pen of France's National Rally said the result pointed to an "obvious truth: membership in the European Union is not the natural horizon for every European democracy".

Türkiye marks 104th Victory Day as Erdoğan visits Anıtkabir amid naval parade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
10:42:27 UTC
19:42:27 KST

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan on August 30 issued a message marking the 104th anniversary of Victory Day, commemorating the decisive victory in Türkiye’s War of Independence. (AA Photo)
Türkiye observed the 104th anniversary of its historic 1922 Victory Day on Aug. 30, marked by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s visit to Anıtkabir, widespread public celebrations and a naval parade on the Bosphorus.
The nationwide celebrations commenced in the capital Ankara, where Erdoğan led top government officials, military commanders and political party leaders to Anıtkabir, the mausoleum of modern Türkiye founder Mustafa Kemal Atatürk.
Erdoğan laid a wreath at the mausoleum and stood in silence to pay tribute before signing the official memorial book. In his message, Erdoğan paid tribute to Atatürk and his comrades-in-arms while expressing Türkiye’s determination to grow stronger in every field.
Following the state ceremonies in the capital, the focus shifted to the seas, where the Defense Ministry coordinated a sweeping maritime display. It deployed 15 naval vessels to transit the strait while 30 ships docked at 30 ports nationwide for public visits.
The Bosphorus procession passed landmarks starting from Rumeli Feneri at 9:30 a.m., reaching the Maiden’s Tower by 11:06 a.m. Concurrently, the Victory Cup yacht race took place on the waterway.
At the Istanbul Aviation Museum, the Air Force SOLOTÜRK team drew massive crowds for a meet-and-greet event before their flight. Pilots Lt. Col. Murat Bakıcı, Lt. Col. Erhan Aydemir, Capt. Ş. Alper Şen and Master Sgt. Muhammed Bölükbaşı signed merchandise for aviation enthusiasts. The pilots hosted 11-year-old cancer patient İkra Acar and gifted her team apparel.
Acar expressed her excitement over the meeting. Her medical treatment has lasted over a year.
“I want to be like them when I grow up,” she said.
Bakıcı said Acar is a warrior and already a fighter pilot.
“We hope she will overcome this illness and become a soldier in the future,” he said.
Aydemir invited citizens to the performances. The team feels immense pride representing the Turkish Armed Forces, he said.
In the northwestern province of Çanakkale, a Coast Guard dive team and civilian experts, including underwater documentary producer Tahsin Ceylan, plunged into the Gallipoli Historical Underwater Park. The divers navigated World War I wrecks and unfurled a Turkish flag featuring modern Türkiye founder Mustafa Kemal Atatürk’s portrait underwater.
Historical artifacts took center stage during the celebrations. A 106-year-old sewing machine used to tailor uniforms for soldiers during the War of Independence went on display at a Türkiye Diyanet Foundation cafe. Meanwhile, 15 women in the western province of Manisa knitted a 1.5-by-2.25-meter Turkish flag using 3 kilograms of yarn over 10 days. The flag features 1,813 motifs.
The Defense Ministry opened military heritage sites free of charge. This granted public access to the Ankara Air Force, Çanakkale Naval, Hatay Naval, Istanbul Naval, Istanbul Air Force, İzmir Museum Ships, İzmit Museum Ships, Mersin Naval and Zonguldak Ereğli Naval museums.
Victory Day commemorates the decisive defeat of occupying Greek forces at the Battle of Dumlupınar in 1922. The Great Offensive, launched on Aug. 26 under Atatürk’s command, culminated in the Aug. 30 victory and paved the way for the republic’s foundation. The day has been officially celebrated across the nation and Turkish Cyprus since 1926.

Hong Kong gives 45 Wang Fuk Court holdouts final call on buyout scheme

Hong Kong gives 45 Wang Fuk Court holdouts final call on buyout scheme
As of noon on Sunday, 1,939 of estate’s 1,984 flat owners have submitted acceptance letters, while 77.7 per cent have signed sale and purchase agreements
As of noon on Sunday, 1,939 of the estate’s 1,984 flat owners – or 97.7 per cent – had submitted acceptance letters, while 77.7 per cent had signed formal sale and purchase agreements, according to the government.
This leaves about 45 homeowners, or 2.3 per cent, who have yet to accept the government’s buy-back offer ahead of the August 31 deadline. The latest figure represents an increase of 25 completed acceptance forms compared with Friday’s official update.
Under the acquisition scheme, the government will buy flats at HK$8,000 (US$1,020) or HK$10,500 per square foot, depending on whether the land premium has been paid. After selling their homes and receiving compensation, flat owners can either buy a property on the open market or join a special sales programme to acquire a new subsidised flat.
A spokesman for the Housing Bureau on Sunday urged the owners who were refusing to sell “not to miss the last opportunity” and to return the signed “Letter of Acceptance” to confirm their intention by 5pm on Monday.
“With the reply deadline approaching, the engagement team coordinated by the Housing Bureau is stepping up efforts to contact owners yet to provide their response and offer the assistance required,” the spokesman added.

Israeli strike kills two people including a 3-year-old boy, Gaza medics say
CAIRO, Aug 30 - An Israeli airstrike killed two Palestinians, including a three-year-old child, in the central Gaza Strip on Sunday, health officials said.
Gaza medics said the Israeli airstrike near a bakery in Deir Al-Balah killed one man, Hussam Nusair, a three-year-old boy, Tayyem Hamdan, and wounded several others.
The Israeli military said it attacked and killed a Hamas militant. It said that Nusair advanced attacks against Israeli forces and civilians.
Hamas did not immediately comment on the military's allegation.
An October 2025 U.S.-backed ceasefire halted major fighting in the shattered territory, but it failed to end strikes by the Israeli military, which it said aimed to thwart attacks by Hamas and other Gaza militants.
Hamas accuses Israel of violating the ceasefire and undermining efforts to implement a broader plan by U.S. President Donald Trump to end the Gaza conflict, which also includes Israeli withdrawals and Hamas disarmament.
More than 1,300 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire took effect last October, according to Gazan health officials, while the Israeli military says four Israeli soldiers have been killed. REUTERS

Malaysia’s Anwar unveils cost of living measures as opposition rises
Anwar has faced declining support over a perceived failure to deliver on reforms as well as the mishandling of several high-profile corruption cases
2-MIN READ2-MIN

Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim on Sunday introduced measures to address rising living costs and support businesses, including restoring higher quotas for subsidised petrol and diesel purchases, as well as more funding for schools and small traders.
The measures are expected to take effect on September 1, Anwar said in a televised address.
“The economic growth of the country must be returned to the people,” he said.
Anwar has been under pressure to tackle higher living costs, even as Malaysia’s economy has outperformed most of its regional peers. The country’s gross domestic product grew 6 per cent in the second quarter this year, surpassing official projections.
Anwar said the government would restore a quota for Malaysian citizens to buy the popular RON95 transport fuel to 300 litres per month, after reducing it to 200 litres a month earlier this year amid a surge in global crude oil prices due to the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The quota for diesel purchases for certain categories of users would be similarly raised to 400 litres per month, he said.

Train drivers have secured a significant pay rise after the threat of strike action was floated on busy routes across the UK, including on the busy London-Manchester line.
The deal, which was agreed on Saturday between Avanti West Coast and the Associated Society of Locomotive Engineers and Firemen (Aslef) union, is the first to be approved by Andy Burnham in his premiership.
As well as the London-Manchester line – likely to see increased ministerial traffic after the establishment of the No 10 North office – the company also operates services to other big British cities such as Birmingham, Glasgow and Liverpool.
Coming after Aslef announced plans in June to ballot members about possible strike action over pay, the deal – first reported by the Sunday Times – will be seen as a victory for the union. It includes a 3.6% pay rise for drivers, 0.7 percentage points higher than the latest inflation rate, as well as time and a half pay for working Sundays, and £720 if drivers work a fifth day in the week.
Avanti is to be renationalised under the Labour government by spring 2027, with all rail companies due to be under government control by the end of that year. The operator, which is seen as having the worst punctuality rating for any major rail company in the UK, based on figures from the Office of Rail and Road, has cut multiple services in the past year, including the 7am train between Manchester and London, which it cut and brought back in the space of a few days after public scrutiny.
The government said it had “prioritised resolving the rail union disputes, improving services for passengers and saving hundreds of millions in lost revenue to ease the burden on taxpayers”.
But the shadow transport secretary, Richard Holden, said the government was “totally capitulating to their union paymasters” and that “taxpayers are being asked to stump up millions simply to save Burnham’s blushes”.
An Aslef spokesperson said on Saturday: “Our job is to enhance our members’ terms and conditions and this deal, struck with Avanti West Coast and approved by the DFTO (Department for Transport Operator), has been accepted.”
A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “We are pleased to see Avanti West Coast work with Aslef to enable a fair and affordable settlement to keep Britain’s railways moving and prevent disruption for passengers.”

CIA chief proposed trilateral talks during Moscow visit – Axios
CIA Director John Ratcliffe proposed a trilateral meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Vladimir Zelensky during his covert trip to Moscow in an effort to find a resolution to the ongoing Ukraine conflict, Axios has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Ratcliffe made an unannounced trip to Moscow on August 25. The following day, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that contact between the two countries’ intelligence services had taken place, but said Putin had not met with the CIA chief. “Of course, President Putin is immediately briefed on everything,” Peskov said, calling the meeting “a positive phenomenon” while declining to give further details.
Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) chief Sergei Naryshkin later confirmed that he had met with Ratcliffe in Moscow. Naryshkin said the issues discussed were related to the intelligence services. Axios reported that Ratcliffe also met with Federal Security Service (FSB) Director Alexander Bortnikov.
US officials briefed Zelensky on the Moscow talks and the plan for a trilateral summit. They also said Ratcliffe had discussed the possibility of restarting peace talks, the outlet reported.
Earlier last week, Trump described the visit as “semi-routine.” When asked by talk show host Glenn Beck whether Putin planned on “testing NATO resolve,” or whether Ratcliffe discussed US sanctions on Iran, Trump replied “none of the above.”
Ratcliffe’s visit was the first known trip to Moscow by a CIA director since William Burns traveled there in November 2021. The last known face-to-face meeting between the CIA and SVR chiefs was in Ankara in November 2022, when Burns met Naryshkin to discuss nuclear escalation risks and detained US citizens.
The last publicly disclosed contact between Ratcliffe and a senior Russian official was a March 2025 phone call with SVR chief Sergey Naryshkin. The two sides agreed to maintain dialogue to “promote international stability and security” and reduce tensions between Moscow and Washington, the SVR said.

Despite the pressure, Tehran has shown no sign of yielding on Hormuz. Pezeshkian has instead called for reviving the June interim agreement with Washington.
“We can solve our problems and gain our privileges with the memorandum of understanding,” he said.

Why the Hottest New Wearables Want to Be Ignored
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

There’s a new kind of gadget on shelves, designed for you to ignore it 99 percent of the time—it only needs attention when its battery is low. I'm talking about the screen-free wearable. You rarely look at it or touch it, yet it collects health stats day and night so you can view them later on in an app, when you get the time—if you can find the time. No pressure.
They have been exploding of late and are only set to grab more attention in the coming months, with the promise of demanding less of your attention once you actually buy one. Today there’s the Garmin Cirqa, Google Fitbit Air, Polar Loop, the Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Whoop series, the original pioneer of this category. Apple is considering its own version of the concept, according to Bloomberg. One answer to that big question of why? Many of us are sick of attention-hoarding tech and social media, not least realizing it is probably doing us no good.
I have reviewed wearables since they went mainstream the first time around with the early waves of Fitbits from 2009 and onward. In some ways this new generation of trackers feels like a callback to those days. Back when I used the Fitbit Ultra, a 2011 tracker that clipped to your jeans, I paid so little attention to it that two days passed before I realized I’d lost it somewhere on the streets of Zagreb, Croatia. While, like many, I fell for the sub-Tamagotchi little cartoon faces of the 2012 Fitbit Zip’s screen, it—like a Fitbit Air—wasn't something you were meant to pay attention to more than a couple times a day, max.
Over the last few years, though, I’ve spent most days referring to a Garmin, Samsung, Fitbit, Coros—the list goes on—dozens or hundreds of times a day. WhatsApp messages and emails buzz on their little screens and my wrist reflexively raises to see what’s up. When I wear a Garmin watch, I’m also lulled into the rhythm of checking evening and morning “reports,” and pathologically looking at my sleep score as soon as I wake up. And let’s not even get into the move alerts, an eye-rolling nag wearables have had for years now.
What Wearables Have Become
Part of the sell-in of new-breed wearables is that they're, in some ways, the antithesis of what other watches have grown into. Fitness watches are more smartwatch-like than ever. OLED screens are near-ubiquitous even in health trackers; hardcore running wearables let you communicate with AI assistants. And this is all even though smartwatches have never really fulfilled the original promise of a life-changing app or feature beyond what people used the first Apple Watch for back in 2015: not much.
Sure, Apple Watches may have saved a life or two, but that’s not necessarily what you’re buying them for. I waited years to report on smartwatch apps that would change things and instead saw entire wearable app ecosystems wither like neglected houseplants. Screen-free wearables want to hit “reset” on the entire category.
The most interesting factor isn't that bands like the Fitbit Air exist now, but why this is all happening now, in 2026. These wearables are largely a case of design subtraction. They are much like a normal fitness tracker—heart rate sensor, battery, accelerometer, Bluetooth transmitter, and whatever other sensors are packed in on a per-case basis—with the display excised.
Whoop has made screen-free wearables since its first proper release in 2015, but the shift in what Whoop considers itself to be about mirrors the change we see in the wider market. Today a Whoop band is made for just about anyone with the spare cash to pay for its $199 annual subscription. It’s a system to “help you improve how you sleep, train, and feel—starting day one,” to use Whoop’s own words. This couldn’t be further removed from the self-serious way Whoop described itself in 2015, as a “performance optimization system exclusively designed for elite athletes and teams.” What a change a decade makes.
Even if Whoop has always been grounded in the now-common concept of “training readiness,” things have altered drastically. So while it’s tempting to say Google's Fitbit and company are playing catch-up with Whoop, that’s not quite it. It has homed in on the “low-distraction” lifestyle selling point just as the other bigger tech companies have.
On at least three fronts this can be attributed—or blamed—on AI, to some extent.
AI as the Good and Bad Guy
AI is a way for these wearable companies to upsell and make money, and on the other side, a major contributor to why a lot of us feel like we need low-distraction tech these days in the first place. While virtually every Whoop rival says it can be used without a subscription, some of these companies lean heavily on AI as an upsell.
Take Google and the Fitbit Air. Without a subscription, the app looks cute enough but is fairly spare. You get stats and charts, but if you want chatty explainers of what any of it means, you need Google Health Premium at $10 a month. Numbers and graph lines become paragraphs that reference specific quirks or events of the day because, to steal a line from humorist and podcaster John Hodgman, specificity is the soul of narrative.
And this is just the beginning. “The use of AI in monitoring and guiding health and wellness is still at the early stage of development but will likely become significantly more advanced as AI matures,” says Peter Richardson, vice president and cofounder of Counterpoint Research.
I find Google Fitbit’s chatbot ramblings quite annoying, with not-that-rare dips into the condescending, and I may even prefer the subscription-free experience. But my job has pushed me through the unenviable task of learning what VO2 Max actually means, what heart-rate variability trends indicate, and so on: not the norm.
AI could solve that long-standing issue with wearables—people glazing over data as soon as they see anything more than their daily step count. This AI use will be better represented on the phone than the watch screen, too, making the lack of screen a strength. It lets the AI shine.
Technostress
The most important influence of AI here is on the other side of the equation, though, as just the latest stage in the tech-ification of our daily lives. I’ve heard from multiple friends about how their recent work appraisals focused on higher-ups demanding greater AI use within their “personal workflow.” Perhaps you’ve had a similar experience.
Elizabeth Marsh, a doctoral researcher at the University of Nottingham who studies the dark side of the digital workplace, finds that digital tools consistently trigger a familiar cluster of harms: technostress, information overload, constant interruption, and blurred work–home boundaries.
“These appear to have become the predictable by-product of environments where the volume and pace of digital demand has risen faster than people's capacity to absorb it,” Marsh tells WIRED, noting that information overload and FOMO correlate strongly with lower well-being and higher strain.
It’s a good argument for not having notifications and alerts pop up on your wrist, phone, and work PC—and wherever else your to-do list of responsibilities takes on a digital form.
“Participants described them in visceral terms—one said the notifications “make me feel sometimes on edge and it does make me feel anxious and it affects my mental health;” another described feeling angry at the sender for taking their time, while simultaneously feeling bad for not replying immediately,” Marsh says about her study on “digital workplace technology intensity.”
But she found simply cutting off notifications wasn’t necessarily a solution either, as people worried they would miss something. Screen-free wearables are a parallel development to this kind of tech cold turkey of banishing wearables from your wrist entirely. You can still get your sleep scores and step count, but without it being advertised consciously through the day. With a Garmin Cirqa, you can even see maps of runs and walks without ever having tapped a “start workout” button. Nothing needs to buzz away or, at a simpler level, require the daily charge coddling of an Apple Watch.
This is perhaps the key. So many tech companies are making these low-distraction wearables because so many of us are close to wanting to opt out altogether, at least in the areas of tech in which we can.
Digital Mindfulness
Marsh’s suggested strategy for dealing with tech strain is what she calls “digital mindfulness,” which is all about having an “awareness of how you engage with technology, rather than operating on autopilot.” That mindless social media feed scrolling? In most cases, you won't convince anyone that’s a digitally mindful practice. Marsh says it involves three things.
“Intention—having a clear purpose for picking up the device in the first place, rather than reaching for it reflexively and then wondering where twenty minutes went,” she says. “Attention—staying with what you've chosen to do and resisting the pull of whatever else is competing for your attention. And attitude—responding to yourself with a bit of kindness and patience when it goes wrong, as self-criticism about our own tech habits tends to make the relationship worse rather than better.”
Buying a screen-free tracker like a Fitbit Air isn’t digital mindfulness in itself. But it’s more intuitively compatible with adopting that mindset than a notification-spewing, buzzing smartwatch.
