‘It makes no sense’ for Moscow to attack NATO – Finland’s president
Finnish President Alexander Stubb has said that he doesn’t believe speculations that Russia is planning to attack NATO countries.
Russia has repeatedly rejected claims that it has aggressive designs against the bloc, saying that they are only made by Western politicians to distract the public from problems at home and justify growing military spending.
During his interview with the German tabloid Bild on Saturday, Stubb was asked to weigh in on the assessment by the Defense Ministry in Berlin that Russia could invade NATO territory by 2029.
“If someone had such a crystal ball – wonderful. But I just don’t see any evidence or facts for it,” he replied.
“First, I have intelligence findings. And secondly, we have a deterrence – and this deterrence is stronger than that of any other military power anywhere in the world,” the Finnish president added.
Given NATO’s conventional forces, missile arsenals and nuclear weapons stockpiles, “it does not make sense for any power in the world to test the resolve of this alliance,” he said.
According to Stubb, Russia is also preoccupied with the Ukraine conflict.
“I simply don’t see that they could now suddenly mobilize forces for two fronts,” he noted.
“I’m not saying: ‘Relax.’ You should always prepare for the worst to prevent it,” the Finnish president said.
He accused Moscow of waging “information warfare” against the West, saying that “Russia wants us Europeans to sit here and discuss: Will Russia escalate?.. Will Russia attack NATO and Europe?”
Stubb again urged NATO to continue its support for Kiev amid the ongoing conflict with Moscow. Finland joined the bloc in 2023, abandoning its longstanding policy of neutrality.
“We have to understand, you in Germany and we in Finland, that Ukraine is the best security guarantee we have against Russia. If Ukraine loses, we lose,” he argued.
Moscow maintains that a conflict with NATO is only possible if the bloc launches an aggression against Russia first.
Earlier this week, Moscow told the UK that its military facilities and equipment in Ukraine and beyond could become legitimate targets for Russia if Kiev continues to use British-supplied weapons for strikes on Russian territory.
Russian officials also previously warned that if Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania knowingly help to facilitate Ukrainian drone attacks against northwestern Russia, Moscow could consider them complicit in those actions and would have the right to self-defense under the UN Charter.

Turkish industry focuses on transformation under Emissions Trading System
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
07:22:04 UTC
16:22:04 KST

Türkiye’s upcoming Emissions Trading System (ETS) will force a major transformation across core heavy industries, driving decarbonization in energy, metals, cement, chemicals, glass and ceramics.
The ETS regulation, prepared by the Climate Change Directorate under the Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Ministry, was published in the Official Gazette last week.
The regulation establishes the rules governing the implementation of Türkiye’s ETS and provides the legal framework for the national carbon market.
Through the ETS, the government aims to encourage reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, accelerate the transition to low-carbon production technologies and support the country’s green transformation process.
The ETS also introduces significant obligations for industrial enterprises. Facilities covered by the regulation will be required to monitor, report and verify their emissions and surrender the necessary emission allowances corresponding to their verified emissions.
Seyit Ardıç, chairman of the Ankara Chamber of Industry (ASO), told state-run Anadolu Agency that the regulation marks an important stage in the green transformation of industry.
“With the new system, carbon is becoming more than an environmental indicator that is monitored and reported. It is turning into an economic parameter that directly affects production costs, investment decisions and competitiveness,” he said.
“The system will directly affect energy, iron and steel, aluminum, cement and lime, glass and ceramics, paper and pulp, as well as certain chemical and hydrogen production activities,” he added.
“The cost impacts of the system could also be felt in sectors such as machinery, automotive and electrical-electronics through supply chains. We must turn this process into a transformation opportunity that strengthens the competitiveness of our industry,” Ardıç said.
“For the transformation to succeed, a predictable implementation timetable, strong financing opportunities and effective incentive and grant mechanisms will be of great importance. In particular, our SMEs need to be supported effectively to help cover the costs of this transition,” he added.
In a report, global energy think-tank Ember said that the introduction of Türkiye’s EST marks a new chapter in the country’s climate policy.
By reducing industrial emission intensity through product-based benchmarks, the system supports the green transition and helps exporters remain competitive under the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), it said.
Under the Turkish ETS, facilities with annual emissions of more than 50,000 tons of CO2 will be required to monitor and report their emissions and surrender certificates equivalent to their annual emissions, it noted.
Türkiye’s decision to launch the ETS is significantly influenced by its trade relations with the European Union, according to the report.
According to CBAM rules, if a carbon price has already been paid in the exporting country, that amount can be deducted from the CBAM costs payable to the EU.
“Therefore, implementing an effective ETS in Türkiye helps keep these carbon costs within Türkiye’s borders and channel them towards the green transition of domestic industry. This also helps Türkiye’s export sectors remain competitive in international markets,” it said.

"It must be absolutely clear that Venezuela retains ownership and sovereignty over its resources," she said.

He claimed the transaction more than doubles existing US oil reserves and will "substantially lower gas prices" for Americans in the long term, while promoting prosperity in the South American nation.
 
The deal will strengthen the rapidly evolving relationship between Washington and Caracas, Trump said.
 
Rubio said the deal is a "huge win" for both nations, and that it will bring nearly $100 billion in private investment to Venezuela.

From doomscrolling to nomophobia: new digital-age conditions reshaping our brains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
07:20:41 UTC
16:20:41 KST

Doomscrolling, nomophobia, FOMO and social media addiction: the new digital disorders, what they mean and when smartphones become a problem
Can you not go five minutes without checking your phone? Do you open Instagram "just for a second" and find that half an hour later you are still there? Do you wake up during the night and the first thing you do is check your notifications? Or do you keep scrolling through bad news even though you know perfectly well it is making you anxious?
Welcome to the age of new digital addictions.
Experts stress that the point is not to demonise smartphones, social networks or video games. The digital world is now part of our lives and can bring huge benefits. The problem begins when use becomes hard to control and starts to crowd out sleep, work, study, relationships or physical activity.
And research is starting to put a name to many of these behaviours.
The first real diagnosis: gaming disorder
One distinction is crucial. Not everything that gets called "smartphone addiction" is officially a disease.
The World Health Organization has, however, recognised in the International Classification of Diseases, ICD-11, gaming disorder.
That does not mean that playing a lot is automatically an illness. The disorder is about a loss of control over gaming, a growing priority given to play over other activities and continuing the behaviour despite negative consequences. To reach a diagnosis, there has to be a significant impact on personal, family, social, school or work life, generally for at least 12 months.
And it affects a minority of players, not everyone who spends a few hours in front of a console.
Social media addicts: when endless scrolling is the problem
Here the picture becomes more blurred.
Social media addiction, often referred to in research as problematic social media use or social media use disorder, is not currently an independent ICD-11 diagnosis like gaming disorder.
But the phenomenon has now been widely studied.
The signs are fairly intuitive: wanting to stop and being unable to, spending more time online than planned, feeling a strong need to check social media, neglecting other activities, becoming irritable when you cannot access platforms, or continuing to use them despite the problems they cause.
The American Psychological Association urges people to pay attention to exactly these behaviours, especially among teenagers.
And the figures are striking. According to the latest major Health Behaviour in School-aged Children (HBSC) survey by the World Health Organization in Europe, carried out among almost 280,000 young people aged 11, 13 and 15 in 44 countries and regions, 11% of adolescents show signs of problematic social media use, compared with 7% in 2018. The share rises to 13% among girls and falls to 9% among boys.
FOMO: the fear of being the only one who does not know
One of social media’s most powerful traps now has an extremely familiar name: FOMO, Fear Of Missing Out.
It is that feeling that makes you think: "What if something has happened in the meantime?".
So we check WhatsApp, Instagram, TikTok, the news and chats even when we have no real reason to do so.
FOMO is not a psychiatric diagnosis. It is, however, a psychological phenomenon studied in relation to problematic use of the internet and social media. A study published in 2024 looked precisely at the link between FOMO, problematic social media use and doomscrolling, and found that emotion regulation mechanisms play an important role.
In other words: the more we feel we need digital tools to manage anxiety, boredom or unpleasant emotions, the more we risk being drawn into a vicious circle.
Doomscrolling: why we keep reading bad news
It is probably one of the most characteristic phenomena of the smartphone era.
Doomscrolling is the compulsive consumption of negative news: wars, disasters, crises, accidents, illnesses, scandals. One story leads to another and your finger keeps scrolling.
The paradox is obvious: we look for information to feel better prepared and often end up feeling even more anxious.
Doomscrolling is not an independent medical diagnosis either, but it has become a focus of research into problematic online behaviour. Studies have linked it to FOMO and difficulties in regulating emotions.
And it can turn into another trap: the more worried we are, the more information we seek; the more negative information we consume, the more our worry grows.
Nomophobia: when the phone is gone, the anxiety arrives
"Nomophobia" is a word coined from no mobile phone phobia.
It does not simply mean "I am annoyed that I left my phone at home". It is the term used to describe the discomfort or anxiety linked to the absence of a smartphone, loss of connection, or the inability to access information and one’s digital relationships.
Again, it is worth being careful with words: it is not an official standalone diagnosis.
But it is a studied phenomenon, increasingly entangled with other problematic behaviours. A study published in 2026 analysed nomophobia, social media addiction and FOMO together, identifying the fear of missing information as one of the most important bridges between these phenomena and symptoms of anxiety and depression.
The phone, in short, can become a kind of "safety object": if we have it, everything is fine. If it disappears, even just for a few minutes, something feels wrong.
Phantom vibration: the phone that vibrates even when it does not
Have you ever been certain that your phone was vibrating in your pocket, only to take it out and realise that no notification had arrived?
This is called phantom vibration syndrome, or the phantom vibration syndrome.
It is not a recognised disease, but a studied perceptual phenomenon: the brain can interpret tiny physical stimuli as a phone vibration, especially when we are used to constantly expecting notifications.
It is almost the digital version of "I hear someone calling me" when nobody has called.
And then there is smartphone-induced insomnia
The issue is not only how much time we spend online. It is when we do it.
Scrolling in bed seems harmless: "I will just watch two videos and then sleep". The problem is that those two videos can turn into twenty minutes, an hour or much more.
The APA notes that using technology close to bedtime, and social media in particular, is linked to sleep disturbances in adolescents.
And a longitudinal study published in 2025 found an association between problematic social media use and later depressive and anxious symptoms, with sleep problems apparently playing a partial role in the connection. The authors themselves stress, however, that the relationship is complex and should not automatically be read as cause and effect.
The practical takeaway is easy to grasp: if the phone steals our sleep, the problem is no longer just the time spent in front of the screen.
Social media and the body: the physical impact
The digital revolution is not only about the brain.
Hours spent in front of a screen can mean less movement, more sedentary behaviour, eye strain and musculoskeletal problems linked to maintaining the same posture for long periods.
The so-called tech neck, the "smartphone neck", is now a common expression for the pain and tension associated with the posture of tilting your head towards your device. It is not a new medical diagnosis, but it describes a very concrete problem: we are spending more and more time with our neck bent over a screen.
The WHO, when discussing the effects linked to problematic use of technology and gaming, also highlights sedentary behaviour, musculoskeletal problems, sleep disturbances and eyesight issues.
The brain is not "ill": it is the behaviour that becomes problematic
And this is perhaps the most important distinction.
We should not turn every digital habit into a diagnosis.
Watching TikTok for an hour, playing a video game at the weekend, checking Instagram or reading the news does not necessarily mean being addicted. Quantity alone is not enough.
What really makes the difference is control and the impact on daily life. The question to ask is therefore not just: "How many hours do I spend on my phone?" It is rather: "Can I stop when I want to? And what am I sacrificing to carry on?"
If the phone starts eating into sleep, work, study, relationships, sport or real life, then the warning bell becomes much more serious.
The new frontier: a possible "social media addiction"?
Research is pushing further.
In 2025, a group of researchers proposed criteria for a possible classification of Social Media Use Disorder, identifying loss of control and a deterioration in everyday functioning as central elements. Among the possible criteria, they also discuss a preference for online interactions and FOMO.
But we are still in the realm of research, not facing a new official diagnosis.
And this is exactly where the future battle lies: understanding when a technology designed to capture our attention stops being a useful tool and starts to turn into a behaviour that is hard to control.
Because the real problem may not be the smartphone itself.
It may be the fact that we have built a digital world that is able to tell us, every few seconds: "Hey, look at me. You have missed something".

Türkiye steel exports rise 2.9 percent year-on-year in July

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
07:19:03 UTC
16:19:03 KST

Türkiye’s steel product exports rose 2.9 percent year-on-year in volume to 1.2 million tons and 4.4 percent in value to $827.3 million in July, according to data from the Turkish Steel Producers Association (TÇÜD).
In the January-July period, steel exports increased 2.4 percent from a year earlier to 9 million tons, while export revenues rose 1.6 percent to $6.1 billion.
Steel imports fell 19.7 percent year-on-year in volume to 1.5 million tons and 17.6 percent in value to $1.1 billion in July.
During the first seven months of the year, imports declined 3 percent in volume to 10.7 million tons and 4.9 percent in value to $7.4 billion compared with the same period of last year.
The ratio of exports to imports rose to 82.1 percent in the January-July period from 76.9 percent a year earlier.
Türkiye’s crude steel production increased 7 percent year-on-year to 3.4 million tons in July. In the first seven months of the year, crude steel output rose 7.9 percent to 23.2 million tons.
TÇÜD Secretary-General Veysel Yayan said an 85 percent increase in steel exports to South America, which reached 762,000 tons, had a positive impact on overall steel product exports.
“All these developments do not yet fully reflect the negative consequences of the quota system, which is estimated to cause a contraction of approximately 4 million tons in our exports to the European Union. The decline in our exports to the EU is expected to accelerate in the coming months,” Yayan said.
“On the other hand, the presence of Chinese-origin steel products in the Turkish market continues to increase and steel imports from China reached approximately 2.5 million tons in the first seven months of the year,” he added.

Swiss daily Blick reported that rave visitors initially mistook the shots for fireworks until somebody shouted "everyone down."
The newspaper wrote that the shooting took place right after the event ended. Police later took the remaining visitors to a nearby gym, where many were interrogated, Graser said.
Police asked any witnesses with videos or photos to share them with investigators.
The Aargau Racing Club, which runs the horse racing track, expressed shock at the shooting.

"Techno and raves are supposed to be a place for freedom and safety, never a place where something like this happens," he added.

Statins can reduce dementia risk by up to 15%, long-term study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
07:00:50 UTC
16:00:50 KST

Statins can lower the risk of dementia by 15%, and the earlier in life they are taken the higher the chances of avoiding the disease, a 15-year study suggests.
The number of people living with dementia globally is forecast to nearly triple to 153 million by 2050. But experts believe almost half of dementia cases could be prevented or delayed.
Now research presented in Munich at the world’s largest heart conference suggests that the cholesterol-busting drugs could dramatically reduce the risk of people developing dementia.
In the largest study of its kind, more than 132,000 people in Denmark were tracked by researchers between 2006 and 2021.
Those who started on statins during the study period were 10% less likely to develop dementia. Those taking them early reduced their risk by 15%. The results were similar in women and men.
The findings were presented on Sunday at the annual congress of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC), and simultaneously published in the Lancet Regional Health Europe journal.
Prof Isabel Goncalves, a member of the ESC communication committee, who was not involved in the research, hailed the findings. “Because statins are widely available and inexpensive, the findings are potentially important,” she said.
Statins are already one of the most commonly used drugs in the world. The drugs reduce low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels in the blood, which can lead to plaque buildup in arteries and increase the chance of heart attacks, strokes and heart disease. But statins could also help protect the brain in the long term.
Experts believe this is because there is strong evidence that high LDL cholesterol can increase people’s risk of developing dementia, by hardening or narrowing blood vessels that supply the brain.
LDL cholesterol (LDL-C) drives plaque formation, and the resulting disruptions to the brain’s blood supply can increase the risk of dementia.
Previous research from the Lancet dementia commission suggested addressing 14 modifiable risk factors, starting in childhood and continuing throughout life, could prevent or delay 45% of dementia cases.
“Detecting and treating high levels of LDL-C from midlife is one such highlighted risk factor,” said Dr Tummas Ternhamar, from Copenhagen University hospital, who presented the results of the new research at the conference.
All those in the 15-year study had type 2 diabetes. But Ternhamar said the findings strengthened the idea that one day everyone might be offered statins as part of a package of measures – such as staying physically active and eating well – to reduce their risk of dementia.
Speaking to reporters in Munich, he said: “Our study supports the idea that dementia risk is best addressed by targeting several factors at once, and that cholesterol may belong on that list.
“The Lancet commission already takes that multicomponent view, recommending that high LDL cholesterol be detected and treated from midlife. What our findings also add is that timing matters within that – acting early looks better than acting late.”
Among the 132,585 people followed by Ternhamar and his colleagues, 2.7% went on to develop dementia.
Compared with no statin initiation, early statin treatment was associated with a 15% lower relative risk of dementia over 10 years. Late statin initiation was associated with a 10% lower relative risk of dementia over 10 years.
Ternhamar said experts were investigating exactly why statins might lower the risk of dementia.
“Statins effectively lower LDL cholesterol and protect against atherosclerosis and atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseases,” he said. “This may in turn protect against cerebrovascular atherosclerosis, ischemic stroke, reduced blood flow, and damage to brain tissue, offering a plausible link to explain our findings.”
Dr Honorine Lebraud, a senior partnerships manager at Alzheimer’s Research UK, who was not involved in the research, said: “This observational study adds to growing evidence linking cardiovascular health and brain health. It reinforces the fact that what is good for the heart is good for the brain.
“More work is needed to show a direct link between statins and reduced dementia risk. This study offers important clues about how cholesterol and cardiovascular health influence dementia risk, while also showing where future research should focus.”
Prof Bryan Williams, chief scientific and medical officer of the British Heart Foundation, said it was important to remember that this was an observational study, which meant it could show an association but cannot prove that statins themselves reduced the risk of dementia.
“That said, there is evidence from trials that do show that statins reduce the risk of dementia so the findings in this study are certainly plausible.”

A lone Black woman’s defiance of Swedish neo-Nazis, 10 years on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
07:00:50 UTC
16:00:50 KST

The striking photograph showed a lone Black woman, her fist raised, standing in the path of hundreds of uniformed neo-Nazis on parade in 2016, and it made headlines across the globe.
At the time, it was held up as a symbol of the resistance to the far right. But 10 years on, as Sweden gears up for elections in which the far right is expected to emerge as the second most-voted-for party, the woman in the photo sees it as a sign of the bewildering change that has gripped the Scandinavian country.
“Ten years ago, people would say: ‘Oh we dislike the far right, the Sweden Democrats, we despise Nazis,’” said Tess Asplund, 52. “And now, they’ve become normalised. It’s like, what happened?”
Her comments hint at the recent reshaping of Swedish politics, where the far right – once a pariah – has steadily marched into the halls of power. “I’m sad, afraid and ashamed of Swedish citizens,” said Asplund in an interview at a cafe in central Stockholm. “It’s pure racism.”
Ahead of a general election on 13 September, polls suggest that the centre-left opposition has a lead over the ruling rightwing coalition, meaning a change of government could be on the cards.
But the Sweden Democrats, a party with neo-Nazi roots, is expected to garner the second-most votes in the country. In the 2022 elections, it also came second, paving the way for it to play a supporting role in a minority-run coalition.
The party has long been dogged by accusations of harbouring violent racists and swastika-wearing Nazi sympathisers. It has used its leverage in government to consistently target migrants, including asylum seekers, as well as Muslims, ushering in ultra-restrictive migration policies and a discourse that routinely disparages the millions of people from around the world who have made Sweden their home and seek to contribute to it.
Earlier this year, the Swedish prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, mused that if his four-party coalition won the upcoming election, the far right could enter government, in what was seen as a watershed moment for Swedish politics.
It was a sharp contrast to the Sweden that Aspland had stood up for on 1 May 2016. She and scores of others had travelled to the central Swedish city of Borlänge to rally against a planned march by the Nordic Resistance Movement, one of the country’s largest neo-Nazi groups.
As she faced off against them, her act of defiance was caught on camera by the photographer David Lagerlöf of Expo, the anti-racism foundation in Stockholm.
It soon went viral, with Swedish media likening it to another iconic image of resistance: a 1985 photo in which photographer Hans Runesson captured a woman taking aim at a skinhead with her handbag in the south-western city of Växjö.
Media requests poured in from around the world. In Sweden, people began stopping Asplund on the streets, thanking her for her gesture, though she also grappled with a stream of online harassment and death threats on her home telephone line.
For Asplund, who has spent much of her life campaigning against racism, it was a sobering frontline encounter with the far-right spectrum of Sweden, which ranges from the extremist Nordic Resistance Movement, which in 2024 was designated as a terror group by the US, to the Sweden Democrats, who have long worked to make over their image.
A 2023 study noted that the presence of the two groups, both of which have shared roots in their militant opposition to immigration, probably works to bolster their causes by keeping issues of immigration and integration on Sweden’s political agenda.
Or, in the words of Mohammad Aluaudt Allah, a Syrian refugee who was kicked unconscious on a street in central Stockholm last year, the politicians who blame immigrants for all of the country’s issues have “created a sense of impunity for violent Nazi groups”.
“They may feel that they are being given permission to exercise their hatred and attack us,” he told the newspaper Dagens Nyheter.
The view was echoed by Asplund. “The Nordic Resistance Movement, they’re kind of small now, we don’t hear so much about them any more,” she said. “They don’t have to be big because Sweden Democrats are big, so they’ve got people doing their work in the government. The Nazis are in the shadows.”
The resulting rhetoric had then been amplified by some in media, she said, pointing to those who had uncritically swallowed the far right’s blaming of all social and economic ills on migration.
What had emerged was a hardened Sweden, one where, for example, dozens of young people who had lived their whole lives in Sweden had been deported to their parents’ countries of birth after they failed to meet the increased earnings thresholds for migrants. “Thirty years ago, we would be on the street fighting against this. Now it’s like, ‘That’s sad for him or her.’ It’s a shift that really scares me,” she said.
“If Olof Palme were alive today, he would turn over in his grave,” she added, citing the assassinated former leader of Sweden’s Social Democratic party, who is credited with many of the progressive policies long associated with Sweden, from the robust social welfare system to a pro-refugee discourse that welcomed those escaping dictatorships and war.
She noted, however, that her disappointment and shame did not extend to everyone in Sweden. “We are many, many people here fighting for human rights and against racism,” she said.
But in some ways, the photo – hailed in 2016 for capturing one of the conflicts of our time – seemed to pit Palme’s Sweden against the march of the far right.
In the years since, Asplund despaired that it may have been the far right who had emerged victorious.
“I’m afraid and heartbroken because when I speak to people they’re like, ‘Oh for God’s sake, forget that. It was 20 years ago that there were Nazis and skinheads, now it’s gone,’” she said. “They’ve normalised it. It’s not my safe Sweden any more, it’s not the Sweden that I’m used to.”

Researchers find Britain’s 11th-century ‘Conquest Man’ was Scandinavian – but did he land with the Norman army?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
07:00:49 UTC
16:00:49 KST

One of the most consequential showdowns in the history of the British Isles, the Battle of Hastings is seen as the foundational event of the Anglo-Saxons’ conquest by their Norman enemy across the Channel.
But researchers who have put flesh on the bones of one man who lived through the turmoil of the era are learning more about the fighters who may have belonged to neither side.
Dubbed Conquest Man, a skeleton of an unknown male was buried at St Peter’s church in Barton-upon-Humber, with previous analyses revealing the oak used to make his coffin came from a single tree felled in 1079 – probably when the man died.
But while this and other details are clear – he died in his 50s or 60s, was of stocky build, had multiple healed fractures and stood just 5ft 1in tall – his origins are not.
According to English Heritage’s head curator of collections, Kevin Booth, who has been leading the project, questions remain over whether the man was even a Norman or Saxon.
“He’s likely neither, and we shouldn’t be shocked by that,” Booth said.
The new work – which has not been peer-reviewed – was produced by researchers at Historic England, the Francis Crick Institute, the British Geological Survey, the University of Southampton and the Face Lab at Liverpool John Moores University.
The results helped the team produce a reconstruction of Conquest Man’s face, suggesting he had thin lips, a receding hairline and a frank gaze.
According to analyses of the man’s DNA, he had substantial continental ancestry, while studies based on his skull shape suggest he had Scandinavian origins.
Levels of strontium isotopes in his teeth are compatible with someone living in the Barton area, while levels of oxygen isotopes suggest he may have spent time in a colder region during adolescence.
And though the man was interred in the cemetery of a pre-conquest church that had been transferred to Gilbert De Ghent, one of William the Conqueror’s knights, his grave goods indicate a Scandinavian influence, with applewood staffs placed by his side.
While it is possible Conquest Man came from Barton, Booth said the most likely explanation is that he arrived from Scandinavia – a situation that would not be surprising given pre-conquest Barton would have been in the heart of the Viking-controlled territory known as the Danelaw, with the River Humber providing access to the sea.
“Our man was born into a world where one king ruled England, Denmark, Norway and parts of Sweden. That pretty much continued through to 1042. The exchange through the Humber and other east coast ports must have been commonplace,” said Booth.
“That our man could have come across in early adulthood within this common North Sea territory makes a lot of sense.”
However, there is another possibility. “It’s entirely plausible that our man comes in through Pevensey beach in 1066,” said Booth, noting it is also plausible the man came to Normandy from Scandinavia, whether because of family connections or trade, or simply in search of a life.
“It’s just perhaps … not the most likely account,” he said. Indeed, the report from the new work stresses it would be “a step” to place Conquest Man with the victorious Norman army.
“While the dukedom of Normandy (land of Northmen) had itself been formed through the intermingling of Danish incursion and settlement in the 10th century, by the mid-11th century that connection and movement of peoples between (largely Denmark) and Normandy seems to have all but ceased,” the report says.
Booth added the work highlights that the events of 1066 were not in isolation, but noted the year was exceptional in putting a final break in the long-lasting connections between Scandinavia and, particularly, the east coast of England.
“Our man grows up in a different world but manages to navigate his way into the new reality,” he said.

Trump’s ‘economic D-day’ against Iran risks driving the stakes even higher | Sina Toossi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
07:00:49 UTC
16:00:49 KST

Donald Trump has found a new way to promise victory over Iran. After months of war have failed to force Iran’s capitulation or collapse, his administration has unveiled what the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, calls Operation Economic Outcast: an effort to cut it off from what remains of the global economy and threaten foreign governments, banks and companies with sanctions if they continue doing business with Tehran.
There is no question that Iran is vulnerable. Its economy has been battered by years of sanctions, war and a months-long US naval blockade. Iranian officials acknowledge that oil exports and access to foreign currency have been severely constrained. Ordinary Iranians are already enduring high inflation, currency depreciation and worsening living standards. Further economic strangulation will inflict significant additional hardship.
Iran also wants an end to the war. Its president, Masoud Pezeshkian, has said it should seek peace while it can still negotiate from a position of “power and dignity”. But Iran needing a deal is not the same as Iran preparing to surrender. That distinction has repeatedly eluded Trump in formulating his Iran policy: ramping up pressure is not the same as having a strategy. Iran gets a move too.
Indeed, Iranian officials increasingly suggest this strategy has the opposite effect than what was intended. Each successive escalation, in their telling, demonstrates why Iran relinquishing its remaining leverage would simply leave it vulnerable to the next round of US pressure. The emerging strategy therefore appears to combine bargaining with endurance: seek an agreement while demonstrating that it can withstand the pressure without capitulating or abandoning its core terms.
This is why recent Iranian rhetoric deserves more attention than it has received.
Mohsen Rezaei, the new head of Iran’s supreme national security council, has called participation in Washington’s economic campaign an “act of war”. He says Tehran will first try to persuade neighbouring states not to participate, but has threatened their interests if they do. He has even warned that Iran could prevent Gulf oil exports through routes designed to bypass Hormuz.
These statements should not simply be dismissed as declarations of defiance for an audience in Iran. They reflect a consistent strategic logic: Iran cannot defeat the US economically, but it can try to make the economic strangulation of Iran prohibitively expensive for Washington and the countries it needs to enforce it.
That could mean tightening pressure on Hormuz, threatening infrastructure that enables alternative oil-export routes or putting greater pressure on US interests across the region. None of this would help ordinary Iranians. Escalation would compound their suffering. But that is precisely why Washington should think beyond the first-order effects of its own actions.
There is another weakness in Trump’s plan. For Bessent’s threat to work, Washington must persuade or coerce much of the world into participating, especially China, the principal buyer of Iranian oil. Yet Beijing is moving in the opposite direction. It has ordered firms not to comply with US sanctions targeting Chinese buyers of Iranian oil, while its top court recently highlighted a ruling penalising a Singaporean company for complying with US sanctions. Beijing has now warned it will take “all necessary measures” if Chinese interests are targeted.
Washington therefore faces an uncomfortable choice: tolerate continued trade between Iran and China, its neighbours and other partners, or dramatically escalate coercion of the governments, banks and companies that keep those channels open. That risks multiplying the US’s economic confrontations at a moment when it needs international cooperation to isolate Tehran. Bessent acknowledged the danger when asked why Washington was not immediately imposing its most sweeping secondary sanctions. “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” he responded. That is quite an admission for an operation advertised as “economic D-day”.
With the midterms approaching, the White House has strong incentives to avoid another major escalation that could further disrupt Gulf energy flows and send fuel prices soaring. Tehran knows this. Its gamble is that it can endure and reroute enough commerce while imposing enough costs that Washington and its partners eventually prefer a settlement to continued confrontation.
That makes this a dangerous contest of endurance. Washington is betting Iran’s economy completely breaks first. Tehran is betting the US’s tolerance for the war and its mounting economic costs breaks first.
This has been the recurring flaw in Trump’s approach. In 2018, he left the 2015 nuclear deal with Iran, in an attempt to secure more favourable terms. Iran instead expanded its nuclear programme. Military conflict was supposed to force Tehran to accept US terms. Instead, the war expanded and Hormuz became a central source of Iranian leverage. Now intensified economic strangulation is supposed to accomplish what military power could not.
Unless Trump starts thinking several moves ahead, his latest attempt to force Iran into submission could leave the US with even higher energy prices, an even more confrontational adversary and yet another escalation it never counted on.
- 
  Sina Toossi is a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, where his work focuses on US-Iran relations, US policy toward the Middle East and nuclear issues

New payment set up? Get in touch! The bank scam where your ‘bank’ is the scammer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
07:00:49 UTC
16:00:49 KST

Your phone pings and it’s a message from your bank about a new payment being set up on your account. If you do not recognise the transaction, it says, you should get in touch. There’s a number for you to call.
The person on the other end of the line tells you that your account has been compromised by scammers. They need details from you so they can help protect your money. Before you know it, they are giving you details of a safe account to transfer your savings to, or asking you to hand over your debit card so it can be replaced.
Impersonation scams suh as this are rife - and costly. Figures from Lloyds bank show that fraudsters posing as representatives of trusted organisations – including the police, banks, HM Revenue & Customs and phone providers – stole 10% more from its customers in the year to the end of June than in the previous 12 months.
While the number of its customers reporting a scam has fallen by 3% this year, the average sum taken rose by 10% to £3,516.
Meanwhile, Santander says more than £3m has been stolen from its customers through bank impersonation scams so far this year, with an average loss of £6,000.
Because the messages are being sent out randomly, the scammer could claim to be from a company you have no financial relationship with. But if a text or phone message does include your bank’s name, it is likely to stop you in your tracks.
What it looks like
It might be a call or email, but it usually starts with a text, says Elaine Ross, head of fraud analytics at Nationwide building society. “A lot of people are more sceptical about people calling them than they are about getting a message,” she says.
The text says that a payment has been set up to someone from your account and asks you to take action if you don’t recognise, or did not make, the transaction. Recent messages seen by Guardian Money show criminals saying that people have paid a specific person or business.
“The value will be a high value, and it will be a person the victim doesn’t know,” Ross says.
In some cases the message will give you a number to call, in others it will ask you to reply ‘Y’ if it was you, and ‘N’ if it wasn’t. “As soon as you press ‘N,’ they will call you back and say they are from Nationwide’s security team or the police. That puts people into a panic,” she says.
Once they have you on the phone, they will attempt to persuade you to move cash or hand over your cards - or both – for your own protection.
What to do
Ignore any message that is from a mobile phone number and not your bank.
Chris Ainsley, head of fraud risk management at Santander UK, says: “If something doesn’t look or sound right, trust your instincts. Stop, check and contact your bank directly using a trusted number.”
Use the number on the back of your card to contact your bank if you are concerned.
Hang up and call back if you are on a call that you become suspicious about. Ross says that when Nationwide contacts people to warn them about scams, “we expect customers to say ‘I’m going to call you back’ – if they are worried during a call, we would absolutely encourage them to do that”. That might mean joining a queue to get through, she says, but it will be worthwhile.
Find out what tools your bank or building society has in place to help you detect and avoid scams. At Nationwide, for example, if you are speaking to someone claiming to be from the building society, you can now check via its app that it is a genuine call: open and go to the “more” section, then tap “call checker”.

(AFP Photo)
Ecuador became the latest Latin American country to declare an emergency over the El Nino climate phenomenon on Aug. 29, which could be the strongest on record, officials said.
This year's El Nino is already wreaking havoc in Central America, which is in the throes of a severe drought, and in Indonesia, where it is exacerbating wildfires.
Scientists predict the current occurrence will reach its peak by the end of the year and cause record global heat in 2027.
Ecuador's Ministry of Risk Management "declared a red alert throughout the country in response to the El Nino episode."
The alert activates emergency committees tasked with coordinating preventive evacuations and other measures.
El Nino causes surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean to rise, altering wind patterns, pressure, and precipitation, and disrupting fishing and bird migrations.
Ecuador is also expecting droughts and wildfires in its Amazon region, in the east of the country.
Panama, Honduras and El Salvador have already declared emergencies over El Nino.
Further south, Peru has declared a state of emergency in a third of its cities over El Nino, warning that intense heat and rain might mean people will not have enough to eat.

Nearly one thousand people swim across Danube in Budapest for first crossing in six years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
07:00:36 UTC
16:00:36 KST

The Danube was closed to river traffic for four hours to make way for the Generali OWT Danube Crossing open-water swim.
Nearly one thousand people took the plunge in Budapest on Saturday along one of the Danube's usually busiest stretches — between Corvinus University and the University of Technology — for the Generali OWT Danube Swim.
It was the first time in six years the event had been held, since organising it requires serious preparation, organiser Balázs Mezős told Euronews.
"This is a very big event: almost 40 paramedics watch over the swimmers, 12 motorboats look after them, and the entire Danube is closed for four hours, so no one can enter or leave. The larger ships have to be cleared from the start and finish areas and moved elsewhere," Mezős explained.
For competitors, it's an extraordinary experience to swim somewhere that would normally be unthinkable, given the boat traffic and safety considerations. Budapest unfolds before them in a completely different way.
"I used to come to university over Liberty Bridge every day," one young woman told Euronews. "I would always look out from the tram, wondering what it would be like to swim across — whether you actually could. It never occurred to me that it was really possible. Then we found out this event existed, and we signed up as soon as registration opened."
According to the organisers, the water is clean, the stretch is safe, and there are no dangerous eddies.
"People are very wary of the Danube," Mezős said. "That basically stems from the fact that they don't swim in it, because usually you're not allowed to. Fortunately, more and more open-water Danube beaches are being built here in Budapest and across the country, so people are slowly getting used to it. You can see that in our swimming races, where the number of participants keeps growing. So I think there's a kind of mistrust that has no real basis. People tend to mention whirlpools first, but there aren't any here — what little current there is wouldn't even be able to pull under a duck. You have to give it a try: the first time or two might feel a bit uncomfortable, or exciting, or even scary, but by the third time it's a real pleasure. Swimming while carried along by a current of about five kilometres an hour is heaven itself."
"A fantastic experience," said a British man living in Budapest, whose wife and two young daughters were waiting for him in front of the University of Technology. "Every Budapest resident should try it once. The start is tough because of the current — you think you're swimming in a straight line, but you're not. But the organisation is excellent; it's a great event."
The Danube Swim is part of the Generali Night Run sports festival, which offers participants a range of distances to run, in the morning or even at night, through some of Budapest's most iconic locations.

Ice-rock avalanche in Nepal triggers deadly mudslide in China's Xizang: experts
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
15:00:08 CST
16:00:08 KST

Su Pengcheng, a researcher from the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, speaks during a press conference held by the information office of the Xizang regional government to brief the rescue and relief efforts after a mudslide struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in the autonomous region, in Xigaze, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, Aug. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Tenzing Nima Qadhup)
GYIRONG, Xizang, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- An ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-mountain glacier in Nepal has been identified as the cause of a devastating mudslide that struck Gyirong Port in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Aug. 26, local authorities said Sunday.
A glacier on the north slope of Mount Langtang Lirung in Nepal fractured at an altitude of about 5,200 meters, triggering an ice-rock avalanche, according to a press conference held by the information office of the regional government.
The avalanche plunged rapidly to an altitude of around 4,000 meters, scouring the mountainside and developing into a massive debris flow, which surged about 22 kilometers before reaching Gyirong Port at an altitude of around 1,800 meters.
The disaster flattened an area of about 0.7 square kilometers, destroying 27 buildings and related facilities in the area.
The findings were made by a cryosphere emergency disaster response team from the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, based on the analysis of remote-sensing monitoring data and field-transmitted data, as well as on-site surveys and investigations.
The deadly mudslide had claimed 16 lives and left 546 others missing at Gyirong Port as of 6 p.m. Saturday, the regional government said on Sunday morning. ■

Hungary's bee population at risk, warns national beekeepers' association
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
07:00:04 UTC
16:00:04 KST

By August, the drought and extreme heat have all but wiped out natural sources of pollen, leaving bees starving and parched.
Prolonged drought and successive heatwaves have wiped out natural sources of nectar and pollen in Hungary, leaving bees facing starvation.
The pollen shortage could affect as much as 80% of the country's bee population, warns the National Hungarian Beekeeping Association (OMME). Experts have also alerted the ministry responsible for agriculture and food policy to the crisis.
Pollen is the most important protein source for bee colonies. It's essential for raising young bees and helping them develop properly. Without it, honey yields suffer—and colonies' chances of surviving winter are directly threatened.
For weeks, around 80% of Hungary's bees have had little or no access to natural pollen. The drought has made things worse: even the damp areas and riverbanks that normally still supply food for bees in late summer have dried up this year.
For a hive to survive, worker bees must carry at least a litre of water back to the queen and her larvae to keep them from drying out. The worse the drought gets, the farther bees must fly to find food and water—burning more energy and dying at higher rates as a result.
A lack of nectar can also cause colonies to turn on each other, driving mortality even higher.
OMME says this could lead to significant colony losses by spring 2027. This matters beyond beekeeping, too: honey bees play a key role in pollinating crops, and by extension, in the food supply.
Because of the crisis, OMME has written to Szabolcs Bóna, the minister responsible for agriculture and food policy. Beekeepers are normally required to maintain a set number of colonies, but because of these exceptional losses, many will be unable to meet that requirement through no fault of their own.
OMME is asking the authorities not to automatically penalize beekeepers for expected losses, but instead to take into account the extreme weather and the unprecedented shortage of natural food sources.
The effects of the drought and heat won't end when the season does. How much pollen is available now could decide whether colonies survive the winter, how well they recover next spring, and ultimately, how much honey Hungary produces next year.

At 22, Lithuanian artisan is keeping centuries-old weaving traditions alive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

“Few people my age probably do this,” 22-year-old folk artist Tomas Antropikas says with a smile as he settles behind a loom to weave a shawl based on an authentic example from the southern Lithuanian village of Marcinkonys.
But weaving is only one part of the young artisan’s craft.
“I weave, I reconstruct details of traditional costumes and textiles, I dye yarn, spin yarn, weave bands, braid baskets, make cords, knit, crochet, sew and embroider,” he said. “I reconstruct the full costume ensemble. I just don't make the shoes.”
His home has four looms. One is currently producing the Marcinkonys shawl; another is being used to weave fabric for a skirt based on a pattern characteristic of the Polish-Lithuanian border region around Punsk.
His fascination with traditional crafts began long before he owned his first loom.
Grandmother's TV
Handicrafts surrounded Antropikas as a child. His mother and grandmother sewed, knitted, crocheted and embroidered.
But a chance childhood discovery set him on a very different path.
“My biggest friend in the village at my grandmother's was the television,” he recalled.
At about age five, he watched a television program hosted by Lithuanian ethnologist Zita Kelmickaitė that featured traditional woven bands. Although he could not yet read, he found a book showing how the bands were made and tried to reproduce the technique himself.
“Something worked, perhaps not very well, but that was the beginning of everything,” he said.
The decisive moment came during his final years of school, when a teacher named Rimutė first allowed him to sit at a loom.
“That's when I realised I needed one. I would bring one from anywhere, find one anywhere, for any amount of money. I was really hooked,” he said.
Since then, weaving has become less a hobby than a necessity.
“If I don't sit at the loom for a week, I get hungry. Something is missing from my life,” he said.
The pleasure starts before the weaving
Antropikas laughs at the idea that weaving itself is the hardest part.
“There is a beautiful saying: If it weren’t for the beginning and the end, even a frog would be a weaver,” he said.
Preparing the loom and finishing the fabric are the most difficult stages, he explained. Once that work is done, weaving becomes almost meditative.
He moves a shuttle carrying a bobbin through the opening between the threads, presses the pedals to change the arrangement of the warp and beats the newly woven thread into place.
“And again I press the pedals, the heddles change, I pass the shuttle through again. That's the monotony of the work,” he said.
During the interview, the shawl steadily grew longer. After several dozen minutes, about 25 centimetres of fabric had been added.
From museum archives to the loom
Antropikas recently completed a bachelor’s degree in cultural history and anthropology at Vilnius University’s Faculty of History and is beginning his master’s studies.
His academic work and his craft feed into each other. His bachelor’s thesis examined traditional skirts from the southern region of Dzūkija, and he spends time researching museum collections, libraries and archives.
“When I get tired of sitting at the loom, I go to the archives. When I get tired of the archives, I return to the loom. Both guarantee a good result,” he said.
A museum fragment cannot simply be copied. Antropikas studies its history, purpose, colours and period. Determining the original colours can be particularly difficult because textiles may fade over centuries.
“You see a piece of skirt fabric in a museum and don’t know whether it really was those colours,” he said. “You have to try to make the reconstruction correspond as closely as possible to the historical reality.”
That attention to detail is central to his philosophy.
“You can do it any way you want. But why do it any way you want if you can do it well?” he said. “So that it is the way it was.”
For Antropikas, traditional dress is about much more than selecting colours associated with a particular region. Understanding how clothing was actually worn is equally important.
“The greatest pleasure for me is making a replica of something that already exists,” he said. “Based on authenticity, we construct both our understanding of the world today and our national costume.”
A grandmother’s shawl
The most meaningful recognition has not come through awards or titles, but through moments when his work connects strangers with their own family histories.
At the annual Kaziukas Fair in Vilnius, a woman stopped at his stall and spent a long time looking at and touching one of his shawls. Antropikas noticed that she had become emotional.
“I asked what happened. She said, ‘It's like my grandmother’s,’” he recalled.
When he asked where her grandmother was from, she answered: Marcinkonys.
The shawl had been reconstructed from a museum example from the same village.
“That’s when you understand that you are doing really important work,” he said.
Traditional crafts are often associated with older generations, but Antropikas believes a younger community is quietly emerging.
“I keep discovering more and more friends who may not weave on such cumbersome looms, but who immerse themselves in handicrafts and traditional culture,” he said. “Those people are out there. You just have to look for them.”

What's the latest on the floods?

Chinese authorities said the dead included over a hundred Nepalis and people from more than a dozen countries.

One dead, five injured in shooting at Swiss rave as major police operation unfolds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
06:55:33 UTC
15:55:33 KST

Shots were fired early on Sunday at an event attended by around 3,500 people in Aarau, Switzerland, killing at least one person and injuring five others. Police have launched a large-scale operation.
A 22-year-old woman was fatally shot at a rave attended by around 3,500 people in the Swiss town of Aarau in the early hours of Sunday, Aargau cantonal police said.
Another woman and four men, aged between 24 and 27, also suffered injuries ranging from minor to serious. All of the victims were residents of Switzerland, according to police.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has named the woman killed in the shooting as Italian national Maria Spinelli.
"I wish to express my deepest condolences on the death of Maria Spinelli, the young Italian woman who fell victim to the tragic shooting in Aarau, Switzerland," Meloni wrote on X.
"My thoughts are also with the other injured, including two Italian citizens, and with all those affected by this tragic incident," she added.
Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis also reportedly expressed his condolences to his Italian counterpart, Antonio Tajani. Tajani has sent a task force to Switzerland to support local authorities, according to the report.
The shooting occurred at around 2.30 am during a rave. Witnesses said they initially mistook the gunshots for fireworks. Around 10 shots can be heard in a video published by Swiss newspaper "Blick," which was reportedly recorded near the scene.
There have also been reports of a possible second crime scene. Swiss broadcaster Tele M1 reported that shots were also fired at members of the travelling community. Police have not yet confirmed those reports.
A manhunt for the suspect is ongoing.
"Possible motives and the exact circumstances of the incident remain unclear," cantonal police said. Authorities have not released further information about the suspect or said whether any arrests have been made.
According to Swiss emergency news outlet BRK News, a Swiss military Super Puma helicopter has also been deployed over the wider Aarau area.
Flight data show the aircraft making several movements around the town. It is not yet clear what role the helicopter is playing in the ongoing operation.
German police have also joined the search operation, a spokesperson for Freiburg police headquarters confirmed. No further details about the specific measures have been released.
Our journalists are currently working on this story. The article will be updated as soon as new information becomes available.

Türkiye marks 104th anniversary of Victory Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
06:55:07 UTC
15:55:07 KST

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Sunday issued a message marking the 104th anniversary of Victory Day, commemorating the decisive victory in the country's War of Independence.
 
"Today, we proudly mark the 104th anniversary of the Great Victory, which went down in history as the 'Battle of the Commander-in-Chief' and constituted the most important stage of our National Struggle," Erdogan said in a statement shared by the Communications Directorate on the Turkish social media platform NSosyal.
 
"I congratulate our beloved nation, the Turkish Cypriot people and our citizens living in different countries around the world on Aug. 30 Victory Day.
 
"I extend my most sincere gratitude to our esteemed guests who share our joy and excitement on this holiday at our missions abroad."
 
Erdogan said the Aug. 30 victory once again affirmed that the lands on which the Turkish nation has lived freely for a thousand years are its "eternal homeland."
 
"The Great Victory, which also paved the way for the establishment of our Republic, proclaimed to the entire world that our nation would never accept captivity, while also helping break the imperialist encirclement of our geography," he said.
 
"The determination, courage and resolve we displayed as a nation 104 years ago despite all kinds of adversity remain our strongest source of motivation today."
 
Erdogan said Türkiye, inspired by and drawing confidence from its "glorious history," is advancing steadily toward its goals through success stories in every field, from energy and the defense industry to science, technology, and foreign policy.
 
"At a time when wars, conflicts, crises, and political uncertainties are increasing around the world, particularly in our region, Türkiye stands out with its proactive policies that are principled, resolute, and centered on humanitarian values," he said.
 
"I would like to state with satisfaction that today there is a Türkiye that strives to prevent oppression regardless of who perpetrates it, stands by the oppressed regardless of who they are, and does not hesitate to pay a price when necessary for this cause."
 
Quoting an ancient Turkic expression, Erdogan said: "Unless the blue sky above collapses and the dark earth below is pierced, no one will be able to make Türkiye and the Turkish nation abandon their blessed struggle."
 
"Despite all the incitements and provocations of those who thrive on instability, we, as a state and a nation, will continue to stand for rights, law, justice, peace and stability," he added.
 
Erdogan thanked all citizens who, "just as 104 years ago," are contributing in unity and solidarity to building the Century of Türkiye.
 
"On this meaningful day, I also embrace with affection all our friends and brothers and sisters in different corners of our shared cultural and spiritual geography whose hearts beat with our nation and who share both our joys and our sorrows," he said.
 
"On this occasion, I commemorate with gratitude Gazi Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, the commander-in-chief of the Great Victory, and his comrades-in-arms. I pray to Almighty Allah to have mercy on our martyrs, whom we regard as the eternal guardians of our independence, and remember our veterans with gratitude.
 
"Happy Aug. 30 Victory Day."
 
Commemoration at Anitkabir
 
The first ceremony commemorating the 104th anniversary of the Great Victory was held at Anitkabir, the mausoleum of Mustafa Kemal Ataturk.
 
The ceremony began with a procession, led by Erdogan, with state officials walking along the Road of Lions.
 
The officials included Turkish Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus, Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz, New Party Chairman Ozgur Ozel, heads of the country's highest judicial bodies, members of the presidential Cabinet, Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) Chairman Devlet Bahceli, Republican People's Party (CHP) Chairman Kemal Kilicdaroglu, Good Party (IYI Party) Chairman Musavat Dervisoglu, Presidential Communications Director Burhanettin Duran, military commanders, representatives of political parties, bureaucrats and other state officials.
 
Erdogan laid a wreath bearing the crescent and star at Ataturk's mausoleum. Following a moment of silence, the Turkish national anthem was played.
 
Erdogan signed the Anitkabir memorial book, writing:
 
"Dear Ataturk, today, as a nation, we once again proudly celebrate the 104th anniversary of the Great Victory.
 
I commemorate with gratitude, foremost Your Excellency, the esteemed members of our Grand National Assembly and the heroic soldiers of our heroic army who contributed to the Great Victory, one of the turning points of our National Struggle."
 
He added: "Just as 104 years ago, today we do not allow sinister plans targeting our country and region, and resolutely safeguard our nation's independence and future."
 
Anitkabir was opened to the public following the state ceremony.
 
Victory Day marks the final battle in western Anatolia against Greek forces in 1922 and is dedicated to the Turkish Armed Forces.
 
Turkish forces fought the Battle of Dumlupinar from Aug. 26 to Aug. 30 in what is now Türkiye’s central Kutahya province, where the invading Greek army was decisively defeated.
 
By the end of 1922, all foreign forces had been expelled from territories that collectively became the Republic of Türkiye one year later.

Some migrants ready to pack bags fearing far-right win in east German state
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
06:54:00 UTC
15:54:00 KST

A general view taken on August 27, 2026 shows the Harzklinikum Dorothea Christian Erxleben, in Quedlinburg, eastern Germany. (AFP Photo)
As a far-right regional election victory looms in an ex-communist eastern German state, many migrants are readying to pack their bags, fearful of the AfD party's threatened "deportation and remigration offensive".
A week from now, the anti-immigration, Islamophobic and Russia-friendly Alternative for Germany party is expected to score a historic win in the small state of Saxony-Anhalt, with hopes of taking its first-ever governing majority.
It is an ominous scenario for Syria-born cardiologist Ayman Alyoussef, head physician in a clinic in the picturesque town of Quedlinburg, who voiced a common sentiment: "I fear that hatred of foreigners will spread."
Alyoussef, who arrived in the country in 2014 and is now a German citizen, said he has been welcomed by patients and colleagues but sometimes faces hostility on the streets, as do his wife and daughter who wear Muslim headscarves.
"There are patients who arrive at 3:00 am with a heart attack. I am able to get them through an acute crisis," Alyoussef told AFP. "Afterwards, they are very grateful when they realize that a foreigner helped them.
"But out on the street, they don't know that I am a cardiologist. They think I am just a foreigner receiving assistance from the city. That is why they say they don't want someone like me here. That is the problem."
Many foreign-born residents share such experiences and fears.
Last week, some 150 migrant-run restaurants, kiosks and barber shops in the state capital Magdeburg temporarily closed their doors to protest what they warned is an increasingly xenophobic climate.
Support group Refugee Council said many migrants had already reported "experiences of racism and social exclusion" and that talk of mass deportations had sparked growing "fear and uncertainty".
'Up in flames'
It is a feeling shared by Afghan migrant Rezwaan Talash, 24, who arrived in Germany six years ago and works in a Magdeburg computer repair shop.
"Whether I'll still have my life the way it is now, that's a question and a fear that's always on my mind," he told AFP.
Talash, who also volunteers in a migrant support group, said that "from our association, quite a few people from Saxony-Anhalt have recently moved away because it could be unsafe here for us after the elections.
"We don't want everything we've worked to achieve here so far—starting a calm, good life here—to suddenly go up in flames."
AfD top candidate Ulrich Siegmund, who wants to become state premier, has vowed to deport all foreigners without legal status "from minute one" in office.
Speaking to AFP on Aug. 29 at a campaign event, Siegmund insisted that his party wants to deport "people who are here illegally, who are required to leave the country", while "regular immigration based on strict criteria ... would not be a problem".
Whatever happens after the election on Aug. 30, the heated campaign rhetoric has already deepened "societal divisions", said Mamad Mohamad, a candidate for the left-leaning Greens party who was recently handing out flyers outside an Islamic cultural center in the city of Halle.
"There are people who want to talk to us and have questions, but there are also people who walk by and hurl insults or shout at us," he told AFP.
Mohamad, a Yazidi Kurd who arrived in Germany from Syria in 1996 as a 16-year-old, said he and his fellow campaigners "always have to keep an eye on where we are, who we are talking to, and ensure we are never alone."
"We always go out in groups of three or four when campaigning in the city."
Demographic crisis
Economists warn that the AfD's anti-migrant campaign, aside from the human toll, would spell an economic own-goal for the small state, which has already lost nearly a quarter of its population since Germany's reunification in 1990.
"Today, for every two people leaving the workforce, only one enters it—a gap that cannot be filled by the residents of Saxony-Anhalt and neighboring regions alone," says conservative CDU candidate Sven Schulze.
The AfD has proposed to counter the demographic crisis with "baby bonuses" for German parents and by seeking to lure back Germans living abroad, but employers say they are already struggling to find qualified staff.
"Saxony-Anhalt definitely has problems finding young talent," said Talash's boss in the IT store, Matthias Herberg. "Many people leave the state. Many school leavers don't have ideal qualifications.
"Well-qualified people with a migration background could absolutely fill these gaps."
Pushing out migrants would especially hit the state's health sector, where thousands of doctors and nurses are foreign-born.
"Without our highly qualified colleagues of foreign origin, we wouldn't be able to function," said Quedlinburg clinic director Matthias Voth. "I would have to close the hospital."
Alyoussef said he wanted to stay but was keeping his options open.
"I have a German passport, and my family too," he said. "I can work anywhere—not just here in Saxony-Anhalt or in other states, but in other countries as well.
"If I get the feeling that hatred is being spread here, then that's it, I'm done."

At least one dead, five injured in shooting at rave in Switzerland

Unknown Publisher

Manhunt under way after one killed, multiple injured at Swiss rave
At least one person was killed and five others injured – some seriously – in a shooting at a rave in the northern Swiss city of Aarau, police and local media reported Sunday. A major police operation is underway at the scene, with authorities urging residents to stay away from the area.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
A shooting at a rave in the northern Swiss canton of Aargau left one person dead and five injured early Sunday, local police and media reported. Police said they are still looking for potentially more than one suspect.
Aargau cantonal police wrote earlier on X that a 22-year-old woman died of injuries at the scene. Four men and one woman, between 24 and 27 years old, were taken to hospital with injuries ranging from minor to severe.
All of the victims are residents of Switzerland, police said. In line with Swiss privacy rules, they did not release their names.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
However, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Sunday evening identified the woman who was killed and two other victims as Italian citizens.
“I express my deepest condolences for the death of Maria Spinelli, the young Italian woman who was a victim of the tragic shooting in Aarau, Switzerland,” she wrote on X, identifying the dead woman by name.
“My thoughts also go to the other injured individuals, among whom there are two Italian citizens, and to all the people involved in this dramatic event,” she said, adding that she trusts “the work of the Swiss authorities to shed full light on what happened and identify those responsible.”
Earlier on Sunday at a press briefing, Aargau police said all its forces were involved in finding the suspect or suspects.
“The manhunt is continuing nonstop at full speed,” police spokesperson Bernhard Graser told reporters.
He said police had not yet any information about possible motives. Asked whether a terrorist attack was a possibility, Graser said that “the fact that the rave was already winding down suggests that’s not the case. A fight could also be a possibility.”
Public shootings are rare in the Alpine country despite relatively widespread gun ownership.
“In terms of its nature, this incident is certainly unique in recent years,” Graser said. “We don’t yet know the full extent of it, but based purely on the circumstances, it is something truly extraordinary. That’s why there’s such a large police presence.”
Authorities were alerted around 2:30am. local time to the shooting in the canton’s capital Aarau, 46 kilometers (29 miles) west of Zurich, police spokesperson Pascal Wenzel told Swiss public broadcaster, SRF.
At the time of the incident, the “Aarau Rave VOL. 7” was taking place at the horse racing track in Aarau’s Schachen district, SRF reported. The fire department cordoned off a large area around the site.
A major police operation was still underway on Sunday afternoon and locals were asked to stay away from the area scoured by investigators for possible links connected to the crime. Officers, firefighters and ambulances were on the scene in large numbers. Police in Freiburg, in neighboring Germany, also took part in search efforts for the suspect, the German news agency dpa reported.
“Right now, virtually the entire Aargau police force is out on the streets,” Graser said, adding that they had no information on where the suspect or the suspects might be. However, police have ruled out the possibility that they could pose a threat again.
Swiss daily Blick reported that rave visitors initially mistook the shots for fireworks until somebody shouted “everyone down.”
The newspaper wrote that the shooting took place right after the event ended. Police later took the remaining visitors to a nearby gym, where many were interrogated, Graser said.
Police asked any witnesses with videos or photos to share them with investigators.
The Aargau Racing Club, which runs the horse racing track, expressed shock at the shooting.
“We extend our deepest sympathy to all those affected and their families, who are facing this difficult and trying situation,” it said on its website. “We would like to thank the emergency responders and all others involved who worked professionally and with dedication on the scene.”
Swiss DJ Tekibo, who performed at the rave, wrote on Instagram that “what happened at Aarauer rave is absolutely heartbreaking.”
“Techno and raves are supposed to be a place for freedom and safety, never a place where something like this happens,” he added.
Aarau has about 22,300 residents. It is located approximately 30 km (18 miles) south of the German border.

Rain, thunderstorms and heat up to +30°C — weather forecast in Ukraine for August 30
Kyiv • UNN
On August 30, rain and thunderstorms are expected in the western and northern regions, while it will be dry in the south and east. In Kyiv, temperatures will reach 26°C.
On Sunday, August 30, partly cloudy conditions are expected in Ukraine. Most western and northern regions will see brief rain showers, locally accompanied by thunderstorms, while dry weather will prevail in the south and east. Daytime temperatures will reach 22–27°C, and up to 30°C in Zakarpattia and the south. This is reported by the Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center, according to UNN.
Details
According to forecasters, brief rain showers are expected on August 30 in most western and northern regions, as well as in Vinnytsia region. Rain is also forecast during the day in Cherkasy region. In some places, the showers will be accompanied by thunderstorms.
No significant precipitation is expected in the rest of Ukraine.
Fog is possible in places in the western regions at night and in the morning. The wind will be predominantly southwesterly, and in the southeastern part of the country, easterly, at a speed of 5–10 m/s.
Nighttime temperatures will be 11–16°C, while daytime temperatures will reach 22–27°C. In Zakarpattia and the southern regions, thermometer readings will locally rise to 30°C.
Brief rain showers are also forecast in Kyiv and Kyiv region, with thunderstorms possible in some places. In the capital, daytime temperatures are expected to be around 24–26°C, and 22–27°C across the region.
At the same time, an extreme fire-danger level will persist across a significant part of Ukraine. Forecasters separately warn of deteriorating weather conditions on the Kyiv and Kaniv reservoirs: during thunderstorms, southwesterly wind gusts of up to 12–15 m/s and an increase in wave height to 1.2–1.4 meters are possible. Danger Level I, yellow, has been declared.
Additional information
On Monday, August 31, the weather will generally stabilize. No significant precipitation is forecast across most of Ukraine; only brief rain showers are possible at night in a number of northern regions and in Vinnytsia region. During the day, the air will warm to 25–30°C.
